title: ‘We get 200 tourists a day’: when your house becomes a TV star | Television | The Guardian
description: What’s it like to live on the set of a soap opera? Or above Ted Lasso’s favourite pub? The residents of the homes made famous by hit TV shows tell all
Author: Alexi Duggins
Headline: What’s it like to live on the set of a soap opera? Or above Ted Lasso’s favourite pub? The residents of the homes made famous by hit TV shows tell all
Content: ‘At any hour of the day or night, there are groups of visitors in front of the house taking flash photos’ …Sarah Jessica Parker filming at the apartment she’s helped to make famous.Photograph: Jose Perez/Bauer-Griffin/GC ImagesView image in fullscreen‘At any hour of the day or night, there are groups of visitors in front of the house taking flash photos’ …Sarah Jessica Parker filming at the apartment she’s helped to make famous.Photograph: Jose Perez/Bauer-Griffin/GC ImagesTelevision‘We get 200 tourists a day’: when your house becomes a TV starWhat’s it like to live on the set of a soap opera? Or above Ted Lasso’s favourite pub? The residents of the homes made famous by hit TV shows tell allAlexi DugginsFri 14 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHalf the world recognises the apartment that Carrie Bradshaw lives in. Or the New Jersey mansion where Tony Soprano ate, slept and obsessed over the ducks in his swimming pool. In the 1990s, if you asked a good chunk of the global population where Will Smith lived, they would instantly picture a huge, white abode in Bel Air.For the real people who call those places home, this can be an issue.“We had loads of problems with people just walking in during Covid,” says Kate Fox, who lives in a house that featured in British soapEmmerdale, for the years it was filmed entirely in her West Yorkshire village of Esholt. “Somebody actually came and just stuck their head through our front door. Maybe once a month you’ll get somebody opening the door or doing something inappropriate like peeking through your windows. People have no issues about completely invading your space – but you get used to it.”View image in fullscreenFenced off … Walter White’s Breaking Bad home in Albuquerque, New Mexico.Photograph: Raisa Macouzet/AlamyPublic intrusion is a common experience for the residents of TV-famous homes. In 2015, Vince Gilligan, the creator of Breaking Bad, had to urge fans to stop paying homage to his show – because they were recreating a scene where an entire pizza is thrown on to the roof of the house whose exterior was featured as Walter White’s bungalow. And last year, the owner of the apartment made famous by Sex and the City’s lead charactererected a gate outside itbecause “at any hour of the day or night, there are groups of visitors in front of the house taking flash photos, engaging in loud chatter, posting on social media, making TikTok videos or just celebrating the moment”. Eventually, the owners of the Breaking Bad house followed suit, erecting a 6ft iron fence – not that it stopped fans. “They still try to throw pizzas even though she’s got a gate, she’s got signage,” said Frank Sandoval, who runs Breaking Bad tours to the house in an RV. “They even try to climb the gate.”But not everyone treats the arrival of hordes of fans as a bad thing. “At first, I was confused why they would want to come in,” says Glenda Kenyon, whose place in Barry, south Wales, features in BBC sitcom Gavin and Stacey as the home of Stacey’s mum, Gwen. “I just said, no, sorry, I can’t do it. Then the second year I thought, no, I’ve got to change it, so I started opening up.”View image in fullscreen‘It has changed my life’ … Knock-off Nessa poses with Glenda Kenyon outside her home, which was made famous by British TV sitcom Gavin and Stacey.Photograph: Francesca Jones/The GuardianGlenda turned her home into a walk-in tribute to the show. It has a collection of memorabilia including fridge magnets, key rings, tea towels and “nearly every T-shirt you can buy”. She’s set up a photo opportunity in the kitchen with the frying pan Gwen uses to cook her infamous omelettes, as well as a face mask of the character visitors can put on. She even ended up partnering on tours with a coach firm, whose “Dave’s Coaches” bus regularly appeared in the show, and another run by Knock-off Nessa – who impersonates Ruth Jones’s character. Last year, she welcomed 168 busloads of people to her home, and it has given her a renewed purpose.“I was lonely before, so lonely,” says Glenda, who lives alone and has experienced depression. “It has changed my life, because before I was so quiet, and now I can open up. I’m a hell of a lot better than I used to be. When you’re meeting people, you’re not thinking about the depression. I had no friends before, and now I got everybody.”View image in fullscreenPutting Barry on the map … Knock-off Nessa with a group of tourists visiting Kenyon’s home in one of the Dave’s Coaches buses that featured in British sitcom Gavin and Stacey.Photograph: Francesca JonesHaving a home that’s famous for being on TV doesn’t just change the life of its owners. If the show is big enough, it can change an entire area – as a pocket of London’s Richmond found out after Ted Lasso was set there. The high-end jewellers and panama hat boutique that line the chi-chi alleyway of the soccer goof’s home are now joined by the Ted Lasso Store, featuring a recreated locker room decked out with a “Believe” poster, and a replica shirt for every player – available to purchase alongside a selection of mugs, scarves and snow globes. Over the road, an Italian restaurant attracts customers with a £5 “Eat like Ted” offer that entitles you to a box of Ted’s favourite shortbread biscuits.“I didn’t realise it would be such a big deal,” says Reece Kent – who lives above, and is the general manager of, The Prince’s Head pub – Lasso’s regular. “Before I started working here, I was like, OK, we might get a few tourists. But I get 150 to 200 a day. At first it was just people from America, but now it’s Germany, Australia, Japan. I had a couple from Jamaica the other day.”View image in fullscreenAnother round … Up to 200 fans a day visit The Prince’s Head pub, the setting of the fictional Crown & Anchor pub in Ted Lasso.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesRichmond is far from the only place this has happened to. Over 37 years, a suburb of Melbourne was thronged by more than a quarter of a million soap opera fans on bus tours, desperate to see the real-life cul-de-sac that moonlighted as Neighbours’ Ramsay Street – resulting in a security guard being permanently stationed there. Esholt had its share of soap fans, too, with regular coach tours turning up. But Richmond is still packed with fans – and the pub has transformed one table into a designated fan area, next to a big AFC Richmond logo, replica shirt and signed pictures of the cast. They’re now the end point of a Lasso tour, which leaves them regularly flooded by big groups of tourists wanting to see the non-existent dartboard that featured in the show, and fiercely competing to sit at the table where Lasso held chats with his footballing assistant coach Beard. There has been one unexpected consequence of it all for Kent, though: needing to convince fans that he didn’t inspire a character in the show, the similarly named Roy Kent.“A couple of weeks after I started, this tourist came in who’d seen my name on the website and had made all these connections that Roy Kent was based on me,” laughs Kent. “Luckily, after a while, they believed that it was actually based on Roy Keane. I would have loved to be Roy Keane, but I’m not.”View image in fullscreen‘I had a couple from Jamaica the other day’ …The Prince’s Head pub, the setting of the fictional Crown & Anchor pub in the ‘Ted Lasso’ Apple TV show.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesBeing confused with a star of the show isn’t the only strange side-effect of having a TV show filmed in your home. “The end of our house had a vet’s waiting room and surgery in when I was growing up,” says Fox, who spent a chunk of her childhood having to pick her way around cables and lights, and being instructed to be as quiet as possible during takes. Until, that is, Emmerdale moved production to a set, and decided to create a mock-up of Fox’s home as one of the highlights of the now-defunct Granada Studios tourist attraction. “So there was an exact copy of my front lounge in a studio. Me and my mum went a few years ago. It was just a bizarre, bizarre place to be.”Its effect on residents’ finances also doesn’t hurt. “When we were kids we sold tours of the house when my parents were out. We’d charge like 50p and let people have a look around,” says Fox. “I think the tourists liked getting a tour from a child. I never got any complaints!”View image in fullscreenSoap life … Kate Fox in Esholt, where Emmerdale was filmed.Photograph: Richard Saker/The ObserverThe owners of TV-famous homes who want to sell up also have very little to complain about. When the owners of Walter White’s Breaking Bad home eventually tired of fan attention, they sold it for $1.3m – reportedly to a streamer who intends to “treat it like a monument” – not bad compared to the $350-400,000 neighbouring homes are valued at. Esholt has attracted superfans “who have moved here specifically for the Emmerdale connection”, according to Fox. And two of the houses featured in Gavin and Stacey have been bought by superfans recently – one of which was sold very much as seen, because, they said, “To be able to own the original furniture was the cherry on top of the cake for us.”Having a house associated with TV stars can also work the other way round too. Fox’s family may no longer have their home if it weren’t for the relationship they struck up with an Emmerdale star.“At one point, Mum and Dad were at risk of losing the house to the council. Leah Bracknell [who played Zoe Tate] contacted the press and said: ‘You need to write about this,’” says Fox. “She’d appear in photos with them as well, and they did end up being allowed to buy the house off the council. We’ve still got all the press clippings now. She was really, really nice.”A number of the Ted Lasso stars also became fond of their filming locations. According to Kent, “they’d pop in on days they weren’t filming – for lunch or just a drink”, although Lasso himself wasn’t the main culprit. “Jason Sudeikis [who plays Lasso] only popped in once. I had Coach Beard in a couple of times. Dani Rojas was the main one – he’d have lunch and bring friends. They were lovely.”Despite getting to meet celebs, living somewhere TV famous isn’t for everyone. “People who moved here during filming or since, they really do struggle with the tourists – they think it’s so rude and shocking that people just walk into your house,” says Fox. But, ultimately, for some people, it brings a real sense of happiness – particularly if you’re a fan of the show.“I was over the moon when I first saw my house on telly. Every time I watch, I’m going: ‘That’s mine! That’s mine!’” says Glenda.“People tell me that I’ve put Barry on the map and I do feel like that’s true. I’ve had people from India, Africa, New Zealand, Swindon – you name it, I’ve had them. I’m very proud. I’ve done something in my life I can be happy about.”Explore more on these topicsTelevisionGavin & StaceySex and the CityAnd Just Like ThatEmmerdalefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: What does Clacton get for its loyalty to stroppy Nige? Next to nothing | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Why bother to improve people’s lives – or even show up – when getting votes is this easy? In many ways, though, the stunt hasn’t paid off
Author: John Crace
Headline: Why bother to improve people’s lives – or even show up – when getting votes is this easy? In many ways, though, the stunt hasn’t paid off
Content: ‘The town’s job is merely to vote for him, whenever he commands.’ Farage arriving to vote in Clacton.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The town’s job is merely to vote for him, whenever he commands.’ Farage arriving to vote in Clacton.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesThe politics sketchClacton byelection August 2026What does Clacton get for its loyalty to stroppy Nige? Next to nothingJohn CraceWhy bother to improve people’s lives – or even show up – when getting votes is this easy? In many ways, though, the stunt hasn’t paid offFri 14 Aug 2026 09.17 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 14.10 EDTShareWhat can Clacton possibly have done to deserve this? Is this some cosmic karma for a past existence in which the town executed hundreds of innocent women and children? Surely, even then, enough is enough. For the past few years Clacton seems to have been the centre of some abusive psychological experiment. The sort the Americans used to run in the 1950s and 60s, that have long since been banned. One run byNigel Farageand designed merely to fuel his narcissistic dreams, with the voters mere cannon fodder.Clacton’s relationship with Nige is and always has been entirely one-sided. The town’s job is merely to vote for him, whenever he commands. Even for byelections that are entirely unnecessary and will possibly have to be re-run before the end of the year. On a turnout of just 44%,little more than 60% of the voters duly obligedon Thursday, even though none of the main parties were standing and Nige’s main opponent was a man with a bin on his head. Maybe parts of Clacton are waking up, and are fed up with Farage taking the piss out of them.Here’s how it works. For a few weeks during an election campaign, Nige breaks the habit of a lifetime and makes two or three visits to theEssexcoast. He gets someone to buy him a beer or an ice-cream – most local businesses don’t take crypto – and poses with a pet supporter his team have rounded up for the day. He then gets the hell out of Clacton as fast as he can. And that’s all it takes for Nige to win. He isn’t a man who puts in the unnecessary hard yards.And what does Clacton get in return? Next to nothing. An MP who scarcely bothers to turn up to Westminster. And who, when he does, invariably fails to give his constituency a second thought. The Jaywick ward of Clacton was the most deprived area in the country when Farage was first elected in 2024 and nothing has changed since. Nor does Nige appear that bothered. All he needs to do is to dispense a bit of unmediated grievance and the votes come tumbling in. Why bother to make people’s lives better when it’s that easy? It’s the ultimate dysfunctional relationship.It was past dawn when the returning officer was ready to announce the result. Ploughing through a ballot paper that’s almost a metre long to accommodate the more than 30 candidates takes time. And where was Nigel at his moment of triumph? Absolutely nowhere to be seen. Surely now was the time for him to put on his public face. The Mr Congeniality. The common man. The politician who can connect with the little people. Except he just couldn’t bring himself to do it. There are limits even to Nige’s artifice. He just couldn’t conceal the fact he was having a giant strop.Nige couldn’t escape the reality that he had been out-thought and out-played at every stage since his disastrous decision to call a byelection. He had hoped to kill off theinvestigation into the £5m gifthe received from the Thai crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne that, even with the benefit of an extra six week’s thinking time, he has been unable to explain convincingly.If anything, Reform’s finances have been looking even murkier over the past six weeks, with money apparently flyingbetween George Cottrell(the man-boy who calls Nige Daddy), Fiona (Posh George’s unfortunate mother), Richard Tice and the Reform bank account. In Reform World everyone gets to be a millionaire for 15 minutes. Except the suckers who vote for the party.Then there was Farage’s absurd attempt to portray the election as the people v the establishment. Only it became ever clearer that Nige was – always has been, always will be – the establishment. No more so than in a two-way fight between himself and a comedian with a dustbin on his head, claiming to be a space warrior from Planet Sigma Nine.This was a psychological wound too far for a Nige close to breakdown. He just couldn’t bear to be seen standing next to a bunch of jokers, losers and Laurence Fox. So he pulled a sicky.So Nigel Farage has beaten a man in a bin. But he’s in deep trouble, and he knows it | Owen JonesRead moreDicky Tice tried to give it a positive spin. The police had insisted there was a “credible threat” and had advised Nige to stay away from the count. However, it is understood Essex police did not advise anyone to stay away, and had believed they had everything in hand. The only disturbance they had been expecting was a few heckles and a Led By Donkeys-style stunt. But that was too much for Nige. His facade too fragile, his self-esteem in tatters. Just a giant ball of childlike need. He couldn’t even bring himself to give the “major speech” he had promised for Clacton at 10.30am. He needed a quiet room in which to lie down. Sulks don’t come much bigger than this.You might have thought Nige’s team could have persuaded him to make an ersatz display of charm, dignity and gratitude. You know the sort. “I’d like to thank the voters of Clacton for placing their trust in me. I won’t let them down.” Through gritted teeth and crossed fingers. Because he had every intention of letting them down. But Nige couldn’t do that.All he could do was post on X: “The result in Clacton speaks for itself.” This was a little too close to the mark. Because 9,500 voters had chosen Count Binface rather than a career politician. The Reform bubble was bursting in front of Nige’s eyes. This was not the landslide he had been hoping for. Just a stunt that had backfired. Indeed, the speech of the night was made by the Count, observing that he was the clear winner of all those who had bothered to turn up.Meanwhile, Reform retreated into their own world. Turning Clacton into a little bit of Glastonbury with their very own Farage Fest. If you can count a few members of the Reform elite dancing awkwardly and trying to look as if they were having a good night. Though perhaps, like some Glastonburys, this was a night where the aim was to forget rather than to enjoy yourself. It felt like the end of days.Come Friday morning, reality was beginning to hit. This wasn’t the end of a victorious election campaign, but the beginning of a new one. With Lee Anderson insisting Reform would thoroughly cooperate with the reopened investigation. There’s a first time for everything.Explore more on these topicsClacton byelection August 2026The politics sketchNigel FarageEssexEnglandReform UKByelectionscommentShareReuse this content

title: Nine life lessons from the happiest man in the world: from embracing tiny changes to not overthinking meditation | Health & wellbeing | The Guardian
description: Stressed out, endlessly scrolling and never satisfied? Yongey Mingyur Rinpoche, the Buddhist monk with off-the-charts levels of contentment, may have the answers …
Author: Joel Snape
Headline: Stressed out, endlessly scrolling and never satisfied? Yongey Mingyur Rinpoche, the Buddhist monk with off-the-charts levels of contentment, may have the answers …
Content: Photograph: Bema Oser Dorje. Illustration: Mel CerriHealth & wellbeingNine life lessons from the happiest man in the world: from embracing tiny changes to not overthinking meditationStressed out, endlessly scrolling and never satisfied? Yongey Mingyur Rinpoche, the Buddhist monk with off-the-charts levels of contentment, may have the answers …Joel SnapeFri 14 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTShareBy some metrics, Buddhist monk Yongey Mingyur Rinpoche is the happiest man on Earth. Inbrain scans, researchers noted that Mingyur’s neural activity showedoff-the-charts levels of activationin the left prefrontal cortex, an area associated with positive emotions such as happiness, enthusiasm and joy. In other tests conducted when he was 41 years old, his brain reportedly “resembled that of a 33-year-old”. He also laughs a lot.Can happiness be taught? I met Mingyur (Rinpoche is an honorary title meaning, roughly, “precious one”) to discover his strategies for a richer life.Less convenience, morecontentment“As the Dalai Lama says, we have everything at the touch of a finger, and so when we start to feel lonely, incomplete, bored – we protect ourselves with whatever: eating ice-cream, our smartphone, coffee,” says Mingyur. “We try to get away from them, but those feelings are wisdom, in a way. The really important thing is to sit with them, embrace them as a path to explore.”For instance, if you find yourself bored while watching a Netflix romcom and simultaneously scrolling on your phone, that’s a signal that ever more stimulation will never be satisfying (science backs this up: one recent study suggestsflicking between videos on social media makes us more bored, not less). Take it as a sign to switch everything off, look inward and stop trying to fill the vacuum with superficial stuff.Embrace changes (even terrifying ones)In 2011, Mingyur left his monastery in the middle of the night with nothing but the clothes on his back, intending to live as a homeless yogi. About three weeks in, he developed severe food poisoning and spent days paralysed by exhaustion and pain – but he now sees this as the moment he started to truly understand the Tibetan Buddhist idea of relinquishing control.Does he think it’s possible to experience that sort of thing without going through something quite so unpleasant? “Absolutely, of course. Especially nowadays – modern life is full of adventure. When you turn 18, start a new job, start a new relationship – each of those are opportunities for change.” But you don’t have to wait for these bigger moments: meeting a new group of people or taking up a new challenge can help increase your comfort levels with new things. Try implementing one small change every time you feel like you’ve spent a day just going through the motions: a new route home from work, or cooking with one ingredient you’ve never used before. Something I find helpful is to keep a little list of things I want to try whenever I come across them, then when things get stultifying, I’ve got a ready-made buffet to choose from.You don’t need quiet to find peace“I felt bored the first time I learned meditation,” says Mingyur. “I said, ‘Today is breathing. Tomorrow, again, breathing. The rest of this week, breathing. This is stupid.’ But for meditation, you need to know two things. One, you can make everything support for meditation – you can meditate anytime, anywhere, with anything. Second, you have to have some creative element with your meditation: everything becomes a friend to the meditation.”To put this another way, if there’s traffic noise outside, or the person next to you is watching TikTok videos, the idea is to let that become a source of focus and calm. This is easier said than done. Mingyur suggests building up to it by listening to music, then waterfalls or birdsong, then loud conversations or construction. Eventually, he says, you should be able to meditate while a baby is crying (I won’t be trying this).Use the ‘three pillars’“We think about three things in Tibetan Buddhism: view, meditation and application,” says Mingyur. “View is the mindset: we believe that everybody has an inner sky, the qualities of awareness, love, compassion and wisdom. We practise meditation, and then we practise application – building new habits. So it’s easy to say: ‘Oh, people aren’t nice.’ But of course there are a lot of great qualities in a lot of people, and if you see that, it will manifest. But it’s a habit: you have to keep doing it, and doing it, and then you change.”Mingyur suggests doing this in a small way every day. Maybe one day try appreciating your family, and the next, find positive things to say about your most annoying colleague.Be grateful (for really specific things)Photograph: Maya Sepulchre. Illustration: Mel CerriYes, gratitude lists can feel a bit peak 2021, but one approach is to go from the incredibly general to the extremely specific. “I appreciate that I have senses, that there’s a roof above me, that I have at least one or two friends or family,” says Mingyur. “When you begin to appreciate these things, you start to appreciate the quality of your life and everything around you.”This doesn’t necessarily mean you need to start a gratitude journal. After a few days, it can feel a bit too easy for your mind to scribble another ‘I’m grateful for my children’. Instead, the idea is to use little moments of downtime to notice how nice it is to be in the specific moment, whether you’re sitting in a comfortable chair or watching your child swing a stick around in the woods.The sky doesn’t change, even in a storm“I had panic attacks when I was young,” says Mingyur. “When I began to learn meditation from my father, I asked him how to fight them. He said: ‘Don’t fight.’ The first reason is that if you fight, panic becomes stronger. It’s like saying: ‘Don’t think about orange’ – suddenly it’s all you can think about.And the second thing my father said is, there’s no need to push panic away, because it’s like a storm cloud in the sky. A storm cloud can’t change the nature of the sky – it comes and then it goes. You just have to connect with the inner sky.” To put this another way, whatever inner turmoil you’re going through, remind yourself that it isn’t actually changing anything fundamental in your brain: it will pass and things will feel better.At times of extreme distress, this might feel impossible. In which case, Mingyur suggests we focus on physical sensations – the temperature of the room, the sounds around you – to help deal with the panic in that moment, rather than trying to tell ourselves everything is fine.Breathe your way tolastinghappiness“Genuine happiness is when we let go of that feeling of dissatisfaction, incompleteness, that something is missing,” says Mingyur. “But if you only look for happiness, then you will get the opposite. People often think, ‘I’ll be happy if I make more money, or if I move to this new country or get this new job or win the lottery’ – but that just changes your happiness a little bit and then you go back to baseline, right? But if you practise breathing, love and compassion, you can move that baseline over time.”To start, simply sit and breathe naturally, focusing on the rise and fall of your abdomen or the sensation of the air passing through your body. As you’re doing this, you might try mentally repeating a simple mantra (“May I be happy and free from suffering” is a common one) to cultivate love towards yourself, and then extending that compassion to loved ones, pets and, eventually, all the other people in your life.Anger is like frost on the grass“What we call awareness is like sunlight, and our emotional patterns are like frost on the grass in the morning,” says Mingyur. “When the sunlight manifests, the frost melts automatically – there’s no fight. I talk to some business leaders who are really stressed. They have to do so many things at the same time, so they build the habit of being stressed or angry all the time. They come to me and say: ‘My relationship is not good,’ or ‘There’s a problem between me and the boss.’ I say, ‘Just catch the anger. Be with the anger. Just for a second.’ Once you catch it, you have a choice, it can transform.”To put this another way, when you’re momentarily furious at someone – at work or at home – you don’t need to meditate for 10 minutes; just avoid your autopilot response of snapping at them by noticing the fact that you’re angry, and then watching as the emotion melts away. From experience, I can say that this takes practice – but it’s definitely worth working on.And it helps to help other people“If you can really help others, you feel a different level of happiness from having an ice-cream or a coffee,” says Mingyur. We all know this, obviously – but how often are we actually doing it? Check in on a neighbour in need today

title: Milk, wine, salad: how your food will be affected by the summer of heat | Farming | The Guardian
description: There are parched fields, overheating sheep and potentially the worst cereal harvest since detailed records began – but it’s a good year for cider apples
Author: Fiona Harvey
Headline: There are parched fields, overheating sheep and potentially the worst cereal harvest since detailed records began – but it’s a good year for cider apples
Content: A lamb on Ditchling Beacon in the South Downs. Grass growth has ‘completely stalled’, says the NFU.Photograph: lemanieh/AlamyView image in fullscreenA lamb on Ditchling Beacon in the South Downs. Grass growth has ‘completely stalled’, says the NFU.Photograph: lemanieh/AlamyFarmingExplainerMilk, wine, salad: how your food will be affected by the summer of heatThere are parched fields, overheating sheep and potentially the worst cereal harvest since detailed records began – but it’s a good year for cider applesFiona Harvey,Sarah ButlerandJoanna PartridgeFri 14 Aug 2026 10.40 EDTFirst published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 09.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs parts of the UK swelter through a fifth successive climate crisis-driven heatwave and nearly three-quarters of England remains in drought, how are six homegrown products faring?LivestockOn her farm in Durham on Monday where she was vaccinating sheep, Clare Wise stopped and stood still. For the first time in weeks, it had begun to rain. “We didn’t think of taking cover, we just stayed out and enjoyed it!” she says.Farmers farther south were less lucky, and thecontinuing drought, as well as causingdistress for animalsin danger of overheating, is storing up problems for livestock farmers this winter. Grass growth has been about half of what it should be by this time of year and mowing excess grass in summer is where most get their winter feed.“This would be the peak season for collecting winter forage, but we have not been able to do that,” says Wise, who is also the acting livestock board chief for the National Farmers’ Union. “Grass growth has completely stalled.”View image in fullscreenCattle on Dorney Common, Buckinghamshire, try to graze in the extreme heat.Photograph: Maureen McLean/ShutterstockSome farmers have been forced to dip into their winter feed stores; others will need to supplement their scant supplies with bought-in feed.Milk production is down, but so far only slightly – by about 1%, according to theAgricultureand Horticulture Development Board (AHDB), as cows have less to eat and are discouraged by the heat. Sheep shearers have been in short supply, making it difficult for farmers to make their flocks comfortable.For future years, farmers can grow trees and higher hedges to provide shade for their beasts, says Tom Cantillon, an analyst at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU) thinktank. Some with bigger herds might consider air conditioning in their sheds and milking parlours.But for many livestock farmers, the fear is thatthis year is just the beginning.FruitFor aficionados of soft fruit, this is turning out to be a glorious summer. Berries are smaller but sweeter as the sunniest July on record in the UK has concentrated flavours.Strawberries and raspberries have done particularly well; stone fruit such as peaches, greengages and plums have ripened quickly, and cherries and blueberries have been cheap and plentiful.Cider drinkers can also rejoice at the smaller and sweeter apples. Supermarkets tend to choose apples based on size, notes Cantillon, so if fewer of them make the grade, shoppers may be disappointed but drinkers will see the benefits. “It could be a bumper year for cider-making,” he says.The picture is “genuinely mixed” forother produce, says Martin Emmett, the horticulture and potatoes board chair at the NFU.View image in fullscreenA grocery shop in London. The hot and dry summer has produced mixed results for fruit growers.Photograph: Leon Neal/GettyMost fruit in the UK is grown covered on substrate, so a lack of rainfall in the fields has been less of an issue. But horticulturalists are worried about their water supplies. About half of the UK’s potato crop, for instance, is irrigated, often using groundwater from boreholes or abstracted from rivers. Many farmers would find it easier to store more of their own water on the farm, but constructing on-farm reservoirs requires complex planning permission.Tougher crops and beaver dams: how UK farmers are tackling droughtRead moreCerealsBritain could be in for itsworst cereal harvest in four decades, with wheat, spring barley and oats all substantially down on their 10-year average, according to estimates from the AHDBanalysedby the ECIU. This year’s cereal and oilseed harvest is forecast to be 18.5m tonnes, which would make 2026 the worst since detailed records began in 1984.After a wet start to the year that affected late planting for spring wheat, a dry April hit winter wheat at a crucial growing stage. The record heatwave in May also deprived grains of the moisture they need to plump out.View image in fullscreenSun bleached stubble covers a field after harvesting in Shropshire.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/GettyFurther heatwaves in June and July added heat stress, while the drought continued to stunt the grains. Since mid-June, there has been no rainfall or none of significance across much of England. July was thedriest monthever recorded in southern England.Yields on wheat are normally about 7.9 tonnes per hectare in the UK; that is forecast to be down by more than a tonne per hectare, at about 6.7 tonnes this year.Estimates taken in early August, with about half the harvest gathered, showed that the loss of about 2.5m tonnes compared to early estimates would amount to about £390m in lost revenue for farmers.Tom Lancaster, an analyst for land, food and farming at ECIU, says: “From the wettest winter on record in 2024, to the hottest summer in 2025, and now unprecedented heat and drought this year, we are in danger of UK farming entering a climate doom loop, as repeated impacts undermine the capacity of farmers to drill next year’s crop.”Martin Lines, the chief executive of the Nature FriendlyFarmingNetwork, who farms in Cambridgeshire, says this year has been “brutal”, especially coming on top of two previous consecutive poor harvests. “Harvest this year has been a real kick in the teeth,” he says. “I’ve never known it this dry and hot on our farm. Even farmers I know who were sceptical of climate change are now saying they’re really worried.”Europe is not faring much better, with heatwaves and fires contributing to a forecast of €2bn (£1.7bn) in lost revenue.WineWhile traditional British crops are suffering, many vineyards are thriving. WineGB, the trade association representing the UK’s wine producers, says it is optimistic about the size and quality of the 2026 harvest. Producers are reporting healthy vineyards, clean fruit and encouraging ripening after stable summer conditions.Nicola Bates, the chief executive of the trade body WineGB, said: “Whilst it’s too early to definitively say the overall impact on this year’s UK harvest – and what happens over the next few weeks will be crucial – the vineyards look strong and we’re optimistic.“That said, seasonal conditions remain variable and producers continue to adapt, so building long-term resilience plans is essential for protecting our vineyards and to future-proof English and Welsh wine.”View image in fullscreenFreshly picked grapes are emptied into storage crates at a Chapel Down vineyard in Maidstone.Photograph: Bloomberg/GettyAlthough some growers in Kent, the heartland of the British wine industry, suffered from late frosts most have managed to maintain fruit health.Tim Spakouskas, a grower with 7 hectares (17.5 acres) of vineyard in North Yorkshire, says his farm has had very little rain for at least two months but his long-established vines are doing well as they have deep roots able to tap into moisture well below the sun-baked surface.He is acutely aware that his wider family, who farm a variety of other crops, are “struggling a bit” in the hot dry weather which is not Yorkshire’s usual fare. Spakouskas says some of his newer vines planted last year are also showing signs of stress and he fears he may lose some if the weather does not change.SaladWe may like to eat salad in the heat but lettuce is not a big fan of very hot weather. Its ideal growing temperature is about 20C, according to farmers, and it starts to get stressed at 24C. Over 35C, it won’t be suitable for sale, so the recent bouts of hot weather have been tricky for growers.Ben Andrews, a salad farmer based in Herefordshire, posted on Instagram on Thursday: “There is still no rain and the veg is really struggling.” He said lettuce heads were likely to be smaller and it would probably take two to make up a portion, hitting takings.View image in fullscreenLettuces grow near Hollesley in Suffolk. Crops start to get stressed at 24C.Photograph: Geography Photos/Universal Images Group/GettyOther leafy vegetables such as spinach and pak choi have also entered “thermal dormancy”, where they stop growing in the intense heat, according to Oddbox, which sells boxes of imperfect or surplus fruit and vegetables.Even those growing in the controlled environments of greenhouses and polytunnels are struggling with the heat which topped 30C in parts of the UK again on Thursday.Jan Bentley, the managing director of WS Bentley, which supplies salad cress, microgreens and pea shoots to restaurants and supermarkets grown in hydroponic systems, said yields had been reduced by “heat stress and some poor germination and crops destroyed when extremely hot”.Oddbox also said the quality of cucumbers had been affected as “plants are stressed in the extreme heat, which causes them to misshape”.FishIt is not just people, animals and crops that have sweltered this summer: the water around Britain’s coast is also hotter.Cornwall’s coastal waters are experiencing marine heatwave conditions for the third consecutive year, registering temperatures 3-4C warmer than at this time of year a decade ago, bringing challenges and opportunities for Britain’s fishers as Mediterranean species of fish and shellfish move into UK waters, while cod and haddock are migrating farther north.View image in fullscreenIncreasing octopus numbers off Cornwall have led to record catches.Photograph: A Martin UW Photography/GettyBritain’s southernmost county is experiencing itslargest octopus bloomin 75 years, according to the Marine Biological Association, thought to be linked to the warming seas.As the octopus population has exploded, a record 130,000 tonnes has landed at Newlyn’s fish market so far this year. In previous years, less than 100 tonnes of octopus would have been brought ashore at the market, says Chris Ranford, the chief executive of the Cornish Fish Producers’ Organisation.The fishing industry is “split down the middle whether it’s an opportunity or a problem”, says Ranford. “The volume has got to the level where it is a really solid export market, and the price has held up fairly well.”Octopus is popular in countries including Spain, but there is little domestic appetite. UK fishers are also finding octopus have broken into their shellfish pots and eaten the crab and lobster inside, reducing catches of these species that are more popular with British diners.Ranford, who is also the current chair of the National Organisation of Fishermen’s Federations, says there are concerns that a very cold winter or drop in water quality could suddenly cut octopus numbers, leaving fishers with little to catch as crab, lobster and scallop populations take time to recover.Explore more on these topicsFarmingFood & drink industryFishingFishing industryMarine lifeClimate crisisDroughtexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Family affair: how pop-star siblings Audrey Hobert and Malcolm Todd stormed the charts in parallel | Music | The Guardian
description: Following in the footsteps of Michael and Janet Jackson, and Kylie and Dannii Minogue, the Hobert siblings have simultaneously struck pop gold – with no rivalry
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: Following in the footsteps of Michael and Janet Jackson, and Kylie and Dannii Minogue, the Hobert siblings have simultaneously struck pop gold – with no rivalry
Content: Audrey Hobert performing at the Lollapalooza festival in July, and Malcolm Todd at Osheaga festival in August.Composite: ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAudrey Hobert performing at the Lollapalooza festival in July, and Malcolm Todd at Osheaga festival in August.Composite: ShutterstockMusicFamily affair: how pop-star siblings Audrey Hobert and Malcolm Todd stormed the charts in parallelFollowing in the footsteps of Michael and Janet Jackson, and Kylie and Dannii Minogue, the Hobert siblings have simultaneously struck pop gold – with no rivalryLaura SnapesFri 14 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe history of rival sibling pop solo acts is a limited but potent one. Most famous, of course, are Michael and Janet Jackson. Kylie and Dannii Minogue, Billie Eilish and Finneas, Beyoncé and Solange, Natasha and Daniel Bedingfield, Neneh and Eagle-Eye Cherry, Jessica and Ashlee Simpson, and Brandy and Ray J all share the intimate and rare understanding of what it was like to share Lego sets and chart space.That strange dynamic recently gained a new pairing. The US artists Audrey Hobert, 27, and her younger brother, who performs as Malcolm Todd, 22, have both scored global hits synonymous with the sound of summer 2026.Two years after Todd released the song Earrings, a lovelorn track sung over the music to Steve Lacy’s 2022 megahit Bad Habit, it started blowing up in April, rising to a peak of No 16 in the UK and No 20 in the US. Just as his song started to slip down the charts, Hobert’s ultra-wordy, ultra-catchy track Sue Me started breaking through, vaulting up the UK Top 40 weekly since early June. It reached a new peak of No 29 this week, and cracked the Billboard Hot 100 two weeks ago.Audrey Hobert: Sue Me – videoIn 2026, music fans are used to family dynasties ruling over music thanks to the rise of the pop star nepo baby: Gracie Abrams (daughter of director JJ Abrams), Willow Smith (Will and Jada Pinkett Smith), Mabel (Neneh Cherry), Maya Hawke (Ethan Hawke and Uma Thurman), Romy Mars (Sofia Coppola and Phoenix frontman Thomas Mars) to name but a few.The Hoberts are not exactly nepo babies, though they have showbiz links: their father is a TV showrunner who worked on Scrubs and the Nickelodeon kids’ show on which Hobert, a screenwriting graduate, got her start. She then started writing songs with Gracie Abrams, a childhood best friend, resulting in six co-writing credits on Abrams’ second album, 2024’s The Secret of Us.Hobert’s work with Abrams earned her a publishing deal and later a solo record contract with RCA. She has cited Taylor Swift, Lena Dunham and the comedian Nathan Fielder as inspirations; her loquacious, rhythmic songwriting, full of offbeat narratives about awkward but hopeful loners, mines the sounds of pure pop and pop-punk synonymous with Y2K MTV. She released her debut solo album, Who’s the Clown?, last August. Fellow breakout pop superstar Role Model recently described her slapstick-heavy live show as “one of the best things I’ve ever seen” on the cult How Long Gone podcast. “She’s doing something very new, which is hard to do onstage.”Todd’s USP, meanwhile, is a sort of blue-eyed, heart-on-sleeve take on indie-R&B inspired by the likes of Steve Lacy and Omar Apollo. He started making music seriously during the pandemic, and postponed going to university in order to pursue pop stardom. It worked: he signed with Columbia and released his debut mixtape for the label, Sweet Boy, in 2024. This week, he appeared ina Gap adcovering Robyn’s Dancing on My Own.There appears to be no rivalry between the pair, who frequently boost each other’s careers. She directed the video for his 2025 single Concrete; after he covered her song Phoebe on Australian radio station Triple J’s noted covers session Like a Version in April, she returned the favour in May, covering Earrings for the same slot. Last weekend, the pair duetted on Phoebe during Hobert’s performance at San Francisco’s Outside Lands festival, where she drew one of the festival’s bigger crowds.Malcolm Todd: Earrings – videoTodd told the Face that it was no surprise his sister had found musical success, even if the aspiring screenwriter always said that her goals were working in film and TV. “You just have to watch 30 seconds of a video of her when she was eight years old and you’d be like, ​‘Yeah, there’s no way in the world this girl doesn’t become a pop star.’”‘The beast inside me wants to move!’ The smart, slapstick world of Audrey Hobert, the Steve Martin of popRead moreHobert told Triple J that Todd “deserves every good thing that’s happening and it’s just gonna keep on happening … the head on his shoulders is so straight and he’s just never strayed from the guy he is. He’s always been this guy. He is funny. He is smart. He knows he’s talented and his ego does not fill up a room.”Hobert and Todd’s respective steady rises are symbolic of how breakout pop careers are made today. Rare is the bolt-from-the-blue debut single such as Olivia Rodrigo’s 2021 smash Drivers License (though that built on her years-long Disney Channel career). It took Chappell Roan seven months to blow up after the release of her debut album, which itself came after years of grinding in the pop underground and being dropped by her former label. This year also saw Zara Larsson tower over pop thanks to two slow-burning older hits, last year’s Midnight Sun – and 2015’s Lush Life. TikTok discovery is often the fuel behind these rises.UK audiences will have to wait to see Todd, who embarks on a long tour of North America in September. But Hobert will appear in the UK later this month, playing solo dates and festival appearances supporting Lorde in London and Bristol.Explore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockFamily filmsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jason Arday, professor at centre of Cambridge plagiarism row, found dead  | Jason Arday | The Guardian
description: Academic was pronounced dead at his home in south London after police called to address after 3pm on Friday
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Academic was pronounced dead at his home in south London after police called to address after 3pm on Friday
Content: Jason Arday was appointed as professor of sociology of education at Cambridge in 2023, and was the university’s youngest black professor.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJason Arday was appointed as professor of sociology of education at Cambridge in 2023, and was the university’s youngest black professor.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianJason ArdayJason Arday, professor at centre of Cambridge plagiarism row, found deadAcademic was pronounced dead at his home in south London after police called to address after 3pm on FridayRichard AdamsandVikram DoddFri 14 Aug 2026 18.10 EDTFirst published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 15.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJason Arday, the academic whoresigned last week as a professor at the University of Cambridge, has been found dead at his home in south London.The Metropolitan police said officers were called to Arday’s address by theLondonambulance service after 3pm on Friday.A spokesperson for the Met said: “A 41-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene. His next of kin have been informed and are being supported by officers.“At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious. The case is being investigated by officers from the Met’s central south command unit. A file will be prepared for the coroner.”The body was believed to be that of Arday. At this stage, police are understood not to believe anyone else was involved in the death.London ambulance service was the first emergency service at the scene. The person discovered inside the home was found unresponsive.Arday’s family said in a statement: “Jason was subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for more than three years since he accepted the role of professor at Cambridge University by those who would leave no stone unturned in their quest to undermine him.“The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone.“We are in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son.“We won’t comment further at this point beyond asking the press to leave us alone now, and to stop the campaign of harassment which has been waged against Jason and his family for too long.”The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, said: “I’m devastated for the family and friends ofJason Arday. He faced an unacceptable public hounding and campaign of abuse. I know many Londoners will be angry and upset this evening.“Jason Arday was the victim of a pernicious public shaming that other people in his position simply wouldn’t have faced. His death was a tragedy, but once again it should be a wake-up call for all of us.”Arday was appointed professor of sociology of education at Cambridge in 2023, and was the university’s youngest-ever black professor. But he resigned last week afteraccusations of plagiarismandinconsistencies in statements about his career and achievements.In a statement announcing his resignation, Arday said: “It is with profound sadness that I write to resign, with immediate effect, from my position at theUniversity of Cambridgeand Jesus College.“When I accepted the extraordinary honour of becoming professor of sociology at Cambridge, it was, without question, the greatest professional privilege of my life.”Arday said he had been driven to resign because the “relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love”.Prof Deborah Prentice, Cambridge’s vice-chancellor, said in a statement: “We are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news. Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday’s family and friends at this incredibly difficult time.”Durham University, where Arday worked between 2019 and 2021, said: “We are shocked and terribly sad to learn of the death of Jason Arday.“He is remembered at Durham as a kind and warm person who actively sought to promote opportunities for PhD students. We want to express our deepest sympathy to his family who are in our thoughts.”Arday’s rise to a prestigious professorial chair was remarkable. Arday said he had been nonverbal until the age of 11, requiring extensive speech and language therapy, as well as being illiterate until 18.That life story contributed to him being made a torchbearer for the 2012 London Olympics flame.After leaving school, Arday went on to further study before completing a doctorate in education at Liverpool John Moores University in 2015. That was followed by a string of academic posts culminating in a professorship at the University of Glasgow and a professorial chair at Cambridge.Arday was initially accused of plagiarising another academic’s work for his PhD thesis. But he denied the accusations, and an investigation by Liverpool John Moores University earlier this year upheld its decision to award him a PhD.But other elements of his life story were increasingly questioned, including claims of prodigious money-raising for charity and feats of long-distance running.He was also challenged about whether he was nonverbal as a child.However those claims meant little in the world of academia. After initially defending Arday as the victim of a smear campaign, as further questions arose about his academic career, the university began to temper its support.On 5 August Cambridge announced it would hold an internal inquiry after it said it received “new information” about his academic qualifications and honorary appointments, as well as what it described as “a number of ongoing complaints regarding academic misconduct”. Jesus College, of which he was a member, said it would also hold an inquiry.But while Cambridge said Arday would remain in post and continue to receive support, Arday immediately announced his resignation.At the end of last week Glasgow University said it would also investigate Arday’s academic credentials.The controversy has stirred considerable anger within Cambridge’s academic community, both between Arday’s supporters and those who said the university had erred in appointing him to such a prestigious position.After resisting calls from senior staff for an independent inquiry, earlier this week Prentice backed down, saying she recognised the “anger and anxiety around this damaging and difficult case”.She described it as an aberration that should not be used to cast aspersions on the abilities of its staff of colour.Arday’s memoir, entitled Great and Unfortunate Things, was published this week in the US by an imprint of Simon & Schuster, with UK publication scheduled for later this month. Simon & Schuster has been contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsJason ArdayLondonEnglandUniversity of CambridgeUniversitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham criticised for EV and North Sea approach amid climate crisis | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: Cut in electric vehicle sales targets could add millions of tonnes of CO<sub>2</sub> to emissions in UK, say green campaigners
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Cut in electric vehicle sales targets could add millions of tonnes of CO2 to emissions in UK, say green campaigners
Content: The UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, speaks to staff during a visit to the Met Office weather and climate service in Exeter on Friday.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, speaks to staff during a visit to the Met Office weather and climate service in Exeter on Friday.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/AFP/Getty ImagesClimate crisisBurnham criticised for EV and North Sea approach amid climate crisisCut in electric vehicle sales targets could add millions of tonnes of CO2to emissions in UK, say green campaignersJasper Jolly,Rowena MasonandMatthew TaylorFri 14 Aug 2026 14.51 EDTFirst published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 09.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has been criticised for moving to cut electric vehicle (EV) sales targets and accept North Sea drilling at a time of devastating wildfires caused by the climate emergency.The prime minister for the first time acknowledged on Friday that the climate crisis was behind hundreds of wildfires that have ripped across the parts of the UK.The scale of the disaster has prompted the government to bring in the military, ban the sale of disposable barbecuesand activate the national alert system to issue safety advice to people across England and Wales in areas at risk on Friday night.However, Burnham was also accused of failing to take the push for net zero seriously enough, as the government took steps towards watering down EV targets on the same day.View image in fullscreenSeveral homes in Stourbridge in the West Midlands were destroyed as a result of wildfires this week.Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/Getty ImagesThe government on Friday launched a consultation on cutting the target for new EVs to as little as 50% of all new cars in 2030, down from 80% under existing rules, in proposals that could add millions of tonnes a year to the UK’s carbon dioxide emissions.The consultation will include several options, including leaving the headline target unchanged, or cutting it to 70%, 60% or 50%.In a video from the West Midlands, where homes have been destroyed and dozens of people injured, Burnham appeared to acknowledge the seriousness of the climate crisis. “We cannot accept this as the new normal,” he said. “This isn’t happening in isolation.“Much of England and Wales is in drought and we are in another period of extreme heat. Farmers are watching crops fail and firefighters have faced hundreds of wildfires in a matter of weeks. This is what climate change looks like, here and now.”View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and the West Midlands mayor, Richard Parker, right, with the West Midlands chief fire officer, Simon Tuhill, during a visit to Stourbridge on Friday.Photograph: Peter Byrne/ReutersBut in a broadcast interview, he alsodefended his “pragmatic” approach on extracting oil and gasfrom the North Sea. His government will shortly have to decide whether to allow new drilling at the Rosebank and Jackdaw fields, with a consultation on the former closing on Monday.Environmental groups have said permitting extraction at the fields should be inconceivable after five heatwaves this summer, with Greenpeace saying it was a “Rubicon that he must not cross”.The decision to consider weakening one of the UK’s key climate policies on EVs was announced hours after the country recorded itshottest day of the year so far– and the fifth hottest ever – after five heatwaves that scientists have said are almost certainly worsened by global heating caused by carbon emissions.Fire services said 19homes were destroyed, 200 hectares (500 acres) burnt and dozens of people sent to hospital in the West Midlands, the UK’s traditional automotive centre, in grassfires that may have been worsened by drought.‘It’s due to climate’: the people of Stourbridge on the town’s wildfiresRead moreSpeaking from Stourbridge, Burnham said it was necessary to bring in a temporary ban on disposable barbecues from Friday, asking retailers to withdraw them from sale.“Please think about the situation we are in,” he said. “Britain is a tinderbox right now. Setting a fire in any outdoor setting is a risk to people’s homes and other people’s lives.”The prime minister also revealed he planned to commission firefighting planes to combat the spread of wildfires and appointed a new fire minister, as he made the case that country had to “face up” to the “changing climate”.Environmental groups largely welcomed Burnham’s words on the climateafter 50 organisations earlier criticised him in a letterfor failing to mention it following a Cobra meeting on the heatwave earlier this week.Hannah Martin, the co-director of Green New Deal Rising which coordinated Friday’s letter, said: “Finally Andy Burnham has said the words ‘climate change’ as prime minister and acknowledged the cause of the wildfires, drought and extreme heat that is raging across the country. Now he needs to put policies in place to deal with the scale of the crisis.“That means saying no to new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea … it also means ramping up new investment in renewable energy and climate jobs, doubling down on insulating homes and improving public transport, and making sure our homes, hospitals, schools and emergency services are properly equipped to deal with extreme weather caused by climate change.”Extreme heat: why our cities can’t cope | OpinionSam Keely from the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU) thinktank also urged Burnham not to row back on the government’s commitment for the rollout of electric vehicles.Keely said: “At the same time as the prime minister was speaking, the government launched itsconsultationon watering down the zero emissions vehicle mandate.“Getting more EVs on the road is one of the single most important policies for cutting UK emissions and will also insulate more British motorists from paying more at the petrol pump as a result of volatile oil prices, saving billions of pounds on the British driving bill.”Electric car sales have soared by 29% in the UK this year, but the automotive industry has said the sales targets, known as the zero emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate, are putting too much pressure on manufacturers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThey say the mandate forces them to sell electric cars at discounts and have threatened job losses or even UK factory closures if the rules do not change.The government said it needed the targets to “remain pro-business and grounded in the real world”.Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, said: “It’s right we keep targets under review to ensure they’re practical and back British industry. The end goal hasn’t changed – but we need to take business with us on the journey.”The changes arestrongly opposed by climate campaignersand by the electric car charging industry, which has plans to spend billions of pounds to install charge points across the country.View image in fullscreenThe electric car charging industry has plans to spend billions of pounds installing charge points across the UK.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThe switch to EVs is expected to be the single biggest contributor to cutting UK carbon pollution in the next decade, according to the government’sClimate Change Committee.Under the existing rules, carmakers need to sell an increasing proportion of pure electric cars every year or face fines. The targets tighten from 33% this year to 80% in 2030. The sale of new petrol and diesel cars is then to be banned from 2035.Ami McCarthy, the Greenpeace UK head of politics, said weakening the rules would be “a wrong turn for drivers, energy security, our climate and the economy”.Milk, wine, salad: how your food will be affected by the summer of heatRead moreShe added: “Both the Iran war and this summer’s extreme weather have shown once again why we’re better off cutting our dependence on fossil fuels.“This mandate is one of the most powerful policies we have to bring down planet-heating emissions, which is the only way to stop more deadly heatwaves in future.“Burnham can’t fulfil his promise of tackling the cost of living crisis and reindustrialising Britain without the green economy. So why put on the brakes now?”It would be the second time that Labour has watered down the targets after itlast year added loopholescalled “flexibilities” to the original rules. The loopholes allowed more plug-in hybrid EVs, which combine a polluting petrol engine with a smaller battery, to count towards the mandate, as well as permitting carmakers to catch up with more battery car sales in later years.Extending the flexibilities to 2034 will also be considered in the consultation, which will run until 23 October. Van sales targets are also likely to be changed.The most extreme change proposed, cutting the headline rate to 50%, could reduce electric car sales by as much as 5.8m, according to analysis by the ECIU. It added that the changes would make the 2035 ban much harder to achieve, with some carmakersalready lobbying for it to be delayed.Colin Walker, the ECIU head of transport, said: “Proposing to water down the UK’s biggest climate policy the day after temperatures hit 38C, and a summer of heat and drought that risks the UK having its worst ever harvest, may seem strange to the increasing number of people concerned by images of homes on fire, and the security and affordability of the food we eat.”Mike Hawes, the chief executive of the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders lobby group, said: “The automotive industry is fully committed to a zero-emission future, investing billions in new technologies, products and incentives.“However, with the ZEV mandate conceived under vastly different conditions, this welcome review is a timely opportunity to adjust the transition so it works for all.”Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisAndy BurnhamElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsAutomotive industryAutomotive emissionsGreenhouse gas emissionsEthical and green livingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump threatens to declare strait of Hormuz ‘territory of the United States’ | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: Seriousness of remark made in New York on Friday, and whether it signaled new policy ​position, not clear
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Seriousness of remark made in New York on Friday, and whether it signaled new policy ​position, not clear
Content: Donald Trump at the David S Mack Center for Training and Intelligence in Garden City, New York, on Friday.Photograph: Samuel Corum/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump at the David S Mack Center for Training and Intelligence in Garden City, New York, on Friday.Photograph: Samuel Corum/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpTrump threatens to declare strait of Hormuz ‘territory of the United States’Seriousness of remark made in New York on Friday, and whether it signaled new policy ​position, not clearMaya YangFri 14 Aug 2026 17.38 EDTFirst published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 17.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trumphas threatened to declare the strait of Hormuz as “a territory of the United States” as his administration struggles to conclude the war with Iran.During a speech at a police academy on Long Island, New York, on Friday, the US president said he would “pretty soon” designate the waterway – a crucial chokepoint for global trade, through which about a fifth of the world’s seaborne oil supplies typically pass – a US territory.The comment came as peace talks withIranremain at an impasse following failed negotiations, with Tehran refusing to reopen the strait, which has been all but closed since the US and Israel launched their war on Iran in February.Almost six months into the war, there is little indication that negotiations will soon yield peace, as Iranian officials continue to defy Trump’s demands. The US has been blockading Iranian shipping and ⁠ports in recent months in an effort to pile economic pressure on Tehran.“After we finish defeating Iran, which is being very badly defeated, pretty soon I’ll be declaring the Hormuz strait a territory of the United States,” Trump said on Friday. “Essentially, that’s what it is. We have the blockade. No ships get through unless we want them to.”The seriousness of Trump’s remark, and whether it signaled a new policy ​position for his administration, was not immediately clear.Responding on X, formerly Twitter, Kazem Gharibabadi, Iran’s deputy foreign minister, said Tehran would not ⁠be intimidated by threats, ​or ‌a show ‌of force, by ‌the US – and added that the strait of Hormuz ​would only ​be opened, ​or ‌closed, under Iran’s ​authority.Earlier this week, the president claimed that the US had “total control” over the strait and said “I think we will keep it” on Truth Social, despite the waterway being an internationally navigable strait bordered by Iran and Oman.Fuel prices have risen sharplysince the start of the war, forcing working Americans to pay significantly more at the pump.Nevertheless, on Friday, Trump said that Americans who have had to “pay a tiny little bit more for your gasoline” should remember that they are “doing it so that a very evil country cannot have a – really, it’s the No 1 state sponsor of terror in the world – we don’t want them to have a nuclear weapon.“When you have to pay a little bit more, you’re at $4, it’s OK, I mean, it’s not. I’ll never apologize. I did the right thing,” he added.Over the past six months, the Trump administration hasrepeatedly claimed victoryin the war, saying Iran’s regime has been pleading for a deal.Tehran has remained steadfast in its demands,sayingas recently as last Saturday that it will not reopen the strait of Hormuz unless the US “corrects its behavior”, “completely compensate[s]” Iran for war damage, lifts sanctions and “unconditionally” releases frozen assets.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpUS-Israel war on IranUS politicsIranStrait of HormuzMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Strong 7.7-magnitude earthquake strikes eastern Indonesia, killing two  | Indonesia | The Guardian
description: Shallow quake hit Indonesia’s Flores region early on Saturday, prompting thousands to seek higher ground
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Shallow quake hit Indonesia’s Flores region early on Saturday, prompting thousands to seek higher ground
Content: Strong earthquake hits IndonesiaIndonesiaStrong 7.7-magnitude earthquake strikes eastern Indonesia, killing twoShallow quake hit Indonesia’s Flores region early on Saturday, prompting thousands to seek higher groundGuardian staff and agenciesFri 14 Aug 2026 19.43 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 22.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA powerful 7.7-magnitude quake struck easternIndonesiaearly on Saturday, killing two people, causing widespread panic and collapsing buildings and homes in a region prone to deadly earthquakes.Authorities initially issued a tsunami warning, but it has since been lifted.The shallow quake hit Indonesia’s Flores region with a depth of 10km at 5.58am local time, according to the US Geological Survey, followed by two aftershocks, including one with a magnitude of 6.1.“At this point there are two reported fatalities” – a man and a woman, disaster agency spokesperson Berton Suar Pelita Panjaitan told reporters in Jakarta, adding that authorities were still determining the full extent of the damage.The epicentre of the quake was located off the north coast of Flores island, about 68km (42 miles) northwest of the coastal town of Ende, US and Indonesian authorities said.Residents in Nagekeo regency, the area closest to the epicentre, raced for higher ground immediately after the earthquake.“Suddenly it started to shake and I panicked,” 31-year-old hospital customer service official, Lukas Lotar told AFP. “Patients also fled the hospital, the jolt was big. I saw some walls were cracked,” he added.View image in fullscreenPeople flee their homes to seek safety after a earthquake in Talibura Village, Sikka, East Nusa Tenggara on 15 August 2026.Photograph: Arnold Welianto/AFP/Getty ImagesNagekeo resident Yohanes Babo, 56, said he was at a market when the quake hit.“The shaking was strong. Thankfully, we were already outside the house,” he said.“People were panicking, running here and there. We’re evacuating for the time being … and trying to get to the hills,” he said, adding: “My family is safe. No one was harmed.”Authorities issued a tsunami warning but later lifted it when Indonesia’s meteorology, climatology and geophysics agency (BMKG) said monitoring showed no significant sea level changes that would pose a threat to coastal communities.“We have ended (the tsunami warning) but we will keep monitoring the sea level,” said BMKG earthquake and tsunami director Wijayanto.Images broadcast on Indonesian television showed hundreds of people in nearby Nagekeo regency evacuating the area surrounded by the rubble of damaged buildings.The quake was felt across much of Flores island with initial reports indicating heavy damage.Yohanna Embu, a resident of Sikka, a regency within East Nusa Tenggara province, said a number of buildings were damaged by the strong shaking and panicked people ran to higher ground.“Many buildings here were damaged … I saw that the waiting room at the port terminal in Maumere had collapsed,” she said.View image in fullscreenHouses were damaged by the 7.7-magnitude earthquake in Ruteng, Manggarai, East Nusa Tenggara, on 15 August 2026.Photograph: SELO/AFP/Getty ImagesIndonesia, a vast archipelago of more than 17,000 islands, is prone to earthquakes and volcanic activity because of its location on the “Ring of Fire”, an arc of volcanoes and fault lines in the Pacific Basin.Separately, Australia’s tsunami ⁠warning centre said the undersea earthquake ​will ​have “no tsunami ​threat to the Australian mainland, ​islands ‌or territories”.*With Agence France-Presse and ReutersExplore more on these topicsIndonesiaEarthquakesAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Standards watchdog resumes Farage probe as rivals slam needless byelection | Nigel Farage | The Guardian
description: Reform UK leader says he did not attend vote count in Clacton to avoid being ‘humiliated by nobodies’
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Reform UK leader says he did not attend vote count in Clacton to avoid being ‘humiliated by nobodies’
Content: If Nigel Farage is found to have broken parliamentary rules, Clacton could face another byelection.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIf Nigel Farage is found to have broken parliamentary rules, Clacton could face another byelection.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesNigel FarageStandards watchdog resumes Farage probe as rivals slam needless byelectionReform UK leader says he stayed away from vote count in Clacton to avoid being ‘humiliated by nobodies’Rowena MasonandPeter WalkerFri 14 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTFirst published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 04.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNigel Farage’s attempt to draw the sting from inquiries into his financial affairs appeared to have backfired on Friday as the standards watchdog reopened its investigation and MPs from all sides condemned the needless byelection.TheReform UKleader declared victory in the Clacton vote as he was returned with an increased majority and gained more votes than in 2024, saying he had “stuck two fingers up at the entire political establishment”.However, parliament’s standards commissioner immediately reopened an investigation into whether he should have declared a series of gifts provided to him shortly before the last general election.These include a£5m personal gift from crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne, first revealed by the Guardian, and further financial support from his friend and convicted fraudster George Cottrell.View image in fullscreenNigel Farage arrives at a polling station on Thursday to cast his vote in the byelection.Photograph: Richard Pelham/APRival parties said the reopening of the inquiry showed Farage’s attempt to avoid scrutiny had failed, with the Labour party chair, Bridget Phillipson, saying he now had “no hiding place” as he tries to “dodge and deflect” criticism.But at an event to celebrate his win, the Reform UK leader attempted to diminish the significance of the allegations under investigation.He told GB News: “If I’ve made one sin, it’s that I haven’t filled in a piece of paper. I’ve broken no law, I’ve broken no tax law, I’ve taken no public money … maybe I haven’t filled in a piece of paper. I’m confident I’m right, let’s see where we go.”double quotation markThe scandal just keeps piling up. And now he’s through that byelection, there’s no hiding placeBridget PhillipsonWhile playing down the inquiry, Farage also appeared to acknowledge the watchdog could well find against him over his failure to be transparent. If a separate standards committee of MPs recommend a sanction of more than 10 days of suspension from parliament, it could then trigger a second byelection.This would require the approval of more than 10% of the electorate of Clacton – about 7,800 voters – which is less than the number who voted for Farage’s main rival, the satirical candidate Count Binface.Farage also faced criticism for failing to turn up to the Clacton count inEssex, saying he had been told by police of an organised attempt at disruption.However, police said they had given no advice to any candidate not to attend and it emerged that an anonymous art collective flashmob in masks were demonstrating 15 minutes away from the venue at Clacton town hall.View image in fullscreenCount Binface, centre, was the second-most popular candidate in the byelection.Photograph: Joe Giddens/PAAt a separate event, Farage gave an explanation for failing to attend the count saying he was “damned” if he was going to stand on a stage to be “demeaned and humiliated by nobodies”. It was not clear if he was talking about the array of more than 30 independent candidates who stood against him or the possibility of a protest.Tim Montgomerie, a Reform UK commentator and supporter, was among those to criticise his non-appearance.“He should be on every TV screen this morning,” said Montgomerie, “underlining his win – and with that cheeky, trademark smile on his face … his recently far too dominant aggrieved tone is still with us.“It’s not good. You don’t skip your own victory count without a much better explanation. Anger from politicians can work but only if it’s on behalf of others – not yourself. He’s distracting from his victory.”Farage called the byelection early in July saying he wanted voters in Clacton to decide if he was fit to be an MP. However, the stunt did not go to plan after all the main partiesdeclined to stand, leaving him taking on dozens of novelty and fringe candidates, most prominent among them Count Binface.2:17Farage declares victory over Count Binface in Clacton byelection – videoAccording to one report, Farage called his own byelection after his team advised that leaving parliament would end the investigation. In fact it only pauses such processes, which resume if the person is re-elected.Farage has said the investigation was “being used as a political tool”. One Reform MP, Sarah Pochin,called the processa “kangaroo court”.Lee Anderson, the chair of Reform, said on Friday it was a “fair comment” to describe the parliamentary standards process as a kangaroo court and argued that there were questions over whether it would be impartial.Farage is expected to be interviewed by the standards commissioner when parliament returns but it is not certain when the investigation will conclude.‘Let’s see what he can do’: will Burnham bring Barnsley voters back to Labour?Read moreLabour said on Friday that the resumption of the investigation showed Farage could not outrun questions about his finances, with at least 10 questions still outstanding, including whether Harborne had given money to any other Reform-linked figures.Phillipson said: “He forced a byelection he didn’t need to have. He stood again. He spent most of the summer chasing a bin around Clacton.“And now he’s going to come back to parliament and have to answer some very serious questions, questions he’s been seeking to dodge, distracting and deflecting from the £5m … gift, his connections to a convicted fraudster.“You know, the scandal just keeps piling up. And now he’s through that byelection, there’s no hiding place.”A Conservative party spokesperson said the byelection was a “farce started by Nigel Farage to try to dodge scrutiny of his fishy £5m personal donation”.“All Farage can brag about this morning is beating a bloke with a bin on his head. What he should do is answer the serious outstanding questions about why he hid his £5m from the public,” the spokesperson said.The Reform UK leader won the contest with more than 22,000 votes – or 63% – on a turnout of 44%.Friends of Farage suggested he would not be taking much of a break and intended to throw himself back into Reform campaigning and building up a presence in target seats in case of an early general election.Get in touchContact Guardian Politics about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know.
