Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don't already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Scroll down and click onSecure Messaging. When asked who you wish to contact please select thePolitics (UK)team.EmailFor encrypted email correspondence you can create a free Proton Mail account and email us at guardian.politics.desk@protonmail.com.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsNigel FarageReform UKParty fundingClacton byelection August 2026EnglandEssexnewsShareReuse this content

title: Israeli military plans to transfer law enforcement in occupied West Bank to police | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Palestine’s vice-president calls plan ‘flagrant violation of international law’ and a step towards full Israeli annexation
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Palestine’s vice-president calls plan ‘flagrant violation of international law’ and a step towards full Israeli annexation
Content: Israeli forces preventing Israeli and foreign peace activists from delivering supplies to a besieged Palestinian home.Photograph: Nasser ishatyeh/SOPA Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenIsraeli forces preventing Israeli and foreign peace activists from delivering supplies to a besieged Palestinian home.Photograph: Nasser ishatyeh/SOPA Images/ShutterstockWest BankIsraeli military plans to transfer law enforcement in occupied West Bank to policePalestine’s vice-president calls plan ‘flagrant violation of international law’ and a step towards full Israeli annexationEmma Graham-Harrisonin JerusalemFri 14 Aug 2026 13.52 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 14.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsrael’s defence minister wants to transfer law enforcement powers for Israelis in the occupied West Bank over to the police, a plan that Palestine’s vice-president described as a “flagrant violation of international law” and step towards full Israeli annexation.Israel Katz announced that he had ordered the military to draw up plans for the handover of responsibility for policing Israeli settlers amid domestic and international criticism ofthe army’s failure to tackle militants besieging three Palestinian families.The Palestinian vice-president, Hussein al-Sheikh, called for international intervention to enforce international law and stop a move that would “entrench the illegitimate annexation of Palestinian land”.Katz unveiled his plan as a settler siege in the Palestinian village of Qusra entered its sixth day. The Israeli army has proved unable or unwilling to removethe group of militants trying to drive out Palestinian residentsthrough a campaign of terror.View image in fullscreenIsraeli soldiers watch Israeli settlers setting up a tent just outside the entrance of a besieged Palestinian family home in the village of Qusra, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, on 14 August 2026.Photograph: Jaafar Ashtiyeh/AFP/Getty ImagesMichael Sfard, a leading Israeli human rights lawyer, said a transfer of law enforcement powers could constitute a major step towards formal annexation.“The military can delegate enforcement but not responsibility [of the law],” Sfard said. “If they want to create a normative legal framework that absolves the army from responsibility and transfers it to police, that would be another brick, a very major one, of annexation.”However, Israel could also legally expand police powers in the occupiedWest Bankunder the current occupation framework, he added, and the lack of detail in Katz’s statement indicated it may have been driven more by politics than clear policy.“This is a cowardly statement made by a minister of defence who is under scrutiny, because the army that reached Syria, Iran and Lebanon and annihilated Gaza cannot evacuate a few Jewish terrorists that invaded a Palestinian home in an area under occupation for six decades.”View image in fullscreenPalestinian, Israeli and foreign activists attempt to deliver basic supplies to three Palestinian families under siege by settlers in Qusra.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesThere has been a surge in attacks on Palestiniansand construction of new settlements across the occupied West Bank, as extremists backed by the most far-right government in Israel’s history intensify a campaign of ethnic cleansing ahead ofnational elections set for October.On Thursday Katz celebrated the re-establishment of a settlement evacuated by Israel in 2005, under then-prime minister Ariel Sharon’s disengagement plan.“Here, this is the land of Israel. Here, we are staying forever,” Katz said at the ceremony in Ganim, where two dozen prefabricated homes have already been installed, and the hillside is being levelled to make space for more.On the road that leads to the settlement the army had levelled Palestinian property and used piles of rubble to block access roads for Palestinian communities.On Friday the commander of Israeli forces for the occupied West Bank, Gen Avi Bluth, made a second visit to Qusra. Two days earlier he told Palestinians the army would remove the settlers, but soldiers retreated from confrontation with the group.Instead they forced one of the Palestinian families out of their home, saying they needed it as a base for the unsuccessful military operation against the settlers.View image in fullscreenIsraeli settlers re-established Ganim on 13 August 2026, starting with two dozen prefabricated homes.Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPAOne of the homes is owned by a US citizen, and US ambassador Mike Huckabee described the Israelis besieging it as terrorists, and said he had requested the Israeli police and army act to remove them.Huckabee, who supports the settlement movement’s vision of establishing a “Greater Israel” on land seized from Palestinians and neighbouring countries, said the militants in Qusra represent a “very small minority” of the settler movement.State and settler violence has driven a surge in displacement of Palestinian communities in the past three years.Since October 2023, Israel has forcibly displaced 64 entire Palestinian communities and parts of 15 additional communities, affecting nearly 5,000 people, according to data from Israeli rights group B’tselem.On Friday Israeli gunmen opened fire at a group of unarmed Israeli and Palestinian activists as they attempted to peacefully reclaim Palestinian land seized by settlers in Beit Sahour, just outside Jerusalem. A Catholic bishop and journalists covering the event were also targeted by the attackers.Israeli settlers had put a large Star of David and Israeli flags on the roof an old, dilapidated house, owned by Palestinians, just 500 metres from a Palestinian family home.View image in fullscreenThousands of residential units under construction in the Giv’at Ze’ev settlement in the West Bank, near Jerusalem and Ramallah, 6 August 2026.Photograph: Debbie Hill/UPI/ShutterstockMia Biran, from the groupCombatants for Peace, said: “They are all the time threatened by the settlers. We were about a hundred activists, our goal was to clean the area, plant some trees, to show presence and to stand with the residents who are very scared. We were on private Palestinian land.”A few minutes after they started work, the group heard gunfire from the settler outpost and were forced to take cover. One gunman moved close to the group, opened fire in the air and aimed the gun at activists, in an attack videoed by the group.He was later joined by three or four others. “We screamed in Hebrew ‘do not fire’ and then they understood there are Israelis among the crowd,” Biran said.“I called the police to tell them we are threatened by settlers, the activists who were at the roof saw there was a military Jeep all the time in the area who did nothing.”After they withdrew from the area, settlers visited the nearby Palestinian home and threatened to burn it down, she added. Settlers regularly launch arson attacks on Palestinian homes. One such attack in 2015 killed a baby and his parents, orphaning their only surviving son.Quique Kierszenbaum and Sufian Taha contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsWest BankIsraelPalestineMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I shot Mr Thompson’: Luigi Mangione describes his planning and the killing of health insurance CEO | New York | The Guardian
description: It was a dramatic twist to the federal case over the killing of UnitedHealthcare’s Brian Thompson – but state charges are still pending
Author: Victoria Bekiempis
Headline: It was a dramatic twist to the federal case over the killing of UnitedHealthcare’s Brian Thompson – but state charges are still pending
Content: Luigi Mangione at his federal trial at Manhattan criminal court in New York City on Friday in this courtroom sketch.Photograph: Jane Rosenberg/ReutersView image in fullscreenLuigi Mangione at his federal trial at Manhattan criminal court in New York City on Friday in this courtroom sketch.Photograph: Jane Rosenberg/ReutersNew York‘I shot Mr Thompson’: Luigi Mangione describes his planning and the killing of health insurance CEOIt was a dramatic twist to the federal case over the killing of UnitedHealthcare’s Brian Thompson – but state charges are still pendingVictoria BekiempisFri 14 Aug 2026 16.29 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 17.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Luigi Mangione stepped into a Manhattan federal courtroom shortly after 11am on Friday, his demeanor was less debonair than at other recent court proceedings.The 28-year-old, wearing tan jail scrubs instead of natty menswear, walked with hands behind his back and ankles shackled en route to the defense table. Mangione sat and then studied a piece of paper alongside his attorney.This morning’s proceeding would mark a dramatic twist in Mangione’s legal saga. Mangione, who faces federal and state cases inUnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson’s 4 December 2024 killing, had long maintained a not-guilty stance.Luigi Mangione pleads guilty to causing UnitedHealthcare CEO’s death in federal caseRead moreBut this hearing would change that with one simple sentence.“On the morning of December 4, 2024, I shot Mr Thompson in Manhattan and he died,” he said.He added: “I knew what I was doing was illegal.”The killing of Thompson – gunned down on a Manhattan street – shocked the US and triggered a manhunt that ended with Mangione’s arrest in a Pennsylvania fast-food restaurant. But it also sparked an outpouring of public anger and rage at the actions of the US’s widely reviled for-profit healthcare industry.Many assumed that as Mangione went on trial, so perhaps would an entire industry, as the defense might seek to explain his actions. But the guilty plea – in the federal case against him at least – has ended that prospect.Much of the emotional proceeding, which saw both members of Thompson’s family and some Mangione supporters crying in the gallery, involved Judge Margaret Garnett engaging in the standard questioning judges use to determine whether someone is capable of admitting guilt.Was Mangione ever treated or hospitalized for any kind of mental illness? Was he under the care of a doctor or mental health professional? Had he been treated for any sort of addiction?Mangione answered “no” to all these questions.Garnett asked whether he had taken anything in the last two days and Mangione said yes: trazodone, “for sleeping”.Garnett then queried Mangione on whether anyone had made any promises – or threats – to induce him into pleading guilty. He said no.Then came the moment many observers had long waited for: Mangione would have to describe what happened, in his own words, potentially shedding light on the grisly slaying.Mangione said that “after years of enduring severe pain from a broken back, navigating the obstacles of the health insurance system and witnessing similar experiences of countless others”, he learned that UnitedHealthcare would hold its annual investor conference on 4 December 2024.The specific location wasn’t publicly disclosed, Mangione said, so “I then researched the event online”.“I observed that the annual conference of America’s largest healthcare organization with the stated mission to make health – excuse me – with the stated mission to make the health system work better for everyone, would be attended by company executives, the board of directors and hundreds of investors, not doctors, nurses and patients,” Mangione said.Mangione then told the court that in November of that year, he traveled into Manhattan and engaged in subterfuge to get more information.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I then emailed UnitedHealthcare leadership posing as an investor at a firm managing over $50bn in assets and requesting information about the conference,” he said. “Unlike my previous interactions with insurers, I received an immediate response within an hour.”Mangione said that he used a 3D printer to forge part of a firearm and affix it with a silencer and magazine.“My travel toNew Yorkand email to UnitedHealthcare was with the intent to shoot Brian Thompson,” he said.Both prosecutors and Mangione’s lawyers, under Garnett’s questioning, said they believed there was “sufficient factual evidence” for a plea.“Mr Mangione, how do you now plead to counts one and two of the indictment?” Garnett said, referring to the federal stalking charges against him.“Guilty,” Mangione said plainly, bringing an end to the prospect of a federal trial against him and throwing his state case into potential disarray.After the proceeding wrapped, dozens of journalists convened outside the federal courthouse in downtown Manhattan.“There can be no celebrity in assassination,” prosecutor Jamie McDonald said afterwards, adding that Mangione had “attempted to send a public message through violence”.Mangione’s team announced that they filed paperwork to dismiss the separate state case, which is due to start in September, and in which he faces murder charges. They argued that he could not be charged in Manhattan state court because of New York’s own double-jeopardy law.However, Manhattan prosecutors said their case wasn’t over, saying: “We are prepared to litigate the defense motions” and the team “remains committed to seeking justice for Mr Thompson and his family”.So the Mangione saga is still not over. Not yet.Explore more on these topicsNew YorkBrian Thompson shootingGun crimeUS crimeLaw (US)US justice systemnewsShareReuse this content

title: Madonna will not be playing Glastonbury in 2027, Emily Eavis says | Glastonbury festival | The Guardian
description: Festival organiser says she has booked next year’s headliners but would not say if Taylor Swift is among them
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Festival organiser says she has booked next year’s headliners but would not say if Taylor Swift is among them
Content: Rumours of a Glastonbury set began when Madonna told Graham Norton she had something ‘big’ planned in the UK next year.Photograph: NDZ/Star Max/GC ImagesView image in fullscreenRumours of a Glastonbury set began when Madonna told Graham Norton she had something ‘big’ planned in the UK next year.Photograph: NDZ/Star Max/GC ImagesGlastonbury festivalMadonna will not be playing Glastonbury in 2027, Emily Eavis saysFestival organiser says she has booked next year’s headliners but would not say if Taylor Swift is among themNadeem BadshahFri 14 Aug 2026 14.38 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 16.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMadonna will not be performing at next year’s Glastonbury, the festival’s organiser, Emily Eavis, has said.The singer, who has the most top 10 singles in UK chart history of any female artist, has never featured at Britain’s biggest music festival.Eavis said Glastonbury had booked all its headliners for June 2027. Asked about the lineup and speculation that the Queen of Pop would make her debut at the event in Somerset, Eavis told BBC Radio 4’s PM programme: “No, it’s definitely not Madonna, I’ll tell you that.”She added: “But we have got three [other] headliners and we’re very excited about it – it’s all coming together really well.”When asked about the possibility of a performance fromTaylor Swift, Eavis laughed and said she did not want to discuss the lineup any further.Speculation about Madonna, 67, appearing at Glastonbury began in June when the singer suggested to theBBC talkshow host Graham Nortonthat she was planning “something bigger” in the UK next summer.Eavis said: “Pretty much 95% of the stories [about Glastonbury] you read are not true, and rumours are pretty much always wrong.“But the good news is that we’ve got our headliners and we’re cracking on, and we just can’t wait to get back.”Last year’sGlastonbury festivalwas headlined by the 1975, Neil Young and Olivia Rodrigo, with Rod Stewart in the legend slot.On Friday, it was confirmed that Madonna’s collaboration with Kylie Minogue, Love Sensation, debuted at No 8 on the singles chart, becoming Madonna’s highest-charting UK song in 17 years.Love Sensation is the second single from Madonna’s latest album, Confessions II, and a remixed version features the Australian singer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMadonna’s last highest-charting single was Celebration in 2009. Her latest track has become her 65th UK top 10 single, spanning four decades since the 1980s.Only two artists have achieved more UK Top 10 singles: Elvis Presley with 76 and Cliff Richard with 68.Last month, Madonna performedduring the half-time show at the Fifa men’s World Cup final in New York between Spain and Argentina.Explore more on these topicsGlastonbury festivalMadonnaFestivalsMusic festivalsTaylor SwiftnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s due to climate’: the people of Stourbridge on the town’s wildfires | Extreme heat | The Guardian
description: Thursday has been described by residents as ‘horrendous’, ‘distressing’ and ‘one of the scariest days of my life’
Author: Neha Gohil
Headline: Thursday has been described by residents as ‘horrendous’, ‘distressing’ and ‘one of the scariest days of my life’
Content: Volunteers and helpers handling donations at Old Swinford hospital boarding school, a makeshift evacuation centre in Stourbridge.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianView image in fullscreenVolunteers and helpers handling donations at Old Swinford hospital boarding school, a makeshift evacuation centre in Stourbridge.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianExtreme heat‘It’s due to climate’: the people of Stourbridge on the town’s wildfiresThursday has been described by residents as ‘horrendous’, ‘distressing’ and ‘one of the scariest days of my life’Neha GohilMidlands correspondentFri 14 Aug 2026 13.17 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 16.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePeople in Stourbridge have described the fires that devastated more than a dozen homes as “horrendous” and “distressing”, with one describing blazes that surpassed the height of residential houses.Multiple fires spread across theWest Midlandson Thursday as temperatures reached record highs of 38.1C in the UK, during the country’s fifth consecutive heatwave.Fifty-four people, including 19 who were taken to hospital, were treated at eight different fires on Thursday, West Midlands ambulance service said, with the fire service confirming 19 homes in Stourbridge, a market town in Dudley, had been fully destroyed and an additional 18 damaged.During a visit to Stourbridge on Friday, Andy Burnham said the UK was like a “tinderbox” and announced the commission of firefighting planes to tackle future wildfires. “I’ve never seen scenes like this anywhere in Britain,” he told the BBC.The Guardian spoke to people who were forced to hurriedly evacuate from their homes in Stourbridge on Thursday, as a wildfire spread near the town’s golf course.View image in fullscreenFrom left: Andy Hobbs, Gemma Hobbs and neighbour John Bairner, were evacuated from their homes on Osmaston Road.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianThey repeatedly praised the support and efforts of local authorities and neighbours, but are yet to return home, with some staying at a nearby hotel or a makeshift evacuation centre that had been set up at a local boarding school.Gemma Hobbs, 46, and her partner, Andy, 61, were evacuated from their home on Osmaston Road on Thursday, as the wildfires raged over a mile away. Andy described seeing a house in flames.Gemma said: “I looked out the windows and all I could see was thick black smoke. My husband came home in a bit of a flap and said: ‘We’ve got to get out. We’ve got to get out immediately.’”Andy added: “It’s just the fact you don’t expect something to be as exponential as this so quickly. From the span of the area, it’s over 40 acres, that’s what we’ve been told.”Gareth Jones, 59, was providing shelter to his neighbour John Bairner, who had to be evacuated overnight and said it was a “scene of devastation”, calling the wildfire “terrifying”.“It was probably one of the scariest days of my life yesterday,” he said. “It was just the speed at which it spread, it was devastating. Absolutely frightening how quickly it spread. Within an hour. It’s a major event.”Bairner added: “All of the fields have gone, they’re all black. There’s a lot of residents up there, with buckets, hoses, just dampening down because it’s still smouldering away up there.”View image in fullscreenVolunteers and helpers handling donations to Old Swinford hospital boarding school in Stourbridge.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The GuardianThe Old Swinford hospital, a boarding school in Stourbridge, was set up as a makeshift evacuation centre for affected people late on Thursday.As queues of cars and volunteers dropped off donations and supplies on Friday, the headteacher of the school, Paul Kilbride, described the fires as a “devastating experience”, with more than 20 people evacuated from a nearby care home.“From what I saw, [the evacuees] were very tired and very anxious. I think they also showed great spirits [and] they obviously want to go home now,” he said. “This community suffered a lot yesterday.”Laurence Green, 66, stayed at the Old Swinford hospital boarding school overnight after he was evacuated from his home on Osmaston Road. Green said he saw “plumes of smoke” on Thursday afternoon before he was directed by police to evacuate to the town hall.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLaurence Green, evacuated from his home.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The Guardian“It’s horrendous … some of the houses look as though they are very badly damaged or completely destroyed,” he said. “People who built up their lives and built up their homes and for some people, it’s all gone.”Green agreed the devastation was a wake-up call for local people and the country about the impact of the climate crisis. “We should have woken up to what’s happening climate wise,” he said, before calling on the government to make the issue a priority.He dismissed thetemporary ban on disposable barbecues, announced by Burnham on Friday, as “pathetic” in comparison.“I had a bit of an argument with one of the Conservative councillors about it because I said: ‘It’s due to climate’ and he told me: ‘We shouldn’t be bringing politics into it.’ Well, yes we should.”The Bishop of Dudley, Martin Gorick, was also evacuated from his home and echoed Green’s concerns. He said climate change had to be taken seriously and the country had to become less reliant on fossil fuels. “The heat yesterday was extreme,” he said. “That doesn’t happen in England normally.”View image in fullscreenBishop Martin Gorick.Photograph: Fabio De Paola/The Guardian“This is not a divisive issue. It’s something that should bring us all together because we all live in one world. This is our only world.”Gorick described witnessing houses “ablaze” and described it as a “pretty awful sight”.“You see bursts of flame when it hits a tree or something like that. The flame is above the height of houses, it’s big and hot,” he said.The bishop, however, praised the local community for rallying together in the face of the devastation, including individuals who put together a list of medications needed by those who had been evacuated, and local churches and mosques who provided bedding.“The shops responded. People giving away drinks and food,” Gorick said. “It was great to see Muslims and Christians coming together, as well as any volunteers from any background, Sikh, Hindu, no faith were coming together.“That’s the best side of the Black Country, coming together in a crisis.”Explore more on these topicsExtreme heatWest MidlandsWildfiresClimate crisisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Disgraceful’: what one election photo tells us about British politics in 2026 | Politics | The Guardian
description: Results from coastal town of Clacton have been interpreted positively by Nigel Farage and Count Binface, but one spoiled ballot tells its own story
Author: Daniel Boffey
Headline: Results from coastal town of Clacton have been interpreted positively by Nigel Farage and Count Binface, but one spoiled ballot tells its own story
Content: Count Binface (centre) poses with other candidates after the vote count is declared at the Clacton byelection early on Friday morning.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCount Binface (centre) poses with other candidates after the vote count is declared at the Clacton byelection early on Friday morning.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesPolitics‘Disgraceful’: what one election photo tells us about British politics in 2026Results from coastal town of Clacton have been interpreted positively by Nigel Farage and Count Binface, but one spoiled ballot tells its own storyUK politics live – latest updatesDaniel BoffeyChief reporterFri 14 Aug 2026 08.23 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 17.38 EDTShareIt ended, perhaps fittingly, on a rather baffling note. After 34 days of campaigning to regain the parliamentary seat of Clacton on England’s east coast,Nigel Farage, the leader of the Reform UK party, declined to turn up to the town’s leisure centre to hear himself declared the winner and MP. It was quite the thing. The last high-profile winning candidate to fail to enjoy his moment of victory was Bobby Sands in 1981. The IRA man had his reasons: he was on hunger strike in a prison in Northern Ireland, and went on to die 26 days later.Instead Farage attended a gathering of his supporters at an airfield on the outskirts of Clacton billed by his party as “Farage Fest”. He told fans he would be damned if he was going to stand on a stage “having won a resounding victory” and “be demeaned and humiliated by nobodies”.But he also said Essex police had advised him of an “organised campaign to disrupt and degrade the result”. AReform UKspokesperson went further: “Essex police advised Nigel not to attend the count tonight due to a credible threat against him.”Not true, suggested the police. No such advice had been given. One of the shoutiest members of Farage’s anti-immigration party,Lee Anderson, had a slightly refreshed explanation by 8.10am when interviewed by the BBC. His leader had not wanted to disrespect those who had flocked to Farage Fest. He was, actually, if you will just listen just for a moment, a man of principle. “It was a great occasion that it is only right that he spends that time with his members, with his activists, with his supporters,” Anderson fumed.View image in fullscreenCount Binface and the other Clacton candidates await the byelection results.Photograph: Victoria Jones/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenElection workers sort through spoiled ballots at Clacton Leisure Centre after the voting closed.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesAll this left one intergalactic explorer, with his arms raised and a bin on his no doubt sweaty head, to take the starring role at Clacton leisure centre. The candidate who went by the name ofCount Binfacemade a declaration on social media: “I came first in the Clacton byelection! Of the candidates who bothered to turn up for the results.”Count Binface, for those who have not been following this latest fever dream of a moment in British politics, is theparody figure who declared himself the unity candidatewhen Farage triggered the byelection by resigning the seat back in July.Farage had explained his resignation at the time as a challenge to the establishment that would show them that the people did not want him scrutinised and investigated by the parliamentary authorities over anundeclared £5m gift from a crypto billionaireor any of the other financial scandals orbiting Reform UK.The other major political parties called his bluff. It was a stunt, they said, and none of them stood, leaving Count Binface, a familiar and striking figure at elections, whose real name is Jon Harvey, to harvest the anti-Farage vote. And he could reasonably be said to have done rather well, given that he won just 95 votes at therecent byelection in Makerfield, in Greater Manchester, where Andy Burnham, now the prime minister, won his parliamentary seat.Binface, who describes himself as an “independent space warrior” from the planet Sigma IX, won 26.93% of the ballot with 9,455 votes, leaving him second to Farage who secured 22,239 votes (63.34%). There was a healthy 44% turnout.Graphic showing vote share of Nigel Farage, Count Binface and next four candidatesPerhaps – and it is only a theory going round the leisure centre in Clacton – Farage was actually not at the count because he did not fancy the inevitable photograph of him next to his ludicrous competition?“That means I’ve got – against Nigel Farage – 10,000% more votes than I got against Andy Burnham,” Binface later said of his electoral tally. “What does that tell you? Well it tells you that Nigel, who said that he didn’t want to be humiliated, maybe has been. As for me, I’m over the moon – I’m over your moon, I’m over my moons – and what comes next, well we shall see. But you know what, we know this for a fact: over one in four people in this constituency would rather have Count Binface as their MP than the leader of Reform UK.”View image in fullscreenThe Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, arrives to vote in the Clacton byelection on Thursday.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesThat was the Binface take on an election estimated to have cost the public purse £250,000. Others were available. For the fired-up Anderson, who scolded the BBC presenter Justin Webb for being “very rude” for interrupting him on Friday morning, there was one clear reading of that night’s events.“[Nigel Farage is] celebrating a stunning victory in Clacton and the people have decided: they’ve stuck two fingers up to people like the BBC, the establishment, the blob, the whole of Westminster,” Anderson said. “There has been a constant witch-hunt by people in the media.“There’s been a witch-hunt against Nigel Farage and he said: ‘You know what? Enough’s enough. Meet me at the ballot box.’ And when it comes to a crunch, when he does throw the gauntlet down to the other political parties, what happens? They run away like the cowards they are. He challenges them at the ballot box and he wins.”So Nigel Farage has beaten a man in a bin. But he’s in deep trouble, and he knows it | Owen JonesRead moreNaturally enough, that wasn’t how the other main parties saw it. “All Farage can brag about this morning is beating a bloke with a bin on his head,” said a Conservative party spokesperson. “What he should do is answer the serious outstanding questions about why he hid his £5m from the public.”Bridget Phillipson, the chair of the governing Labour party, said: “There’s no hiding place now and Nigel Farage needs to answer to the public as to exactly what’s going on.”As election workers sorted through the voting ballots at the leisure centre in the early hours of Friday morning, one moment caught by photographers also tells a story.Across the 90cm long ballot paper containing all the names of the parody and independent candidates for the seat of Clacton (it was the longest ballot paper in UK electoral history), a disgruntled voter had made their mark: “What a disgraceful waste of money.”Three hours after Farage’s victory was declared, the suspended parliamentary standards investigation into the Reform UK leader over accusations he failed to declare gifts and donationshad resumed.

title: He Had It Coming review – this messy crime-comedy has all the subtlety of a mallet to the crotch | Television | The Guardian
description: It’s sporadically very funny, but the tone of this blackly comic murder-mystery is all over the place. It want to tackle big issues, but seems afraid of its own politics
Author: Sarah Dempster
Headline: It’s sporadically very funny, but the tone of this blackly comic murder-mystery is all over the place. It want to tackle big issues, but seems afraid of its own politics
Content: Barbara (Natasha Liu Bordizzo) and Elise (Lydia West).Photograph: BBC/2025 Jungle Entertainment Pty Ltd, Stan Entertainment Pty Ltd, Screen Australia/Lisa TomasettiView image in fullscreenBarbara (Natasha Liu Bordizzo) and Elise (Lydia West).Photograph: BBC/2025 Jungle Entertainment Pty Ltd, Stan Entertainment Pty Ltd, Screen Australia/Lisa TomasettiTV reviewTelevisionReviewHe Had It Coming review – this messy crime-comedy has all the subtlety of a mallet to the crotchIt’s sporadically very funny, but the tone of this blackly comic murder-mystery is all over the place. It wants to tackle big issues, but seems afraid of its own politicsSarah DempsterFri 14 Aug 2026 18.40 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 21.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘But I can’t get an F,” wails Elise (Lydia West) in the first episode of the Australian campus comedy He Had It Coming, shoulders slumping like soufflés as her tutor peers pityingly at her terrible paintings. “I’m here on a scholarship? I’m hereto be an artist?!”Alas, poor Elise. No amount of wounded upspeak can disguise the fact that she is an aspiring artist in much the same way a bag of flour is an aspiring pastry.Her “work”, bless it, consists of daubing clothes on to impressionist nudes – a “protest”, apparently, against the patriarchy and its preoccupation with “ancient bush”. Unctuous Professor Phoenix (Harry Greenwood) is unimpressed. “Hmm,” he sighs, pouting affectedly at Elise’s “feminist reimagining” of Manet’s Le Déjeuner sur l’herbe; the picnic’s enigmatic nude now sporting a pair of jeans and oversized novelty spectacles.Mon Dieu! The problem, explains Phoenix, slowly, is a lack of ambition. Feminist art isn’t foramateurs. “Be radical,” he smirks, as Elise quietly broils with rage. “Don’t settle formediocrity.”The nerve! “These men are holding us back,” she roars later at new pal Barbara (Natasha Liu Bordizzo), a prickly fashion influencer who is being slut-shamed by the campus jocks for having tipsily humped a stranger’s thigh at a party. “Yes,” agrees Barbara. “Let’s go vandalise something!” And so to the quadrant, where, in the dead of night, a mallet is applied to the genitals of the statue of the university’s hopelessly male namesake.“FTP!” tee-hees Elisedrunkenly. “That means Fuck The Patriarchy!”The next morning, however, brings trouble with a capital strewth. The body of an alpha-jock has been discovered, sans penis, at the foot of the malleted effigy. “Oh, that poor boy,” gasps Elise’s lovely mum. “And his doodle.” Others are less gracious. “Hell, yeah,” whoops a member of the university’s feminist collective. The victim was, it seems, a rapist and a bully. “He had it coming.” As, apparently, did the next victim – a men’s rights activist whose corpse has been similarly de-doodled. Who, we gasp, dunnit?View image in fullscreen‘The series is much too cartoonish to be in any way offensive.’Photograph: BBC/2025 Jungle Entertainment Pty Ltd, Stan Entertainment Pty Ltd, Screen Australia/Lisa TomasettiHe Had It Coming’s tagline is “Bad feminists. Worse detectives”, which makes it sound like an edgy Rosemary & Thyme reboot in which Pam Ferris and Felicity Kendal trample topsoil through a succession of crime scenes while shouting about Mooncups. But this Sydney-set series has loftier ambitions. What happens, it asks, when it is men, rather than women, who are forced to live with the constant threat of sexual intimidation and assault? Among the hot potatoes swept up in the ensuing eight episodes are misogyny, victim-blaming and social media’s complicity in harassment. And yet it quickly becomes clear that this black comedy is not entirely comfortable with the task it has set itself. It seems alarmed, somehow, by its own politics. Like poor Elise’s hopeless paintings, He Had It Coming appears to believe that simply pointing at something bad while going “nyer” is enough to convince onlookers that this constitutes a searing analysis of said bad thing. Which it most certainly does not. Instead, it spends most of its time avoiding the tricky stuff and focusing on its gleefully silly murder investigation, which entails Elise and Barbara galumphing around campus like pantomime horses while neighing quarter-witted theories into their neon-pink walkie-talkies. Consequently, the tone is all over the place. The second episode involves a man’s trousers falling down, a discussion about radical feminism, and a dog that can wink.All of which ensures that the bits that do attempt to make a serious point land with the finesse of a mallet to the genitals. Still, He Had It Coming is, sporadically, very funny. It’s also much too cartoonish to be in any way offensive.Instead, the series seems perpetually distracted by its own puppyish daftness, wagging its tail as it drags yet another mutilated corpse across the refectory floor. Here, everyone is an idiot.The women are as self-delusional and/or unpleasant as the men, and everyone, ultimately, is offered a chance at redemption.It’s a mess, but it’s an energetic mess and its heart – if not its doodle – is in the right place.Not an F, then. But a well-earned C.He Had It Coming aired on BBC Three and is available on iPlayer in the UK and on Stan in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’ve never done anything like this in my life’: Marina Abramović on making art with balloons | Marina Abramović | The Guardian
description: The artist’s latest swerve sees her creating an alien inflatable landscape for New York’s Balloon Museum
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The artist’s latest swerve sees her creating an alien inflatable landscape for New York’s Balloon Museum
Content: Marina Abramović with her new work Snowy/Windy/Spring on Planet Z at New York's Balloon Museum.Photograph: Courtesy of Balloon MuseumView image in fullscreenMarina Abramović with her new work Snowy/Windy/Spring on Planet Z at New York's Balloon Museum.Photograph: Courtesy of Balloon MuseumMarina AbramovićInterview‘I’ve never done anything like this in my life’: Marina Abramović on making art with balloonsDrew ZeibaThe artist’s latest swerve sees her creating an alien inflatable landscape for New York’s Balloon MuseumFri 14 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 10.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOversized inflatable blades of grass graze my face as I wind a path through the glowing white gallery space. Little papery squares of snow blow, some sticking to my hair. The path through the room curves so that only what is right in front of me is visible: initially, it seemed like I would reach the far side of the room in mere seconds but still my journey, magically, continues. I am at Snowy/Windy/Spring on Planet Z, the latest installation by the performance artistMarina Abramović. It opened earlier this month at New York’s newly openedBalloon Museum, which bills itself as “the first permanent home for inflatable art”.“I’ve never done anything like this in my life,” a smiling Abramović said, speaking on Zoom from her Manhattan apartment. “But if you give me an assignment then I’ll try to see what I can do with it.” As she began researching balloon art her first thought was that it was “so kitschy – basically for kids and games”. However, the more she contemplated the balloon, the more she saw its resonance with her own practice. “You put air in it, and at some point the air comes out. Or you pinch it and it disappears. The temporality of this is very close to what I’m doing: performance art.”Following the success of a 2023 pop-up in New York, the Rome-born Balloon Museum chose the city for its flagship. It rented and revamped the hollowed innards of Jean-Georges’s ill-fated Tin Building, replacing the chichi food hall with an inaugural exhibition titled Daydream, which presents 14 installations from artists including Turner Prize-winnerMartin Creed, Balloon Museum mainstay Karina Smigla-Bobinski and the commercial AV installation studio Onionlab.View image in fullscreenRendering of Abramović’s Snowy/Windy/Spring on Planet Z at the Balloon Museum.Photograph: Courtesy of Balloon MuseumThe installations I liked best were those that destabilized me: Swiss composer and artist Thom Kubli’s Black Hole Horizon showed oversized gramophone-style horns that bellowed resonant sounds and spat out soap bubbles. To experience the work of Boris Acket, a Dutch artist, I lay on a padded floor, hypnotized by a fabric wing that revealed and then obscured my reflection in the mirrored ceiling.Oh, the mirrors. As is the case at many of these immersive sites, the Balloon Museum is full of them, and it sometimes felt as if the museum was tailoring the installations to meet visitors’ desires to take selfies. (My tour guide insisted that all the mirrors were the artists’ own choices.)Isaac Mizrahi on stage, style and the legacy of Unzipped: ‘Fashion has no real spine any more’Read moreAt her institute in Greece, Abramović asks attenders to walk through the forest backward using a hand mirror to see, challenging people to disorient themselves and submit to slowness. But her installation at the Balloon Museum is among those that forgoes reflective surfaces. Before entering Planet Z, I donned wireless noise-canceling headphones through which the artist recited the names of exoplanets in a slow monotone. This personal soundscape added to the sense that I wasn’t only moving through an alien space, but that I was somehow outside of earthly time too. As Abramović said: “I’m giving you the work, but you have to give me time. This is the exchange. If you invest yourself into the work, then you have an experience.”When we speak she is dressed in red, a color that she’s said she wears to energize her. After many years of performing, the now-79-year-old thinks “it’s time for the public to have a direct experience” of the kind of presentness she’s advocated for throughout her career.“I really love the completely random propositions people give to me,” Abramović chuckles. In the past couple years, she’s applied her approach to products such as olive oil and a series of tinctures, plus a facial lotion. Since 2002, she’s created arty espresso cups with the coffee purveyor Illy. She’s appeared in avideoby Jay-Z inspired by her blockbuster MoMA retrospective The Artist Is Present. The Balloon Museum is just another challenge.View image in fullscreenAbramović with her ex partner Ulay at The Artist Is Present at MoMA, New York, 2010.Photograph: Patrick McMullan/Getty ImagesAbramović compares her taking on these projects to Renaissance artists who were commissioned by the clergy and aristocracy. Most of the time, the patrons wanted the depictions of the same conventional pieces: the Madonna and Child or the crucifixion of Christ. “How many of these crucifixions were made for just a few incredible masterpieces?” she asks. “I like it when a team gives you very strict rules, then you have to make a masterpiece out of them. It’s very difficult to do. Sometimes you completely fail, and failure is a very good thing. It’s about courage.”Roberto Fantauzzi, the Balloon Museum director, hopes that the institution will split the difference between kid-friendly “playgrounds” such as New York’s Museum of Ice Cream and traditional art institutions. “We are completely in the middle, and this is our strength,” he said, as we spoke beside the museum, overlooking the wide-eyed inflatable outdoor sculptures that have become its mascot (you can buy plushy keychain versions in the gift shop).‘Sade wasn’t particularly friendly’: the stories behind music’s most iconic portraits – in picturesRead more“I haven’t seen the final result yet,” Abramović told me when I asked her about her response to Planet Z.I knew she wouldn’t say if she felt she’d “failed” or succeeded; when we speak, she recounted a performance she knew in her stomach was a failure “right away”, but refused to say the name or year. It was “famous” and beloved, but the thought of it made her sick. “I don’t care what the public says or the critics say,” she said.The Balloon Museum is fun, sure. I smiled; at times I felt disarmed by the sense of wonder evoked by some pieces and the contemplative quiet offered by others. I don’t doubt that if I were a child, it might have opened me to possibilities of contemporary art. But I left and the levity dissipated; I was unchanged. The experience had been consumed.But what did I expect? As Abramović said in a droll tone when I asked her my final questions about the show: “What else do we need to talk about? I mean, it’s just the Balloon Museum.”Snowy/Windy/Spring on Planet Z is at the Balloon Museum, New YorkExplore more on these topicsMarina AbramovićMuseumsArtSculptureExhibitionsNew YorkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Belt and braces PM: what wearing suit braces says about Burnham | Andy Burnham | The Guardian
description: Mod fashion, nod to 80s excess or symbol of tradition? Andy Burnham’s wardrobe choice transcends class divisions
Author: Morwenna Ferrier
Headline: Mod fashion, nod to 80s excess or symbol of tradition? Andy Burnham’s wardrobe choice transcends class divisions
Content: Andy Burnham wears braces (just about visible) on his visit to Ilkeston in Derbyshire. ‘This stuff is simply what he wears,’ said one insider.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham wears braces (just about visible) on his visit to Ilkeston in Derbyshire. ‘This stuff is simply what he wears,’ said one insider.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersAndy BurnhamBelt and braces PM: what wearing suit braces says about BurnhamMod fashion, nod to 80s excess or symbol of tradition? Andy Burnham’s wardrobe choice transcends class divisionsMorwenna FerrierFri 14 Aug 2026 10.09 EDTFirst published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe sartorial evolution ofAndy Burnhamreached another milestone this week when the prime minister appeared at a photocall in Derbyshire wearing a pair of braces under his suit.Navy, slimline and button-on rather than clipped, they were barely visible while he posed for a photo in Ilkeston. It was only when he unbuttoned his suit jacket to embrace members of the public that they were on view.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, pose with a member of the public in Ilkeston, Derbyshire, on Tuesday.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersBurnham’s £595 navy suit was made by Oliver Brown, a traditional tailor with shops in London and Chester, and is the same style worn in his official portrait. Called the Eaton suit, it is made from a 100% merino wool cloth woven by Alfred Brown in Yorkshire, and is made to measure. A spokesperson for the tailor said that while the suit was definitely theirs, the braces were not.If the trousers didn’t fit, wearing a belt would have been out of the question as they don’t have belt loops. And yet, says Chloe Chapin, a fashion historian and author of the forthcoming bookSuitable: The Sartorial Revolution and the Fashioning of Modern Men, “the trousers do have side fasteners, so he doesn’t really need braces at all, at least functionally”.View image in fullscreenGary Cooper in the 1932 film A Farewell to Arms.Photograph: ER Richee/Paramount/Kobal/ ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMichael Douglas wears braces in the 1987 film Wall Street.Photograph: Sunset Boulevard/GettyA political insider who has worked on Burnham’s campaigns for the last two years told the Guardian: “Andy is not the teleprompter type of politician. This stuff is simply what he wears.” The former Greater Manchester mayor and his team think about his clothing and context, though, and it certainly isn’t an afterthought. “His clothes are trying to strike a balance between professional and capable politician – but also let people know that he’s different to other politicians,” the source says. As the first TikTok PM, no one understands this better than Burnham. “The optics are not divorced from the reality.”Braces originated in France in the 1700s as strips of fabric that were buttoned to a waistband. They quickly spread across Europe, like many French trends, though it wasn’t until 1820 that Albert Thurston started making the leather versions we know today. Back then, they were considered undergarments and to show them was inappropriate.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSkinhead teenagers pose in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire, in June 1970.Photograph: Mirrorpix/GettyNo apologies, no freebies: the man who makes Andy Burnham’s jackets on how to weather a stormRead moreBraces had a resurgence in the UK during the 1960s and 70s, worn by mods and skinheads as a form of subversion. The pinnacle of this probably occurred in the 80s, when they became as popular on Wall Street financiers as they did on punks. Wearing this “underwear as outerwear intentionally was a bit like Madonna wearing her Jean Paul Gaultier cone bra, a real statement”, says Chapin. If the 60s version represented working-class pride and anti-establishment rebellion, the 80s “was about a heightening of excess. They transcended class and in an age of abundance showed just how subversive fashion could be.”While Burnham has always been transparent about his journey from Westminster yes-man to “king of the north”, particularly through his wardrobe, could the braces signal a move to formality? In many ways they are the ultimate symbol of tradition, especially in politics, where Winston Churchill and Michael Portillo were fans.It’s more about context, says Chapin. Just as aLabourpolitician will wear red if they want to convey strength, grey or purple if they want to be bipartisan, or blue if they’re talking to Tory voters, if something can be posh and working class at the same time, this is precisely the sort of ambiguity a politician might want to exploit if they’re trying to connect with the public.If nothing else, Burnham wearing braces points towards fashion’s core tension – is clothing about function or aesthetics? Much like his approach to politics, the answer is probably both.Explore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamLabourMen's fashionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: As online dating goes into ‘salvage mode’, can AI solve all its problems? | Online dating | The Guardian
description: Dating apps such as Bumble forced to adapt as ‘swipe fatigue’ grows
Author: Amelia Hill
Headline: Dating apps such as Bumble forced to adapt as ‘swipe fatigue’ grows
Content: Bumble has abandoned its proposition that women make the first move, and is about to ditch the swipe. Photo posed by modelPhotograph: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBumble has abandoned its proposition that women make the first move, and is about to ditch the swipe. Photo posed by modelPhotograph: Getty ImagesOnline datingAs online dating goes into ‘salvage mode’, can AI solve all its problems?Dating apps such as Bumble forced to adapt as ‘swipe fatigue’ growsAmelia HillFri 14 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 12.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBumble was supposed to be different. When it launched in 2014, it offered women a simple proposition: if you matched with a man, you had to make the first move. The rule was meant to make online dating safer and less intimidating, while giving women control over who got to speak first.This week, Bumble abandoned it.The change follows the introduction of Opening Moves, which had already softened the original rule, and comes as Bumble prepares to abandon another defining feature: the swipe.The company says it is responding to changing user behaviour and wants to encourage more meaningful connections.But there is another way of reading the changes.Bumble was created to fix what many saw as Tinder’s chaotic and aggressive hookup culture by shifting the power dynamic entirely to women. Now it is dismantling those features. And it is not alone. Across the dating-app industry, the swipe-and-match model that transformed how people met is being quietly reworked while companies race to put artificial intelligence at the centre of whatever comes next.“Bumble is in salvage mode,” says Luke Brunning, a philosopher who studies the ethics of technology and relationships. “They’ve already reorganised, restructured and cut jobs in response to declining revenue. This risky, standout pivot suggests they’re wondering how, despite all that, to keep going.”The number of Bumble’s paying users fell sharply over the past year and its share price has been under sustained pressure. The company cut about 30% of its workforce this year.“It’s going to be fascinating to see whether they can weather it,” Brunning says. “But they’re not alone: a lot of the major players are also in salvage mode, trying to figure out how to position themselves in a market that is increasingly fed up with them.”Brunning’s research shows dating apps are now often used grudgingly, because people feel that they are necessary, rather than with the excitement that accompanied their rise.The online dating industry, estimated to be worth almost £10bn globally, is keenly aware of this. Its solution? To go full AI.Grindr – seen as a testbed for the wider industry – is transitioning into an “AI-first” platform. Tinder is testing Chemistry, an AI-powered system intended to reduce “swipe fatigue”. Bumble has been developing an AI matchmaking assistant called Bee.Other startups are dispensing with swiping altogether. London-based Fate describes itself as an “agentic AI dating app”: instead of browsing profiles, users are interviewed by an AI about what they want from relationships to find similarities with potential partners.So why aren’t we talking about being on the brink of a brave new world of dating apps, where AI will successfully sift the candidates to find our one true love? Why, instead, is the debate about whether the apps will even survive?Adam Peacock, a researcher of technology and intimacy, thinks the issue is that the industry is misreading what people are objecting to.“There’s a kind of emerging cultural backlash against allowing AI into our intimate lives as well as the additional concern that someone you’re talking to on these apps, is actually filtering the whole conversation through an AI concierge,” he says.Peacock says gen Z in particular are concerned as to whether dating apps are even being designed to make good connections between users but are, instead, opaquely tweaked to monetise the time users spend on the site. That, in a cynical twist, the apps are deliberately profiting from keeping people lonely.“The dating industry has turned intimacy into an enormous source of data,” Peacock says. “Dating apps can know where people live, what they look like, who they are attracted to, what they say to potential partners and, increasingly, how they behave.”Elsa Kugelberg, a philosopher who researches gender and relationships, says online dating has become too embedded in modern life to fail. But the first generation of dating apps – the era of the profile, the swipe, the match and the message – may be reaching its end.Peacock thinks the apps may evolve into something broader: “More of a social media, lifestyle product than a dedicated dating app.”But the question is whether any iteration of dating app will make the experience better, or whether the extra layers of AI will simply function as a temporary facade on an exhausted model.Brunning believes AI on dating apps doesn’t have to be like this. “There can be ways of trying to do digital better, that doesn’t involve giving people AI tools to talk to each other with,” he says.Better moderation, clearer policies, better ways of presenting yourself and more control over how the environment works could all improve online dating without handing more of it to machines, he says.The critical point is this, he says: “You can’t just take a product that’s out of favour, put AI on top of it and say: ‘OK, now we have a product that works.’”Explore more on these topicsOnline datingDatingAppsInternet safetyAI (artificial intelligence)featuresShareReuse this content

title: Why does everything feel meh? We're in the era of joyless decadence – Stateside with Kai and Carter | Society | The Guardian
description: Hosts Kai Wright and Carter Sherman wrestle with why so many of us feel joyless in a time when we have access to so much with academics Michèle Mendelssohn and Charlie Tyson, who argue that we are living in an era of decadence without pleasure.
Author: Kai Wright
Headline: Hosts Kai Wright and Carter Sherman wrestle with why so many of us feel joyless in a time when we have access to so much with academics Michèle Mendelssohn and Charlie Tyson, who argue that we are living in an era of decadence without pleasure.
Content: 36:43Stateside with Kai and CarterSocietyWhy does everything feel meh? We're in the era of joyless decadence – Stateside with Kai and CarterWe should, in theory, be happy. Thanks to our phones, we can do practically anything – listen to our favorite bands' entire discographies, have extravagant meals delivered to our door, travel the world through an endless scroll. So why do so many of these experiences feel so joyless? Why do so many of us feel so empty all the time? HostsKai WrightandCarter Shermanwrestle with these questions with academicsMichèle MendelssohnandCharlie Tyson, who argue that we are living in an era of decadence without pleasure. While decadence always arises in times of extreme inequality, they say that tools like AI and GLP-1s reveal how we've lost our ability to truly enjoy things – and, ironically, reclaiming decadence may help us finally have fun.Michèle Mendelssohn and Charlie Tyson’s Guardian essay:Why does everything feel joyless? title: Donald Trump can’t beat Iran and Nigel Farage can only beat a bin. When it counts, these populists are just losers | Jonathan Freedland | The Guardian
description: The pattern in the US and Britain is clear. They serve up stunt after stunt to mask incompetence and the betrayal of all those who trusted them, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Author: Jonathan Freedland
Headline: The pattern in the US and Britain is clear. They serve up stunt after stunt to mask incompetence and the betrayal of all those who trusted them, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Content: Nigel Farage at CPAC in London, July 2026, and Donald Trump at CPAC in Maryland, February 2025.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNigel Farage at CPAC in London, July 2026, and Donald Trump at CPAC in Maryland, February 2025.Composite: Getty ImagesOpinionDonald TrumpDonald Trump can’t beat Iran and Nigel Farage can only beat a bin. When it counts, these populists are just losersJonathan FreedlandThe pattern in the US and Britain is clear. They serve up stunt after stunt to mask incompetence and the betrayal of all those who trusted themFri 14 Aug 2026 12.03 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 12.59 EDTShareIt’s a shame Nigel Farageducked the announcementof his victory in the Clacton byelection, which confirmed his return as MP for the seat he had needlessly resigned from just a few weeks earlier. You’d have thought he would have loved it. It was the culmination of a stunt, an exercise in politics as performance. It was a display animated by – and seeking to inflame – grievance, a million miles away from the hard, grinding work of tackling the problems that underlie those grievances. It was an attempt to deflect scrutiny, distract attention and evade responsibility. It was, in other words, everything nationalist populists like him excel at. Indeed, the only thing.Reform UK said Farage stayed away because Essex police had warned of a “credible threat” to his security, a claim swiftly denied by Essex police. (Add a flexible approach to the truth to that list of nationalist populists’ talents.) Still, it was a slightly odd claim to make. Recall Farage’s favoured explanation – there are others – for the undeclared £5m gift he received from the Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne, which prompted the very parliamentary investigation that so riled the Reform leader he felt compelled to quit his seat and seek a preemptive not guilty verdict from the people of Clacton: namely, that he needed the money to pay for private, enhanced security. It seems £5m was not quite enough to ensure the lucky recipient would be safe standing next to a man dressed as a bin.Unless, maybe, security was not the whole story. Farage also said he skipped the count because he didn’t want to be “demeaned and humiliated by nobodies”. Quite right. If Nigel Farage is to be demeaned and humiliated, it should be by people of standing. As it happens, he may get his wish. Now that he’s an MP again, the probe into the multiple financial questions that surround him, including over the undeclared support he received from the convicted fraudster George Cottrell,has resumed. A finding against him could necessitate yet another byelection, except this time the major parties will not repeat their boycott and he will have to do battle with opponents even more formidable than an aristocratic trash can.Naturally, Farage regards the likes of Count Binface and Baron von Thunderclap as beneath him, perhaps because it would be painful to admit the crucial thing they all have in common. To understand what that is, look no further than the man who is both Farage’s hero and the exemplar of nationalist populism.Ten years ago, less than five months after the Brexit referendum that represents Farage’s greatest triumph, Donald Trump rode a similar wave of US discontent with the status quo and did it in a similar way – by railing against an ill-defined establishment that had ruined everything. A vote for him would make it all better because, as Trump put it: “I alone can fix it.” In 2024, he was elected once again, on a similar promise.That victory proved Trump’s mastery of a certain strain of politics. His gift for seizing public attention, for channelling a society’s collective anxieties and for persuading people that a simple remedy is at hand, is unrivalled. While Farage plays the same tunes, Trump is the virtuoso.And yet, look at what happens once the carnival of the campaign is over and the governing begins. Trump’s record is disastrous. He was elected to tackle inflation, which he claimed was out of control under Joe Biden, butinflation is higher nowthan it was in November 2024, when he defeated his predecessor.Petrol prices, the indicator Trump repeatedly invoked on the stump in 2024, have leapt up. This, more than any other single factor, helps explain whyTrump’s approval ratingshave cratered, falling to just 34%.And yet Trump, whose appeal centred on his persona as a successful businessman – a persona that held, despite a career of failure and serial bankruptcy – is doing almost nothing to improve the economic fortunes of those who voted for him. I don’t mean that he’s trying to pull various policy levers and they’re not working. I mean he’s not trying. As Jonathan Swan, co-author of Regime Change, an eye-popping account of the first 15 months of this second Trump term,told me for the Politics Weekly Americapodcast: “He’s bored by economic policy.”Of course, those petrol prices did not rise all by themselves. What drove up the price of oil was the decision that seems set to define this presidency: the war on Iran that began on 28 February. It has proved a calamity. It has failed to achieve any of the admittedly shifting goals Trump declared for it: there has been no regime change in Tehran; Iran’s nuclear threat remains unchecked, while its nuclear ambition is now surely greater, if only to deter a repeat of that US-Israeli attack. And it has barely set back Iran’s conventional capability, judging by the regime’s continuing ability to strike its neighbours. As if all that were not bad enough, Trump has succeeded in making the Iranians stronger than they were on 27 February, by handing them an economic weapon of mass disruption, a chokehold on the global economy in the form of their control of thestrait of Hormuz.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMillions of US tax dollars sent to rightwing European thinktanks. Did any Trump supporters vote for that? | Arwa MahdawiRead moreTrump can do the performance, claiming to have “obliterated” the enemy one moment or to have made a breakthrough peace deal the next – but performance is all it is. While the Iranian missiles keep coming, the US military is fast running out of the munitions it needs either to intercept or hit back. Trump’s top general warned him of this danger from the start, but Trumpwaved away those objections, convinced that the war would be over quickly. Trump’s gut told him that Iran would go the way of Venezuela, that it would be fast and easy. His gut was wrong.It keeps happening the same way. Trump will announce an agreement with Iran or between Hamas and Israel, only for it rapidly to become clear thatno deal has been done. Trump lacks the patience for the long, painstaking, detailed work such diplomacy requires. He wants the sugar-rush of a social-media post or a headline. Put simply, he is a maestro of politics as it is now conducted, but he is useless at governing.In this, the nationalist populists who take their lead from Trump are no different. They are good at raging at how things are, but incapable of making them better. They can articulate resentment and exploit grievance, but they cannot cure the ills that fuel that unhappiness. This, ultimately, is what unites Farage with Trump and indeed with those 33 “nobodies” who fought the byelection in Clacton. They are all protest candidates. It’s just that some of them get elected.Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: So Nigel Farage has beaten a man in a bin. But he’s in deep trouble, and he knows it | Owen Jones | The Guardian
description: The Reform leader claims vindication from the people, and it’s too early to write him off. But the problems he now faces may be more than he can bear, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Author: Owen Jones
Headline: The Reform leader claims vindication from the people, and it’s too early to write him off. But the problems he now faces may be more than he can bear, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Content: Count Binface celebrates his second-place finish at the Clacton byelection count, 14 August 2026.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenCount Binface celebrates his second-place finish at the Clacton byelection count, 14 August 2026.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAOpinionClacton byelection August 2026So Nigel Farage has beaten a man in a bin. But he’s in deep trouble, and he knows itOwen JonesThe Reform leader claims vindication from the people, and it’s too early to write him off. But the problems he now faces may be more than he can bearFri 14 Aug 2026 06.29 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 09.56 EDTShareNigel Farage is a rattled, embattled politician. Perhaps he feels buoyed up by securing slightly more votes in a byelection boycotted by all the main parties than he did in the general election two years ago. That was despite 10,000 fewer people turning out to vote. But there was never any question that he was going to win a byelection he called purely to deflect scrutiny of his undeclared £5m personal gift from a Thai-based crypto-billionaire and donations from a convicted fraudster.Farage chose Clacton as his parliamentary launchpad for a reason. It was here that his previous outfit, Ukip, secured its breakthrough in the byelection of 2014. It is one of the most pro-leave seats in Britain, whileElectoral Calculusestimates that almost no other constituency is this rightwing.When I visited, I found no shortage of voters who were defiant about Farage’s scandals. They saw no problem with a politician being showered with dosh by a foreign-based billionaire, arguing that Farage deserved it because he was a “nice man” and even suggesting he might invest it locally. They bought the narrative that the establishment was out to get their man, as if a millionaire ex-City broker who is a sometime friend of the US president is some plucky outsider.They are representative of about a fifth of the country who laud Farage as themainstream politician most hostile to immigration, and who are contemptuous of a Conservative party that failed even on its own terms in office. What should concern Farage, however, is thatmost Britons are more opposed to him than ever, and are determined to block him from power. That majority delivered victory to the Greens in February’s Gorton and Denton byelection, and to Andy Burnham in June’s Makerfield byelection.That the parody candidate Count Binface won more than a quarter of the vote in this ultra-rightwing heartland is a warning in itself. Yes, this “independent space warrior” secured plenty of media attention, but he had precious little ground game – that is, an army of volunteers to get out the vote. Many voters I spoke to hadn’t even heard of him. It seems plausible that some of those who made Count Binface the most successful joke candidate in history had previously voted not justLabour, Lib Dem or Green, but Conservative too.Farage refused to attend the official declaration of this election he chose to call. That suggests not just petulance and contempt for his own voters, but the insecurities of a jittery man.He claims Essex police had told himabout an “organised campaign to disrupt and degrade the result”, but the local force said there had been no “incidents or issues” related to the byelection and that attendance was up to candidates. And did Farage not claim that his £5m personal gift was needed to pay for his security?The explanation is probably more mundane. Being mocked on stage by a man in a bin does not exactly provide the optics of a heroic struggle against the establishment.What next for the Farage show? If he thought the byelection was an effective ruse to deflect from his money issues, reality caught up with him quickly. The parliamentary watchdog has nowreopened its investigationinto Farage’s gift and donations, and another byelection may be forced if there is an adverse ruling.But it is not just finances that have plunged Reform UK into crisis.Farage’s proud association with Donald Trump– toxic even to most Reform voters – has become an ever greater drag. Absorbing so many former Conservatives was surely another big error. The last government was bitterly rejected for a reason, not least by Farage’s own supporters, and filling Reform’s ranks with its former leading lights hardly helped the party’s anti-establishment pretences.And then there is the pivot to ever moretoxic rightwing politics, perhaps partly driven by pressure from the even further right Restore Britain, founded by the former Reform MP Rupert Lowe. Farage now talks of “anti-white discrimination” – rhetoric once confined to the ugliest reaches of the far right. His talk of “pure cold rage” after the conviction of Henry Nowak’s murder – just hours before riots over it – rightly disturbed many.Then there’s Zia Yusuf, his home affairs spokesperson, whose increasingly aggressive social media posts speak to Reform’s authoritarian underbelly. Yusuf repeatedly describes his opponents as “traitors” – his latest target was the Tory former defence secretary Ben Wallace – and threatens that an unspecific “reckoning is coming”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAll of this alarms most Britons, who have concluded that Reform must be kept from power and will vote tactically if needs be. Yet this is of scant comfort to the absurdly underscrutinised Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, because Reform’s hardened core shows no interest in returning to her camp. Rightwing Britain, then, is divided.It would be a mistake to write Farage off, however. We are in the midst of theAndy Burnhambounce. Voters are relieved to be rid of Keir Starmer, and for now Labour is tempting back some progressive voters who defected to the Greens. But Burnham has yet to be forced into many big decisions. Britain’s economic plight, its crisis-stricken public services and Burnham’s slowness to hike taxes on the booming rich could all come to a head in October’s budget. Disillusionment could swell, and Reform could benefit – unless, of course, Burnham calls a snap election first.But you have to ask whether Farage’s heart is really in this. Reports that he received his £5m gift after saying he would need“a million a year”to serve as an MP are telling. Here is a man who appears to enjoy the high life and feel parliamentary politics damages his earning potential. He seems increasingly riled by the sort of scrutiny he has long managed to avoid. Perhaps, after a pointless triumph over a bin, he may simply decide he has had enough.Owen Jones is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsClacton byelection August 2026OpinionNigel FarageByelectionsReform UKRestore BritainAndy BurnhamLabourcommentShareReuse this content
