title: How can we talk about this extreme weather now that it’s a battleground in the culture wars? | Andy Beckett | The Guardian
description: Weather forecasts once gave Britons something safe to chat about. Not any more, and that’s a problem for the experts – indeed, for all of us, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Author: Andy Beckett
Headline: Weather forecasts once gave Britons something safe to chat about. Not any more, and that’s a problem for the experts – indeed, for all of us, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Content: Illustration: Nate Kitch/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Nate Kitch/The GuardianOpinionExtreme weatherHow can we talk about this extreme weather now that it’s a battleground in the culture wars?Andy BeckettWeather forecasts once gave Britons something safe to chat about. Not any more, and that’s a problem for the experts – indeed, for all of usFri 14 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 12.59 EDTShareIn this fragmented but supposedly mild country, watching and talking about the weather forecast is meant to be a reassuring, unifying activity. Collectively, we have created and maintained a national climate narrative of small disappointments and pleasures.The first weather forecaster to appear on British TV, George Cowling, made his debut on the BBC in January 1954, predicting that “tomorrow would be rather windy”, but “a good day to hang out the washing”. For most of the 72 years since, such brief, carefully calibrated broadcasts have provided people from Aberdeen to Penzance with practical information, small talk and minor grumbles about essentially the same situation: living in a country where the weather is constantly changing, in a paradoxically unchanging way.Yet like the traditional British climate, that common weather culture may now be evaporating. “Met Office considers issuing red ‘extreme heat warning’ across Britain while nation enjoys ‘incredible summer’,”said the headlineabove the forecast on the GB News website on Monday, caught between terror and delight at the latest heatwave. As the climate crisis has affected this country in more and more unmistakable but uneven ways, TV weather forecasters have increasingly struggled to find the right language to describe this transformation’s daily consequences. Their struggle influences and exemplifies that of many Britons to understand, and work out what we think about, the apparent end of the weather patterns we expected to shape our whole lives.Across all the British TV broadcasters, sometimes within the same bulletin, or even the same sentence, weather forecasters now present sunshine as welcome and oppressive; high temperatures as miraculous and unbearable; rain as an inconvenience and desperately needed; cloud cover as depressing and a relief. Tanned forecasters in sundresses, emphasising the positives for domestic holidaymakers of another record-breaking summer, alternate with grim-faced forecasters suggesting we are experiencing a weather apocalypse.Meanwhile, the wildly differing effects of the climate crisis on different areas, and from one season to another, are further fracturing Britain’s weather conversation into a babble of separate, sometimes conflicting discourses. This year, parts of the country have experienced such contrasting summers –wetter than usual in western Scotland, desert-like in southern England – that we can no longer say they share broadly the same northern European climate, as had been assumed for centuries. In an era of separatism and nationalism, another major binding element of the UK may be falling away.Beneath the relatively placid surface of our previous weather culture, there were always some tensions and contradictions. In a 2025 academic paper,British Heatwave Discourse (1985–2023): from Ice Cream to Armageddon?, Thijs van Dooremalen and Philip Smith analysed articles about heatwaves in the national press. They found that until 2000 positive and negative coverage coexisted in roughly equal quantities, “often in the same newspaper”. From 2000 to 2014, the balance shifted slowly towards the negative, as the climate crisis became a mainstream worry. Yet only from 2015 did an “Apocalyptic genre” of heatwave articles begin to become dominant; and a “Romantic genre” of celebratory coverage remains. In a country where many people still spend much of the year feeling cold, the idea of hot weather as a liberation is likely to linger, for some, for decades to come.For other Britons, heatwaves have become political flashpoints, their causes to be furiously contested, their existence even denied. During the record heat of 2022, “weather forecasters faced unprecedented levels of trolling”,the BBC reported, including “hundreds of abusive tweets or emails questioning their reports and telling them to ‘get a grip’… ‘it’s just summer’”. Some of these climate crisis deniers described advice on how to stay cool as “pandering to the ‘woke brigade’”, and accused the BBC and Met Office of “scaremongering” to help the then Conservative government impose unneeded green policies.This summer, some of these conspiratorial arguments have re-emerged. But with the Tories having in effect turned against net zero, joined by Reform UK, Restore Britain and most of the rightwing media, disagreeing with weather forecasters who express alarm about our changing climate has become more mainstream. Discussing the weather is no longer just small talk, but also a battlefield in the culture wars.No wonder forecasters often sound unsure or extremely cautious about what tone to adopt on air. In 2023, the BBC’s Tomasz Schafernaker gave a very carefulinterview to the Big Issue. “While our language remains largely the same,” he said, “we have adapted it to include references to climate change. We must be mindful that prolonged periods of sun and heat are not always good news … However, there are often areas in the UK where the weather is much more comfortable, [so] highlighting that it’s not ‘all bad’ is important. It’s a balance that we assess on a daily basis.”Yet three years on, his broadcasts have become less neutral. “The savage summer continues across Europe,” he said on the BBC weather website last Thursday afternoon. “It’s been excruciatingly hot …” On BBC One last Sunday evening, while giving this week’s UK forecast, he kept making gestures of helplessness and disbelief. It was like a weather bulletin from a dystopian drama.Such interventions no longer seem melodramatic. “The climate of the 20th century has now gone,” says Mike Kendon, a Met Office scientist and co-author ofState of the UK Climate in 2025, published last month. So far, this year’s weather has been more extreme. Even more than the heat, summer drought and winter floods, its key feature has been the weather getting stuck in one state for months – a characteristic of harsh continental climates, rather than the changeable one around which our society has been built. So it’s possible that next summer will feature relentless rain, not drought, and that other seasons will continue to stall as well, damaging the economy, everyday life and public health.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBritons are world famous for their weather stoicism. But this stoicism has been created by centuries of relatively minor weather discomforts and disasters. How the forecasters, and the rest of us, will react as the climate crisis intensifies – in our private behaviours and assumptions as well as our public lives – is a question we are only in the early stages of answering.Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsExtreme weatherOpinionExtreme heatUK weatherClimate scienceClimate crisisDroughtFloodingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Karoline Leavitt leaves behind a legacy of lies. What’s next for the Trump aide? | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: The press secretary’s communication style made her eminently qualified for a role in this administration
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: The press secretary’s communication style made her eminently qualified for a role in this administration
Content: ‘As well as her flair for numbers, Leavitt will also be remembered as a consummate professional who remained dignified under pressure.’Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APView image in fullscreen‘As well as her flair for numbers, Leavitt will also be remembered as a consummate professional who remained dignified under pressure.’Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APOpinionTrump administrationKaroline Leavitt leaves behind a legacy of lies. What’s next for the Trump aide?Arwa MahdawiThe press secretary’s communication style made her eminently qualified for a role in this administrationFri 14 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 12.30 EDTShareKaroline Leavitt, 28, is leaving her demanding job as Donald Trump’s press secretaryto spend more timewith her two young children and her 60-year-old husband. According to apostby Trump On Truth Social, Leavitt will be departing her role at the end of the month and will serve as one of Trump’s “top outside advisors”.In other words: the official version of events is that Leavitt is resigning on her own terms for family reasons and not because Trump’s approval ratings are atrecord lowsand she’s a rat fleeing a sinking ship.But is the official version of events the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth? Don’t bother asking Leavitt – I’m not sure she knows much about the T-word. She may have been the youngest White House press secretary in history, but there’s no denying her communication style made her eminently qualified for a role in theTrump administration. I won’t muck about with euphemisms such asmisrepresentedorstated without evidenceormade false claims.Leavitt’s legacy in government was attacking Trump’s enemies and spouting lie after lie after lie.Being a lowly writer means I am held to far higher standards about what I can say than the departing press secretary or her boss, the president of the United States. Unlike Leavitt or Trump, I actually have to provide facts and evidence to back up my assertions. So here we go: here are a few fun facts about Leavitt’s tenure in public office.Karoline Leavitt: six key takeaways from 20 months as Trump’s press secretaryRead moreFirst, there’s her role in promoting lies about the economy. One of the most significant economic policies of Trump’s second term has been his global tariffs, which were initially extended even to volcanic islands inhabitedonly by penguins. During a press briefing in March 2025, Leavitttoldreporters that tariffs were a “tax cut for the American people”. Economists havesaidthis is nonsense. “Economists don’t agree on much, but we agree tariffs are taxes on consumers,” Tara Sinclair, a George Washington University economist told the fact-checking website Politifact. The non-partisanTax Foundationhas also run the numbers and said that in 2025, the Trump tariffs “amounted to an average tax increase of $1,000” per US household.But what’s $1,000, eh? It’s nothing to Trump, who made astaggering $2.2bnduring the first year of his second term in various questionable ways. One imagines it’s also not much to Leavitt, who earns just under $200,000 in her role and whose husband, Nicholas Riccio, manages what has beendescribed asa multimillion-dollar real estate business.And if you feel aggrieved about tariffs increasing the already sky-high cost of living, according to Leavitt, you should just work harder (or marry a real estate tycoon). “Some of these kids, and I call them kids because they are in their 20s and have never had real jobs, and they’re complaining things are expensive,” Fox News’Jesse Watters told Leavittlast month during a conversation about young Democratic party voters. “Yes, things are expensive when you don’t have a real job.” Leavitt agreed, adding that her generation had been raised with “silver spoons in their mouths, just getting everything handed to them”. That was un-American, she suggested, because this country “was built on meritocracy and hard work, pulling up your sleeves, pulling yourself up from your bootstraps”.It’s not just tariffs where Leavitt’s math seems to be off. In January 2025, the press secretary justified Trump’s order to freeze federal funding to the US Agency for International Development (USAID) by claiming it was wasting money.“[T]here was about to be 50m taxpayer dollars that went out the door to fund condoms in Gaza,”Leavittsaid. “That is a preposterous waste of taxpayer money. So that’s what this pause is focused on: being good stewards of tax dollars.”24:30Trump’s great plane escape | Politics Weekly AmericaTo be very clear: that condom claim was a lie. Documents shows that no condoms were sent anywhere in the Middle East, let alone to a place undergoing what many experts have termed a genocide. The US did, however, provide billions of taxpayer dollars to helpIsrael destroy Gaza, which has arguablyreducedbirths a lot faster than condoms would have. The dismantling of USAID, justified by Leavitt, has also increasedpregnancy complicationsand maternal death in poor countries. Astudy published in the Lancetjournal last year estimated that US funding cuts could result in more than 14 million deaths, including more than 4.5 million children under age five, by 2030. I guess, if you’re Leavitt, being “good stewards of tax dollars” means contributing to mass death and immiseration. Money well spent!As well as her flair for numbers, Leavitt will also be remembered as a consummate professional who remained dignified under pressure. Last October, for example, SV Dáte, Huffington Post’s senior White House correspondent,asked Leavittvia text message who had suggested Budapest for a meeting between Trump and Vladimir Putin to discuss Ukraine. Herresponse? “Your mom did.” When Dáte then asked if Leavitt thought that was funny, shereplied: “It’s funny to me that you actually consider yourself a journal [sic]. You are a far left hack who nobody takes seriously, including your colleagues in the media, they just don’t tell you that to your face. Stop texting me your disingenuous, biased, and bullshit questions.”That was a brief look at Leavitt’s past. What’s in store for her future? Despite her comments about her family, don’t expect her to go full tradwife. None of the ambitious women advancing the Trump administration’s anti-woman agenda want to devote their own lives to the domestic drudgery they extoll for others. They’ve got less privileged women to do the childcare and the cooking and the cleaning for them. No, rather than being a tradwife, one imagines Leavitt might end up with a nice little gig on Fox News orBari Weiss’s CBS. Or perhaps, like Sean Spicer, her predecessor under Trump 1.0, she might go the reality TV route and regale us all onDancing With the Stars. No doubt there will also be a “tell-all” book in her future in which, depending on which way the political winds are blowing, she’ll tell us all the things she thinks will rehabilitate her reputation.Will Trump’s next press secretary be a better liar than the first five?Read moreAnd, of course, for now there’s her new role as an “outside advisor”. I can’t tell you exactly what that entails but I can tell you that, going forward, communications with Trump and his outside advisers can apparently beconsidered privileged. On Monday, after Todd Blanche was sworn in as attorney general, the justice department’s office of legal counsel issued a 21-page opinion about the president’s “executive privilege” which protects communication between Trump and advisers whodon’t work for his administration. This makes a future Democrat-led investigation into the Trump administration a lot harder as his advisers – who will now include Leavitt – will not be able to be comprehensively questioned by Congress. Exactly the sort of move you’d expect from a president that Leavitt has called the “most transparent” in history.Best of luck, then, to Leavitt in her future endeavors. I’m sure she’ll roll up her designer sleeves, pull herself up by her bootstraps and find a way to make huge amounts of money. And best of luck to all of us. If there’s one thing that you can be sure about when it comes to the revolving door that isthe White House, it’s that no matter how bad the person leaving is, the replacement is always worse.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationOpinionUS politicsRepublicanscommentShareReuse this content

title: Digested week: Humid New York or London’s oven-blast heat? Tough one to call | Emma Brockes | The Guardian
description: Plus, heartbreakingly brilliant Cats: the Jellicle Ball, summer reads and Taylor Swift’s low-key wedding
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: Plus, heartbreakingly brilliant Cats: the Jellicle Ball, summer reads and Taylor Swift’s low-key wedding
Content: A boy cools off during a heatwave in New York City.Photograph: Jordan Tovin/ReutersView image in fullscreenA boy cools off during a heatwave in New York City.Photograph: Jordan Tovin/ReutersDigested weekNew YorkDigested week: Humid New York or London’s oven-blast heat? Tough one to callEmma BrockesPlus, heartbreakingly brilliant Cats: the Jellicle Ball, summer reads and Taylor Swift’s low-key weddingFri 14 Aug 2026 11.01 EDTFirst published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 07.44 EDTShareMondayI’ve been inNew Yorkfor two weeks, where the unthinkable has happened. Even for a city accustomed to extremes, it is so hot, so humid, so reminiscent of Mobile in Alabama, or Mumbai that, all over New York, people have been forced to break persona to talk about the weather. “Was it always like this?” (No.) “Can you believe this?” (No.) “Are you having a stroke?” (Possibly.)Received wisdom has it that heatwaves in Britain and Europe are worse than in the US because we don’t have air conditioning, but as I write this, on my first day back in heatwave London, it’s a tough one to call.If the south ofEnglandfeels like Riyadh, with its oven-blast of dry heat, New York comes with total humidity. It is so dense, so impenetrable, so vastly more furnace-like than any previous summer that it makes you angry just walking down the street.Air conditioning takes the edge off, but it’s like trying to disguise medicine with a mouthful of Coke; it only goes so far. Meanwhile, the sweat pours down your back and the sky burns white.New Yorkers are about as keen to complain about the weather as they are to point out a celebrity, but in these conditions you can’t not talk about it. While the mayor’s office discusses plans to extend cooling systems to subway platforms, individuals devise strategies to be outside for as little time as possible – like Minnesotans planning a trip across town in a snowstorm.At least the hospitals are temperature-controlled. In Britain, where nurseskeel overwith heat exhaustion, it can feel, at times, as if the single adequately air-conditioned space is the Apple Store; only the iPhones stay cool.TuesdayView image in fullscreenThe cast of Cats: The Jellicle Ball perform at the Tony awards in New York City.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/GettyCurrent trends in New York that may or may not make it over here: frozen yoghurt is having a resurgence but it’s the posh kind – Greek, not Pinkberry. The newest snack craze is “dot cake”, an $11 cube of dry sponge topped with icing and hundreds and thousands and served in a cup, which,according tothe New York Times, New Yorkers have been lining up at 6am all summer to buy. Not at our local Gourmet Garage, I will say).Beyond food, two things worth mentioning: “dog Crocs”, seen on several pets in the street to protect their paws from the punishing heat of the pavement and, as the name implies, tiny canine versions of their owner’s shoes, only these come in a four-pack.And on Broadway,Cats: The Jellicle Ball, a heartbreakingly brilliant interpretation of the original show in which a tired-seeming vehicle, badly damaged by the terrible film version, gets a radical makeover. Jellicle Ball is set in the Black and Latino drag pageants of the 1980s ballroom scene and is led by two legendary performers, André De Shields, who at 80 still brings it, and Junior LaBeija, who many will recognise from the classic 1991 documentaryParis Is Burning. The costumes, by Qween Jean, and choreography by Omari Wiles and Arturo Lyons, all rightfully won Tony’s.As Andrew Lloyd Webbersays, it’s criminal the show closed early last week. It’s the best thing I’ve seen for years. Anyway we went, we screamed, we clacked the massive Jellicle Ball fans and at intermission, the theatre played DJ Murphy’s ballroom remixes of Lloyd Webber’s songs while people lost their minds. Pray it comes to London.WednesdayHow did youeclipse? We were circling Heathrow in the air with the sun behind us when the sky became marginally less sunny. I will add it to the drawer of memories of other, underwhelming eclipse experiences, including that big one in 1999, when I was stuck on a motorway in France and everyone pulled over, looked up at the sky, then got back into their cars. And theGreat American Eclipse of two years ago, when I stood in a big crowd and everyone turned to one another and said: “Is that it?” It’s worse than bird watching.After it’s all over, there is a lot of anticlimactic posting on social media, although a friend in Spain sends a video and they seem to have enjoyed the real thing. As with so many things, I think the enjoyment is chiefly in the anticipation and the pretext it gives everyone to hang out, however briefly, in a single, unifying experience – and the opportunity to do crafts.View image in fullscreenParliament Hill, Hampstead Heath. The eclipse was a chance to hang out and do crafts.Photograph: Denise Baker/GettyThursdayMy summer reading is haphazard but heartfelt, and I’m flipping between Playworld, Adam Ross’s excellent, coming-of-age novel set in Great Neck, New York;Once the Deed Is Doneby Rachel Seiffert, a brilliant examination of camps for displaced people in Germany after the second world war; and Caroline Fraser’sbiography of Laura Ingalls Wilder. The book I’ve loved most so far this summer, however, is a reread ofElizabeth Jane Howard’s memoir, Slipstream, and now I’ve gone down the wormhole and want to read everything she ever wrote.The writer died in 2014, at the age of 90, and is best known for the Cazalet Chronicles, but Slipstream is a piece of social and literary history it’s hard to match. Given how a great central theme of the book is Howard’s low self-esteem, what’s interesting is how bold she was, insisting on a life that met none of the requirements of her time and class; despite a very well-to-do background which ensures the book is stuffed with cameos by people called Minky and dinner-party guests who, she might add casually, “was home secretary at the time”, Howard bolted out of three marriages, left her child in the care of others, and lived for many years a rackety, bohemian existence characterised by lack of funds and adventurous, penniless travel. Quite apart from her writing talent, it’s a study in courage and resolve.View image in fullscreenElizabeth Jane Howard in 1962.Photograph: Ronald Dumont/GettyFridayIt’s been six weeks sincethe weddingof Taylor Swift to Travis Kelce and, amazingly, no one has cracked. All the NDAs are holding! The only public utterance about the event has been from Kelce himself, who said the wedding had been “the best night of my life”, which was “full of a lot of celebration”. Perhaps this is what happens when so many of the guests are near-strangers who simply feel grateful for the invitation.None of the rest of us, meanwhile, will ever forget it; the spectacle of people who’d met the bride and groom once, if at all, dropping everything to scurry across the country or the Atlantic to celebrate the big, celebrity wedding next to Penn Station. It’s hard, in hindsight, to put your finger on who the most embarrassing attendee was, but I’d say Hugh Grant was right up there, as well as Tom Hanks, and Andrew Scott, most of whom seem to have met Swift backstage at the Eras tour in 2024 – or possibly the Toy Story 5 premiere in 2026 – since when, I guess, they’d forged meaningful friendships. Oh, to be world famous, and have this as your life.Digested week in picturesView image in fullscreenNigel Farage makes an appearance in Clacton. ‘The look on that guy’s face is pure admiration.’Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham visits Ilkeston with Angela Rayner. ‘What I love is I was rejected as leader twice and you’ve literally breached the ministerial code, and yet here we are!’Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Keir Starmer takes a shot on … hang on, no one cares.’Photograph: Jeremy SelwynExplore more on these topicsNew YorkDigested weekExtreme heatEnglandAndrew Lloyd WebberMusicalsTheatreTaylor SwiftcommentShareReuse this content

title: Donald Trump’s spying on leftwing groups recalls J Edgar Hoover’s Cointelpro | Kenneth Roth | The Guardian
description: The FBI from the 1950s to the 1970s tried to infiltrate and discredit leftist organizations. Trump seems to be repeating that sordid practice
Author: Kenneth Roth
Headline: The FBI from the 1950s to the 1970s tried to infiltrate and discredit leftist organizations. Trump seems to be repeating that sordid practice
Content: ‘This latest Trump abuse shows the importance of continuing to stand up to his lawless vision of his presidency.’Photograph: Alex Brandon/APView image in fullscreen‘This latest Trump abuse shows the importance of continuing to stand up to his lawless vision of his presidency.’Photograph: Alex Brandon/APOpinionTrump administrationDonald Trump’s spying on leftwing groups recalls J Edgar Hoover’s CointelproKenneth RothThe FBI from the 1950s to the 1970s tried to infiltrate and discredit leftist organizations. Trump seems to be repeating that sordid practiceFri 14 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 13.17 EDTShareIt is bad enough that the Trump administrationblockeda federal criminalinvestigationwhen an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent killed Renee Good as she was turning her carawayfrom him in Minneapolis the past January. Just before the shooting, Good and her partner had been observing andprotestingagainst ICE officers.Instead, it turns out the administration has beeninvestigatingprogressive and evenmainstreamgroups that have been involved in protests against Donald Trump’s sweeping deportations, according to newly released government documents.That Trump’s deportations have prompted widespread outrage is hardly surprising. The president arguably had an electoral mandate to secure the US-Mexican border butnotto raid workplaces and neighborhoods to deport undocumented immigrants.We are US civil rights lawyers. Trump’s policies have driven us to seek justice internationally | Thomas Becker and Antonio RomanucciRead moreMostsuch immigrants in the United States are now settled. They have been in the country for more than five years, and many have US-citizen children, work at regular jobs, pay taxes and are active members of their communities. Few Americans want their neighbors or work colleagues summarily deported.In January, Minnesota was a center of Trump’s deportation efforts. He deployed about3,000federal agents to this blue state to comb the streets in search of immigrants to deport. The public soon took to the streets in opposition, with some protesters using their phones to record detentions while others sounded thealarmthat Trump’s agents were in the vicinity.Yet rather than conduct an inquiry into the deportation agents’ often-unbridledviolence, the administration turned its prosecutorial sights on the protesters. In what it called “Operation Puppet Master”, it used its enormous investigative powers to pursue a vendetta against an array of groups that opposed its deportation agenda.Federal investigators justified the investigation by claiming that these groups might have provided help and money to theallegedly“violent opportunists and agitators” on the street. They also claimed that these groups provided “domestic terrorist financing”. This language parallels Trump’sdirectivelast September expanding the definition of domestic terrorism to include using violence or intimidation to obstruct the rule of law.Even if violence or other lawlessness occasionally broke out among the protesters, it is a huge leap to suggest that civic groups were criminally complicit. Federal conspiracy law is broad but not limitless. Itrequirestwo or more people to agree to commit a federal crime and for the accused to be a part of that agreement.It would hardly be surprising that various progressive groups banded together to monitor and oppose Trump’s deportations. But those activities are protected by the first amendment to the US constitution. They are completely lawful.For the Trump administration to transform coordinated protests into a criminalconspiracy, it would have to show that the targeted groups knew the protests wouldobstructfederal agents “by force, intimidation or threat” and that such criminality was a purpose of their coordination. That is an enormous stretch.double quotation markTrump’s criminal hounding of groups that oppose him shows no deference to the requirements of justiceThe role of federal prosecutor is powerful. A prosecutor can destroy a target’s life with the reputational sting and financial burden of a criminal prosecution. Before I joined Human Rights Watch, I served for more than four years in the 1980s as a federal prosecutor, mainly in New York City. My experience was that most federal prosecutors were aware of their power and tried to wield it in good faith.Trump’s criminal hounding of groups that oppose him shows no such deference to the requirements of justice.The first warning sign was that the Trump administration didn’t even use the justice department or its FBI, which traditionally pursue criminal investigations. Even though Trump hasdecimatedthe department, sparking the departure of many career officials who refused to be tainted bythe president’spersonal vendettas and politicized prosecutions, the administration chose instead to deploy the Department of Homeland Security.The DHS in turn issued administrative subpoenas, which donotrequire judicial authorization, and used other intrusive techniques to collect records and wire transfers from certain progressive groups going backthreeyears – long before the anti-deportation protests began. That suggests what prosecutors refer to as afishing expedition– the abuse of prosecutorial powers, in the absence of concrete evidence of wrongdoing, in the blind hope that something untoward might surface.Undercover federal investigators alsospiedon public meetings and even infiltrated group chats on Signal as activists discussed protests and their political opinions. Agentsrecordedlicense plate numbers to determine who was attending protest meetings.For example, at a 31 January meeting in a Minneapolis library, a homeland security undercover officerlistenedas supporters of a progressive climate group, the Sunrise Movement, discussed sit-ins, de-escalation tactics, and “having a police liaison and safety marshal present during events”. The agent at least had the honesty toreportback that the Sunrise Movement organization focused on “peaceful” protests.However, the Trump administration hascharged15 people with obstructing federal immigration operations in Minnesota using vehicles and other objects. The 94-page indictment does notallegeinjuries to specific ICE officers or serious violence, butassertsthat activists set up blockades around government buildings, threw chunks of ice at federal vehicles and “stalked” agents. Similar charges in parallel cases have already been dismissed or dropped at anunusually high rate.So far,noneof the groups under investigation has been criminally charged, but prosecutors showed a grand jury a PowerPointslideclaiming that 18 groups were part of a conspiracy to impede Trump’s deportation agents in Minnesota.The broad investigation brings back memories of a prior example of egregious federal misconduct targeting perceived leftist groups. Under the notorious J Edgar Hoover, the FBI from the 1950s to the 1970s conductedCointelproto infiltrate and discredit leftist organizations, especially those that promoted Black civil rights or opposed the Vietnam war. Exposure of these outrages led to majorreforms, which the Trump administration now seems determined to reverse.Many hope that the coming midterm elections in November will repudiate Trump’s lawlessness. Republicans are at risk of losing one or both houses of Congress. Yet this apparent abuse of criminal investigative powers reminds us that the presidency is powerful even without the legislative power of Congress.Fortunately, the judicial system has managed tohaltmuch of Trump’s deportation overreaching. Even grand juries, which traditionally show enormous deference to prosecutors, have beenrejectingrequests to bring charges. Moreover, while politicized federal prosecutors have ignored much of the misconduct by Trump’s deportation agents, some state prosecutors havetriedto pick up the ball.Yet much remains to be done as Trump seems determined to find ways toevadeeven adverse supreme court judgments. Exposure by journalists, protests by civic groups and outrage by the public are often the only tools we have.Responding to the Trump administration’s misconduct, Unidos MN, a human rights group in Minnesota,saidthat the government is “lashing out desperately in hopes of intimidating people and organizations that have shown the power of communities acting together”. This latest Trump abuse shows the importance of continuing to stand up to his lawless vision of his presidency.Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. He is the author ofRighting Wrongs: Three Decades on the Front Lines Battling Abusive GovernmentsExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationOpinionUS constitution and civil libertiesUS policingDonald TrumpICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)US immigrationProtest (US)commentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Nigel Farage: Clacton cannot acquit him | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Reform won a contrived byelection, but scrutiny continues – while the party increasingly attacks the watchdogs and journalists asking awkward questions
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Reform won a contrived byelection, but scrutiny continues – while the party increasingly attacks the watchdogs and journalists asking awkward questions
Content: ‘Mr Farage won because his toughest opponent was a comedian in a jumpsuit with a bin on his head.’Photograph: Ben Montgomery/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Mr Farage won because his toughest opponent was a comedian in a jumpsuit with a bin on his head.’Photograph: Ben Montgomery/Getty ImagesOpinionClacton byelection August 2026The Guardian view on Nigel Farage: Clacton cannot acquit himEditorialReform won a contrived byelection, but scrutiny continues – while the party increasingly attacks the watchdogs and journalists asking awkward questionsFri 14 Aug 2026 13.06 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 14.10 EDTShareNigel Farage didn’t attend the count of the byelection he forced upon Clacton. Instead, Reform UK’s leader celebrated his win with supporters at a “Farage Fest”, filmed by a friendly TV channel. For a politician who claims to speak for the people, it was telling that at his triumph he preferred an audience of believers.Mr Farage won because his toughest opponent on the campaign trail was a comedian in a jumpsuit with a bin on his head. ThatCount Binfacenevertheless won 27% of the vote captured the absurdity of a contest the main parties had boycotted as a Faragist stunt. Reform UK’s leader wanted to turn scrutiny of his finances – notably an investigation into whether he failed to report a £5m gift from an overseas crypto billionaire – into a “fight” with the “establishment”. But the result determined who represents the Essex seat, not whether he brokeparliamentaryorelectoralrules.There is no drop in enthusiasm among Mr Farage’s Clacton supporters. But he engineered an election in the safest territory – and despite facing no significant competition,had 37% vote against him. If even this part of the country can mobilise a substantial anti-Reform protest vote when the main parties stand aside, then imagine what might be possible in marginals where a mainstream challenger would prove more formidable.View image in fullscreenCount Binface.Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty ImagesMr Farage also hasn’t escaped the accountability he was trying to outrun. The parliamentary commissioner for standards suspended the investigation when he stopped being an MP; his re-election means the inquiry hasresumed. It covers both the millions from the Thailand-based crypto magnate Christopher Harborne, and alleged undeclared support from the convicted fraudsterGeorge Cottrell.A mandate is not an acquittal. If the commissioner finds a serious breach of the rules and Mr Farage is suspended for 10 or more Commons sitting days, a recall petition in Clacton would follow. If10% of electorssigned it – roughly 1,500 fewer than voted for Count Binface – another byelection would be triggered. This time Mr Farage would face voters after parliamentary censure and a successful recall campaign, not just, as Labour claimed, reeking of the “stench of sleaze”. With the main parties likely to stand, the anti-Farage vote could also coalesce behind one serious challenger – and present a tougher test.A disturbing pattern is emerging around Reform’s intimidatory tactics. Questions about its funding are repeatedly answered not openly but by attacking those asking. A parliamentary watchdog becomes a “kangaroo court”; Reform deputy leader Richard Tice’s lawyers seek material that could identify sources behind the Guardian’sinvestigation; and a prominent Farage allyreportedlyhired private investigators to examine a Sunday Times journalist investigating the party’s finances.This is likely to backfire for Reform. Last September the party was polling 32% nationally. After Mr Farage announced in July that he was triggering a byelection, itdropped from 27% to 24%– squeezed by a resurgent Labour, recovering Conservative party and Restore Britain’s more extreme policies. As even supporters such asTim Montgomerieacknowledge, a political party built on voters’ grievances has now become increasingly preoccupied with its own grievances about the media, investigations and treatment of Mr Farage. The result is that Reform appears inward-looking, defensive and sleazy. That will probably damage the party more than its angry, divisive nationalism, which demonisesminoritiesand shreds Britain’s traditions oftoleranceandpluralism.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on booming poetry sales: Homer, meet the Instapoets | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: In an unexpected twist, a Hollywood epic has contributed to Britain’s best-ever half-year in poetry sales
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: In an unexpected twist, a Hollywood epic has contributed to Britain’s best-ever half-year in poetry sales
Content: Rupi Kaur. ‘Since the emergence of Instapoetry, a fault line has developed among poets as well as critics’.Photograph: Rob Latour/Shutterstock for Hollywood MindView image in fullscreenRupi Kaur. ‘Since the emergence of Instapoetry, a fault line has developed among poets as well as critics’.Photograph: Rob Latour/Shutterstock for Hollywood MindOpinionPoetryThe Guardian view on booming poetry sales: Homer, meet the InstapoetsEditorialIn an unexpected twist, a Hollywood epic has contributed to Britain’s best-ever half-year in poetry salesFri 14 Aug 2026 13.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 14.10 EDTShareIn a short story called Career Move, published in the New Yorker in 1992, Martin Amis imagined a world in which screenwriters wrote for little magazines and earned a pittance while poets were global superstars. Amis’s story, a wonderfully ironic inversion of the time-honoured norm, was surprisingly prescient: the film and TV industries have been struggling, with screenwriters facingcontracting outletsfor their creations, whereas poets are nowbig business.The Bookseller reported recently that poetry sales were at ahistoric high. Part of the increase can be attributed to Christopher Nolan’s film The Odyssey, which has made Homer hot: editions of The Odyssey and its prequel, The Iliad, have garnered almost £1m in book sales in the UK this year. (As well as valiantly trying to keep the ailing film industry afloat, Nolan has also created a craze for epic poetry.) But Nolan’s film does not solely account for the boom in poetry sales. Even without the Homer run, sales of poetry texts and anthologies were still up by 7.2% from what was historically already a very high base.The poets leading the charge are not the traditional behemoths – Berryman and the Brownings, Marvell and Milton, Pope and Pound. These remain acquired tastes, read (if at all) in the beleaguered bowers and tottering towers of organised “Eng lit”. The publishing sensations fuelling the poetic sales surge are “Instagram poets” such asDonna Ashworth,Rupi Kaur,Amanda LovelaceandLucas Jones, whose collection, I Still Believe in Miracles, hasnetted £400,000 in salesthis year.The appeal of this new generation lies in their directness. They want to be our new best friend. “Maybe you kinda feel how I feel,” says Jones in the introduction to I Still Believe in Miracles. The American poet Lovelace dedicates her 2022 collection, unlock your storybook heart (she eschews capital letters throughout), to “anyone who feels like they’ve yet to find themselves: i promise it’s not too late”. Lovelace advises readers to practise “self-care before, during and after reading”.Criticsdismiss such work as more therapy than poetry, and argue it should be filed under self-help. Since the emergence of Instapoetry online in the middle of the last decade, a fault line has developed among poets as well as critics. Rebecca Watts’dismissalin a 2018articlein PN Review, a poetry journal, of poets such as Kaur, Kae Tempest and Hollie McNish as “artless and amateur”,laid bare the divisions. The Instapoets have now successfully migrated to print, but the arguments continue. Is this literature for apost-literate age, or ahealthy riposteto canonical poets (mostly “male, pale and stale” in the eyes of their detractors)?A corrective to the canon is no doubt overdue, and poets who appeal to a young readership beset by mental health issues should not be written off. But there are dangers. In June, Faber publishedTalking in Bed, a slim anthology of Philip Larkin poems in which there is a sense of Larkin being co-opted by the poetry-as-therapy movement. “He finds a way of admitting and delineating our nagging questions and most complicated feelings,” intones the blurb. The acerbic Larkin would not, one suspects, have appreciated this. Poetry should be allowed to be hermetic as well as accessible, and threatening as well as therapeutic.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Reckless ebike users put all of us at risk | Ebikes | The Guardian
description: Letter: Kevin Lloyd is angered by the sheer impunity that radiates from users and calls for regulation
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Kevin Lloyd is angered by the sheer impunity that radiates from users and calls for regulation
Content: ‘Their irresponsibility imposes externalities on other road users and pedestrians.’Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Their irresponsibility imposes externalities on other road users and pedestrians.’Photograph: AlamyEbikesLettersReckless ebike users put all of us at riskKevin Lloydis angered by the sheer impunity that radiates from users and calls for regulationFri 14 Aug 2026 11.20 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 12.15 EDTShareThere may be something in the argument identified by Andy Beckett that increased use of ebikes reflects broader changes in urban areas, including the cost of housing (Lime bikes hurtling around the city: is this the revenge of a priced-out generation?, 8 August). Yet none of that excuses the sheer impunity that radiates from ebike users, worsened by the design of city bikes which encourage the rider to sit back as if on a magic steed from which to survey their kingdom.Their irresponsibility imposes externalities on other road users and pedestrians: riding through red lights and across junctions with no heed to other traffic, wearing headphones (but seemingly never helmets), being on the phone or apparently scrolling while riding, carelessly weaving just to maintain a conversation, riding far too fast on paths shared with pedestrians, dropping bikes like litter. As for riding home after drinking in the pub – seriously?As a helmet-wearing cyclist, it is maddening to dodge people who seem barely familiar with a bike, let alone being in traffic. The behaviour needs to change. In the first instance, that must be through regulation and for riders and suppliers to be liable for the consequences of their actions, which sadly are sometimes serious.Kevin LloydHighbury, LondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Smart glasses controversy sidelines the benefits for disabled people | Meta | The Guardian
description: Letters: Guardian readers reflect on the ableism rife in the debate about Ray-Ban Meta eyewear, despite the life-changing difference they can make
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Guardian readers reflect on the ableism rife in the debate about Ray-Ban Meta eyewear, despite the life-changing difference they can make
Content: A woman trying on Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses. ‘A week of coverage branding them “pervert glasses” has now added a new anxiety’.Photograph: Bloomberg/GettyView image in fullscreenA woman trying on Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses. ‘A week of coverage branding them “pervert glasses” has now added a new anxiety’.Photograph: Bloomberg/GettyMetaLettersSmart glasses controversy sidelines the benefits for disabled peopleGuardian readers reflect on the ableism rife in the debate about Ray-Ban Meta eyewear, despite the life-changing difference they can makeFri 14 Aug 2026 11.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 12.15 EDTShareYour editorial on Meta’s smart glasses acknowledges their value to blind and visually impaired people, then asks that this “not be allowed to distract” from the harms (The Guardian view on Meta’s smart glasses: regulators must get on the front foot, 10 August). As an optometrist who owns a small independent practice, I’d suggest that it is visually impaired people who are being treated as the distraction.I was reluctant to stock Ray‑BanMeta, having no fondness for Meta or Luxottica, but colleagues persuaded me of the benefits for people with sight impairment. The reality has surpassed that. The majority of our buyers have a visual impairment or learning difficulty. One man, practically illiterate, now has the world read to him.For many of these patients, leaving the house is already an act of courage. Unfamiliar streets, unreadable signs, the constant low-level anxiety of navigating a world built for the fully sighted. These glasses have quietly made that easier. A week of coverage branding them “pervert glasses” has now added a new anxiety: not whether they can manage the journey, but whether strangers will assume the worst of them for wearing the thing that makes it possible.A colleague of mine was recently branded a misogynist online, by another optometrist, simply for suggesting the glasses were useful. Opening a Guardian leader with a nickname worthy of a Murdoch red-top – “pervert glasses” – makes that hostility respectable.The harms you describe are real and worth regulating. But on a recent holiday I left my own pair in the hotel room, yet watched hundreds of people photographing poolside on their phones, my daughters frequently in the background, with no permission sought and no bans imposed. The glasses at least announce themselves with a recording light. Pubs, parks and beaches are indeed not film sets, but they have been full of cameras for 20 years. Regulate by all means. Just remember who ends up wearing the stigma.Aled BrassingtonRomiley, Greater ManchesterMuch of the coverage of Meta’s smart glasses has been dominated by the language of “spy glasses” and “predator glasses”, while disabled people’s experiences have barely featured. To its credit, your recent report recognised how useful the glasses can be for blind and disabled people (‘I’m not spying’: how Meta’s smartglasses have divided opinion, 6 August). Even so, accessibility still feels like a side issue in the wider debate around smart glasses.I have severe muscular dystrophy and cannot pick up or operate a smartphone. My Ray-Ban Meta glasses let me make calls, send WhatsApp messages, take photos and record moments by voice. I can start a video call without touching a phone. These are not gimmicks. They give me independence and help keep me connected and safe.I can’t speak for Mark Zuckerberg or defend Meta’s wider record on privacy. But I’ve met Meta developers and scientists working on accessibility. Their commitment is real. They are listening to disabled people and building features that can change lives.There are legitimate privacy concerns. Secretly filming anyone is unacceptable. Meta should improve the recording light, prevent people disabling it, act against abusive content and be clearer about data use. Regulation must keep up.But it is wrong to treat everyone wearing these glasses as suspicious, or to impose blanket bans that may exclude disabled people who rely on them for communication, information or safety. Venues can ban recording without banning the glasses themselves.Phones, doorbells, dashcams and other cameras can all be misused. The answer is to tackle misuse, not demonise a technology or the people who depend on it. Many disabled people are tired of seeing this demonisation while our voices remain absent from the debate raging around smart glasses. We should not have to choose between privacy and independence. We should insist on both.Colin HughesLondonAs it happens, I am visually impaired and find smart glasses very useful. They enable me to read menus and notices and will even translate foreign notices for me. However, I consider recent moves to ban these products from certain premises to be ludicrous.There have been cases of people using smartphones for illicit purposes, for example surreptitiously filming up women’s skirts. However, nobody has dubbed smartphones “pervert phones” or sought to ban them. Some of the same premises which are now trying to do this to smart glasses also have CCTV, which films everybody without their consent, as do many cameras in our streets including doorbell cameras and dash cams.I am sure that the vast majority of smart glasses wearers use the product responsibly and would not dream of filming people without their consent. The theoretical possibility that they might do something bad is not a reason to ban the product entirely. You might as well ban the sale of kitchen knives, in case we use them to stab each other, or even cars in case we use them to run somebody over!Dr Alastair ForbesBridport, DorsetHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Life in the theatre is most revealing | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Letter: Cathy Scott-Willars responds to an article about the secret lives of theatre workers
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Cathy Scott-Willars responds to an article about the secret lives of theatre workers
Content: ‘It has provided me with some of the most entertaining stories.’Photograph: GettyView image in fullscreen‘It has provided me with some of the most entertaining stories.’Photograph: GettyTheatreLettersLife in the theatre is most revealingCathy Scott-Willarsresponds to an article about the secret lives of theatre workersFri 14 Aug 2026 11.21 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 12.02 EDTShareI enjoyed your article (The secret lives of theatre workers: ‘People were having full sex in the stalls’, 9 August). I worked many roles front of house and later as operations manager at a busy regional theatre, and it has provided me with some of the most entertaining stories.My favourite was working at a performance of The Rocky Horror Show in the large main theatre, while in the smaller studio was a play aimed at teenagers. The programming team had provided some post-show entertainment in the form of a DJ and breakdancer for the studio show, which happened to time with the interval of Rocky Horror. The scene I was met with was an usher crying, a furious college tutor shouting at her because her students had witnessed a man in a corset and thong attempt breakdancing, and his balls had fallen out, exposing himself.Another moment that stayed with me was locking the building up at the end of the night. I was late doing my lockdown and was on autopilot, knocking on dressing room doors and popping my head round to ensure everyone had gone. As I swung open one door, not giving the recipient time to answer, I walked in on Rufus Hound in his pants! Mortified, I apologised and quickly closed the door, while worrying I may get into trouble. Instead he passed on a message at stage door to apologise for leaving late and giving me a fright. What a nice guy.Sadly, audience aggression towards front-of-house staff was commonplace, and after three years as an operations manager, I decided it was time to move on.Cathy Scott-WillarsPrestatyn, DenbighshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: At a loss as to which Stephen Moss you’re referring to? So are many others | The Guardian | The Guardian
description: Letters: Stephen Moss and Stephen Moss find the humour in having the same name and working for the same company
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Stephen Moss and Stephen Moss find the humour in having the same name and working for the same company
Content: ‘I manage to write a book about once a decade, usually on some minority pursuit such as chess or cricket. The real, remarkably productive Stephen Moss knocks off bestsellers every other month.’Photograph: Getty/Tetra ImagesView image in fullscreen‘I manage to write a book about once a decade, usually on some minority pursuit such as chess or cricket. The real, remarkably productive Stephen Moss knocks off bestsellers every other month.’Photograph: Getty/Tetra ImagesThe GuardianLettersAt a loss as to which Stephen Moss you’re referring to? So are many othersStephen MossandStephen Mossfind the humour in having the same name and working for the same companyFri 14 Aug 2026 11.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 12.02 EDTShareAt least the Guardian’s Ewan Murray and Sky Sports’ Ewen Murray work for different outlets (A tale of two Murrays: when Ewan met Ewen to talk Tiger Woods, stiff gins and 15 years of mistaken identity, 8 August).Stephen Moss(former literary editor, and chess and classical music expert) and I (Birdwatch columnist) both write for the Guardian, causing endless confusion.A member of Sedgemoor chess club once told me that “We would be very honoured if you could come and give us a game” (they wouldn’t), while a woman, after admitting that she “quite enjoyed” my birding articles, spoiled it by adding “but when you write about classical music, it’s absolutely wonderful!”To my shame, I did not credit my talented doppelganger.Stephen MossMark, SomersetWith reference to Ewan Murray’s article about meeting Ewen Murray, and the two being mistaken for each other, these days I have resigned myself to being “the other Stephen Moss”.I manage to write a book about once a decade (at best), usually on some minority pursuit such as chess or cricket. The real, remarkably productive Stephen Moss knocks off bestsellers every other month. The Owl, The Robin, The Swan, The Swallow, The Wren. There are 11,000 bird species. That’s a lot of potential books. But I am NOT bitter.We are about the same age and, though we have never met, have tracked each other’s careers closely. He wrote for BBC Wildlife; I wrote for BBC Music magazine. The BBC sometimes used to send me his cheques as payment for pieces. Always very welcome. We have both had long associations with the Guardian.I get very tempting offers of birdwatching holidays across Europe and the US. One day I will accept one, even though I can barely tell a buzzard from a blackbird. I frequently get emails, with a detailed description, reporting a rare bird that a Guardian reader has seen on their local lake. My stock response is to say it’s a short-eared Siberian warbler – the first one seen in the UK since 1711 – and they should report it to the RSPB.It could all have been so different. Radio 5 Live once confused us and asked me to appear to discuss the killing of garden birds by domestic cats. I politely pointed out their mistake, but now realise what I should have done: go on and welcome this bird massacre. That would have caused a dent in the real, annoyingly successful Stephen Moss’s reputation and sales, leaving me to rule the roost. But I am not bitter!Stephen MossSurbiton, LondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Audrey Werro holds off Britain’s Keely Hodgkinson to win European 800m gold | European Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: The Swiss runner set a 1:54.81sec championship best to win European 800m gold, ahead of Keely Hodgkinson in 1:55.01
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: The Swiss runner set a 1:54.81sec championship best to win European 800m gold, ahead of Keely Hodgkinson in 1:55.01
Content: Audrey Werro crosses the finish line to win gold in the women's 800m final at the European Athletics Championships.Photograph: Julian Finney/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAudrey Werro crosses the finish line to win gold in the women's 800m final at the European Athletics Championships.Photograph: Julian Finney/Getty ImagesEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsAudrey Werro holds off Britain’s Keely Hodgkinson to win European 800m goldSwiss runner sets 1:54.81sec championship bestFemke Broeders-Bol secures bronze in 1:55.54Sean Ingleat Alexander Stadium, BirminghamFri 14 Aug 2026 17.16 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 19.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Audrey Werro was a child, she was so painfully shy that her father told her she had to become a lion every time she raced. In a European women’s 800m final for the ages, she followed that advice to the letter.As the 22-year-old Swiss superstar came around the final bend, she could feel Britain’sKeely Hodgkinsonon her shoulder, waiting to strike. The Dutch flyer Femke Broeders-Bol was also close enough to dream too. But Werro was ready to flash her teeth.European Athletics Championships 2026: Werro holds off Hodgkinson for gold in 800m, Hughes takes silver in 200m – liveRead moreIt didn’t matter that she had been spiked by Broeders-Bol after 200m. Or that she had led the pack into the face of a swirling wind for most of the race. She didn’t succumb. She roared.The noise from the full house of 23,000 home fans was deafening as Hodgkinson tried to pass her on the outside. But the gap never closed. Instead Werro took gold in 1min 54.81sec – a time that broke a championship record that had stood since 1982.It left Hodgkinson looking mightily disappointed after running 1:55.01 to take silver, with Broeders-Bol claiming bronze. But the Olympic champion was also gracious in defeat after.“It doesn’t sting because I was beaten by a great athlete,” said Hodgkinson. “I think I put together a pretty good race. I don’t think I did anything wrong. The thing about the 800m is you have a million different ways of going in your head but I covered every move well. I just didn’t have enough.”There was a moment, though, that she did believe. “In that last 50, I thought I had it,” she said. “But she’s a strong athlete.” As for Werro, her smile told the story given that on Thursday lunchtime it appeared she was out of these Championships after being tripped in the semi-finals. “I am really happy with this medal after a crazy 24 hours,” she said. “When I was a child, my dad used to tell me I had to be a lion. So I decided to do a celebration with that when I crossed the line.”Before the final, Hodgkinson had asked the weather gods for no wind to help her bid for a third successive European title. But they had other ideas. It was whippy and blustery throughout.But that didn’t deter Werro, who went to the front early. And as the bell sounded with the clock showing 56.45, the big three began to stretch away. “Audrey wanted to take it on and, with that wind, I was happy to let her,” said Hodgkinson. “We’re all great athletes and I knew it was going to be close.”It was. And that allowed Hodgkinson to be philosophical after. “We’re all going to win some, lose some,” she said. “Shit happens. Audrey fell over yesterday. She’d made it back. I know what that took out of me a few weeks ago. So yeah, incredible for her. And yeah, life goes on. I’ll go back and train and just hope I get it next time.”View image in fullscreenAudrey Werro is all smiles after her 800m success.Photograph: Morgan Harlow/APThat may prove easier said than done given that Werro has run the third, fourth and ninth fastest times in history since June. But only a fool would write the British runner off.There was a second silver medal on the night for Britain in the form of Zharnel Hughes in the men’s 200m. Hughes ran a creditable 20.16, especially given that he has been battling a groin injury. However, he had no answer to the speed of Germany’s Owen Ansah, who powered to victory in 19.95. There was a rare dead heat for bronze between Italy’s Eseosa Fostine Desalu and Switzerland’s Timothé Mumenthaler, who both ran 20.26.However, Ansah’s gold medal was instantly controversial given that last week Germany’s National Anti-Doping Agency had recommended that he should receive a four-year suspension over a possible anti-doping violation.The German authorities claim that is because Ansah missed a test in July. Ansah disputes this. But Hughes will be upgraded to gold if Ansah is banned.Earlier in the night, some of Europe’s biggest stars also shone brightly. First Italy’s Nadia Battocletti added the European 10,000m title to her 5,000m crown with a devastating 28-second burst over the last 200m. Then Norway’s Karsten Warholm ran a championship record time of 46.63 to storm to gold in the men’s 400m hurdles.View image in fullscreenNadia Battocletti crosses the line to win the gold medal in the 10,000 metres final.Photograph: Sona Maleterova/Getty ImagesBut perhaps the sweetest moment of the night came when another Italian star, the high jumper Gianmarco Tamberi, asked the crowd to sing happy birthday to his one-year-old daughter, Camilla, after he leaped 2.32m to win gold. They duly obliged too.But there was little joy for Katarina Johnson-Thompson in the women’s heptathlon. The 33-year-old felt the effects of a calf niggle as she finished day one in 16th place with just 3,644 points – a long way behind the leader Adrianna Sulek-Schubert of Poland on 3,968.Explore more on these topicsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsKeely HodgkinsonAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Europe’s top clubs threatened Club World Cup boycott before Fifa plan collapsed | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Europe’s leading clubs threatened not to participate in future Club World Cups unless Gianni Infantino withdrew his Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme, issuing their ultimatum hours before the plan was scrapped
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: Europe’s leading clubs threatened not to participate in future Club World Cups unless Gianni Infantino withdrew his Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme, issuing their ultimatum hours before the plan was scrapped
Content: Nasser al-Khelaifi (right), chair of European Football Clubs, and the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, pictured together in 2025.Photograph: Fabrizio Corradetti/APView image in fullscreenNasser al-Khelaifi (right), chair of European Football Clubs, and the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, pictured together in 2025.Photograph: Fabrizio Corradetti/APFifaEurope’s top clubs threatened Club World Cup boycott before Fifa plan collapsedUltimatum issued hours before plan was scrappedEuropean Football Clubs demanded Infantino back downExclusive byNick AmesFri 14 Aug 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 18.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEurope’s leading clubs threatened not to participate in future Club World Cups unlessGianni Infantinowithdrew his Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme, issuing their ultimatum hours before the plan was scrapped.In a letter to the Fifa secretary general, Mattias Grafström, the influential European Football Clubs (EFC) group warned that its cooperation with future tournaments would hinge on Infantino backing down. It said the threat would hold unless a joint venture between EFC and Fifa – a framework for which has already been agreed – is completed before television rights can be sold for the 2028 Women’sClub World Cup.Continental clash: where world football stands on Fifa and Infantino – explainedRead moreThe letter, dated 31 July and signed by the EFC chief executive, Charlie Marshall, said Infantino’s actions could constitute a “substantial breach” of the bodies’ existing memorandum of understanding (MoU) and suggested this could be grounds for its termination. It floated the idea that EFC and its clubs may push back against the international match calendar and its player release rules, which are crucial to ensuring national team tournaments can function. Infantinoshelved the privately backed Football Forward Enterprise (FFE)in the early hours of 1 August after widespread condemnation.Fundamental to EFC’s complaints was the impression FFE would bring all broadcasting, commercial and sponsorship rights under its own umbrella. The letter askedFifato confirm this and said it would take decisive action if these elements were not included in the long-proposed joint venture, whose creation is enshrined in the MoU and intended to involve managing the commercial side of global club competitions. It witheringly wrote that the tie-in had, “unlike the FFE proposal, made no meaningful progress over the past year”. EFC already has a similar joint venture with Uefa, named UC3, which was launched in 2025.A potentially incendiary section read: “Unless a fully operational Fifa-EFC CWC joint venture, with exclusive authority over, among other things, all commercial and operational matters, is established well ahead of the women’s 2028 Fifa CWC rights cycle, EFC will not support – and its member clubs will not participate in – any future edition, including the women’s and men’s 2028 and 2029 Fifa CWC.”In theory the threat still holds although Fifa, in a response to EFC’s letter since Infantino climbed down, is understood to have promised a swift meeting to keep the joint venture on track. EFC’s position followed concerns raised by a vast number of clubs around Europe, who were angered by the lack of consultation around the design of FFE. One major European club expressed concerns in its own letter saying it would support EFC in any “firmer collective action” if necessary and called for “more rigorous and transparent governance processes”.Any European withdrawal from Club World Cups would in practice mean those tournaments could not run. EFC and Fifa operated last year’s Club World Cup, the first to take place with 32 teams, using a short-term prototype for any future joint venture. No hosts have yet been announced for the new-look Women’s Club World Cup or the next edition of the men’s tournament in 2029.View image in fullscreenChelsea won the Club World Cup in July 2025 by beating Paris Saint-Germain in the final.Photograph: Chris Brunskill/Fantasista/Getty ImagesEFC’s letter also raised the continuing delay,first reported in February, in distributing £185m of solidarity money to clubs that did not participate in the Club World Cup. Transparency over the event’s financial performance was also requested.“We ask that you urgently share the final surplus revenue generated by the 2025 Fifa WC, together with a full profit and loss statement, so that all revenues, expenses and costs can be properly assessed in line with our partnership in this competition,” it said. “The absence of information on this matter, as with the lack of a solution on CWC solidarity for over a year, is also of serious concern and disappointment to EFC and our member clubs.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt is understood there is increasing optimism that this issue is on the verge of resolution, although a notional average £50,000 windfall for every global top-flight club, if the pot was divided equally, pales in comparison with the £84m reward long since banked by last year’s winners, Chelsea.Referring to clubs releasing players for international duty, EFC continued: “Our memorandum of understanding, set to expire on 30 December 2030, includes EFC’s and its member clubs’ acceptance of the international match calendar and the release rules. Both are directly relevant for Fifa’s non-European member associations and to any value FFE may have.” It said Fifa’s apparent commercial vision for FFE constituted a “serious breach of trust” and warned the MoU could be jeopardised.The letter demonstrates the extraordinary level of leverage EFC, which is chaired by the Paris Saint-Germain president, Nasser al-Khelaifi, can claim over Fifa and its increasing influence on football’s future. The organisation, set up in 2008 as a lobby group for clubs around the continent, now has well over 800 members although only a minority hold full voting rights. Some stakeholders elsewhere in football’s ecosystem have expressed fears about the level of power it has assumed. A separate representative body,the Union of European Clubs, was created in 2023 to represent smaller sides but is not recognised by Uefa.One potential consequence of EFC’s discussions with Fifa could, in the medium term, be its expansion into a group representing clubs around the world. More immediately, last month’s letter demanded that Fifa deliver on a previous promise to fully integrate Al-Khelaifi into the Fifa council, which is purportedly its main decision-making body.Explore more on these topicsFifaClub World CupGianni InfantinoEuropean club footballFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Liverpool owner FSG seals £1.65bn sale of 30% stake to consortium including Jeff Bezos | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: Liverpool’s owner has confirmed the sale of 30% of the club to a consortium including Amit Bhatia, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Liverpool’s owner has confirmed the sale of 30% of the club to a consortium including Amit Bhatia, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin
Content: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos is the third richest man in the world but FSG will remain in operational control at Anfield.Composite: ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAmazon founder Jeff Bezos is the third richest man in the world but FSG will remain in operational control at Anfield.Composite: ShutterstockLiverpoolLiverpool owner FSG seals £1.65bn sale of 30% stake to consortium including Jeff BezosConfirmed deal values club as a whole at £5.5bnAmit Bhatia will become club’s new vice-chairmanAndy HunterFri 14 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 16.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLiverpool’s owner,Fenway Sports Group, has confirmed it has agreed the sale of 30% of the club to a consortium including Amit Bhatia, the Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and the Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin. The deal is understood to be worth £1.65bn, valuing Liverpool at £5.5bn, and will see Bhatia become the club’s new vice-chair on an expanded board.Bhatia, the son-in-law of Indian steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, initiated and led talks with FSG on behalf of the 1892 Holdings consortium, a reference to Liverpool’s founding year. The former co-owner of Queens Park Rangers has received financial backing from the Mittal Family Trust, the K5 Sports fund, of which Bezos is the lead investor, and EE Capital, the family office of Elaine and Eduardo Saverin.Arsenal in talks over Quansah; transfer news; Giuliani slams Infantino’s critics: football – liveRead moreElaine Saverin, wife of Eduardo, and Bryan Baum, co-founder and managing partner of K5 Global, will also join the Liverpool board. Bezos is considered a passive investor and will not have a seat on the board.Despite the involvement of Bezos, the third richest man in the world with $272bn (£201bn), Eduardo Saverin, worth an estimated $33bn and the Mittal family, worth around $17bn, FSG will remain in operational control of Liverpool as well as majority owners. 1892 Holdings’ investment remains subject to regulatory approval, which could take up to 90 days, and will have no impact on Liverpool’s transfer budget or strategy for this summer. There is also no change to the leadership or day-to-day running of Liverpool.FSG insist the deal is not part of an exit strategy from a club they acquired in 2010 for £300m after the near-ruinous ownership of Tom Hicks and George Gillett. The transaction does not compel FSG to sell more of the club to 1892 at a future date, or include obligations for 1892 to increase their stake, but it does give Bhatia’s consortium options to purchase more of Liverpool should the majority owners eventually decide to sell.It is the makeup of Bhatia’s consortium, rather than any financial need, that FSG claim attracted them to the British-Indian businessman’s proposal. The FSG leadership team of principal owner John W Henry, chair Tom Werner and president Mike Gordon have spent almost a year getting to know Bhatia and believe the deal will create further opportunities for Liverpool in global business, technology and investment, including in the important markets of India and Asia.View image in fullscreenThe sale will have no impact on Liverpool’s transfer budget or strategy for this summer.Photograph: News Images/NurPhoto/ShutterstockGordon, who has resumed a more hands-on role at Liverpool following the departure of Michael Edwards as chief executive of football at FSG, said: “Liverpool has always been built by thinking beyond one season and making decisions with the club’s long-term interests in mind. That approach continues to attract interest from respected investors and business leaders around the world.“As we considered this opportunity, it became clear that Amit and the consortium shared our long-term philosophy and appreciation for what makes Liverpool special. Their experience and perspective will complement the strong foundation already in place, and we look forward to working together.”With Premier League and Uefa financial regulations linking a club’s spending to turnover, the new investment will not have an immediate benefit for head coach Andoni Iraola and his Liverpool team. However, the commercial opportunities presented by the involvement of Bezos, Bhatia and Saverin will enable the Anfield club to grow their annual revenue significantly. Liverpool’s annual revenue increased to a record £703m in the year ending May 2025.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSpeaking on behalf of 1892 Holdings, Bhatia said: “We are incredibly proud to be investing in Liverpool Football Club and to be doing so alongside FSG. We have the utmost respect and admiration for FSG as owners and for everything they have achieved at Anfield.“To be welcomed as a partner in a club of this stature is a huge privilege. We are making this investment because we believe deeply in Liverpool and its leadership, and we look forward to supporting the club’s continued success for years to come.”Bhatia was involved in QPR for almost 19 years and took on numerous roles, from chair of the club to chair of the club’s community trust, until transferring his shareholding in July. He is likely to have a more visible presence at Anfield than fellow members of his consortium or FSG.Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolFenway Sports GroupJeff BezosFinancesBusinessnewsShareReuse this content

title: Concern grows as British Athletics coach Leon Baptiste vanishes on trip to Morocco | European Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: The coach and former international sprinter has not been seen for two months, with one former teammate calling the situation ‘very worrying’
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: The coach and former international sprinter has not been seen for two months, with one former teammate calling the situation ‘very worrying’
Content: Leon Baptiste with a coaching award at 2023’s Sporting Equals ceremony. He won two golds at the 2010 Commonwealth Games.Photograph: John Phillips/Getty Images for Sporting EqualsView image in fullscreenLeon Baptiste with a coaching award at 2023’s Sporting Equals ceremony. He won two golds at the 2010 Commonwealth Games.Photograph: John Phillips/Getty Images for Sporting EqualsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsConcern grows as British Athletics coach Leon Baptiste vanishes on trip to MoroccoFormer international sprinter not seen for two monthsSituation ‘very worrying’, says former teammateSean IngleFri 14 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 18.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMystery surrounds a highly regarded BritishAthleticscoach who has not been heard from since visiting Morocco around two months ago.Leon Baptiste, 41, who coaches a number of elite athletes including the Paris Olympic 4x400m relay bronze medallist Charlie Dobson, is believed to have gone to Morocco for the weekend with some close friends for a stag do or golf trip.Seb Coe insists empty seats in Birmingham won’t harm London’s bid for 2029 worldsRead moreHowever, he has not been heard from since by his athletes or the UK Athletics officials who pay him as a Loughborough-based consultant, with messages to his phone not returned.UKA have declined to comment, citing confidentiality. The Guardian spoke to a former British teammate of Baptiste, who said: “He was a very calm and sensible chap, in my experience. No one knows what has happened.
