It is very worrying.”Dobson has struggled with injuries in Baptiste’s absence and failed to make it out of the 400m semi-finals at the European championships in Birmingham earlier this week.After finishing fourth in his semi-final in a time of 45.18sec, over a second outside his personal best of 44.14 set last year, Dobson alluded to the situation when he said it had been “an interesting eight weeks”.He also said he had been struggling with some injury niggles that had contributed to his withdrawal from the recent Commonwealth Games. He did not compete in the heats of the men’s 4x400m on Friday morning and it remains to be seen if he returns to the track for Sunday evening’s final.In the meantime UKA staff have stepped in to help Dobson and the rest of Baptiste’s group, with former European 400m champion and relays coach Martyn Rooney taking Dobson under his wing.Baptiste was a talented sprinter who won 200m and 4x100m relay gold at the 2010 Commonwealth Games in Delhi before being forced to retire aged 28 because of a serious knee issue.View image in fullscreenLeon Baptiste (left) wins the 200m final at the 2010 Commonwealth Games.Photograph: Suzanne Plunkett/ReutersSurgery resulted in him missing the London 2012 Olympics before he moved into coaching after deciding not to defend his Commonwealth titles at the 2014 Games in Glasgow.“As much as I am sprinting and progressing, my body has never fully recovered from my knee surgery,” he said that year. “My coach and I feel that Glasgow Commonwealth Games qualification is a tall order – so the time has come for my focus to move elsewhere.“The decision for an athlete to retire is never easy, but in essence the decision has been made for me.”The British Embassy in Rabat has been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Not going to be an issue’: Mikel Arteta relaxed about Arsenal contract situation | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: The Arsenal manager, whose current deal expires at the end of the new season, said of his future: ‘They don’t have to worry about that, I want to be here’
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: The Arsenal manager, whose current deal expires at the end of the new season, said of his future: ‘They don’t have to worry about that, I want to be here’
Content: Mikel Arteta’s Arsenal will play Manchester City in the Community Shield on Sunday.Photograph: Marc Atkins/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMikel Arteta’s Arsenal will play Manchester City in the Community Shield on Sunday.Photograph: Marc Atkins/Getty ImagesArsenal‘Not going to be an issue’: Mikel Arteta relaxed about Arsenal contract situationManager’s deal expires at end of the new season‘They don’t have to worry … I want to be here’Ed AaronsFri 14 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 17.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMikel Arteta has said he is relaxed about his Arsenal contract expiring at the end of the new season and believes his side will need to be better than last year to defend their title successfully.The Premier League champions will face Enzo Maresca’s Manchester City in the Community Shield in Cardiff on Sunday and are heavy favourites to win back-to-back league titles for the first time since the 1930s. The departure of Pep Guardiola from their traditional rivals City means Arteta is now the Premier League’s longest-serving manager, with the Spaniard having joined in December 2019.Arsenal open talks with Bayer Leverkusen over deal for Jarell QuansahRead moreHe signed a three-year contract extension in September 2024 afterArsenalfinished as runners-up to City and had been expected to agree a new deal over the summer that would make him one of the highest-paid managers in the world. Arteta acknowledged on Friday that his priorities have been elsewhere this summer as he attempts to strengthen his squad before the new season but reassured supporters that he is fully committed to the club.“They don’t have to worry about any of that, because I want to be here. I am extremely happy. I feel very grateful to work with the people that I work with and when we have the possibility, we will resolve that. And that’s it,” he said.Asked if he expects talks over a new contract to continue after the transfer window, Arteta added: “There is always another priority, I think. And that’s the way we have been treating it, I think because everybody feels comfortable that the time on the contract is not going to be an issue. I think because my will, certainly, is to be here and I am very happy here. My feeling from the club is the same one. That is why everyone is doing things in a really organic way.”Arsenal have opened negotiations with Bayer Leverkusenover a move for Jarell Quansahas they seek cover for William Saliba and Jurriën Timber, while they are still in the market for another attacker if they can offload Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus. After missing out on Vinícius Júnior when the Brazil forward opted to sign a new deal with Real Madrid, Arteta defended Arsenal’s strategy this summer and is hoping that they can still add to their squad.“I am really happy with the squad, the players that I have and I am really happy with the ambition of the club. There is zero question about that. We have shown that in the manner we have tried to act,” he said.“But I think we need to do it our own way. We have super strengths and we have other areas we need to be very conscious [of] because we don’t have the elements or the structure that other clubs have. We need to do it our way. We are always on it that way and we will do what we believe is the right thing to do. To have the best possibility to compete in every competition that’s for sure.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArteta added: “We’re going to prepare to elevate our level, expecting that the rest will do the same. That’s traditionally what happened in the league in the last few years, and that’s the way we have planned the season, and the way we want to evolve the team.”Explore more on these topicsArsenalMikel ArtetanewsShareReuse this content

title: Raúl Jiménez’s injury-time penalty salvages point for Wolves against Blackburn | Championship | The Guardian
description: Wolves drew 2-2 against Blackburn in the Championship season opener after Raúl Jiménez scored a spot-kick deep in stoppage time
Author: Peter Lansley
Headline: Wolves drew 2-2 against Blackburn in the Championship season opener after Raúl Jiménez scored a spot-kick deep in stoppage time
Content: Raúl Jiménez slots home his penalty for Wolves in stoppage time.Photograph: Brett Patzke/WWFC/Wolves/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRaúl Jiménez slots home his penalty for Wolves in stoppage time.Photograph: Brett Patzke/WWFC/Wolves/Getty ImagesChampionshipRaúl Jiménez’s injury-time penalty salvages point for Wolves against BlackburnPeter Lansleyat MolineuxFri 14 Aug 2026 17.21 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 19.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRaúl Jiménez marked his return to Wolves with the stoppage-time equaliser that saved them from an embarrassing start to their return to the Championship. The Mexico striker, whoscored against Englandduring the World Cup, came off the bench to convert a penalty given for handball by Ryan Alebiosu that would have had VAR questioning whether the defender was in the area when Jackson Tchatchoua’s cross struck his arm.One minor consolation from Wolves’ relegation is that the video assistant referee is no longer their problem. Jiménez, who had bought scarves for all supporters in the South Bank in gratitude for their welcome home, tucked away his first goal in this second spell for the club he graced during their recent heyday before leaving for Fulham.Wolves 2-2 Blackburn: Championship opener – liveRead more“He’s an important striker,” César Peixoto, Wolves’ new head coach said. “He lives for scoring and making goals. Raúl is a key player for us. He helped the team inside and outside the pitch but we have to go slowly with him because he is 35 years old and comes back from the World Cup. We want him to stay good and scoring for us is good for him and for the team.”Goals from Sean McLoughlin and Andri Gudjohnsen allowed Blackburn to provide Wolves with a reality check after Marshall Munetsi had scored early. Confidence is a fragile commodity and, after their decision to replace Rob Edwards with a manager with no experience of English football, the Wolves board know that their supporters’ patience is thin. Leading Gil Vicente to sixth place in the Portuguese first division does not make Peixoto a guaranteed winner.Conceding the equaliser, through Jiménez’s first goal for Wolves in 1,311 days, denied unfancied Blackburn a deserved victory after Wolves lost their shape. Tony Mowbray, their head coach, felt the penalty decision was harsh. “I’ve just been shown an angle by my analyst where he [Alebiosu] is outside the box; another angle I’m told shows he’s just inside the box. I just felt like more and more decisions were starting to sway their way,” the former West Brom manager said. “It’s harsh to take because I don’t think they deserved that second goal.”Molineux was awash with fading golden sunlight and rising optimism at kick-off. A summer that started with such a surprising managerial departure was promising to end with renewed faith in the team’s direction of travel, until Peixoto’s admired high press came unstuck as his team started to “play with their hearts more than their heads”.View image in fullscreenMarshall Munetsi (right) celebrates scoring Woves’ first goal with Fer López.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAThe Blackburn defence had split generously to allow Munetsi a clean run through on to Fer López’s sumptuous pass. The left-footed finish from the Zimbabwean, himself coming back to Molineux after a loan at Paris FC, strengthened the feelgood factor.Peixoto’s tactics do currently lead to gaps on transition. Blackburn, who have not done so much in the transfer market to suggest they should aim higher than last season’s 20th place, got behind Wolves on several occasions. It was no great surprise when, from Ryoya Morishita’s superb right-wing cross, McLoughlin headed beyond Dan Bentley to equalise.Some of Wolves’ best business this summer has been bringing players back to Molineux. While Jiménez started the night on the bench, after a late start to pre-season following his impressive World Cup for Mexico, López was the classiest player on view. Back from a loan at Celta Vigo, he has been invited to make the No 10 position his own, and the Spaniard nearly regained Wolves the lead only to curl his shot wide.View image in fullscreenBlackburn’s Andri Gudjohnsen gives his side a 2-1 lead early in the second half.Photograph: Simon Davies/ProSports/ShutterstockBlackburn continued to benefit from Wolves’ soft centre however. Oladapo Afolayan’s shot needed tipping over by Bentley before the right winger again got space down Wolves’ left – where David Møller Wolfe, in for the injured Hugo Bueno, showed he is still not match fit after his World Cup endeavours with Norway – to cross for Gudjohnsen to turn in Rovers’ second goal. “The team lost some organisation and played with their heart rather than their head and brains,” Peixoto said. “It’s a lesson for us in the future, we need to stay with mental stability for the 90 minutes.”By the hour mark, the South Bank were swirling their Jiménez scarves above their heads and chanting “Si Señor” in honour of the veteran striker who was such an esteemed figure at Molineux for five of the club’s best years in modern times. Before his horrific head injury, he was the pivotal attacking player as Nuno Espírito Santo’s team reached the later stages of the FA Cup and Europa League. The scene was set for the Mexican. Could he deliver? Si, señor.Explore more on these topicsChampionshipWolverhampton WanderersBlackburn Roversmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Iga Swiatek takes swing at critics after ending title drought in Canada | Iga Swiatek | The Guardian
description: Poland’s Iga Swiatek beat Elena Rybakina to win the Canadian Open before hitting out at the ‘unfair judgment’ she gets, particularly in her own country
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: Poland’s Iga Swiatek beat Elena Rybakina to win the Canadian Open before hitting out at the ‘unfair judgment’ she gets, particularly in her own country
Content: Iga Swiatek lets it all out after winning her first title of the year and later admitting she has struggled with the intense scrutiny she faces.Photograph: Robert Prange/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIga Swiatek lets it all out after winning her first title of the year and later admitting she has struggled with the intense scrutiny she faces.Photograph: Robert Prange/Getty ImagesIga SwiatekIga Swiatek takes swing at critics after ending title drought in CanadaPole beats Rybakina to win her first title in 11 months but is angry about disapproving voices from her own countryTumaini Carayolin CincinnatiFri 14 Aug 2026 15.24 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt came as no surprise that almost a year of pent-up emotion exploded fromIga Swiatekthe moment she slotted her final backhand winner to clinch the Canadian Open title by defeating Elena Rybakina in two clean sets on Thursday night.As she screamed towards her team members on her corner of the court, pointed to her head and furiously pumped her fist, though, it was the tenor of Swiatek’s emotion that made her reaction noteworthy: she was angry. Her anger, she explained later, stemmed from the doubtful, disapproving voices she has heard throughout these difficult periods, most of it coming from viewers and the media alike in Poland.Ben Shelton prevails in all-American final to retain Canadian Open titleRead more“After I won, I kind of let myself feel it [anger] a little bit because there are plenty of things that athletes, not only athletes, all the people have to struggle with,” she said. “Sometimes we need to fight things that we shouldn’t.”Considering her generational achievements, Swiatek is one of the most famous people in Poland, and certainly one of the country’s most famous athletes. Her fame has reached a point where she rarely ventures outside when in her home country, only really going to her friends’ apartments or inviting them to hers, to avoid being watched. Last year, Swiatek explained how she had to negotiate with paparazzi after they took photos of her apartment building.“I can accept it when it’s like at work or when I’m going to practise and everything, but for example, like when it’s close to my home or when I’m having just a walk with a friend or with a family member I’d rather them not doing that, because it’s my time off,” she said. “I had an incident, actually, after Miami, when I was home, when paparazzi followed me almost to my apartment. But I stopped them, and I said: ‘OK, tomorrow I’m going to practise. You can make photos of me when I go there, but this is off limits.’ So also they kind of understand sometimes. And I think I understand what their job is about, and we can have a nice, even cooperation if they want to be supportive.”While fame is something that Swiatek has had to accept, the additional scrutiny that comes with her status is what she refuses to tolerate. Practically every tennis player receives some level of social media abuse, hate and threats, one of the many pressing issues in the sport, but the criticism Swiatek receives is distinct because of the amount that comes from home. Every result and decision is the subject of intense public scrutiny, something that has increased during her more difficult past two years on tour, and they have further complicated her attempts to rediscover her confidence. One of the biggest points of contention has been her relationship with her team, with ample focus on the role of her psychologist, Daria Abramowicz. Asked why so much negativity comes from home, which should be a safe space, Swiatek shrugs: “That’s an interesting question, I think, for a sociologist or someone, because honestly, it’s not only in Poland, but in Great Britain as well, in different countries, for different sports, not only for individual athletes.“There is unfair judgment from different parts coming to us, and we need to handle it. For sure, last month I faced it, my team faced it. My goal was for it to not interrupt my process and define who I am. Being sure about my decisions, not letting this disrupt anything and focus on growing because it’s just the world that we live in. It shouldn’t be like that so I took yesterday’s opportunity to just talk about it a little bit more even if it helps one person, or one young athlete knows that we all try to do something with it, maybe it will help a little bit.”This is a significant moment for Swiatek, her first title in 11 months and after so much enthusiasm about their partnership, her first alongside her new coach Francisco Roig. Such are the demands of this gruelling sport she had no time at all to savour it. Swiatek closed out her 6-2, 6-3 win over Rybakina at about 7.30pm and her press duties ended around 10pm on Thursday.By midday on Friday, she had packed her bags, taken a private jet to Cincinnati, provided by the tournament, and was addressing the media before her title defence in Ohio. “It’s intense, but it’s OK,” said Swiatek. “I’ll find my time to appreciate what happened and to be grateful about it, for sure. Because without it, it doesn’t make sense to keep going. You need to get a taste of these moments and remember them.”Explore more on these topicsIga SwiatekTennisfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Belgian student strikes gold worth €9m while digging a new sewer | Belgium | The Guardian
description: Kobe, 18, who made discovery on site of former brewery in Sint-Gillis-Dendermonde, at first thought trove was €1 coins
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Kobe, 18, who made discovery on site of former brewery in Sint-Gillis-Dendermonde, at first thought trove was €1 coins
Content: Kobe said the gold was ‘really bricked in there – not in a safe or anything’.Photograph: Gianni Barbieux/Photo NewsView image in fullscreenKobe said the gold was ‘really bricked in there – not in a safe or anything’.Photograph: Gianni Barbieux/Photo NewsBelgiumBelgian student strikes gold worth €9m while digging a new sewerKobe, 18, who made discovery on site of former brewery in Sint-Gillis-Dendermonde, at first thought trove was €1 coinsJon HenleyEurope correspondentFri 14 Aug 2026 11.52 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 12.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor a student with a summer job working on a Belgian building site, “money down the drain” has taken on a whole new meaning: excavating the trenches for a sewage system, he stumbled across a hidden trove of gold worth an estimated €9m (£8m).“We suddenly saw something lying there,” 18-year-old Kobetold the Belgian news network VTM. “At first I thought it was €1 coins. So we started digging them up. Then we saw a gold bar. It turned out to be a bit more than we thought.”The student, who has not been further identified, was working with colleagues on the site of a former brewery on Van Langenhovestraat in Sint-Gillis-Dendermonde, about 19 miles (30km) north-west of Brussels, when they made the discovery on Tuesday.View image in fullscreenThe hoard was stashed in a bag in a bricked-in cellar wall beneath the grand villa.Photograph: Facebook/Dendermonde Local PoliceThe hoard, which includes gold coins, nuggets and numbered bullion bars, was stashed in a bag in a bricked-in cellar wall beneath the grand villa originally built for the brewery’s owner, Theophilus Van Assche, in the late 19th century.Kobe said: “It’s just not something you expect when you’re working on a regular Tuesday morning,” adding that the treasure trove appeared to have been deliberately hidden. “It was really bricked in there – not in a safe or anything.”Brewing on the site began in 1899 and ceased in 1970, and the listed property – the wrought-iron gates of which still bear the initials “VA” – is being completely renovated by the social welfare organisation CAW Oost-Vlaanderen to create new offices and housing.View image in fullscreenThe trove included gold coins, nuggets and numbered bullion bars.Photograph: Facebook/Dendermonde Local Police“The Brouwershuis was a beautiful building, but it is being completely gutted,” Geert Hillaert, of CAW,told the news outlet HLN. “Ultimately, only the walls will remain. Labourers were laying drainage pipes when they stumbled across the gold.”Kobe and his colleagues called the police and notified CAW as soon as they came across the gold hoard. The treasure has since been transferred to a secure facility in Brussels pending a detailed official investigation to establish its legal ownership.Hanne Ollevier, of the East Flanders public prosecutor’s office, told HLN that authorities must first verify that the bullion was not stolen property or the proceeds of criminal activity, and was likely to spark a complex civil dispute.View image in fullscreenBelgian law requires finders to wait at least five years for potential owners to claim any treasure.Photograph: Facebook/Dendermonde Local PoliceThe building contractors, the welfare organisation and any descendants of the once-wealthy Van Assche family could all have a claim to part of the fortune. Belgian law requires finders to wait at least five years for potential owners to claim any treasure.A former mayor of Dendermonde,Piet Buyse, told HLNthat the Van Assche’s fortune had “certainly stayed in the family. It wouldn’t surprise me at all if they had decided to put at least some of it in gold, and then to hide it in a safe place.”For his part, Kobe said he and his colleagues had understood straight away that they had to hand over such a big find. “If it had been a few coins, maybe not,” he said. “But maybe we’ll get some kind of finder’s reward eventually.”Explore more on these topicsBelgiumEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Students squeezed out of university courses after bumper A-level grades | Admissions | The Guardian
description: Students narrowly missing grades are being rejected, while some on oversubscribed courses are asked to defer
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Students narrowly missing grades are being rejected, while some on oversubscribed courses are asked to defer
Content: Cardiff University has asked ‘a small number’ of students on two programmes to defer until 2027.Photograph: Matthew Horwood/AlamyView image in fullscreenCardiff University has asked ‘a small number’ of students on two programmes to defer until 2027.Photograph: Matthew Horwood/AlamyAdmissionsStudents squeezed out of university courses after bumper A-level gradesStudents narrowly missing grades are being rejected, while some on oversubscribed courses are asked to deferRichard AdamsEducation editorFri 14 Aug 2026 11.54 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 18.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStudents across the UK have found themselves unexpectedly squeezed out of their desired university courses as this year’sbumper crop of A-level grades​h​as not always translated into ​​the places many were hoping for.​With close to a third of the A-levels awarded in England, Wales andNorthern Irelandachieving the top A and A* grades this year, universities are taking a tougher stance by rejecting students who narrowly missed their expected grades and who in previous years would still have gained a place.The stronger competition has tipped record numbers of applicants into clearing, or settling for their second choices, with universities in some cases wanting students to defer for a year.Cardiff ​University ​h​as asked students on two programmes to defer until 2027, after more than expected achieved their required grades, leaving it with a surplus of qualified applicants for courses such as midwifery.​The university said it had asked “a small number” of applicants to defer, with limits on its intake previously agreed with the Welsh government.“We understand this will be deeply disappointing for those affected, and our immediate priority is to support these students and ensure they receive clear guidance as they consider their next steps,” a spokesperson for Cardiff said.“It is important to be clear thatCardiff Universityhas not over-offered places. As with all universities, offers are made based on detailed modelling of applicant behaviour and historical acceptance patterns. This year, an exceptionally high number of applicants met the conditions of their offers and accepted places, resulting in demand exceeding the number of commissioned places available.“This has been an extremely difficult decision … and we explored every possible option to avoid activating the university’s oversubscription policy for these two courses.”At least one applicant said she had complained to the Office for Students,telling Wales Onlinethat Cardiff had offered her a £750 bursary to defer or lose her place. The Office for Students does not regulate universities in Wales.View image in fullscreenGeography course closures have been announced at Exeter’s Cornwall campus, with students told to change courses or move to the Devon campus (pictured).Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianUcas figures show that this year, 73% of students inEngland, Wales and Northern Ireland were given firm offers after grades were issued, below the 76% with firm offers in 2024 and 2025. A record 23,000 students have already deferred their places this year.Figures published on Friday show record numbers of students were eligible for clearing, the post-results process to apply for courses with unfilled places.UK universities face ‘financial crisis’ amid collapse in international studentsRead moreThe proportion of applicants receiving their first-choice course offer was lower this year at 79%, compared with 82% last year, while the proportion placed at their “insurance” choice increased.The competition for places has increased as a result of selective universities growing less slowly than last year, despite record numbers of applications. While selective universities received almost 10% more applications this year, the universities have only increased offers by 5% compared with 2025.The swathe of course closures and staff cuts set off by university restructuring has also affected students. Those offered places on geography courses at the University of Exeter’s Cornwall campus near Falmouthhave now been toldto either change courses or be moved to Exeter’s main campus in Devon, after the course closures were suddenly announced on Thursday.Explore more on these topicsAdmissionsStudentsHigher educationUniversitiesA-levelsCardiff UniversityWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump downplays concerns about sailors onboard USS Abraham Lincoln amid record deployment | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: President said nine months at sea ‘not nearly long enough’ even as families call for attention to mental health crisis
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: President said nine months at sea ‘not nearly long enough’ even as families call for attention to mental health crisis
Content: The USS Abraham Lincoln has been supporting the US war against Iran.Photograph: Abaca/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe USS Abraham Lincoln has been supporting the US war against Iran.Photograph: Abaca/ShutterstockDonald TrumpTrump downplays concerns about sailors onboard USS Abraham Lincoln amid record deploymentPresident said nine months at sea ‘not nearly long enough’ even as families call for attention to mental health crisisMarina DunbarandJoseph GedeonFri 14 Aug 2026 18.12 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has downplayed concerns about US sailors enduring a record-setting deployment of nearly nine months onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln on Friday, saying the deployment was “not nearly long enough” as concerns mount over mental health and supply issues onboard the aircraft carrier.The US president made the comments during a brief exchange with reporters before flying toNew Yorkfor an event highlighting falling violent crime rates across the US.“That ship is moving right now, or very shortly, and it’s being replaced with another very similar ship,” Trump said when asked about the lengthy deployment. When asked by reporters whether family members were worried about the situation, the president claimed: “No, they’re not.”The Lincoln has been supporting the US war against Iran, and several Democratic lawmakers are pressing the Pentagon for accountability over conditions onboard the carrier. The defense secretary,Pete Hegseth, on Thursday said those conditions had been “completely misrepresented”.Trump orders Pentagon to redesign US aircraft carrier to use steam catapults to launch jetsRead moreMilitary families and US Congress members have called attention to the intensifying mental health crisis for those onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, as its 5,000 sailors and marines endure a record-breaking deployment at sea tied to the war with Iran.The scrutiny comes as the navy hasreimposed a blockadeon Iranian ports in the crucial strait of Hormuz, even as hostilities between the US and Iran have calmed in recent weeks. The Trump administration has offered no clarity on how it intends to wind down the war, while Hegseth has suggested the US military can maintain the blockage of Iranian ports “indefinitely”.Another aircraft carrier, the USS George Washington, left port in Da Nang, Vietnam, last week and is expected to replace the Lincoln, one of two aircraft carriers currently deployed in the Middle East.Two leading specialist military papers, theNavy TimesandStars and Stripes, reported that there have been multiple attempts by sailors tojump overboardas poor conditions and mental stresses on the Lincoln reach a breaking point in its ninth month at sea.One sailor succeeded in early August, a US official confirmed. “The sailor was quickly recovered by an air wing search and rescue helicopter, treated by Abraham Lincoln’s medical department, and transferred off ship for follow-on care.”Worried families expressed their concerns about loved ones onboard the Lincoln at an emotional town hall meeting with navy leaders in San Diego last week, Stars and Stripes reported. One spouse among the 200 or so family members said that her husband had texted her that day saying “he hopes he doesn’t wake up tomorrow”.The US navy said it has “not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship”, but declined to provide data, citing operational security and patient privacy concerns.The Lincoln is “operating in a highly contested environment where traditional supply hubs in the Middle East were disrupted by combat actions”, the US official said, adding that navy leaders had “prioritized mission-critical supplies: first food, then hygiene items, then mail”.“Current reports from the ship confirm continuous access to clean water, functional [air conditioning], and healthy meal options,” the official claimed.In astatementreleased on Friday, Hung Cao, the acting secretary of the navy, similarly downplayed the reports, saying that “sailors and marines are expected to dig deep” and accused the media of “trying to paint our warriors as victims”.The statement acknowledged that a “small number” of mental health cases were “treated with no loss of life”, and added that “there is no question our young men and women have been pushed to their limits”.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpUS militaryPete HegsethUS politicsTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: At least six people dead and one wounded in mass shooting in rural Michigan | Michigan | The Guardian
description: Suspected gunman fled the scene, prompting a manhunt, before he and another individual were found deceased
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Suspected gunman fled the scene, prompting a manhunt, before he and another individual were found deceased
Content: The shooting happened in a rural area of northern Michigan.Photograph: Westend61/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe shooting happened in a rural area of northern Michigan.Photograph: Westend61/Getty ImagesMichiganAt least six people dead and one wounded in mass shooting in rural MichiganSuspected gunman fled the scene, prompting a manhunt, before he and another individual were found deceasedUwa Ede-OsifoFri 14 Aug 2026 19.32 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 19.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA mass shooting on Friday has left six people dead, including the suspected gunman, in Missaukee county, a rural area of northernMichigan, according to state police. Another person is in critical condition at a local hospital.Michigan state police identified the suspected gunman as 39-year-old Chad Hickman ina statementposted on social media.Hickman fled the scene, prompting a manhunt, the police said. The Missaukee county sheriff’s office hadappealed to the publicfor help in locating the “armed and dangerous” Hickman, before he was located by state police.Investigators tracked Hickman’s vehicle to a wooded area, where he and another individual were found deceased. It is unclear what circumstances led up to the shooting.“This situation is heartbreaking for the community and challenging for the investigators involved,” said Lt Ashley Miller, a Michigan state police spokesperson. “We remain committed to conducting a thorough investigation and will provide updates as new information becomes available.”Court records indicate Hickman was in the process of a divorce. He also had been sentenced to more than a year in county jail, after pleading guilty in 2024 to two misdemeanors. He was charged with contributing to the delinquency of a child and child abuse in the fourth degree, which can mean under state law a reckless act that harmed or endangered a minor. Both charges dated back to a 2010 offense.More details soon ...Explore more on these topicsMichiganGun crimeUS crimeShareReuse this content

title: Putin’s recruiters scramble to avoid second mass mobilisation as Ukraine losses mount  | Russia | The Guardian
description: Russia is losing 30,000 casualties a month, and the country’s regions are under pressure to feed the ‘meat-grinder’. Experts say it may not be enough
Author: Pjotr Sauer
Headline: Russia is losing 30,000 casualties a month, and the country’s regions are under pressure to feed the ‘meat-grinder’. Experts say it may not be enough
Content: With Putin showing no sign of abandoning his far-reaching territorial demands, even as Russia’s summer offensive stalls, the Kremlin faces a growing manpower headache.Photograph: Igor Ivanko/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWith Putin showing no sign of abandoning his far-reaching territorial demands, even as Russia’s summer offensive stalls, the Kremlin faces a growing manpower headache.Photograph: Igor Ivanko/AFP/Getty ImagesRussiaPutin’s recruiters scramble to avoid second mass mobilisation as Ukraine losses mountRussia is losing 30,000 casualties a month, and the country’s regions are under pressure to feed the ‘meat-grinder’. Experts say it may not be enoughPjotr SauerFri 14 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 14.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn kitchens and Telegram chats across Russia, the same question is being asked with growing frequency: willVladimir Putinorder another mobilisation?Nearly five years into the war, Russia is scrambling to find enough soldiers to replenish its ranks, as voluntary recruitment slows and its forces suffer heavy losses on the battlefield inUkraine.With Putin showing no sign of abandoning his far-reaching territorial demands, even as Russia’s summer offensive stalls, the Kremlin faces a growing manpower headache.“The problem for the Kremlin is that it is getting much harder to find people willing to fight, even for crazy money,” said Aleksei Tabalov, a human rights activist and director of an organisation that helps Russian conscripts.Putin lastresorted to mobilisationin September 2022, when a series of dramatic battlefield setbacks forced the Kremlin to call up 300,000 reservists to stabilise the front.View image in fullscreenA billboard advertising ‘contract military service’ beside a highway outside Krasnodar, Russia.Photograph: APSince then, Moscow has avoided another deeply unpopular call-up by relying largely on high paid voluntary contracts to fill the ranks with roughly 1.3 million contract soldiers Russia has recruited since.Men, particularly from Russia’s poorer regions, have been offered life-changing signing bonuses and salaries on open-ended contracts amounting to several years of local wages, alongside substantial payouts to their families if they are killed.But Russia’s heavy losses mean it must continue finding new soldiers at a high rate.Western estimates put Russian casualties atmore than 30,000killed and wounded a month, a toll that reflects the army’s attritional “meat grinder” tactics, in which troops are repeatedly sent forward in small assault groups despite heavy losses.Moscow, meanwhile, now recruits roughly 1,000 soldiers a day, according to calculations by Janis Kluge, a Russia expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, which means most new recruits are used to replenish depleted units rather than expand Russia’s offensive capacity.That has once again raised the prospect of mobilisation.Top Russian officials have dismissed reports of an impending call-up, with former president Dmitry Medvedev describing them as “nonsense” and a “lying provocation” by Ukraine.Two people familiar with discussions in Moscow also said there was no indication that Putin had decided to order another mass mobilisation. A senior western official likewise said there were no signs that a decision had been taken.View image in fullscreenA firefighting helicopter drops water over a food warehouse damaged during Russian drone strikes near Kyiv, 12 August 2026.Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/ReutersBut fears that another call-up may be on the way have nevertheless increasingly entered everyday conversations.In Telegram chats used by local sports teams, work colleagues and groups of friends, Russians swap rumours about a possible mobilisation and share advice on securing exemptions or avoiding the draft. Some speculate that a new call-up could come after September’s elections to the Duma.“It’s guesswork right now whether mobilisation will actually happen,” said Ivan Chuviliaev, a spokesperson for Get Lost, a group that helps Russian soldiers desert.But he said the renewed speculation was already being exploited to boost recruitment.“The panic around mobilisation is being used by officials to pressure men into signing contracts,” Chuviliaev said. “The message is: mobilisation is coming anyway, so you might as well sign a contract now and get a payout before you’re forced to fight.”View image in fullscreenPutin recently signed a law expanding the pool of convicted prisoners eligible to sign contracts with the army.Photograph: Russian President official/APAImages/ShutterstockFor now, people familiar with the Kremlin’s thinking say the authorities appear determined to strong-arm more men into signing contracts rather than risk another mobilisation.Over the summer, lawyers and activists have documented increasingly coercive recruitment tactics in several regions, with men detained on the street by police, taken from workplaces or summoned to stations – before being brought to military recruitment offices and pressed to sign contracts.“It has turned into a hunt for people,” said Tabalov. “Under various pretexts, through deception, blackmail, violence and threats, they are forcing them to sign contracts.”Tabalov said recruiters were increasingly targeting what he described as “socially marginalised” men, including those with debts, criminal cases or other vulnerabilities that could be used to put pressure on them to enlist.In the southern Penza region, where some of the most aggressive draft methods have been reported, videos posted online have shown men being driven away in vans as relatives protested outside recruitment offices. Activists say some have been threatened with prosecution or beaten until they agreed to sign.The search has widened elsewhere too. Universities, technical colleges and vocational schools have been encouraged to recruit students into newly formed drone units, offering another source of manpower for the military. Putin recently signed a law expanding the pool of convicted prisoners eligible to sign contracts with the army, including people convicted of “serious and especially serious crimes”.Much of the responsibility for finding soldiers has been pushed down to Russia’s regions.Governors and local administrations are expected to meet recruitment targets set by Moscow, giving the Kremlin some distance from the drive while leaving regional officials responsible for finding enough men in their own territories.Around that system, a lucrative recruitment industry has emerged. Regional governments offer thousands of dollars not only to soldiers who sign contracts but also to those who find them, with “bring a friend” schemes paying residents for every person they persuade to enlist.View image in fullscreenSmoke rises from an oil refinery after a Ukrainian drone attack in Moscow, 18 June 2026.Photograph: Social Media/ReutersPrivate recruiters and public-sector employees scour social media for candidates, while advertisements for military contracts have become ubiquitous online. Russian regions have paid recruiters at least 7.7bn roubles ($96m) since such schemes were introduced,according to the independent Russian outlet IStories.One recruiter in central Russia, speaking to the Guardian on condition of anonymity, said his organisation was expected to find between 20 and 30 men each month, with bonuses for exceeding the target and penalties for falling short.“It was easier last year,” the recruiter said. “Now it is getting harder.”The recruiter said mobilisation was also being discussed in his office, but that there had been no orders or indications that a new draft was imminent.Another mass call-up, however, would carry significant political risks for the Kremlin.The 2022 call-up triggered one of the biggest episodes of domestic disruption since the invasion began,prompting a mass exodusof Russians and a sharp drop in Putin’s approval ratings.It would also come at a potentially sensitive moment. Recent polling suggests confidence in the course of the war is weakening, with the share of Russians who believe the campaign in Ukraine is going wellfalling to its lowest levelsince April 2022.For now, analysts say Moscow is more likely to step up recruitment efforts through higher bonuses, pressure on regional officials and increasingly coercive tactics.Whether that will be enough could ultimately determine if Putin resorts to another mobilisation, said Tabalov, the activist.The options before the Kremlin, Tabalov said, could range from another mass call-up to a more selective mobilisation, sending existing conscripts to the front or quietly calling up reservists for frontline service.“I don’t think they’ll be able to recruit enough people under the current system,” Tabalov said. “Then they’ll be faced with the question of what form mobilisation should take.”Explore more on these topicsRussiaUkraineVladimir PutinEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Iberian orca known for ramming boats seen with suspected gunshot wounds | Whales | The Guardian
description: Marine conservationist says deliberate attack would be ‘act of extreme cruelty’ against endangered population
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: Marine conservationist says deliberate attack would be ‘act of extreme cruelty’ against endangered population
Content: Toñi, the oldest orca in her pod, has been seen with markings on her dorsal fin that suggest pellet gun fire.Photograph: Cristina Otero Sabio/WeWhale.org and Iberian Orcas GuardiansView image in fullscreenToñi, the oldest orca in her pod, has been seen with markings on her dorsal fin that suggest pellet gun fire.Photograph: Cristina Otero Sabio/WeWhale.org and Iberian Orcas GuardiansWhalesIberian orca known for ramming boats seen with suspected gunshot woundsMarine conservationist says deliberate attack would be ‘act of extreme cruelty’ against endangered populationAshifa Kassamin MadridFri 14 Aug 2026 11.07 EDTFirst published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 10.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpanish officials have launched an investigation after the matriarch of an orca pod known for jostling and ramming boats off the Iberian Peninsula was spotted with wounds suggesting she had been shot by a pellet gun.On Friday, Spain’s environment ministry said Toñi, the oldest living member of the pod,had been seen swimmingin the Strait of Gibraltar with markings on her dorsal fin that were “consistent with shots from a pellet gun”.Humpbacks return to Rio: the whales are back from the brink of extinction – but will tourism help or hinder?Read moreA source from the ministrytold El Paísthat some of the projectiles remained lodged in her fin, posing a risk of infection. The ministry was in touch with officials in Portugal, the source added, as the markings were detected after the orcas had travelled from the waters off the Portuguese city of Faro.The orcas of the Iberian Peninsulaburst into headlinesin 2020 after sailors shared stories of rudders that had been rammed and boats that had been spun 180 degrees or tipped sideways. Since then, a small group of orcas from the pod have been blamed for damaging scores of vessels and sinking at least four boats, leaving scientists scrambling to explain the baffling behaviour.Scientists have long pushed back against the assertion that the orcas are attacking vessels, instead suggesting that the behaviour could be a form of play or a means of practising their hunting skills.In the days since Toñi’s injuries came to light, the WeWhale and Iberian Orca Guardians (IOG) association have been closely tracking the animal for any sign of weakness. “We know Toñi. We were with her a few weeks ago and these wounds were not there,” the IOG co-founder Janek Andre said.“Seeing Toñi,laabuela[the grandmother], like this is devastating,” he added. “If someone has deliberately fired a shotgun at her, this is not only an act of extreme cruelty against an individual animal. It is an attack on one of the last remaining members of a critically endangered population.”Researchers have long sought to highlight the many stressors faced by this population of orcas as they navigate life in a major shipping route. Food scarcity, injuries and pollution have left the population on a knife’s edge, reduced to between 30 and 40 individuals.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn 2023, video emerged thatappeared to show people launchingfirecrackers into the sea as orcas rammed the rudder of their vessel, hinting that the animals were now facing another threat as sailors push back against their actions.“There has been enormous public discussion about Iberian orcas and their interactions with vessels,” said Andre. “Whatever someone’s opinion about those interactions may be, shooting at these animals can never be an acceptable response. These orcas need protection, not retaliation.”Explore more on these topicsWhalesSpainEuropeCetaceansMarine lifeWildlifenewsShareReuse this content

title: El Niño may peak at the worst time for the Amazon – and it should worry us all | Amazon rainforest | The Guardian
description: Delay to rainy season in forest already damaged by human-driven heating could trigger powerful ‘Godzilla’ El Niño
Author: Jonathan Watts
Headline: Delay to rainy season in forest already damaged by human-driven heating could trigger powerful ‘Godzilla’ El Niño
Content: Fires burn along the Trans-Amazonian highway near the Aripuana national forest in the state of Amazonas, Brazil, in 2021.Photograph: Lynsey Addario/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFires burn along the Trans-Amazonian highway near the Aripuana national forest in the state of Amazonas, Brazil, in 2021.Photograph: Lynsey Addario/Getty ImagesView from the AmazonAmazon rainforestAnalysisEl Niño may peak at the worst time for the Amazon – and it should worry us allJonathan WattsDelay to rainy season in forest already damaged by human-driven heating could trigger powerful ‘Godzilla’ El NiñoFri 14 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTShareAs a supercharged climate scorchesEurope with wildfireand delugesAsia with floods, the Amazon is bracing for a drought that strikes fear into the hearts of forest defenders and food producers alike. But it should worry even more of us.Scientists arepredicting that the peakof El Niño will occur at the worst possible time for the world’s biggest tropical rainforest: the end of the dry season between October and December, when rivers are at their lowest and undergrowth is most likely to be tinder dry. This will be a period of extreme vulnerability for the forest, which plays a globally important role in stabilising the climate and irrigating crops.The planet’s life-support system is already reeling from a double whammy. Human-driven climate disruption, caused by burning fossil fuels and trees, is relentlessly heating the world and amplifying extreme weather events, such as heatwaves and storms. On top of this long-term trend is the latest El Niño, a naturally occurring phenomenon of high Pacific Ocean temperatures that leads to warming – and drought and fire – for much of the rest of the world.View image in fullscreenFirefighters battling a major wildfire burning through a pine forest in the Gironde department of France in July.Photograph: Le Gonidec Margot/Abaca/ShutterstockScientists say this El Niño is on course to be the strongest in 150 years by a“mind-blowing margin.”Even in its incipient phase, it is wreaking havoc havoc across the planet.Western Europe has endured the hottest June and July in history, with exceptionally low rainfall, sparking extreme wildfires in France, Greece and other Mediterranean countries and water shortages in the Seine, Rhine and Danube basins. Three-quarters of Englandis in droughtand baked by what is forecast to be thehottest UK summeron record.Forecast maximum temperatures for 13 August 2026In Asia, South Korea and Japan are sweltering ina record heatwave, while China has beenbattered by Typhoon Dolphin, which has turned Shanghai’s streets into rivers, torn roofs from houses and forced the evacuation of more than 1 million people. Floods have killed more than 100 peoplein India’s Assam state, with more rain forecast.View image in fullscreenFlooding in Wenzhou, in China’s Zhejiang province, after Typhoon Dolphin made landfall on Sunday.Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesSwathes of the world are burning. In Canada,“out of control” wildfireshave forced tens of thousands to flee British Colombia and darkened the skies of distant New York. Huge fires are also raging on Java Island in Indonesia and Utah in the US, which has also been scorched by a recordJuly heatwave.In Africa, the UN is predicting a severe hit to food production. In the Middle East, local temperature records are being broken almost every day, with the United Arab Emirates registering 51.2C in Al Dhafra.A line graphic show daily global sea temperatures between 1991 and 2026Meanwhile,sea surface temperaturesare trending far outside previous parameters, threatening coral reefs and other marine life. Because the oceans arethe world’s main heat absorber, their temperatures are a prelude to what follows on land.But among the greatest concerns about what comes next is the Amazon, which is essential for maintaining biodiversity and ensuring rainfall for food-producing regions across South America.View image in fullscreenThe Curuá River, an Amazon tributary, flows through Caxiuanã national forest in Brazil.Photograph: Jorge Sáenz/APA few decades ago, the idea of drought in the rainforest would have seemed outlandish. The Amazon is the world’s biggest river and its principal tributaries – the Xingu, Negro, Tapajós, Madeira, Purus, Juruá and Japurá –are among the planet’s main sources of freshwater. The forest around them has always been famed for humidity, with giant trees that sucked up moisture and pumped it into the atmosphere, generating “flying rivers” that cooled and watered an entire continent. The trillions of trees and plants in the Amazon also draw down huge quantities of carbon dioxide with benefits to the entire planet. Anyweakening of this functionadds to the risks of instability, food insecurity and extreme weather.Now, theBrazilian meteorological agency has released a forecastthat the unusually strong El Niño will delay the onset of the Amazonian rainy season, raise temperatures, deplete rivers and intensify fire risks.A line graph showing average daily temperatures from January to December for 1979 through to 2026As in many other parts of the planet, this creates an emergency within an emergency: the onset of a natural but extremely powerful “Godzilla” El Niño that could last well into the new year, on top of human-driven warming.Scientists and Indigenous residents say the Amazon isstruggling to recoverfrom the devastation caused during the last El Niño in 2023-24, which left some of the world’s greatest rivers at record-low levels, sparkedunprecedented fire outbreaksand causedmass deaths of dolphinsand fish.With a third of the Amazon now degraded by farming, mining and human-caused climate disruption, the trees and undergrowth are more flammable and vulnerable to“megafires,”raising concerns that many parts may tip beyond thepoint of no return.View image in fullscreenHouses and boats stranded along a dried-up Negro River, a major Amazon tributary, in Brazil’s Amazonas state in October 2023.Photograph: Michael Dantas/AFP/Getty ImagesThe government is trying to address this with satellite monitoring, enforcement operations andgreater investment in firefighting capacity. This produced positive results last year, when the burned areas of the Amazonfell to their lowest levelsince records began in 1985.But one year is not long enough for the forest to recover, and it now faces a far greater threat.Three previous El Ninõs (1997-98, 2015-16 and 2023-24) proved disastrous for the Amazon. Prof Jos Barlow, an Amazon specialist at the Lancaster Environment Centre, said the prospect of a still stronger phenomenon was deeply worrying: “It is hard to imagine the outcome of even more severe droughts and heat.”The Amazon fire season has already started but the peak is still a couple of months away.Indigenous communities are setting up their own firefighting units to cope with outbreaks in deeper parts of the forest. Dr Erika Berenguer, a forest expert at Oxford University and author of a book on how to deal with rainforest fires, said: “It’s crazy. The humid forest should not be burning.”A major part of the problem, Berenguer said, was multiple El Niños hitting in a relatively short space of time: “It’s similar to if you are already sick and then you get an infection. That infection is going to have much greater impacts on your body because your immune system is already compromised fighting the sickness.”View image in fullscreenFields and rainforest burning uncontrollably in the Amazon in October 2023.Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty ImagesThe brutal conditions are likely to drag on – and possibly intensify – in 2027 because there is alag of about three monthsbetween the peak of El Niño warming in the Pacific Ocean and temperature rises elsewhere in the world.Carlos Nobre, a professor at the University of São Paulo and one of Brazil’s leading climate scientists, said: “The Amazon has to be very prepared from now through the beginning of 2027, at least up to March, because this El Niño is very likely to induce a severe drought.”Farmers are bracing for a turbulent year. “Fellow ranchers, GET READY FOR EL NIÑO,” reads a post on a popular WhatsApp group for beef producers in the Amazonian state of Pará. “El Niño will impact Brazilian cattle farming by causing heat stress in animals, reducing pasture quality, and leading to ‘water scarcity’. This drives up supplementation costs and can reduce weight gain and milk production.”Other agricultural businesses post apocalyptic images of parched soil or flooded cities (the south of Brazil is forecast to get much more rain). “The 2026 Super El Niño has evolved from a mere weather phenomenon into a symbol for a new era of global instability,” warns one post.The industry magazineAgrofortereports that Brazil’s soya bean harvests have fallen during previous strong El Niño years, but omits any mention of the human causes for the more hostile climate: deforestation – usually by farmers – and the burning of fossil fuels.View image in fullscreenA soya harvest at a farm near Senador Guiomard, Acre state, Brazil.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesIndigenous groups, in contrast, tend to preserve the forest and help to maintain a stable climate – but they, too, face the triple threats of a global heating, forest clearance and El Niño.The government has warned that traditional lands will face increased fire risks, and has stockpiled food in case of shortages. During the previous El Niño, some forest communities in the Xingu and Tapajós basins were left isolated, thirsty and worried about hunger when rivers – the main transportation route – ran dry and vegetable gardens shrivelled up. Anything worse next year and Brazil could face the apocalyptic scenario of drought refugees in a rainforest.That this is even a possibility should alarm the world. A severely weakened Amazon will further disrupt the climate and agricultural production at a time when farmers across many parts of the world are already saying thatchanges are too quickfor them to adapt. Global food prices are at a three-year high as falling harvests combine with the fuel inflation caused by the US-Israeli attack on Iran. The UN is predicting that49 million more people are likely to face acute hungerbecause of El Niño.Much more needs to be done to protect biomes such as the Amazon, on which the world depends. Investing more in firefighters is a necessary short-term step, but it only deals with the consequences rather than the local and global causes. Unless deforestation is halted and fossils fuels are phased out, the atmosphere will continue to warm and amplify extreme weather. Even this year’s Godzilla El Niño will seem like a pussycat compared with what is coming.Explore more on these topicsAmazon rainforestView from the AmazonEl Niño southern oscillationTrees and forestsFood securityDroughtClimate crisisExtreme weatheranalysisShareReuse this content

title: ‘They do look majestic’: tears and pride as first white storks set free in Cornwall | Birds | The Guardian
description: Twenty-one birds released on Bodmin Moor where it is hoped they will one day return to produce their own young
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Twenty-one birds released on Bodmin Moor where it is hoped they will one day return to produce their own young
Content: One of the storks in the air after its release. Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianTwenty-one birds released on Bodmin Moor where it is hoped they will one day return to produce their own youngBySteven Morris; photographs by Jim WilemanFri 14 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThey took a little coaxing at first – after all, they had got used to a safe, comfortable aviary tucked away in woodland on the edge of Bodmin Moor. But after a few minutes, the birds stepped out into freedom and the bolder ones were soon soaring into the blue, the first white storks to be released into the wilds ofCornwall.Yan Swiderski, the founder ofthe Cornwall Stork Project, had tears in his eyes. “I do feel a bit emotional,” he said. He sounded a little like a proud father wanting to play down the achievements of his offspring – and failing. “They’re a little bit clumsy at the moment. They aren’t used to flying free … but they do look majestic, don’t they?”Stork released in CornwallTwenty-one white storks, most of whom hatched on the moor this year, were released on Thursday. They will probably spend a couple of months in Cornwall getting used to freedom before heading south for the winter, perhaps to southern Spain or Morocco.If all goes well, they will return in a few years’ time to the area where they hatched and produce their own young. “That will be so exciting,” Swiderski said.View image in fullscreenThe storks in their enclosure before releaseView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenThe project is based atHamatethy farm, which produces organic beef and pork but also runs rewilding schemes. Its stork project began in 2021 and it now has five pairs of adults that were either rescued or bred in captivity.Swiderski, a fund manager turned farmer, said it was not possible simply to release any oldwhite storkinto a landscape as it would try to return to the place where it was born.Storks in Hamatethy farm“The way to do it is to set up breeding aviaries. You can then release the chicks that are born in those aviaries. They’re like swallows, they have a very strong homing instinct, so they will migrate in the autumn, then hopefully come back and nest pretty much where they came from.”The project follows the model establishedat the Knepp estatein West Sussex, which has been operating since 2016 and has successfully reintroduced storks. It is possible the Bodmin storks will team up with the Knepp ones to fly away for winter.View image in fullscreenJan Swiderski speaking at the eventView image in fullscreenStaff at Hamathey farm listen to SwiderskiNatural England, the government’s adviser for the natural environment in England, does not sound very enthusiastic about white stork releases, though it says they are not banned. It argues thatneither white nor black storkswere ever native breeding birds in England.It said there was one breeding record of the white stork in Scotland in 1416 and records of imports of storks from Calais in the 16th century.While recognising the value of white storks as a visible and charismatic species in engaging people, NaturalEnglandsaid releases of white storks “are not a priority for us”.View image in fullscreenStorks after being released from the enclosureView image in fullscreenSwiderski said: “To head off any controversy about native versus non-native, I think the important point here is that with climate change, the European natural range of birds is moving northward. We can point to the European bee-eater, the glossy ibis, the pallid harrier.”Swiderski was distracted as one of the storks came in low over the trees. “I don’t think I’ll get tired of the sight of them – they’re so brilliant,” he said.There was a tense moment when a crow appeared to be alarmed at the sight of a stork in its airspace and swooped in close, but nothing came of the confrontation.View image in fullscreenOne of the storks flying highView image in fullscreenCapturing the big momentSwiderski said upland Cornwall was a decent habitat for white storks. “Bodmin Moor is good in the sense that you’re not in the middle of a chemical landscape. They just need healthy soils, earthworms and insects and a bit of wetland here and there,” he said.“People sometimes ask me what the ecological function of a white stork is and my answer is always that they engage humans with nature. If you can interest people in birds like storks – what they eat, where they come from, where they go – you can have all those conversations about healthy soils, the importance of organic farming for insects, the importance of not overgrazing for small mammal populations, thriving wetlands. And that is worth a lot.”Explore more on these topicsBirdsWildlifeCornwallEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Police Scotland warns ‘robust security’ needed to stop attacks on AI datacentres | Scotland | The Guardian
description: ‘A great deal of public opposition is likely’ to a proposed datacentre near Edinburgh, the force says
Author: Aisha Down
Headline: ‘A great deal of public opposition is likely’ to a proposed datacentre near Edinburgh, the force says
Content: A protest on Thursday in Larbert, about 30 miles west of Edinburgh, is said by campaigners to have been attended by more than 100 people.Photograph: Larbert residents groupView image in fullscreenA protest on Thursday in Larbert, about 30 miles west of Edinburgh, is said by campaigners to have been attended by more than 100 people.Photograph: Larbert residents groupScotlandPolice Scotland warns ‘robust security’ needed to stop attacks on AI datacentres‘A great deal of public opposition is likely’ to a proposed datacentre near Edinburgh, the force saysAisha DownFri 14 Aug 2026 12.05 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 14.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice inScotlandhave issued a stark warning about the need for “robust security measures” to stop proposed AI datacentres from being attacked by protesters.There has been mounting opposition to AI infrastructure globally, including in the US where such projects have become asignificant political rallying point.Police Scotland said “a great deal of public opposition is likely” to a datacentreplanned in Larbert, about 30 miles west of Edinburgh, in a letter submitted as a part of a planning consultation this month.The letter encouraged the datacentre’s developer to liaise with the police to prevent “unplanned incursions for the purposes of disruption”.‘It’s smoke and mirrors’: hope turns to fear in Scottish village chosen for AI datacentreRead moreIt appears to be one of the first official acknowledgments ofmounting public uneaseabout datacentre development in the UK. Police Scotland declined to comment.There are hundreds of datacentre projects in various stages of planning in Britain. Only some of these appear to be viable developments, with research groups warning of a glut of“zombie projects”waiting to connect to the grid.In Scotland there are at least 23 “hyperscale” datacentre developments in the planning process, according to the Edinburgh-based charity Action to Protect Rural Scotland (APRS). Combined, they would use more than one and a half times the power that Scotland uses at peak demand.View image in fullscreenNearly 7,000 people have filed objections to the proposed datacentre in Larbert.Photograph: Larbert residents groupGroups across Scotland have started organising opposition to planned datacentres. More than 100 people attended a protest in Larbert on Thursday, according to local campaigners. Nearly 7,000 people have filed objections to the proposed development.Similar protests are planned in the coming weeks, including one in Edinburgh in early September, when the Scottish parliament will be back in session.This summer, the Scottish National party passed a motion tofreeze all new datacentresin Scotland. If that motion becomes Scottish government policy, it could pose a serious threat tothe UK’s AI strategy. British officials have been pushing datacentre developers to build in Scotland.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRevealed: landmark Scottish AI project has no prospect of meeting renewables promiseRead moreSome of the opposition to datacentres is about the physical footprint of the projects. Michael Maciocia, a Larbert resident who attended Thursday’s protest, said he and others were worried about the 200 diesel generators that Apatura, the site’s developer,planned to installas backup power for the datacentre.APRS is concernedthat these could release significant quantities of nitrous oxide into the air, which could negatively affect the health of people living nearby.“Where this datacentre is planned to be built, within 50 metres of one of the buildings is a 56-bed care home for the terminally ill … Within 400 metres, there’s the 860-bed Forth Valley Royal hospital,” said Maciocia. “The amount of pollution and the noise created by these things will be horrendous in every direction.”View image in fullscreenCampaigners in Larbert are concerned about the potential health and environmental impacts of the proposed datacentre.Photograph: Larbert residents groupHazel McQueen, who also lives nearby, said: “I live extremely close to the proposed site, and since this application was submitted it has become a huge part of my life.” She says she has spent hours on top of her full-time job reading about the datacentre, attending meetings and helping to organise opposition to it.She says she is concerned for the health of her family, and of her grandson who has leukaemia. “I need to fight this for his future and the future we are leaving for him.”Scotland’s ‘green datacentres’ policy ignores emissions impact of AI, analysis showsRead moreCecilia Rikap, a professor at University College London, says there is a larger, symbolic dimension to public anger around datacentre development.“It’s the physical manifestation of AI, and there is a growing opposition to AI. People are seeing how AI is replacing the good part of their work, people are seeing how AI is undermining younger people’s capacity to think,” she said. “Ultimately, if you want to protest against generative AI or the role of big tech, you would protest at a datacentre. That’s what you can see. All the rest is much more invisible.”A spokesperson for Apatura said: “We’re committed to developing data centres in line with world-leading safety and environmental standards and in compliance with all planning regulations. We recognise that there has been opposition to the planning application and remain committed to working closely with government and local community throughout the planning process to ensure concerns are listened to and carefully considered.”Explore more on these topicsScotlandDatacentres - UKPoliceProtestEdinburghPlanning policyScottish politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: National Rail says heat poses ‘exceptional challenges’ after two trains derail in 24 hours | Rail transport | The Guardian
description: Incident near Essex town of Wickford happens day after two passengers seriously hurt in East Sussex derailment
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: Incident near Essex town of Wickford happens day after two passengers seriously hurt in East Sussex derailment
Content: Rail workers and police officers investigate the scene where a Greater Anglia train derailed near Wickford.Photograph: Lucy North/PAView image in fullscreenRail workers and police officers investigate the scene where a Greater Anglia train derailed near Wickford.Photograph: Lucy North/PARail transportNational Rail says heat poses ‘exceptional challenges’ after two trains derail in 24 hoursIncident near Essex town of Wickford happens day after two passengers seriously hurt in East Sussex derailmentRachel HallFri 14 Aug 2026 13.20 EDTFirst published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 10.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK’s fifth heatwave of the summer has “presented exceptional challenges to the railway”, Network Rail has said, after two trains derailed in less than 24 hours.On Friday, BritishTransportPolice (BTP) confirmed the rear carriages of a Greater Anglia train derailed “in an upright position” at Wickford railway station in Essex, adding that there were no reported injuries. On Thursday, two people were seriously injured when several Southern train carriages left the track near Lewes in East Sussex and ended up on their side, trapping passengers onboard.Martin Frobisher, the group safety and engineering director at Network Rail, said it was “working quickly to understand the situation and to provide assistance where needed”.He urged people to avoid speculating on the causes of the Wickford and Lewes derailments and said that Network Rail would conduct internal investigations to look at causes and factors.The derailed train inEssexwas travelling from Southend to Liverpool Street with about 40 people onboard. It left Rayleigh at 2.06pm but failed to reach Wickford at 2.11pm as planned.View image in fullscreenThe Greater Anglia train derailed near Wickford.Photograph: Lee EastonA post on the National Rail website said all lines were closed between Wickford and Southend Victoria. This meant trains running between London Liverpool Street and Southend Victoria were unable to operate.The Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) said on X that it had deployed inspectors to the site to gather evidence.BTP declared amajor incidenton Thursday afternoon after the derailment near Lewes. About 150 people had been on the service from London Victoria to Eastbourne, which was evacuated. Two people were taken to major trauma centres with severe injuries. BTP said on Friday the injuries were not deemed to be life-threatening.Southern urged customers planning to travel this weekend to check ahead as significant disruption was expected across parts of the network until further notice. Trains are expected to be extremely busy, with customers advised to allow at least one extra hour for their journey.Frobisher said: “The unprecedented hot and dry weather that we have experienced this summer has presented exceptional challenges to the railway. In response, we have taken several additional proactive steps to manage and mitigate the impact on the railway, including closely monitoring the temperature of tracks, implementing speed restrictions where it is appropriate to do so, and planning track renewals around high temperatures.”He added: “We will also conduct our own internal investigations, in which we will look at all possible causes and factors. I appreciate the public will be concerned at the news of two derailments of passenger trains over a short period of time, but I want to reassure them that Britain’s railways still rank among the safest in the world and that safety is always our first consideration on the railway.”View image in fullscreenEmergency services arrive near the scene of the derailment on Friday.Photograph: Lucy North/PAJohn Whitehurst, the chief executive of Greater Thameslink Railway (GTR), which operates Southern, praised four railway workers onboard the Lewes train – the driver, onboard supervisor, a spare driver and an off-duty member of staff – who initial reports suggested had “acted quickly to help make the railway safe and support passengers during the evacuation”.“Their actions are a powerful example of colleagues putting passengers first in very difficult circumstances,” he said.After the incident, Whitehurst insisted the railway was safe in hot weather. He told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that derailments were “incredibly rare”, adding that what happened “was a very serious incident and I’m deeply saddened by it”. He said “a full investigation” was under way with the RAIB.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRichard Bowker, a former chair of the Strategic Rail Authority, told the same programme that the inquiry would look at the effects of heat on the damaged track, including whether the ground below the track had dried out.James MacCleary, the Liberal Democrat MP for Lewes, told Times Radio that concerns had been raised about tracks being “a bit bumpier in recent months” in the area as a result of the sustained heatwaves.View image in fullscreenThe scene of the derailed train in Lewes on Thursday.Photograph: James Manning/PAGareth Dennis, a railway engineer and author of How the Railways Will Fix the Future, said although there was no firm evidence to connect the two derailments, “the likelihood of two similar derailments in the hottest part of the country happening in quick succession without a common cause is extremely low”.He added that there was a high likelihood that the derailments were caused by a track buckle, where steel rails that have expanded in the heat snap into a buckled shape under the wheels of a passing train, though there are other possible causes.Xueyu Geng, a professor in ground engineering at the University of Warwick, said steel rail was known to expand significantly in extreme heat, with a 1C rise in temperature causing approximately 11mm of expansion per kilometre of track.A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “We are aware of a derailment involving a Greater Anglia train near Wickford, Essex. The train is upright, there are no reported injuries and investigators have already been deployed to the site.“Our railways remain amongst the safest in the world and while incidents like this are extremely rare, when they do occur, they are taken very seriously.”Explore more on these topicsRail transportEssexEnglandTransportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cheryl Hall obituary | Television | The Guardian
description: Actor who played Shirley Johnson in the sitcom Citizen Smith, and whose dozens of other roles included EastEnders, Doctor Who and The Bill
Author: Anthony Hayward
Headline: Actor who played Shirley Johnson in the sitcom Citizen Smith, and whose dozens of other roles included EastEnders, Doctor Who and The Bill
Content: Cheryl Hall as Kathleen and David Jason as Shorty Mepstead in Lucky Feller, one of the many sitcoms in which she appeared in her 40 years on screen.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCheryl Hall as Kathleen and David Jason as Shorty Mepstead in Lucky Feller, one of the many sitcoms in which she appeared in her 40 years on screen.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockTelevisionObituaryCheryl Hall obituaryActor who played Shirley Johnson in the sitcom Citizen Smith, and whose dozens of other roles included EastEnders, Doctor Who and The BillAnthony HaywardFri 14 Aug 2026 14.53 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 14.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCheryl Hall, who has died aged 76, was an actor best known for her roles in 1970s sitcoms. As Shirley Johnson in Citizen Smith, she was the girlfriend of Wolfie, the would-be revolutionary leading the Tooting Popular Front with the battle cry “power to the people”.Wolfie Smith, played by Hall’s then husband, the actor Robert Lindsay, and his small “army” of self-styled urban guerrillas, are simply inept, concocting plans such as stealing a Scorpion tank in order to mount an attack on the House of Commons, only to discover that parliament is in recess.Nevertheless, Shirley supports her boyfriend’s ideals while wishing they could settle down together in something resembling her parents’ middle-class lifestyle. Her father, initially played by Artro Morris, and then byPeter Vaughan, is less damning of Wolfie’s Marxist revolutionary politics than of his unemployed status and unkempt hair.The sitcom, beginning in 1977, was written byJohn Sullivanshortly before he created Derek “Del Boy” Trotter, another south London antihero, in Only Fools and Horses.
