Citizen Smith ran for four series, finishing in 1980, but Hall left at the end of the second run in 1979, reportedly frustrated at her character’s lack of comic dialogue.View image in fullscreenCheryl Hall, seated second left, holding a poster with Robert Lindsay, and posing with the rest of the Citizen Smith cast, 1977.Photograph: BBC/AllstarAlthough it did not help Hall’s career, Sullivan later admitted that she was right to be dissatisfied with her Citizen Smith role, and went on to prove he could write comedy for female characters with Just Good Friends (1983-86).Hall’s departure also coincided with the end of her marriage, and she and Lindsay divorced in 1980. Later, ina 2022 interview with Zoe Williamsin the Guardian, Lindsay said it was a result of his obsession with achieving success. “That single-mindedness broke up my first marriage,” he said.Hall was born in Whitechapel, east London, to Lilian (nee Cole), a civil servant at the Royal Courts of Justice, and George Hall, a woodworker and market trader. She was brought up in Bethnal Green and attended Coborn school for girls, Bow, where she appeared in school plays.While studying at the Corona Theatre School in London, she worked as a cleaner to supplement her grant. One day, she glanced up from her work and saw Stewart Granger, the British Hollywood film star, looking down at her. “Starstruck is the only way to describe how I felt,” she recalled. “But, when he heard that I was a drama student, he made me some tea and spent the rest of the afternoon talking about acting.”View image in fullscreenCheryl Hall with Colin Blakely in Tales of the Unexpected, 1981.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockHer early stage appearances included the role of Helen, a schoolgirl, in a 1971 revival ofBarry Reckord’s groundbreaking drama Skyvvers, set in a London comprehensive, at the Royal Court’s Theatre Upstairs.She was already in demand on television by then. Between 1968 and 1971, she appeared as a jobseeker in the ITV schools series You and the World. Then came roles in both dramas and comedies, from Special Branch (in 1969) and On the Buses (in 1971) to Callan (two parts, in 1970 and 1972), Sykes (in 1972) and Albert (also 1972), in which she played Doreen Bissel, the fiancee ofRodney Bewes’s factory worker of the title.Hall lost out to Katy Manning for the part of the Doctor Who companion Jo Grant, alongsideJon Pertwee, but the programme’s producer,Barry Letts, gave her a guest role as Shirna, the assistant to a travelling showman, who rescues Jo in the 1973 adventure Carnival of Monsters. A year later, in the prison drama Within These Walls, Hall played an inmate in the drugs unit.View image in fullscreenCheryl Hall with Martin Shaw in The Villains, 1972.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockBack in sitcoms, she played Sid James’s secretary in 1974 episodes of Bless This House, then Kathleen, the girlfriend of a shy plumber, Shorty Mepstead (David Jason), who lives with his mother, in both series of Lucky Feller (1975-76). As Shorty’s girlfriend, she also has eyes for his elder, more worldly-wise, brother, Randolph (Peter Armitage), and at one stage fears she is pregnant by him.Hall’s other roles, in a television career in which she clocked up almost 100 parts in 40 years, included Mrs Jackson in the children’s foster home series Dodger, Bonzo & the Rest (1985); a short run in EastEnders (1988) as Christine, who provided a safe house to Den Watts (Leslie Grantham) – and was seduced by him – when he was on the run from the police; and seven different characters in The Bill (between 1984 and 2007).Although she kept busy, starring roles remained elusive and Hall was able to focus on her interest in local politics. In 1993, she ousted a sitting Conservative on Kent county council to give Labour its first win in the Ramsgate South ward. She eventually became leader of the party’s group, in opposition, on the council.View image in fullscreenCheryl Hall, second from left, with Ronnie Corbett and the rest of the cast of No Sex Please We’re British, 1973.Photograph: Ronald Fortune/ANL/ShutterstockAt the 1997 election she stood as a parliamentary candidate for Canterbury. Although she gained 31% of the vote, the Conservative MP retained the seat. She lost her county council seat in 2001 and, from 2010, spent much of her retirement in Greece.Before her marriage to Lindsay (1974-80), Hall was in a three-year relationship with the actor Robin Askwith. In 1985, she married Robert Potter; they divorced four years later. She is survived by their sons, Benjamin and Joshua.Cheryl Georgette Hall, actor, born 23 July 1950; died 9 August 2026Explore more on these topicsTelevisionThe BillDoctor WhoEastEndersDramaobituariesShareReuse this content

title: British cyclist Finlay Tarling, 19, dies in Volta a Portugal accident | Cycling | The Guardian
description: The British cyclist Finlay Tarling, a 19-year-old rider for the NSN Development Team, has died in a crash during the eighth stage of the Tour of Portugal
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: The British cyclist Finlay Tarling, a 19-year-old rider for the NSN Development Team, has died in a crash during the eighth stage of the Tour of Portugal
Content: Finlay Tarling in action at the Tour of  Britain in 2025.Photograph: Huw Fairclough/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFinlay Tarling in action at the Tour of  Britain in 2025.Photograph: Huw Fairclough/Getty ImagesCyclingBritish cyclist Finlay Tarling, 19, dies in Volta a Portugal accidentTeenager involved in an accident in PortugalRider’s NSN Development Team ‘heartbroken’Jeremy WhittleFri 14 Aug 2026 13.42 EDTFirst published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 12.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFinlay Tarling, the younger brother of Netcompany Ineos rider, Josh Tarling, has been killed while racing in stage eight of the Volta a Portugal.Although the details are yet to be confirmed, reports in the Portugese and French media suggest that the 19-year-old Welsh rider was hit by a non-race vehicle travelling on the course in the opposite direction to the peloton.In a statement, the race organisation said: “The organisers of the Volta a Portugal em Bicicleta, Jogos Santa Casa, deeply regret to announce the death of British cyclist Finlay Tarling, from the NSN Development Team, following a serious accident that occurred during the eighth stage of the race, between Melgaço and Fafe.“At this time of profound sorrow, the organisers of the Volta a Portugal and the PortugueseCyclingFederation extend their deepest condolences to Finlay Tarling’s family, his teammates, the NSN Development Team, and all his friends and loved ones.”Tarling was a highly-rated young talent and time-trialling prospect and had placed third in the under-23 time trial at the British National Championships this summer.His NSN Development Team posted: “We are heartbroken to announce the passing of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal today.”“Fin was a much-loved member of our team but most importantly, he was a son, a brother, and a friend to so many. He will be deeply missed. Our deepest condolences go out to Fin’s parents Michael and Dawn, his brother Josh, and everyone who was lucky enough to call Fin a friend. Rest in peace, Fin.”Finlay Tarling’s progression had been through track and road racing. He joined the then Israel-Premier Tech Academy prior to 2025. He continued with the team after it was rebranded as the NSN Development Team for 2026, and, developing a reputation in European racing as a time trial specialist, finished 11th in the opening prologue stage of the Portugese race in Lisbon.The eighth stage, of 166.8 kilometres from Melgaco to Fafe, was neutralised with 23 kilometres to race, following Tarling’s death and the podium ceremony cancelled. His teammates rode together to the finish line in a show of solidarity.In a post on X, cycling’s governing body, the UCI, said it was “deeply saddened by the tragic death of British rider Finlay Tarling, who passed away following a serious accident during today’s eighth stage of the Volta a Portugal.”The Portugal prime minister Luís Montenegro also expressed his condolences to Tarling’s family and team, adding on X that the news of his death “leaves us deeply shaken.”Stephen Park CBE, the performance director for the Great Britain cycling team, said: “All of us at British Cycling are heartbroken to learn of the tragic passing of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal. Fin was a talented rider with a fantastic future ahead of him, a loyal teammate and an all-round brilliant young man.“Our deepest sympathies are with his parents and brother, Josh at this tragic time.”Explore more on these topicsCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ontario free to axe Toronto bike lanes, region’s top court rules | Toronto | The Guardian
description: Win is significant for region’s premier, Doug Ford, who blames protected zones for city’s traffic ills
Author: Olivia Bowden
Headline: Win is significant for region’s premier, Doug Ford, who blames protected zones for city’s traffic ills
Content: A bike lane in downtown Toronto. It’s been estimated that ripping up the lanes would cost taxpayers C$48m.Photograph: Andrew Francis Wallace/Toronto Star/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA bike lane in downtown Toronto. It’s been estimated that ripping up the lanes would cost taxpayers C$48m.Photograph: Andrew Francis Wallace/Toronto Star/Getty ImagesTorontoOntario free to axe Toronto bike lanes, region’s top court rulesWin is significant for region’s premier, Doug Ford, who blames protected zones for city’s traffic illsOlivia BowdenFri 14 Aug 2026 17.03 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 17.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Ontario government is now free to rip out Toronto’s bike lanes on its busiest streets after the region’s top court ruled in favour of the province on Friday, overturning a lower court’s decision that decreed removal would violate constitutional rights.The win is significant for Ontario’s premier, Doug Ford, and his government, who have long railed against Toronto’s bike lanes, blaming the protected zones forthe city’s traffic ills.In 2024, the Ford government passed legislation that would allow Ontario to axe Toronto’s lanes, despite the recent installation of the infrastructure by the municipality.But the effort to tear up the lanes covering 19km (12 miles) of road was paused after cycling advocacy organisations levelled a legal challenge against the province.Their challenge was supported in July 2025, when a superior court judge ruled removing the lanes was unconstitutional, as it would create a heightened risk of death or injury, in turn violating the right to life and security of the person. Those rights are protected under Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms.Friday’s decision from the Ontario court of appeal reverses that ruling. Michael Longfield, executive director of Cycle Toronto, one of the groups that launched the legal challenge, said he is disappointed in the decision.“This isn’t just about keeping people on bikes safe. It helps pedestrians. It helps other drivers. It has a very strong traffic calming effect that we need in major cities,” he said.The court of appeal judges in their decision wrote that there is no charter right to bike lanes and the government is free to change legislation on the lanes if it wishes. They explained that courts cannot find legislation unconstitutional because experts predict the government’s policies will fail.“Neither the government nor the legislature is under any obligation to accept policy advice,” wrote Justice Huscroft in the decision.In reaction to the ruling, Toronto’s mayor, Olivia Chow, said she has been working with the province to negotiate a path forward “that keeps every road user safe”. There’s hope the municipality will negotiate an alternative with the Ford government that still makes room for cyclists, said Longfield.Ontario’s transportation minister, Prabmeet Sarkaria, said in a statement the top court’s decision is a “victory for common sense”. The government has not yet announced when or if they plan to remove the lanes.It was estimated by a city report in 2024 that ripping up the lanes would cost taxpayers an additional C$48m (£26m). Internal briefings obtainedby the Trilliumalso found the province’s own staff reported that bike lane removal would not reduce congestion and could make it worse. Those staff members also warned Ontario may be seen as encroaching on municipal decision-making.Fundamentally, Ford targeting bike lanes is a gross overreach of the provincial government into city affairs, said Longfield. It is “frankly ridiculous”, he said, to believe the key to solving urban congestion is barring bike lanes.“The more we can focus on real, evidence-based solutions … the better it will be,” he said.Explore more on these topicsTorontoCanadaCyclingAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: French court blocks Macron’s social media ban for under-15s | Social media bans | The Guardian
description: Constitutional council says curbs infringe freedom of expression and privacy as president vows to rework legislation
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Constitutional council says curbs infringe freedom of expression and privacy as president vows to rework legislation
Content: The EU plans to seek stronger protections for children from harmful social media features.Photograph: Jeremy Piper/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe EU plans to seek stronger protections for children from harmful social media features.Photograph: Jeremy Piper/ReutersSocial media bansFrench court blocks Macron’s social media ban for under-15sConstitutional council says curbs infringe freedom of expression and privacy as president vows to rework legislationDan MilmoGlobal technology editorFri 14 Aug 2026 13.12 EDTFirst published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 12.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrance’s top court has blocked a ban on social media access for under-15s, ruling that it infringed freedom of expression and privacy.The decision is a blow to PresidentEmmanuel Macronas momentum builds around the world for Australian-style restrictions on children’s use of social media.A lawapproved by parliament in Julywould have barred under-15s from opening social media accounts from the beginning of September. Tech platforms would also have been required to close existing accounts within four months and use age-verification tools approved by ⁠France’s privacy regulator.However, the constitutional council found that while the law required users to provide proof ​of age, it failed to specify the “conditions and limits” ‌under which this should happen. It also found that the restrictions infringed freedom of expression and privacy.“The council holds that the contested provisions, on ‌the one hand, disproportionately infringe upon the freedom of expression and communication and, on the other, fail to provide the legal safeguards necessary to ensure the right to respect for private life,” it said.Several countries havefollowed the example of Australia, which barred under-16s from leading social media platforms in December last year. Indonesia and Malaysia have introduced restrictions for under-16s on certain platforms, while the UK is preparing toblock leading apps for the same age group next year.1:40‘Growing up too young’: Londoners praise under-16s social media ban – videoIn Australia, the affected platforms are Facebook, Instagram, Kick, Reddit, Snapchat, Threads, TikTok, Twitch, X and YouTube.The EU has also said it plans to seek stronger protections for children from harmful social media features, building on the digital services act that already sets rules for tech platforms.Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, said last month that “it is clear we need age-appropriate restrictions to platforms”. She did not refer to a specific age limit, instead raising the prospect of “phased and gradual access for different age ranges”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSocial media companies generally oppose blanket bans, arguing that they already have measures to protect younger users, including a minimum age of 13. They ⁠have also said they would comply with government restrictions.Macron, who in April ​urged teenagers to turn off their devices and read in order to become better ​citizens, has asked the French prime ‌minister, Sébastien Lecornu, to ​rework the legislation to address the constitutional council’s concerns, according to the Élysée.The Élysée said Macron remained determined for the reform to take effect before spring 2027, whenFrance holds its presidential election. Macron is ineligible to stand for a third term.Explore more on these topicsSocial media bansFranceEmmanuel MacronSocial mediaDigital mediaEuropean CommissionEuropean UnionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Canadian plasma clinics pause collections after deaths of two donors | Canada | The Guardian
description: Grifols, which runs private chain of clinics, to temporarily stop taking donations after new government investigation
Author: Olivia Bowden
Headline: Grifols, which runs private chain of clinics, to temporarily stop taking donations after new government investigation
Content: An autopsy showed Rodiyat Alabede, 22, died of cardiac arrest shortly after donating plasma in Winnipeg in 2025.Photograph: gofundmeAn autopsy showed Rodiyat Alabede, 22, died of cardiac arrest shortly after donating plasma in Winnipeg in 2025.Photograph: gofundmeCanadaCanadian plasma clinics pause collections after deaths of two donorsGrifols, which runs private chain of clinics, to temporarily stop taking donations after new government investigationOlivia Bowdenin TorontoFri 14 Aug 2026 12.21 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 13.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA chain of private plasma donation clinics inCanadahas said it is pausing collections after the deaths of two donors and a new government investigation into potential unsafe practices.Grifols, a Spanish healthcare company which runs 17 clinics in Canada and is the country’s only private clinic for plasma donation, said it informedHealthCanada of its decision to temporarily pause collections on Wednesday.On the same day, the agency had issued a formal notice of non-compliance for failure to follow blood regulations, a senior officialtold the Globe and Mail newspaper.The two deaths occurred after plasma donations in October 2025 and January 2026,Health Canada said in March of this year. The donors, both of whom were in the province of Manitoba, went into “distress” while donating, people familiar with the cases said.Though Health Canada did not release the identities of the donors, friends said one was Rodiyat Alabede, 22, an international student and aspiring social worker who donated plasma in Winnipeg on 25 October.Patientadvocates reported at the end of Maythat there were concerns about whether Alabede had been properly screened.“They had staff taking plasma from donors who did not know how to extract plasma in a safe manner,” alleged Kat Lanteigne, a safe blood campaigner who represents Alabede’s family.“The [failures] were so egregious that … now we have more questions than answers,” she said in May.An autopsy showed Alabede died of cardiac arrest shortly after donating. Health Canada reported that it found “no link” between Alabede’s death and plasma donation.Patient advocates have called for a new inquest into her death, however, after alleging that “significant medical discrepancies” had been uncovered between her autopsy, which was completed two days after her death, and the medical summary drafted by Health Canada published on 27 March of this year.The Guardian has also seen Health Canada inspection reports from May that found deficiencies at Grifols clinics, including inadequate training for staff, failures in standard operating procedures, poor record-keeping and a failure by Grifols to remedy past issues.The Health Canada report also found that staff did not stop plasma collection when alarms went off, and described the company’s reporting as “incomplete” and “inaccurate”.Prior to the newly announced pause, donations were permitted at Grifols twice a week. The company paid donors up to C$100 (£55) for each donation.Plasma is a pale yellow, protein-rich liquid in blood that assists in moving red and white blood cells, along with platelets, through blood vessels, according to Canadian Blood Services, the non-profit that operates Canada’s national blood supply.Plasma also helps prevent excessive bleeding and is used to create medications for a variety of conditions including haemophilia, liver disease and various cancers.The plasma donation process differs from donating blood overall. A medical device called an apheresis machine draws the blood, separates it into individual parts, collects the components needed and then returns the remaining blood back into the body, according to Canadian Blood Services. The process takes about 90 minutes, whereas a general blood draw takes about 10.In Canada, provinces and territories decide whether paid plasma clinics are permitted. British Columbia and Quebec do not allow the practice, for example, but Manitoba, where the deaths occurred, does not prohibit companies from paying donors for plasma.Grifols said it decided to pause collection “proactively and voluntarily” due to what it deemed “unfounded attention”. It said the pause would allow it to work with Health Canada and Canadian Blood Services.The company has denied the two deaths were connected to plasma donation.On Friday, Health Canada said it found “various deficiencies” specifically at the Taylor Avenue Grifols location in Winnipeg. A spokesperson for that location said it was working closely with the company so that it could return to operations.“Canadians can be assured that this decision will have no impact on the safety and security of Canada’s blood and plasma supply,” Grifols said.Explore more on these topicsCanadaHealthAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Scientists hope to shed light on young universe by using far side of the moon | The moon | The Guardian
description: UK team seeking to put suitcase-sized satellite in orbit around moon in search for 21cm line radio frequency signal
Author: Nicola Davis
Headline: UK team seeking to put suitcase-sized satellite in orbit around moon in search for 21cm line radio frequency signal
Content: By collecting data when the CosmoCube passes the far side of the moon, the team hopes to avoid interference caused by FM radios and other technology on Earth.Photograph: RAL Digital Creative Services./STFC/UKRIView image in fullscreenBy collecting data when the CosmoCube passes the far side of the moon, the team hopes to avoid interference caused by FM radios and other technology on Earth.Photograph: RAL Digital Creative Services./STFC/UKRIThe moonScientists hope to shed light on young universe by using far side of the moonUK team seeking to put suitcase-sized satellite in orbit around moon in search for 21cm line radio frequency signalNicola DavisScience correspondentFri 14 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 12.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLittle is known about what was happening shortly after the big bang, but now researchers are hoping to shed fresh light on the matter by harnessing the far side of the moon.Scientists plan to put a suitcase-sized satellite into orbit around the moon, using the data it collects as it passes the far side to search for a radio frequency signal emitted by neutral hydrogen atoms in the early universe.More specifically, the satellite, nicknamed CosmoCube, will be looking for what is known as the 21cm line. Crucially, the older the signal, the more its wavelength has been stretched, or redshifted, to longer wavelengths, providing a way for its strength to be tracked over time relative to the cosmic microwave background radiation.“The main thing we track by looking at this signal is what’s the physical temperature of the gas during the early universe,” said Prof Eloy de Lera Acedo, the lead author from the University of Cambridge’s Cavendish Laboratory.With the 21cm signal acting a bit like a thermometer, the team are hoping to study events from the start of the so-called “dark ages”, about 380,000 years after the big bang, through the cosmic dawn, when the first stars and galaxies emerged, to the end of what is known as the epoch of reionization, approximately 1bn years after the big bang.“The temperature of the gas is affected by the things happening in the universe at the time,” said de Lera Acedo. In addition he noted the amplitude and shape of the 21cm signal was expected to be influenced by dark matter, offering a way for experts to investigate the nature of this mysterious component of the universe.View image in fullscreenA representative model of the CosmoCube undergoing tests. The 21cm line is the radio frequency signal emitted by neutral hydrogen atoms in the early universe.Photograph: RAL Digital Creative Services/STFC/UKRIResearchers have attempted to detect the 21cm line before but it is difficult to do using Earth-based instruments. Not only is the signal weak but human-made technology – from FM radios to plane communication – can cause interference.Writing in the journal Nature Astronomy, de Lera Acedo and his colleagues said other challenges included disturbances created by the Earth’s ionosphere.While experts at the Edges (Experiment to Detect the Global EoR Signature) radio telescope in Australia claim to have found the 21cm line, questionshave been raised over the results.The team behind the CosmoCube mission, which is expected to last two years, said taking observations from the far side of the moon should avoid many of the challenges faced by Earth-based instruments.“The total cost is estimated to be just under £50m and the launching date – we expect it to be about five years from now,” said de Lera Acedo, adding that CosmoCube had already been granted more than £2m of funding by the UKSpaceAgency.Phil Bull, a professor of cosmology at the Jodrell Bank Centre for Astrophysics who is not involved in the project, welcomed the mission.“The CosmoCube measurements will help us understand the major ingredients of our cosmic origins – the processes that led to the formation of the first stars and galaxies, and lit up the Universe after a period called the cosmic dark ages,” he said.But, Bull noted, CosmoCube was not the only mission trying to make these measurements, and others may get there first.“More ominously, other planned lunar missions might bring with them exactly the type of human-generated radio noise that the mission is trying to escape,” he said, “making this a race against time.”Join us on 3 September for a live recording of the Guardian’s Science Weekly podcast with Black Box host Michael Safi at Kings Place in London. Purchase your tickethere.Explore more on these topicsThe moonSpaceAstronomySatellitesnewsShareReuse this content
