Board/APView image in fullscreenThe Serbian entrepreneur Ljubisa Karović, sitting in seat 11F, had his head and right arm sucked out of the broken window in the incident.Photograph: National Transportation Safety Board/APRyanairRyanair window that passenger was partly sucked out of was broken by engine debris, report findsFan blade broke off shortly after takeoff on 10 July flight from Greece to Germany, preliminary findings showBusiness live – latest updatesJoanna PartridgeFri 14 Aug 2026 06.28 EDTFirst published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 03.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBroken engine parts were responsible for shattering a window on a Ryanair plane, causing apassenger to be partly sucked outmid-flight in July, US investigators have said.A preliminary report by the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) found an engine fan blade broke off shortly after takeoff on the 10 July flight from Greece to Germany shattering the window and damaging the fuselage.The Serbian entrepreneur Ljubisa Karović, sitting by the window in seat 11F, had his head and right arm sucked out of the broken window in the incident.Karović was saved from being completely sucked out of the window by other passengers, who grabbed hold of him.The 61-year-oldtold the Guardian he was lucky to be aliveafter the incident on Ryanair flight FR1879 and said his wife, Svetlana, told him he had fainted several times, including after he had been pulled back inside the cabin.View image in fullscreenLjubisa Karović was saved from being completely sucked out of the window by other passengers, who grabbed hold of him.Photograph: Svetlana GrkovicThe NTSB said the flight, which was scheduled to fly from Thessaloniki inGreeceto Memmingen near Munich, “experienced a No 2 (right) engine fan-blade-out (FBO) failure during climb out from the Thessaloniki international airport (SKG)”. The flight was operated by the budget airline’s subsidiary Malta Air.Investigators found the cabin depressurised and the two pilots decided to return to Thessaloniki airport, where they “made an uneventful landing”.A few days after the incident, the NTSB was “delegated the investigation in full” by the Greek authorities. The flight crew’s timeline of the event was set out by the NTSB, detailing how they experienced a “high vibration” engine alert during the flight climb. They reduced the engine power in response and carried out a series of checks.The engine vibration reduced and the crew continued the climb on autopilot. However, the vibrations then increased significantly and the crew heard a loud bang. The flight crew put on their oxygen masks, declared an emergency and began an immediate descent.The flight attendants reported “hearing and feeling a loud continuous vibration and seeing a small amount of fog/smoke before the oxygen masks dropped”, the report found.Four bird strikes to the plane’s right engine were reported by flight crews in the 12 months preceding the incident, the report found, adding that bird remains were reportedly found in two of the cases. The fan blades had undergone ultrasonic inspections in recent months with “no findings”.Karović told the Guardian less than a fortnight after the incident that he did not remember much but had a painful head and neck. “It could have been the seatbelt, the fact that I was still strapped in. But maybe it is fate. I believe in God and I thank him every day,” he said.The Boeing 737-800 plane had 149 passengers and four flight attendants on board.Ryanair said it would not comment on the preliminary report, or on whether Karović would receive compensation, until after the final report was published.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe airline’s finance chiefsaidlast month it was “way too early” to discuss whether Ryanair would have to compensate the couple while the airline awaited the outcome of an investigation into the incident.Boeing and CFM, the engine maker, are assisting with the investigation.Jeff Guzzetti, a former NTSB and Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) investigator who reviewed the preliminary report, told the Associated Press that the required maintenance appears to have been performed on schedule.However, investigators are expected to examine how the previous inspections were conducted and whether the previous suspected bird strikes contributed to pre-existing damage. “We know what happened and even to some extent why it happened, but there’s still unanswered questions that the NTSB will get at,” Guzzetti said.In 2025 the FAA issued three directives requiring airlines to strengthen parts of the engine coverings on Boeing 737 planes, following two previous fan blade failures that sent pieces of the engine covering flying. In one accident,a passenger was killedon a Southwest Airlines plane in 2018, after debris knocked out a window.The FAA gave airlines until July 2028 to complete the modifications, and the NTSB report found the required changes had not yet been made to the Ryanair plane.Guzzetti said the latest accident could prompt the FAA and NTSB to examine whether that deadline should be moved up.Explore more on these topicsRyanairAirline industryTravel & leisureTransportEuropeGermanyGreecenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Murakami saw his book come alive!’: the Japanese company bringing the author’s science fiction masterpiece to the stage | Theatre | The Guardian
description: A play based on the writer’s dreamlike novel Hard-Boiled Wonderland and the End of the World is touring the world, riding a wave of interest in Japanese culture. Its creators talk about how they adapted the famously cryptic tale
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A play based on the writer’s dreamlike novel Hard-Boiled Wonderland and the End of the World is touring the world, riding a wave of interest in Japanese culture. Its creators talk about how they adapted the famously cryptic tale
Content: Skull set … Narushi Ikeda in End of the World and Hard-Boiled WonderlandPhotograph: Takahiro WatanabeView image in fullscreenSkull set … Narushi Ikeda in End of the World and Hard-Boiled WonderlandPhotograph: Takahiro WatanabeTheatre‘Murakami saw his book come alive!’: the Japanese company bringing the author’s science fiction masterpiece to the stageA play based on the writer’s dreamlike novel Hard-Boiled Wonderland and the End of the World is touring the world, riding a wave of interest in Japanese culture. Its creators talk about how they adapted the famously cryptic taleMarigold WarnerFri 14 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTatsuya Fujiwara is no stranger to London’s Barbican theatre. It was here nearly 30 years ago that one of Japan’s biggest film stars, now 44, made his stage debut. He was just 15, plucked out of an audition of more than 5,000 hopeful youngsters by the revered theatre director Yukio Ninagawa for his play Shintoku-Maru. It kickstarted Fujiwara’s career, and three years later he landed a role in the cult dystopianfilm Battle Royale, going on to star in hit TV dramas and blockbuster films, all the while continuing to perform in Ninagawa’s acclaimed productions.Now, Fujiwara returns to where it all began, to perform in a stage adaptation of Haruki Murakami’s science fiction novel Hard-Boiled Wonderland and the End of the World. The story alternates between two seemingly unrelated narratives: a cyberpunk thriller set in Tokyo, and a surreal fantasy that unfolds within a mysterious walled town. Directed by the French choreographer Philippe Decouflé, the play premiered in Tokyo in January, toured Japan until March, then Singapore in April. After the Barbican run this autumn, the tour will wrap up in Paris.“When performing in Japan, you become accustomed to your own audience,” says Fujiwara. “You develop a feel for what reaches them and how they receive you. The moment you cross a border, that certainty disappears.”View image in fullscreenFlowered up … Tatsuya Fujiwara and Miu Tomita in End of the World and Hard-Boiled Wonderland.Photograph: Takahiro WatanabeWe meet in April, backstage at the Esplanade theatre in Singapore just a few hours before the production’s first performance to an English-speaking audience. (The play is performed in Japanese, with English surtitles.) The response was rapturous, the audience more animated than with any performance during the Japan run, according to the director and cast. The Singapore house laughed freely, while in Japan the comic moments did not land with such warmth.Whether that’s due to cultural differences in self-expression or humour is up for debate, but backstage during intermission the cast are giddy. “It definitely gives us confidence for London,” says the director.This play arrives at a time when Japanese culture is experiencing a global boom, particularly in London. The last five years alone have seen a cluster of UK exhibitions about Japan. The British Museum has curated shows on manga, Hokusai and the samurai; the V&A did the history of kimonos; Oxford’s Ashmolean explored art and photography from Tokyo; and Somerset House celebrated 50 years of Hello Kitty. However, productions that have broken through to a mainstream audience overseas have largely been based on anime and manga. This summer saw a musical adaptation of Death Note at the Barbican, as well as Pretty Guardian Sailor Moon at the West End’s Here at Outernet and Koko in Camden Town, and Spirited Away, which enjoyed a six-month run at the London Coliseum in 2024.double quotation markToday, there is a curiosity about Japanese storytelling and aesthetics. Audiences approach our work with more familiarity“The barriers are considerably lower,” says Miyako Kanamori, senior executive and veteran producer at HoriPro. As one of Japan’s largest entertainment companies, HoriPro has been exporting Japanese theatre to the UK for many decades. “Thirty years ago, when we first brought [Yukio] Ninagawa’s productions to Britain, that cultural landscape simply did not exist. Today, there is a far broader curiosity about Japanese storytelling and aesthetics, and I feel audiences approach our work with a greater sense of familiarity.” Perhaps now is the time for homegrown theatre to shine. Plus, as a global bestseller, Murakami’s name carries instant esteem and recognition.However, the world of Murakami does not naturally lend itself to the stage. His novels can be cryptic and allegorical, making them hard to adapt for its native audience, let alone an international one.Hard-Boiled Wonderland and the End of the Worldspans 400 pages and features curious creatures such as unicorns and the “Murks”, monsters that lurk in the sewers. Fujiwara plays Watashi, the protagonist ofthe cyberpunk narrative the Hard-Boiled Wonderland,a human data processor known as a “Calcutec” who is essentially a cyborg. He encrypts data using a technique known as “shuffling”, described as a supernatural kind of mind alteration. His routine job slowly reveals a darker conspiracy buried deep within his own consciousness.View image in fullscreenPage turners … Tatsuya Fujiwara and Misato Morita in End of the World and Hard-Boiled Wonderland.Photograph: Takahiro WatanabeThe parallel narrative is even more peculiar. End of the World unravels within a mythical walled town. Upon entering, the second protagonist, Boku – played on alternating nights by Kiita Komagine and Ryunosuke Shimamura –is stripped of his shadow and all his memories, and tasked with reading dreams from the skulls of dead unicorns. The two plots eventually converge, and while they are both totally removed from the reality we know, the stories are strangely relatable.Murakami wrote the novel more than 40 years ago, but in an age of AI and algorithmic control, his questions about what remains when memory and selfhood are stripped are more pertinent now than ever.“At first I thought it was impossible to do anything with [the material],” says Decouflé, who is best known for directing music videos for New Order and Fine Young Cannibals, as well as France’s 1992 Winter Olympics opening ceremony. “I’m not Japanese, so I can never fully grasp what lies beneath the text, but then I thought: ‘They’ve asked me to do it, so I’m going to do it my way, with my dreams, my ideas, my vision.’”For the production company, bringing in a European director with a background in movement was a deliberate decision. Having worked on several adaptations of Murakami’s novels – Ninagawa’s Kafka on the Shore in 2015 and Simon McBurney’s The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle in 2023 – producer Kanamori learned that expressing the spiritual and psychological dimensions of the author’s world through dialogue alone was “profoundly difficult”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShe came to realise that “music and physical expression might offer a more truthful theatrical language for his work”, particularly for a play that was intended to be performed to a non-Japanese-speaking audience. Working closely with Japanese scriptwriter Ako Takahashi to decode the text, Decouflé has made a highly visual adaptation. He casts ballerinas as unicorns, dressing them in golden leotards and pointe shoes with stilted forelimbs. Street dancers armoured in urchin-like spikes writhe and scuttle through the sewers, while Tokyo-based dancer Rikubouz moves in long, liquid phrases to connect the two worlds between scenes.Murakami came to rehearsals himself. “He was always very contained, very still,” says Decouflé. “And then suddenly he saw the stage. He saw it alive. And I could see that he was happy – happy that I had given life to his dreams, to his book.” After the premiere, the author made a short speech. “He said something like: ‘I wrote this novel 40 years ago, and I had forgotten everything. Tonight, you all reminded me of what I created.’”View image in fullscreenShuffle vision … Tatsuya Fujiwara in End of the World and Hard-Boiled WonderlandPhotograph: Takahiro WatanabeDecouflé had made two productions in Japan before – once 30 years ago, another 15 years ago – and has observed the rise of Japanese dance in that time. “Thirty years ago, we could not find dancers of the quality we needed. Even 15 years ago it was so-so. And now Japan has some extraordinary dancers.” He was also impressed by the professionalism of the performers. “I never heard anyone complain,” he says. “I gave them hard work, I really pushed them. And at the end, they were overjoyed. It was a great luxury to work that way.”Cultural exchange has always been a crucial part of Japan’s story and how its art travels. Back in the Edo period, artisans commonly used discarded Ukiyo-e prints to package ceramics. These were later discovered by the impressionists, inspiring the Japonisme movement and artists such as Monet, Van Gogh and Klimt. The dialogue that followed, between eastern aesthetics and western modernism, moulded the development of modern art on both sides.Perhaps something of that pattern persists here. The play’s star hopes international interest in Japanese theatre will also ignite a new energy back home. “It would be amazing if theatre in Japan could one day command the kind of broad cultural engagement it has in the UK, where it’s truly part of public life,” says Fujiwara, who knows better than most what it takes to carry culture across borders. At the Barbican in 2015, performing Ninagawa’s Hamlet on Shakespeare’s home turf, the pressure was paralysing.“It’s a bit like a British company staging kabuki in Japan,” he says. “But this time it’s different because it’s Murakami. There’s more room to breathe, and more hope that we can offer something that reaches people broadly.”End of the World and Hard-Boiled Wonderlandis at Barbican theatre, London, 8 to 11 October.Explore more on these topicsTheatreDanceScience fiction booksJapanfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A critical mauling: Brian Logan on comedy critics being portrayed as horrible snobs | Stage | The Guardian
description: Two Edinburgh fringe shows feature savage send-ups of reviewers. Is this petty revenge or do they have a case? Our writer finds one ‘a hoot’ – and thinks the other let him off lightly
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Two Edinburgh fringe shows feature savage send-ups of reviewers. Is this petty revenge or do they have a case? Our writer finds one ‘a hoot’ – and thinks the other let him off lightly
Content: Poison pen … the critic in Andrew Doherty’s Reviewers Welcome … To Die!Photograph: PR handoutView image in fullscreenPoison pen … the critic in Andrew Doherty’s Reviewers Welcome … To Die!Photograph: PR handoutStageA critical mauling: Brian Logan on comedy critics being portrayed as horrible snobsTwo Edinburgh fringe shows feature savage send-ups of reviewers. Is this petty revenge or do they have a case? Our writer finds one ‘a hoot’ – and thinks the other let him off lightlyBrian LoganFri 14 Aug 2026 09.06 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 10.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNo one ever built a statue to a critic, they say – but plenty of art gets made about them. There wasWild Bore at the Traversea few Edinburgh fringes back, an eye-catching performance-art attack on the notion of critical authority. There was Tom Stoppard’s The Real Inspector Hound, Sheridan’s The Critic, and the 70s horror movie (later a play)Theatre of Blood, in which critics are subjected to gruesome murder at the hands of a deranged thesp. And while we’re talking unspeakable gore, one feature of Sarah Kane’s queasy play Cleansed, currently enjoying arevival, is that (in a wanton act of literary vengeance) its sadistic torturer antagonist is named after a theatre critic, Jack Tinker, who’d panned Kane’s work.Runts of the reviewing litter though we are, there’s even a sub-genre of art about comedy critics. The comic Russell Kane wrotea novelabout one who was unable to laugh. Ex-critic Charlotte Runcie wroteanotherabout a journo giving a woman a one-star review for her standup, then sleeping with her.double quotation mark‘Who wants to be a comedy critic?’ barks Riches, eyeballing the audience. I sink back into my seatSo there’s a precedent for the two shows on this year’s fringe that take comedy reviewing as their subject, one of them in direct response to so-so notices at last year’s festival. That show is Andrew Doherty’s Reviewers Welcome … to Die! It’s a folk-horror spoof about an up-himself critic obliged by demons to learn the error of his ways. It springs from Doherty’s dismay at receivinga three-star crit(“one of the three worst scores you can get!”) for his sophomore show Sad Gay Aids Play – after critical hosannahs greetedhis debut the year before.So where does Reviewers Welcome fall on the all-important five-star spectrum? Happily, given that this is not a review, I am under no obligation to rate his show, which characterises those in my profession as preening, nepotistic snobs, scorning the talent they purport to judge while nursing their own thwarted artistic delusions. “How sad, lonely and pathetic I am,” trills Doherty’s anti-hero Felix Chatelier, at least until popular and sexy playwriting genius “Andrew Doherty” shows up to shepherd our unlovely critic towards redemption. This happens at a fringe festival in the fictional Midlands town of Billington, a name that long-time readers of Guardian theatre reviews may recognise.View image in fullscreenClose to the bone? … Adam Riches, AKA Caliban Monroe, performs The Critic’s Way.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianAll of this unfolds in the spoof scary-movie style familiar from Doherty’s hit Gay Witch Sex Cult, another Wicker Man-ish affair pitting a dopey outsider against yokel locals and dark forces beyond everyone’s ken. Just as it trades in genre stereotype, so the show’s take on critics seldom outpaces cliche – although I did enjoy the closing gag about Chatelier’s constitutional inability to dole out that final, fifth star. But we critics get off lightly here, in that Reviewers Welcome is as much a mickey-take of thin-skinned artists bearing grudges as of those arbiters of taste who decorate or dismiss them with a swish of our pen.And now to the second show. When Adam Riches bounds on stage in character as eminent comedy critic Caliban Monroe, it looks like his show The Critic’s Way might land uncomfortably closer to the bone. Scottish accent? Replica Scottish football sportswear? Why do I feel like I’ve seen this (stylish, smooth-talking) guy before? But The Critic’s Way soon devolves into another of Riches’ familiar burlesques on swaggering but shallow masculinity (ah, so it can’t be me then) with strictly limited insight into Caliban’s critical calling. The persona makes Chatelier look multidimensional by comparison, as Riches loudly deplores comedians, claims to have invented star ratings and reads from his now-remaindered titular treatise on the art of what he calls “the ’tique”.double quotation markThere’s ridicule there (fair enough) but perhaps grudging affection tooThere’s little of the promised “razor-sharp satire”, although – like most of Riches’ uproarious interactive work – his show is never less than a hoot. “Who wants to be a comedy critic?” he barks, eyeballing the audience as I shrink in my seat. Inevitably, behind the arrogant veneer, Monroe is another “sad, lonely and pathetic” individual. The “voice of a veneration” no longer, he’s out of a job after a victim of his hatchet work hits back against one particularly indelicate review. You could just about read this as an exploration of a changing climate for criticism, in which speech is neurotically policed, and ideas like objective judgment and the single authoritative voice are both critically (as it were) out of fashion.Or you could enjoy Riches’ exuberant faux-workshop for what it is: a 50-minute piece of nonsense revelling in the archetype of the cultural snob, in love with his own supposed erudition, seething with resentment that to deploy it he must piggyback on the work of – shudder! – mere comedians.Considering these two shows together as a critique of the service we comedy reviewers render – well, there’s ridicule (fair enough) but perhaps grudging affection too. It’s probably a three-star review then for me and my counterparts – but I like to think it reads like a four.Andrew Doherty’s Reviewers Welcome … to Die!is Upstairs at Pleasant Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 August;Adam Riches’ The Critic’s Wayis at Cow Cafe at Underbelly, Cowgate, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustExplore more on these topicsStageComedy (Culture)Comedy (Stage)featuresShareReuse this content

title: These Violent Delights review – Scottish Ballet’s feverish Romeo and Juliet is bold and unsettling | Movies | The Guardian
description: A taut, dreamlike reimagining of Shakespeare’s tragedy strips away romance in favour of dread, creating an engrossing and fiercely physical dance film
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: A taut, dreamlike reimagining of Shakespeare’s tragedy strips away romance in favour of dread, creating an engrossing and fiercely physical dance film
Content: All-consuming passion … Kayla-Maree Tarantolo and Ishan Mahabir-Stokes in These Violent Delights.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicView image in fullscreenAll-consuming passion … Kayla-Maree Tarantolo and Ishan Mahabir-Stokes in These Violent Delights.Photograph: Mihaela BodlovicMoviesReviewThese Violent Delights review – Scottish Ballet’s feverish Romeo and Juliet is bold and unsettlingEdinburgh film festivalA taut, dreamlike reimagining of Shakespeare’s tragedy strips away romance in favour of dread, creating an engrossing and fiercely physical dance filmPeter BradshawFri 14 Aug 2026 11.55 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 11.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleScottish Ballet, under the direction of Christopher Hampson and Oscar Sansom, gives us an engrossing dance riff on Shakespeare’sRomeo and Juliet. The title alludes to Friar Lawrence saying, at the couple’s secret wedding ceremony, that “these violent delights have violent ends”, that their passion will consume itself in the act of marriage – which is true, but not in the way he thinks.The ballet is fierce, athletic, knotty and sensual; it is not a filmed event beneath a proscenium arch but a film that inhabits its own theatrical space. The whole event is a radically impressionistic compression of the play’s action, bringing it down to just 70 minutes, an extended nightmarish dream sequence with a repeated and disturbing scene of Juliet being dragged across the grass by an unseen force. This version chucks out, among other things, the balcony scene, and it interestingly modifies the ending, suggesting that the double-suicide might not be a trick that goes wrong but an anguished mutual gesture of despair.Intriguingly, it is only really at the end that Romeo (Ishan Mahabir-Stokes) and Juliet (Kayla-Maree Tarantolo) have much time together alone. From the beginning, we see Juliet, frustrated and lonely within her family who are trying to marry her off to the milksop Paris; at one point Paris (Yuri Marques) and Lord Capulet (Christopher Akrill) make her do a bizarre kind of abusive “trust exercise” movement between the two of them. Her nurse (Grace Horler), incidentally, is dressed in the uniform of an NHS-style nurse, as if getting ready to put Juliet in the psych ward if she defies her parents’ wishes.In her mind, at the outset, she haunts the life of Romeo, as if in a kind of choreographed trance, as he spends parallel time with his family. She has predicted that this is the man who destiny has in store for her. The party scene where they are to meet is held at a club ominously called the Apothecary, and the dance hums with nervous energy and MDMA excitement, but the ballet never permits any simply euphoric private moments of pure love for the star-crossed leads. They are always entangled with other people, vibrating with suspicion, confronting the future that is crowding in on them.This is a reading of Romeo and Juliet that is all about the alienation of love and the brevity of youth: a dark and pessimistic reading, in its way, but performed with vehement commitment and style.These Violent Delights screened at theEdinburgh international film festivaland is in UK and Irish cinemas from 21 October.Explore more on these topicsFilmEdinburgh film festivalBalletRomeo and JulietWilliam ShakespeareScottish BalletDancereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Out There review – saucer-eyed teen searches for aliens in YA comedy drama  | Edinburgh film festival | The Guardian
description: Wales, 1999: Maz is convinced her dead father was abducted by extraterrestrials in Simon Ryninks’s likable film, with a funny turn from Michael Sheen as a new age type
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Wales, 1999: Maz is convinced her dead father was abducted by extraterrestrials in Simon Ryninks’s likable film, with a funny turn from Michael Sheen as a new age type
Content: Close encounters … Aneurin Barnard as Bryn in Out There.Photograph: courtesy EIFFView image in fullscreenClose encounters … Aneurin Barnard as Bryn in Out There.Photograph: courtesy EIFFEdinburgh film festivalReviewOut There review – saucer-eyed teen searches for aliens in YA comedy dramaWales, 1999: Maz is convinced her dead father was abducted by extraterrestrials in Simon Ryninks’s likable film, with a funny turn from Michael Sheen as a new age typePeter BradshawFri 14 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 15.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFeature first-timer Simon Ryninks writes and directs this likably daft but big-hearted YA comedy drama, inspired by West Wales’s reputation as a hotspot for UFO sightings – particularly Broad Haven in Pembrokeshire, where many saucer-eyed people in 1977 really did report close encounters of the first kind. Now the scene is the fictionalised Welsh town of Caradoc in 1999, a world of smoking in pubs, dot-matrix computer printouts, Sony Handicam video cameras and droll references to the New Labour government.Maz (Nerys Amber Stocks) is a teenager doing A-levels, haunted by the death of her dad five years before: a scientist working at a top secret Ministry of Defence base who was killed in a mysterious incident involving a flash of white light from above. She witnessed this terrible event as a kid, having cheekily smuggled herself into the base in the back of his car, but now can’t quite remember it in detail. PTSD? Or have aliens wiped her memory?She is obsessed with the idea that her dad isn’t dead but rather was abducted by aliens, and that she might yet be able to see him again. So she conceives a plan to get back into that heavily guarded base, a scheme that is to involve her loyal but nervous best mate Elis (Tom Maya) and gibbering local ufologist Bryn (Aneurin Barnard).And for extra help with understanding the vast reaches of the cosmos and opening the doors of perception, they ask new age shop owner and drug enthusiast Shifty Gruff (an amusing turn from Michael Sheen), Caradoc’s own Howard Marks, who supplies shrooms to the local youth and offers to give hypnotherapy to Maz to unlock memories and visions. “Have you done regression therapy before?” asks Elis suspiciously. “I have in a past life …” says Gruff smoothly. When his hypnosis is unexpectedly successful, Gruff becomes very excited. Elis warns him: “With great ability comes great …” and Gruff interrupts: “Commercial opportunity!”Amid the extraterrestrial shenanigans, there’s room for some melancholy thoughts that UFO belief is just an inability to accept death, to accept that this, here on Earth, is all that there is. This is entertaining stuff from Ryninks, though I was sad that there wasn’t a bigger role for the excellent Kimberley Nixon. It could spin off nicely as a TV series.Out There screened at the Edinburgh film festivalExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh film festivalEdinburgh festival 2026Science fiction and fantasy filmsEdinburgh festivalUFOsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Something Wile E this way comes: how the Looney Toons reboot movie came back from the dead | Movies | The Guardian
description: Cartoon royalty were lined for a live-action toon hybrid Coyote vs Acme. Then it was shelved as a tax write-off. But its cast, crew and fans fought for its release. Three years later it’s set to be a surprise summer hit
Author: Nick Duerden
Headline: Cartoon royalty were lined for a live-action toon hybrid Coyote vs Acme. Then it was shelved as a tax write-off. But its cast, crew and fans fought for its release. Three years later it’s set to be a surprise summer hit
Content: That’s not all folks … Will Forte as Kevin Avery in Coyote vs Acme.Photograph: AltitudeView image in fullscreenThat’s not all folks … Will Forte as Kevin Avery in Coyote vs Acme.Photograph: AltitudeMoviesSomething Wile E this way comes: how the Looney Toons reboot movie came back from the deadCartoon royalty were lined for a live-action toon hybrid Coyote vs Acme. Then it was shelved as a tax write-off. But its cast, crew and fans fought for its release. Three years later it’s set to be a surprise summer hitNick DuerdenFri 14 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 07.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBack in 2020, Dave Green started making his new film, Coyote vs Acme. Mixing live action with animation, it would be an unconventional courtroom drama that pitched actor Will Forte against a host of 2D Looney Tunes characters – including cartoon royalty such as Foghorn Leghorn, Porky Pig and Bugs Bunny. This, Green believed, would weave a heady spell for cinemagoers of all ages. Six years later, his film is finally about to be released. When Green first called “Action!”, his dark hair was not yet flecked liberally with grey. It is now.“We’ve held on to a lot of hope these past few years,” Green says from his home in Los Angeles, “and we never really let go of it.”That sustained hope was necessary because, just three months after filming wrapped in 2023, Warner Brothers announced that it was shelving the movie, alongside two others, Batgirl and Scoob! Holiday Haunt, as part of a major tax write-off. It would never see the light of day.View image in fullscreenThe need for speed … Wile E Coyote in Coyote vs Acme.Photograph: AltitudeFor Forte, the project’s palpably human lead, this came as an abrupt shock. “We’d gotten a call from our producers on a Tuesday night saying they were excited about it, that it had tested really well with audiences,” Forte says. “But then, the very next day, came the Warner Brothers news.” He palms his forehead hard enough to leave a mark. “We still went ahead with our own screening of it, but it became a funeral screening.”While it seems reasonable enough to assume that Scoob! Holiday Haunt would prove no great loss to cinematic history, the fate of Coyote Vs Acme was far less explicable. Looney Tunes holds a special place in the hearts of millions of people who grew up in front of televisions at any point between the 1950s and 1980s, and Green had done a commendable job in breathing new, and slyly modern, life into them.Cast and crew were stunned by the cancellation. Then came the anger. “Oh, I just got to this very angry place,” Forte says, “and I needed to release it somehow. I wrote a bunch of very angry posts, really scorched-earth stuff, and I’d send them to my agents asking if it was OK to post. They were like:‘Don’t you dare!’”Nevertheless, when Forte was interviewed about it by Entertainment Weekly magazine in the US, he said that it had left him feeling “extreme frustration, fiery frustration, a lot of anger, white-hot anger”.It was his wife who suggested he calm down. “She made me see that it was doing me no good to have these feelings in my system all the time. I tried to let it go. It was a grieving process, really.”View image in fullscreenDirector Dave Green … ‘We got this incredible outpouring of support. That really buoyed us.’Photograph: Chris Pizzello/APForte eventually moved on, as actors will, most recently with the hit Netflix seriesThe Four Seasons. Green, meanwhile, stewed over his apparent failure, wondering what he’d done wrong. “But then,” he says, “we got this incredible outpouring of support from so many people. That really buoyed us.”Green, whose previous credits include 2016’s Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: Out of the Shadows, first got the idea for Coyote vs Acme after readinga humorous article in the New Yorker magazine from 1990by the writer Ian Frazier, in which Wile E Coyote sues Acme for their faulty products.“I grew up watching family movies that were very close to what was going on here,” he adds. “Films like Beetlejuice, Ghostbusters, Tim Burton’s Batman, ET. All were, in certain ways, dark and adult, but also fun and bright, and silly and funny. I wanted to make something that didn’t talk down to viewers.”Green’s film was funded by an initially enthusiastic Warner Brothers with a $70m budget. On finishing the film, Forte was wildly optimistic. “Dave did such a terrific job and I just wanted people to see it. After the Warner Brothers thing, I started to fantasise about helping it reach an audience. I’d dream I was going to win the lottery, then release the movie myself and give all the proceeds to charity.”His frustrations, publicly aired as they were, were not in vain. Indeed, they encouraged others to follow suit. Fans of the cartoons, who had read about the film’s plight, took to the internet in their thousands to express discontent, as did members of the production crew. The film’s composer Steven Price (who won an Oscar in 2013 for Gravity) shared an online clip of his work withan orchestra and a choir at Abbey Road“because no one will see it now”. The post got 6.8m views.View image in fullscreenJohn Cena as Buddy Crane in Coyote vs Acme.Photograph: AltitudeWhile it is not yet a matter of public record how Warner Brothers reacted to all this, they nevertheless became increasingly aware that they’d let go of a hot property. The prospect of selling it on to another production company was appealing from a financial perspective, but less so if it then went on to be a smash hit. Last year, the film finance and distribution company Ketchup Entertainmentbought it for about $50m. A global release is imminent.“I still can’t believe it’s happening,” says Green. “There are so many parallels. This is a movie about an underdog and it’s become an underdog itself. Truly, we are here because everyone spoke out on its behalf, which is just – well, it’s insane, really. I’m sorry,” he says. “I still haven’t found a way to articulate it any better than that. It feels like a miracle. We just got extremely lucky, I guess.” Eventually, yes. They did.Coyote vs Acme is out in the UK on 21 August, 28 August in the US and 17 September in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsFilmAnimation in filmWarner BrosfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How the mob took Hollywood: the story of organized crime and the movies  | Documentary | The Guardian
description: Hollywood Crime Story: The Mob Takes Over the Movies looks back at how criminals insinuated themselves in the film business
Author: Zach Vasquez
Headline: Hollywood Crime Story: The Mob Takes Over the Movies looks back at how criminals insinuated themselves in the film business
Content: A photograph used in Hollywood Crime Story: The Mob Takes Over the Movies.Photograph: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA photograph used in Hollywood Crime Story: The Mob Takes Over the Movies.Photograph: Getty ImagesDocumentaryHow the mob took Hollywood: the story of organized crime and the moviesHollywood Crime Story: The Mob Takes Over the Movies looks back at how criminals insinuated themselves in the film businessZach VasquezFri 14 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 16.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“From the foundation of Hollywood, organized crime is there.” So claims Tom Patterson, producer and director of new three-part documentary series, Hollywood Crime Story: The Mob Takes Over the Movies.American witchhunt: how the McCarthy blacklist annihilated the Hollywood leftRead moreOrganized crime’s connection to the film industry actually predates Tinseltown, being present for the foundation of the medium itself, when inventor Thomas Edison sicced his hired goons on competitors in an attempt to maintain total control over early motion picture technology. As covered in Hollywood Crime Story, this resulted in said competitors – mostly Jewish businessmen from the east coast – fleeing westward and establishing the town and studio system that would become synonymous with movies as we know them.That same period also begat the rise of organized crime syndicates on the other side of the country – The Outfit in Chicago, the mafia in New York – a result of the criminal economy created by Prohibition. It didn’t take long for the two worlds to collide. Combining archival footage with talking head interviews, Hollywood Crime Story charts the interdependent relationship between the mob and the movies from development of cinema through to the year 1990, when the dual releases of The Godfather Part III and Goodfellas, per Patterson, “put a nice cap on that era of Hollywood”.View image in fullscreenAl Capone in 1931.Photograph: APEpisode one covers the dawn of the motion picture through the 1960s, a period that saw the ascension of the Chicago kingpin Al Capone, who dispatches one of his underlings, Johnny Roselli, out west to explore new business opportunities. Roselli finds a Hollywood ripe for the picking, quickly establishing himself among its top stars and moguls, including and especially Harry Cohn, the vicious co-founder and president of Columbia Pictures. It was thanks to a half-million-dollar loan from Roselli that Cohn was able to buy out his partners at Columbia, thus giving the mob its first real stakes in one of the major studios.We learn about Capone’s short but lively trip to Hollywood and his initially antagonistic but ultimately positive reception to the loose biopic made about him in 1932, Scarface. We meet suave but volatile gangster Benjamin “Bugsy” Siegel, who moves to town and immediately starts rubbing shoulders with the industry elite; his underling and future replacement as head of vice in LA, the brutish Mickey Cohen, who got his start in crime at age nine when he held up a movie theater; Cohen’s abusive thug Johnny Stompanato, who dated movie star Lana Turner and was eventually stabbed to death by her teenage daughter; and the corrupt union officials whom the mob inserted as heads of the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees (IATSE) and the Teamsters. We get the startling tale of the bosses putting a hit out on the Screen Actors Guild president, James Cagney, when he wouldn’t hand his union over to them (his life only spared thanks to Scarface lead Paul Muni personally asking Capone to intervene) and a funny anecdote about Cohen robbing leading lady Betty Grable only for her to laugh it off when they reunite years later.Most of these violent characters meet violent ends, but nature abhors a vacuum, so it isn’t long before new shady figures take the reins. Episode two of Hollywood Crime Story is set between the late 60s and the early 80s. “Rather than disappearing after the fall of the studio system,” explains Patterson, “organized crime becomes more intertwined with Hollywood than ever, but in more mainstream-accepted ways.”View image in fullscreenLana Turner and Johnny Stompanato.Photograph: Getty ImagesIn one of the series’ best moments, one-time president of Universal Studios Tom Mount tells of attending a meeting presided over by director Alfred Hitchcock, super-agent Lew Wasserman (whose uber-powerful agency MCA rose to prominence with the direct backing of Capone), former mobster and Las Vegas mogul Mo Dalitz, and lawyer Sidney Korshak, one of if not the most powerful man in Hollywood thanks in no small part to his large mob clientele. Mount recalls listening to these men “carve out” parts of Hollywood for themselves.Wasserman and Korshack are two of the central figures in this middle chapter, as they were at the heart of a cadre made up of Jewish gangsters and businessmen known as the Supermob, or, alternatively, “the Kosher Nostra”. The Supermob ran every aspect of Hollywood, from casting to funding to unionizing – as well as off-the-books wheeling and dealing, such as negotiating the release of Frank Sinatra’s kidnapped son – but, as summed up by series narrator Jeff Rechner, “where the mob once used violence to exercise control, these new figures wield the boardroom as their weapon.”Their story leads directly to the creation of the most iconic mob movie of all time: The Godfather. Shepherded by Korshack protege and maverick president of Paramount Pictures Robert Evans, secretly funded in part by mafia and Vatican banker Michele Sindona, and given an unofficial greenlight by crime boss and Italian civil rights campaigner Joe Colombo (who’d be gunned down during a public speech while the film was in production), the huge success of The Godfather went on to reshape how both film-makers and criminals operated.“When The Godfather came out, mobsters were trying to keep it low-key,” says Patterson. “Then they see this grand, wonderful old school depiction and think, ‘I want to live like that.’ You start hearing stories of the gestures becoming bigger – the kissing the ring of the capo, the big weddings, the whispered meetings, the code names.”View image in fullscreenRobert Duvall and Marlon Brando in The Godfather.Photograph: Paramount/Kobal/ShutterstockAs with the rogue’s gallery from episode one, this renewed attention and heightened profile leads to tragedy for most of these individuals. But even as this second generation of shadowy powerbrokers are either dragged into the light or snuffed out for good, they manage to reshape the future of entertainment. Hollywood Crime Story argues: “In squeezing the life out of prestige film-making and transforming studio economics, Korshack and the Supermob may have unknowingly set the stage for the blockbuster age.”That age truly dawned in the next decade, alongside mainstream cinema’s disreputable sister industry: pornography. Episode three explores how mob-affiliated figures, such as Louis “Butchie” Peraino, parlayed the money they made from producing porno flicks into purchasing and distributing legitimate films (in his case, titles such as Andy Warhol’s Frankenstein, Enter the Dragon, Dark Star and The Texas Chainsaw Massacre), thus creating an early model for independent film-making that we’d see take off in the 90s.Alongside pornography, the other big revenue stream for Hollywood mobsters was cocaine, which became the drug de rigueur of the town’s elite. Robert Evans and his fall from grace become the focus for much of this episode, particularly his involvement in the disastrous production of the 1984 historical crime drama The Cotton Club. Reuniting with Godfather director Francis Ford Coppola in the hopes of recreating that film’s success, Evans made a desperate decision to secure funding by partnering with two members of Florida’s cocaine cartel. The subsequent falling-out between the pair resulted in a highly publicized murder trial that would destroy what was left of Evans’s reputation (at least until his unlikely third-act reinvention 20 years later).View image in fullscreenRobert Evans in 1974.Photograph: Jeff Robbins/APThese stories are just a sampling of those covered in Hollywood Crime Story, which, by its directors’ own admission, barely scratches the surface. Inspired during the development of respective docuseries about Marylin Monroe and Elvis Presley’s connections to the mob, Patterson found that “Once you start diving into it, another story pops up, and another story pops up, and another story pops up. The hardest part was deciding what to include in the three episodes.”To that end, Patterson is greatly helped by the expert team he assembled behind and in front of the camera, a mix of mob historians, such as senior director of education at Las Vegas’s Mob Museum Claire White and author Gus Russo, and film experts like Jonathan Kuntz and Christina Newland. The documentary succeeds not only as a breezy, but expertly researched look behind the Hollywood curtain, but also as a critical examination of the mob genre itself, its evolution from the silent era to the final decade of the 20th century. Patterson explains his decision to end in 1990 by asking, “Has there been a truly great gangster movie since Goodfellas? They either tend to look to the past or they’re on TV.”Regardless of one’s opinion on post-2000 mob cinema, Patterson notes that “Organized crime in Hollywood ranges today from Ukrainian mobsters taking over streaming services to African gangs running piracy, etc, etc. We don’t live in the world of concentrated power in either a physical or psycho-geographic Hollywood any more.”However diffuse organized crime’s impact is on the industry in today’s digital age, you can bet the relationship remains a symbiotic one, with movies influencing how gangsters think and act, and vice versa, ad infinitum.Hollywood Crime Story: The Mob Takes Over the Movies airs on Sundance Now and is available on AMC+This article was amended on 14 August 2026. It was originally stated that Lana Turner was married to Johnny Stompanato, but they only dated.Explore more on these topicsDocumentaryFactual TVTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It was lonely being a young queer artist’: Sam Smith on finding health, happiness – and their hazel-eyed fiance | Sam Smith | The Guardian
description: On their new album, Smith is subverting their singer-songwriter roots to tell a queer love story. They talk about their shifting fanbase, the nasty undercurrents of fame – and finding sanctuary in New York City
Author: Juan A Ramírez
Headline: On their new album, Smith is subverting their singer-songwriter roots to tell a queer love story. They talk about their shifting fanbase, the nasty undercurrents of fame – and finding sanctuary in New York City
Content: ‘On Hazel Eyes, I wanted to capture the bloom of falling deeply in love’ … Sam Smith.Photograph: Collier SchorrView image in fullscreen‘On Hazel Eyes, I wanted to capture the bloom of falling deeply in love’ … Sam Smith.Photograph: Collier SchorrSam SmithInterview‘It was lonely being a young queer artist’: Sam Smith on finding health, happiness – and their hazel-eyed fianceJuan A RamírezOn their new album, Smith is subverting their singer-songwriter roots to tell a queer love story. They talk about their shifting fanbase, the nasty undercurrents of fame – and finding sanctuary in New York CityFri 14 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 05.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSam Smith logs on to our video call with the username “Lily of the Valley”, the May-born singer’s birth flower. It sets a serene tone. They’re in Guadalajara, Mexico, for the latest stop of a residency tour, titled To Be Free, in support of their fifth studio album. Instead of Smith’s usual jet-lagged arena itinerary, this lower-key excursion stops at smaller venues in only six cities and sheds the ostentatious theatricality of their last outing.On stage on their last tour, “I was flailing around on a massive gold bum and had, like, seven costume changes,” Smith says with a chuckle. It’s intimacy they’re after now, the ability to satisfy their “craving to look at people again”, which matches the romantic feeling of their fifth album, Hazel Eyes. But for Smith, whose genre-shifting stardom has been accompanied by harsh controversies, it’s also a chance to observe who’s still in their corner: “There’s some wonderful people that have stayed, but it’s a completely different room than it was with In the Lonely Hour,” their 2014 debut.View image in fullscreenSmith performs at the Castro theatre in San Francisco on their To Be Free tour.Photograph: Steve Jennings/Getty Images for Capitol RecordsSmith broke out at 20, as the featured vocalist on Disclosure’s massive 2012 hit Latch. That 2014 debut, featuring the mega-hit Stay With Me, heralded them as a soulful chart-topper, if one whose knack for heartbreak could verge on self-pity. It was good enough for Bond: in 2015, Smith sang the Spectre theme Writing’s on the Wall and won an Oscar. Their subsequent releases veered into a glossier pop sound and generally remained as successful. But since coming out as non-binary in 2017, the British singer has frequently been attacked and vilified by rightwing commentators. The peace that emanates from the 34-year-old during our call, and from this latest album, was largely achieved after relocating from the UK to New York three years ago to be with their fiance, the (hazel-eyed) designer Christian Cowan.“When I got here and was able to walk in the street and feel no judgment, I realised that I was very happy to have found a sanctuary in New York City as a queer person,” they say. Smith, who has been wearing “makeup and wild femme clothing from a very young age”, found that “tensions were a little high” after the 2023 release oftheir expressive last album, Gloria. “With a body like mine and the person that I am, it created a bit of a media storm.” (The videos for Unholy and I’m Not Here to Make Friends were accused of being oversexualised, with a rhetoric that felt transphobic to many observers.) “But I moved to New York for positive reasons. I wasn’t running away from anything.”After Gloria, Smith “was looking for safety and comfort in music”, something to capture “the bloom of falling deeply in love” and buoy their cross-continental move. They found it by downsizing their process. Simon Aldred, with whom Smith had co-written one song on their debut, had long told Smith to call whenever they were ready for a more intimate collaboration. For Hazel Eyes, Smith took him up on it.View image in fullscreen‘I was flailing around on a massive gold bum’ … Smith on stage in Berlin for the Gloria tour, 2023.Photograph: Frank Hoensch/RedfernsThe result is a more clear-eyed assessment of the reality of relationships than Smith’s lovelorn previous albums. They wrote the first half of what became the smoky opener, Everlasting Love, the night before meeting Cowan; the second half reflects on their three years together. It’s also Smith’s first time co-producing an album. “I’ve always been very hands on with my music, but I never felt like I could really put my name on the credit,” they say. “I’ve realised that I’m not just a singer and a songwriter, I’m an artist.” Hazel Eyes’ soundscape channels a dusky, 70s blend of blues and folk, R&B and outlaw country.The process was looser than Smith’s past experiences in more professional, structured writing rooms, where they felt that recording had to be done “completely sober and all had to happen between the hours of 10am and 5pm”. Hazel Eyes was written at all hours, thanks in part to their near-constant conversations with Aldred; Smith mentions tequila-tinged 1am studio sessions with the Dap-Kings, the late Sharon Jones’s band, as a high point: “It just felt so freeing, what music’s about.”These relaxed, more intimate collaborations scared Smith, who says they had operated as “a pop ho for a long time – in the best way. I loved it, and I will be that again, but every two, three records were written with a different group of people. It was like a speed-dating process of making music.”Watch the video for My Guy.Hazel Eyes is also a return to the singer-songwriter style of Smith’s debut. They don’t see it as a rehash, but a new angle on traditional songwriting tropes. “A song like My Guy, that lyric is so simple and one that maybe we’ve all heard before – ‘He’s mine, mine, mine, he’s my guy’ – but you haven’t heard it from a non-binary person who’s 34 years old in 2026. I was very interested in that type of lyric-writing for this album, to take the traditional and sing it through my lens and sing it freely.”It was only after the success of Unholy, their 2023 duet with Kim Petras, that Smith found the freedom to return to that classic sound. With its baroque electropop and panic-baiting live performances (at the Grammys, Smithsported a pair of devil hornsin a red-lit, fiery set), the global No 1 single earned them a Grammy – andcondemnation from conservatives. “When Unholy happened, I felt like I’d been fighting for that song for a long time,” says Smith – they had always wanted to top the US charts, having previously peaked there at No 2 with Stay With Me.Global competition is no longer a concern for Smith. “As a queer artist, I have different parameters and rules, so it’s just not a healthy way for me to think,” they say – that for any artist whose existence is, to some, contentious, fame is always rigged with a nasty undercurrent, no matter how quantifiable their success. Smith says they were at their “most depressed or creatively stunted” during that chase. With Hazel Eyes, they wanted to focus on emotional truth rather than “worrying about hooks, even though I love hooks”. They’ll return to that, says Smith, “but it’s my prerogative to choose when I want to use that tool”. This led to some “uncomfortable moments” with their label, with Smith having to say “I just wanted to keep the business out of the music”.View image in fullscreen‘I wanted to keep business out of the music’ … Smith.Photograph: Collier SchorrHazel Eyes was the first time Smith set a colour palette (“this brown, sepia filter”) and ethos to which every song must be upheld: a familiar guiding image, based on a lifelong affinity for rivers born out of a bucolic spot near their Cambridgeshire home town. Any ideas, sounds or lyrics, even the more urbane, New-York-inspired ones, would have to sound at home in that domesticated image in order to make it on to the record. They found that rigour liberating – it allowed Smith to lean into the maximalism of carrying through a single idea. “I like spilling over the sides,” they say. “There’s something for me in the imperfection of it that feels so pop.”It’s a point of pride for Smith to have reset their relationship with the public on their own terms. Becoming a celebrity at 20 meant that they quickly found an “incredibly traumatic” side to fame, “especially to a younger, queer brain, because it felt quite lonely at times within the industry”. For a few years, from 27, they shunned the “huge part of the job” that is constantly taking selfies with fans. Doing so allowed them to recover some semblance of privacy, but led to depression, “because I felt like I was upsetting people all day”.After a lot of therapy, they say, “I actually have started to find the happiness and the joy of meeting people. I’m a healthy person right now, so I’m able to juggle more. The trajectory of fame that I went through at such a young age, and trying to navigate my life as a gay person, then changing my pronouns – the weight of doing that so publicly in my 20s meant that I could juggle less.”Occasionally, there is a protective edge to Smith’s conversation, such as when they point out that they “juggled a lot, because I brought out four records and toured the world multiple times”. But it doesn’t feel confrontational; more demarcating well-defined boundaries and a hard-won ability to claim their achievements.Watch the video for Unholy.It’s true that controversy has hounded Smith from day one. They have never concealed their sexuality and have evolved almost entirely in the public eye, which has included some stumbles. In 2016, when collecting the Academy award for best original song for their Bond theme, they incorrectly claimed to be the first openly gay Oscar winner (that was John Schlesinger as best director of Midnight Cowboy, in 1970); shortly into the 2020 lockdown, they were ridiculed for sharing photosdepicting their “quarantine meltdown” that some felt to be tone deaf.Whatever anyone says, Smith’s sales and streaming figures put them in the echelons of Elton John and Freddie Mercury in terms of queer pop success stories, although Smith is cautious about placing themselves within that legacy. “George Michael was always a beautiful inspiration to me,” they say, but they’ve found a “deep comfort and understanding about the type of artist I am” from conversations withthe artist Anohni, with whom they’ve grown close, “because I am not like George Michael. I’m a femme queer and when it comes to that, and the people that came before me in the UK, it’s a different type of lineage.“What I’ve experienced as a queer femme artist on the global pop stage, I don’t think there’s others that I can compare my career to,” they continue. “I’ve learned to see that as a strength when, at times before, I just found that incredibly isolating. I’m trying not to compare or to look left and right in that sense any more.”Smith finds that, after a period of increased LGBTQ+ acceptance in the UK and abroad, the pendulum has swung back. “For trans people in the UK, it’s incredibly hard.” I ask if they ever find solace in the thought that history will probably only remember their successes: Michael’s cruising scandal, I point out, has been almost entirely vindicated on queer social media. Smith takes a beat to think.View image in fullscreenSmith at the Grammys in 2015, where they won four awards.Photograph: Frazer Harrison/Getty Images“I want to answer this honestly,” they say. “I’m encouraged sometimes, especially by straight people around me, to think of that. It doesn’t necessarily bring me comfort, because of the state of things. I think it’s important to be educated as a queer person, to know that things could get better, but things could also get worse in my lifetime, and we have to work hard for kindness and peace.” Two years ago, they established the Pink House foundation, a charity that will provide support for the LGBTQ+ community. It gives Smith a chance to “focus on the realities of situations and hope for a better future”, they say, more than focusing on their own legacy.But there’s at least one tribute to Smith’s life in New York. Julius’ is a gay bar in the city’s West Village with a history of community and rebellion. Alongside shots of icons such as Judy Garland and John Cameron Mitchell, some images of Smith line its walls. They were taken there by a friend, years ago. “I’m English, right? I love a pub.” It’s since become their favourite haunt; some of Hazel Eyes was written on the counter.‘Experimental, queer and kind of magical’: Sade and Sam Smith feature on 46-track album for trans rightsRead moreWith a self-effacing grin, they point out that those photos are “in the back” of the venue. Still, one is by the noted fashion photographer Alasdair McLellan. “I love Alasdair McLellan – so that’s just a slay.” The other is of Smith and Alicia Keys from a small performance they hosted at the bar for a 10th anniversary celebration of In the Lonely Hour. “It was such a beautiful, triumphant moment for me, as someone who was moving to New York, to get to sing with Alicia fucking Keys in this gay bar.” Smith beams. “If I could be part of the legacy of Julius’, that’s a legacy I’m proud to be a part of.”With all but their third album topping the UK charts (Love Goes peaked at No 2), there’s a confidence that, no matter what they release, Hazel Eyes will find an audience. “I’m a political artist, whether I want to be or not, so my audience is in flux at times,” Smith says. “I am singing for me, ultimately, and I’m singing to the sky and whoever hears it.”Hazel Eyes is released via Capitol on 21 AugustThis article was amended on 14 August 2026. Hazel Eyes is released via Capitol, not Polydor as previously stated.Explore more on these topicsSam SmithPop and rockLGBTQ+ rightsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Add to playlist: the heartbreak post-mortems of Cape Town’s Rowlene and the week’s best new tracks | Music | The Guardian
description: The South African singer has been a memorable guest artist, but the unhurried, emotional tracks on new album Some Strings Attached show she’s ready for the spotlight
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: The South African singer has been a memorable guest artist, but the unhurried, emotional tracks on new album Some Strings Attached show she’s ready for the spotlight
Content: An R&B balladeer at heart … RowleneView image in fullscreenAn R&B balladeer at heart … RowleneAdd to playlistMusicAdd to playlist: the heartbreak post-mortems of Cape Town’s Rowlene and the week’s best new tracksThe South African singer has been a memorable guest artist, but the unhurried, emotional tracks on new album Some Strings Attached show she’s ready for the spotlightMary Chiney andLaura SnapesFri 14 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 08.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromCape Town, South AfricaRecommended if you likeSummer Walker, SZA, ShekhinahUp nextSome Strings Attached out nowRowlene Bosman learned to sing in a Cape Town school choir, and the discipline never left her: she is a precision vocalist in a scene that rewards volume. Most South Africans first heard her in 2018, delivering the hook onNasty C’s SMA– she was the first signing to his Tall Racks label – and the featured artist circuit kept her busy for years. But while South African pop stampeded towards amapiano, Rowlene held her ground as a balladeer, writing slow, confessional R&B in which heartbreak is examined instead of danced away. Her 2020 debut album 11:11, a set of aching, close-quarters soul songs, brought a South African music award nomination for best pop album, and three of her originals –Cupid,Stayand the Nasty C collaborationI Need You– landed on the soundtrack of Netflix’s SA teen crime drama Blood & Water, carrying her voice far beyond home.Hurts 2b Reminded, from her new albumSome Strings Attached, is the best argument yet for that patience. Over spare, unhurried production with a faint Afropop pulse ticking underneath, she sings about the ambush of memory: the places and small details that resurrect someone you thought you had let go. The twist is who she is mourning: not the dead, nor an ex, but friends who are alive and well yet simply elsewhere, people whose lives moved on without her. Losing them, she has said, was the price of finding herself. After 10 years of stealing the show from other artists, she sounds ready to headline her own.Mary ChineyThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreenHayley Williams.Photograph: Zachary GrayPower Snatch – Born DeadParamore’sHayley Williamscontinues her fruitful artistic evolution with her new band’s surprise second EP. Balancing murky alt-rock grandeur and serpentine intimacy, this highlight winds its vines around you. [Stream atBandcamp]Heavensouls – Dawn of the CityChidi Obialo, 20, has already released an album of the year in Westside Trapped. Now comes a 10-minute odyssey evoking a malfunctioning Dance Dance Revolution machine, dreamy chiptune and frenetically lapping IDM. [Stream atBandcamp]Sophia Stel – Now I’ve Got a Lot You KnowThe breakout Vancouver star’s latest song threatens to spill from robot ballad to confetti-canon rager, although the EDM risers that peak two minutes in bring surprising clarity and warmth to her devotional.Axel Boman and Superpitcher – True CrimeNew Boman is always cause for celebration, not least when it’s seven delicious minutes of ribboning, swirling synth trills undercut by a beat as fine and spangly as tinsel fronds.King Gizzard& the Lizard Wizard – Kill for the Steel“We don’t wish death upon you,” a alien voice incants reassuringly on the latest from Gizz’s Cyberdog techno turn; instead, their apparent wish is a state of dripping, warehouse-induced transcendence. [Stream onBandcamp]Shabazz Palaces – Ahh World (I Won the Alpha Bet)Ishmael Butler delivers life lessons – never gossip, hit fastballs, take risks – on a shadowy, bassy track so cool and imperious you could imagine it emanating from an ancient court.Garefowl – Buthaigir/PuffinFrom the Scottish archipelago of St Kilda come this avian-inspired group, whose new album for AD93 contemplates the island’s birds. The lead single is a gorgeous, violin-led lament.Laura SnapesSubscribe to the Guardian’s rolling Add to Playlist selections on Spotify – or transfer it toApple,Tidalor other servicesThis article was amended on 14 August 2026. Ishmael Butler’s son does not appear on the new Shabazz Palaces song as previously stated.Explore more on these topicsMusicAdd to playlistSouth AfricaPop and rockR&BfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Hillborg: Lost Landscapes album review – sonic imagination and luminous colours | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Unconventional instrumentation adds to the filmic feeling of these three works by the Swedish composer, played on this recording by a powerhouse orchestra on top form
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Unconventional instrumentation adds to the filmic feeling of these three works by the Swedish composer, played on this recording by a powerhouse orchestra on top form
Content: Stylistically eclectic: composer Anders HillborgPhotograph: https://www.hillborg.com/View image in fullscreenStylistically eclectic: composer Anders HillborgPhotograph: https://www.hillborg.com/Classical musicReviewHillborg: Lost Landscapes album review – sonic imagination and luminous coloursGothenburg Symphony Orchestra/Kuusisto/Lubman/Falk Winland(Alpha)Unconventional instrumentation adds to the filmic feeling of these three works by the Swedish composer, played on this recording by a powerhouse orchestra on top formClive PagetFri 14 Aug 2026 06.06 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 06.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnders Hillborg’s stylistically eclectic work resists easy categorisation as these three rewarding works, performed by the Gothenburg Symphony Orchestra, demonstrate. Lost Landscapes opens with signatureglissandi, features a filmic, jazz-inflected chase and ends in an orchestral death spiral. Pekka Kuusisto draws out its luminous colours and richly clustered harmonies.View image in fullscreenAnders Hillborg: Lost Landscapes.Photograph: Alpha ClassicsThe Strand Settings, a four-movement song cycle to texts by Canadian poet Mark Strand, was composed at the behest of Renée Fleming. Nature, the elements and a certain forlorn eroticism infuse poetry that Hillborg responds to with tonal and dynamic restraint. Gently pulsing strings with piquant woodwind and brass build atmospheric soundscapes over which Swedish soprano Ida Falk Winland spins haunting vocal lines in impeccable English.Finally, Sound Atlas, stylishly conducted by Brad Lubman, showcases Hillborg’s sonic imagination and affection for unusual instruments. Here it’s theverrophone, invented by German musician Sascha Reckert, where the rims of glass tubes are rubbed with wet fingers, similar to playing wine glasses. The orchestra is often instructed to play slightly sharp or flat, their microtonal clashes lending the work a spectral quality. A pair of gleaming slow movements pitch into the glittering Vaporised Toy Pianos followed by the roiling Vortex before concluding with Hymn, a noble finale in the manner of Sibelius.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com. title: Henry Threadgill, Vijay Iyer, Dafnis Prieto: Fifteen review – Pulitzer winner stirs gorgeous improv patterns | Music | The Guardian
description: By turns gleeful, sensitive, urgent and ruminative, this is a brilliant set that plays to the trio’s formidable strengths
Author: John Fordham
Headline: By turns gleeful, sensitive, urgent and ruminative, this is a brilliant set that plays to the trio’s formidable strengths
Content: Brilliant … (from left) Dafnis Prieto, Henry Threadgill and Vijay Iyer.Photograph: Michael WilsonView image in fullscreenBrilliant … (from left) Dafnis Prieto, Henry Threadgill and Vijay Iyer.Photograph: Michael WilsonJazz album of the monthMusicReviewHenry Threadgill, Vijay Iyer, Dafnis Prieto: Fifteen review – Pulitzer winner stirs gorgeous improv patterns(Nonesuch)By turns gleeful, sensitive, urgent and ruminative, this is a brilliant set that plays to the trio’s formidable strengthsJohn FordhamFri 14 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThough the century-old Pulitzer prize – launched as a celebration of the craft and social necessity of good news reportage – was eventually expanded to include fiction and music by 1943, the US-born art of jazz has only been represented by Ornette Coleman and Wynton Marsalis in their lifetimes, Duke Ellington, John Coltrane and Thelonious Monk posthumously – and most recentlyHenry Threadgill, for his four-part suiteIn for a Penny, In for a Pound, in 2016.View image in fullscreenHenry Threadgill, Vijay Iyer, Dafnis Prieto: FifteenPublisher Joseph Pulitzer once declared his dreams for his readership were “to arrest their attention, enlist their sympathy … stimulate their imagination, convince their reason, and awaken their conscience”. Contemporary-classical composer and flautist Threadgill has been doing all that with his music,his personal story, his internationalism and his charisma since the 1960s. Now 82, he releases Fifteen, joining him in a brilliant trio featuring pianist/composer Vijay Iyer and creative Cuban percussionist Dafnis Prieto.The album title references the number of years since this collective originally convened on a fundraiser for New York’sJazzgallery. It’s simpler and more explicitly improv-oriented than Threadgill’s Pulitzer winner, the instrumentally diverse, polyphonically dizzying In for a Penny: all three members here are simultaneously composers and free-improvisers who cherish the communality of recurring patterns in ways some free-jazz players avoid.Trio Piece is begun by Prieto and Iyer in staccato interval-hops and asymmetrical snare-drum snaps before Threadgill’s skimming flute lines glide in. Last Night is an urgently pressing piano groove powered by Iyer against Prieto’s supple, sensuous drum sounds, while Threadgill’s own Where Coconuts Fall is a rumination for piano, frothing cymbals and imploring alto-sax long tones. Prieto’s closing On the Way is a coquettish Latin frolic, edited by the stately Threadgill to clipped sonic punctuation marks, but gleefully stormed all over by Prieto and Iyer. Hearteningly delightful contemporary music-making.Also out this monthBassist/composerLinda May Han Ohalso celebrated the arts of the jazz trio onStrange Heavenslast year, but the Malaysia-born bassist/composer gets even more closely conversational onBeneath Lifted Skies (Biophilia)in a duo partnership with Chilean saxophone starMelissa Aldanathat will entrance jazz traditionalists and newcomers alike. A hurtling interchange on the Charlie Parker classic Anthology, lyrically haunting wanderings on Wayne Shorter’s Dance Cadaverous and Oh’s beautiful solo reflections on Billie Holiday’s God Bless the Child are among 15 exquisite vignettes, likely destined for the end-of-year faves lists. Three-volume set The Riverside Years 1959-1962 (Acrobat) captures the effortless lyrical fluency of short-lived guitar geniusWes Montgomeryin some of his hottest company, including saxist Johnny Griffin and Miles Davis pianist Wynton Kelly between those years. And innovative UK-based guitarist/composerNicolas Meierdraws on the work of Argentine composer Astor Piazzolla, flamenco and new configurations of his jazz, Turkish and Middle Eastern roots onElysian Drift (MGP).Explore more on these topicsMusicJazz album of the monthJazzreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Rebecca Perry: ‘Lorca hit me like a bolt of lightning’ | Culture | The Guardian
description: The poet and novelist on the power of fairytales, being inspired by Frank O’Hara and the joys of Doris Lessing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The poet and novelist on the power of fairytales, being inspired by Frank O’Hara and the joys of Doris Lessing
Content: ‘Percival Everett made me feel I might be able to write a novel’ … Rebecca Perry.Photograph: Ross JonesView image in fullscreen‘Percival Everett made me feel I might be able to write a novel’ … Rebecca Perry.Photograph: Ross JonesThe books of my lifeCultureRebecca Perry: ‘Lorca hit me like a bolt of lightning’The poet and novelist on the power of fairytales, being inspired by Frank O’Hara and the joys of Doris LessingRebecca PerryFri 14 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 05.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy earliest reading memoryReading On the Ning Nang Nong by Spike Milligan, aged five or so, sitting on the floor of the bedroom I shared with my brother – who, in my memory, was sitting on the carpet next to me.My favourite book growing upI had a collection of fairytales in a big yellow hardback, which I was totally entranced by from around the age of seven to 10. I’ll never forget the feeling of despair on turning the page and discovering that the Little Mermaid had become foam on the surface of the water; it was a very early lesson in the helplessness of the reader in the face of a story’s destiny. In particular, though, I loved a Scottish fairytale called The Black Bull of Norroway, which I think, in many ways, has been under the surface of everything I’ve ever written.The book that changed me as a teenagerCollected Plays by Federico García Lorca, which I studied for GCSE drama and led me to seek out his poetry. It would be impossible for me to think about my adolescent relationship to reading, and my relationship as an adult to language, without Lorca. I remember these lines from City That Does Not Sleep hitting me like a bolt of lightning: “… and the man who rushes out with his / spirit broken will meet on the street corner / the unbelievable alligator quiet beneath / the tender protest of the stars”.The writer who changed my mindFrank O’Hara, which I know is one of the most predictable answers a poet can give, but for good reason. All of the poetry I’d studied up to the point of discovering him felt deeply serious, almost something not to be touched. Then you read O’Hara and it’s like: OK, life!The book that made me want to be a writerI really don’t think this is something that happened to me. I have just written for as long as I can remember and, at a certain point as an adult, I realised that normal living people can write books if they want to, if they’re lucky, and that maybe I would like to try to do that. To answer a slightly different question,Percival Everett’s astonishing The Treeswas the book that made me feel I might be able to write a novel.The book I rereadAnne Carson’s Glass and God, in particular The Glass Essay. It’s basically perfect – my go-to text for resetting my brain and being reminded, within the space of a page, about the capacities of writing.The book I could never read againJK Rowling’s Harry Potter series was a huge part of my childhood, but it’s art that’s firmly not to be separated from artist, in this case.The book I discovered later in lifeI don’t think I read Doris Lessing’s The Golden Notebook until I was in my 30s – but really, any time is the perfect time to discover this novel.The book I am currently readingA proof of Compensation by Augustine Cerf, which so far is brilliant, and My Garden (Book) by Jamaica Kincaid, which I often pick up and read a page or two of between other things. I’m also rereading Doom Painting by AK Blakemore, out in September. It’s a phenomenal achievement – I don’t know how she did it.My comfort readThe poetry collection Adam by Gboyega Odubanjo, who died in 2023. I keep this book on the shelf directly above my desk and when the loss of him feels particularly impossible, I take it down, read a poem and remember he’s there on the page.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories.
