title: The best recent crime and thrillers – review roundup | Books | The Guardian
description: The Amateur by Chris Bohjalian; Claws Out! by Bella Mackie; Plant Lady by Minyoung Kang; Children of Wolves by Lawrence Osborne; Mad Mabel by Sally Hepworth
Author: Laura Wilson
Headline: The Amateur by Chris Bohjalian; Claws Out! by Bella Mackie; Plant Lady by Minyoung Kang; Children of Wolves by Lawrence Osborne; Mad Mabel by Sally Hepworth
Content: Incisive social satire … Bella Mackie.Photograph: Kate Peters/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIncisive social satire … Bella Mackie.Photograph: Kate Peters/The GuardianCrime and thrillers roundupBooksReviewThe best recent crime and thrillers – review roundupThe Amateur by Chris Bohjalian; Claws Out! by Bella Mackie; Plant Lady by Minyoung Kang;Children of Wolves by Lawrence Osborne; Mad Mabel by Sally HepworthLaura WilsonFri 14 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 08.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenThe Amateurby Chris Bohjalian (Hutchinson Heinemann, £18.99)American bestseller Bohjalian deserves to be far better known in the UK, although, as the first line of his 26th novel points out, “It is neither virtue nor might that rules the world; it’s luck”. Mira Winston’s luck began early, as she was born into a rich family, clever enough to secure a place at Yale, and a talented enough golfer to consider turning pro, but things change dramatically in 1978 when, at the age of 18, a ball she hits on a driving range smashes the temporal bone of a young caddy, killing him almost instantly. The freak accident turns out to be rather more complicated than first thought, not least because it becomes karmically conflated, in Mira’s mind, with her relationship with a married man twice her age. Told as a memoir, with Mira looking back on the derailment of her life and chronicling society’s changing perceptions of agency and privilege, this literary thriller is a masterfully executed ace.View image in fullscreenClaws Out!by Bella Mackie (Borough, £20)Mackie’s third novel centres on Diana, a manipulative grifter whose previous three husbands have died, apparently of natural causes. She’s in the process of getting her feet under the fourth mark’s prosperous Hampstead table when she encounters opposition. David Farrand’s “entitled but otherwise entirely average” daughter Catriona isn’t going to give up her father or her inheritance without a fight, and when she starts investigating Diana’s past, she discovers that her former stepchildren are convinced of foul play. Meanwhile, Diana’s own son, a feckless charmer, is also hoping to benefit from his mother’s matrimonial plans. Some readers may find the arch authorial tone grating, and the sharp-eyed will spot at least one major plot development before it occurs, but the incisive social satire, vinegary humour and expert pacing will keep you laughing as you turn the pages.Plant Ladyby Minyoung Kang, translated by Shanna Tan (Doubleday, £14.99)In a fictional Korean city, green-fingered trauma survivor Yoohee realises her dream of opening a plant shop. Although she remains courteous and self-effacing, her long-held conviction that humans, like plants, repay attention and tenderness, has worn thin, and when an errant boyfriend fails to improve, she repurposes him as fertiliser. She begins offering her overwhelmingly female customer base an additional service, ridding them of abusive men, but a young detective notices that the shop is the only common point of reference in a string of otherwise unconnected disappearances, and a game of cat and mouse ensues. This “weird girl” tale of female revenge is politely told, the mechanics of dismemberment happening off the page, and although the villains tend towards the cartoonish, the atmosphere is such that one can almost inhale the damp, scented air of our heroine’s lush botanical haven as she calmly puts the world to rights.View image in fullscreenChildren of Wolvesby Lawrence Osborne (Chatto & Windus, £18.99)Osborne’s books often feature morally ambiguous expats in exotic locations; here it’s American investigator Tyler Sedgewick, in Turkey to track down Chana Knight at the behest of her father. Posing as a writer, Tyler worms his way into the young woman’s friendship group; Chana, Adam, Diana and Marco are the delinquent, sensation-seeking offspring of wealthy parents, who first met at a California reform school for rich kids, and became self-styled radicals. Now, they have walked out of their respective lives with the intention of atoning for their privileged existences through a “meaningfully violent act” against “a prominent American target”. Tyler, who has become dangerously drawn to Chana, does not realise the extent to which he is being used, and soon attracts the attention of the Turkish intelligence agency. There are echoes of both Graham Greene and Patricia Highsmith here, but Osborne’s sense of place and ability create an undercurrent of menace all his own.View image in fullscreenMad Mabelby Sally Hepworth (Macmillan, £16.99)The titular character of Australian Hepworth’s latest is a stroppy, sarcastic 81-year-old, living under a pseudonym in a quiet Melbourne suburb. More than 60 years earlier, Mabel Waller became the youngest person in Australian history to be convicted of murder. Now she keeps herself to herself, but Persephone, the lonely young daughter of a neighbour, is determined to be friends, and slowly Mabel, whose own desolate childhood with her wealthy but uninterested parents is gradually revealed in flashbacks, begins to thaw. But someone has discovered her past and is sending anonymous letters, and when the elderly man next door dies unexpectedly, she becomes the prime suspect. Although crime fiction aficionados may figure out at least one plot twist early on, Mabel’s cantankerous facade, behind which the fuzzy outlines of loss, trauma and misunderstanding gradually sharpen into focus, and the growing warmth of the intergenerational friendship, make this a genuinely moving and surprisingly funny read.Explore more on these topicsBooksCrime and thrillers roundupFictionThrillersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Beverly Hills Housewife by James Cahill review – a trip inside Hockney’s world | David Hockney | The Guardian
description: Muse Betty Freeman sits at the centre of this sun-drenched book about art, eccentricity, and the spirit of Los Angeles
Author: Ben Eastham
Headline: Muse Betty Freeman sits at the centre of this sun-drenched book about art, eccentricity, and the spirit of Los Angeles
Content: David Hockney and Betty Freeman.Photograph: John Kasmin. Courtesy of the artist and  Lyndsey IngramView image in fullscreenDavid Hockney and Betty Freeman.Photograph: John Kasmin. Courtesy of the artist and  Lyndsey IngramBook of the dayDavid HockneyReviewThe Beverly Hills Housewife by James Cahill review – a trip inside Hockney’s worldMuse Betty Freeman sits at the centre of this sun-drenched book about art, eccentricity, and the spirit of Los AngelesBen EasthamFri 14 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 03.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDavid Hockney was 29 years old when he came to Betty Freeman’s house to photograph her swimming pool. Scouting locations for the pool paintings that would make him a household name, he took preparatory snaps of his partner, Peter Schlesinger, emerging naked from the water. And yet something about his aloof and quietly eccentric host, who dusted the hunting trophies while a handsome young man padded around her patio in the altogether, intrigued the artist. So he asked whether he might photograph her too, and she agreed.Completed a year later, Beverly Hills Housewife (1966/7) shows a beautiful woman standing outside a beautiful house. The scene is lit by an unbroken sun, her blond bob is undisturbed by any breeze, a lush fern sets off her popping pink dress. She is surrounded by the symbols of mid-century American prosperity: a chair by Le Corbusier, a tasteful modernist sculpture. We don’t need the title to know the place and time, because Hockney’s paintings have come to define them in our imagination: shimmering water and scattered light, bright colours and reflective surfaces, a clean and impassive contentment.In this comparably polished mix of anecdote and art history, James Cahill uses Hockney’s painting as a “primary source” for his own multifaceted portrait of the working-class Yorkshireman who fell in love with Los Angeles, of the wealthy art collector who became his friend and ally, and of the city that would go on to shape the culture in which we now live. After potted introductions to these central characters, Cahill starts by unpacking the “lifestyle-magazine version of bourgeois affluence” that Beverly Hills Housewife presents to us.double quotation markA portrait always tells us as much about its maker as its museIn doing so, he provides an object lesson in how to read a picture, drawing the reader’s attention to the details that illuminate it. Note, for example, that Freeman’s face is doubled by the stuffed head of an antelope shot by her husband and mounted on the wall. Recast as a cultured woman trapped in a loveless marriage with a conspicuously absent big-game hunter, Freeman’s blank expression comes to seem melancholy rather than merely vacant (that the self-deprecating title was her idea suggests a disillusioned kind of wit). Hockney at his best was a narrative painter, and his pictures invite and are animated by such interpretations.Yet a portrait always tells us as much about its maker as its muse, and so Cahill moves on to what this painting might reveal of the artist’s own ideas and affinities. Most instructively, he shows how Hockney adopted the compositional model of the annunciation, in which the Virgin Mary receives news of her fate from the angel Gabriel, and painted Freeman into Mary’s place. This allows Cahill to elaborate on the artist’s debt to the early Renaissance masters, and then to speculate on the dynamic between this young, gay man and the glamorous older woman he represents (with gentle irony) as the Madonna: victim and mother, protector and icon. Like all good criticism, the simple observations underpinning these speculations seem so obvious once pointed out that they cannot be unseen, and change the picture for ever.The difficulty the book runs into is that there is only so much to unpack. Hockney was a painter of enclosed worlds, from which the otherwise inescapable facts of Los Angeles life – the Watts riots, choking smog, Vietnam – are excluded. This does not diminish him as an artist any more than it diminishes Vermeer, and Cahill is justified in arguing that “meaning might reside in so-called veneers” as much as in what lies beneath them. But it does make his work a difficult subject for the kind of ekphrastic exercise that requires hidden layers of meaning to excavate.So, recognising that Hockney was more interested in the “concealments of portraiture, its feints and deflections” than in exposing any hidden truth, Cahill follows his lead. Rather than digging up the painting’s glossy surface, he glances off it into anecdotal histories of vanguard American music (of which Freeman was an influential supporter), the mythologised Los Angeles art scene (with Edward Kienholz’s darkness as counterpoint to Hockney’s light), and much else besides. There are heroes (the hobo composer Harry Partch) and villains (the painter Clyfford Still, whose egomania and vanity is entertainingly monstrous even when set against the high bar maintained by the abstract expressionist movement).At times this can feel tendentious, and the connections that link the period back to the painting somewhat strained. But it is testament to the agility of his prose and the lightness of Cahill’s touch that the reader is unlikely to mind, and so this portrait of multiple subjects continues to feel enlightening and engaging long after the painting at its heart has been exhausted. His book is in this respect much like its primary source: charming, clever, and difficult to pin down.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: Alien: Isolation 2 – another strong female protagonist stalked in a terrifying new world | Games | The Guardian
description: Creative Assembly could strike gold again with this follow-up to their fan-favourite, film-inspired game … if you’re brave enough to venture outdoors
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Creative Assembly could strike gold again with this follow-up to their fan-favourite, film-inspired game … if you’re brave enough to venture outdoors
Content: ‘The player and the alien are going to have to adapt to survive’ … Alien: Isolation 2.Photograph: SegaView image in fullscreen‘The player and the alien are going to have to adapt to survive’ … Alien: Isolation 2.Photograph: SegaSummer games previewsGamesAlien: Isolation 2 – another strong female protagonist stalked in a terrifying new worldCreative Assembly could strike gold again with this follow-up to their fan-favourite, film-inspired game … if you’re brave enough to venture outdoorsGraeme MasonFri 14 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlien: Isolationredefined Alien games on its release in 2014, bringing the original taut, haunted house theme of thefirst movieto fans who had mostly been fed action-packed shooters. Cowering under desks and inside lockers wasn’t a new thing; being hunted by an intelligent and lethal xenomorph that could spring down from a duct at any moment was.“I was thinking about what we could do for a sequel while we were still finishing the first game,” reveals Creative Assembly’s Alistair Hope, creative lead on Alien: Isolation and its sequel. “But we didn’t actually start the project until around the time of the 10th anniversary. We’ve seen the response grow over time, watching [Alien: Isolation] continue to find new players, even though it’s a relatively old game. And they’re surprised there isn’t a sequel.”Details are slight, but here’s what we know so far: a Weyland-Yutani survey team discovers a crashed vessel on a planet that resembles LV-426 crossed with a windswept forest. It’s a vessel that’ll appear familiar to fans of Alien: Isolation – it’s the part of Sevastopol that the duplicitous Marshal Waits jettisons from the station in the first game, with Amanda Ripley and the alien inside. Ripley escapes. The alien does not. Until now.“We were super proud of Amanda. She’s really important to the Alien: Isolation experience. But we wanted to tell a new story, in a new location, and to do that, it felt like we needed a new protagonist,” says Hope. That new character is Blake, although Hope is tight-lipped on any details beyond her employer, Weyland-Yutani. It seems likely, however, that this new lead, thrust into the dangerous world of the xenomorph, will follow the IP’s tradition of strong female characters.View image in fullscreen‘We’ve been effectively training it to hunt in the exterior’ … Alien: Isolation 2.Photograph: SegaA fascinating part ofAlien: Isolation 2will be how the alien reacts to its new environment. “The alien uses its senses to track you down, and it’s very effective in those interior spaces. So we’ve been effectively training it to hunt in the exterior. Those core survival skills that you needed in the first game will be the same – but the player and the alien are going to have to adapt to survive.” That’s not to say Alien: Isolation 2 won’t have plenty of claustrophobic interiors, creating a seesaw of emotions whether trapped inside or exposed outside. “We can play with that, and mess with it. It feels like a really exciting opportunity.”Carcass Clad: stifling tank combat promises tension, terror and surprising laughsRead moreTaking place months after the events of Alien: Isolation, the sequel will retain the low-fi sci-fi universe, leaning heavily once more on the first Alien movie. There’s a glimpse of a Working Joe in the trailer, suggesting that, once again, the alien might not be the only antagonist the player has to avoid. Could hostile humans enter the mix? Hope is guarded. “Alien: Isolation 2 absolutely is building on that core foundation that we established in the first [game],” he says. “And, yeah, we love that rock, paper, scissors setup and scenario.” Draw your own acid blood-spattered conclusions.Sevastopol, the decommissioned and slowly decaying space station of Alien: Isolation, became an evocative extra character in the original game. Creative Assembly appears well placed to repeat the trick with Alien: Isolation 2’s forbidding colony world, home to a remote Weyland-Yutani outpost, Kurosaki Station. Just don’t forget your umbrella.Alien: Isolation 2 is coming soon to PC, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S and Nintendo Switch 2.Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsAlienShooting gamesAction gamesAdventure gamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kristen Schaal: The Legend of Crystal Shell review – flighty Conchords comic is still kooking on gas | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: As a half-horse half-woman who dreams of being a unicorn and performing Swan Lake, Schaal sheds little light but has plenty of sparkle
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: As a half-horse half-woman who dreams of being a unicorn and performing Swan Lake, Schaal sheds little light but has plenty of sparkle
Content: Wilfully dotty … Kristen Schaal in The Legend of Crystal Shell at Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenWilfully dotty … Kristen Schaal in The Legend of Crystal Shell at Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewKristen Schaal: The Legend of Crystal Shell review – flighty Conchords comic is still kooking on gasPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghAs a half-horse half-woman who dreams of being a unicorn and performing Swan Lake, Schaal sheds little light but has plenty of sparkleBrian LoganFri 14 Aug 2026 11.54 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 11.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor a happy handful of years in the noughties, around the time she made her TV name onFlight of the Conchords’ sitcom, Kristen Schaal was a fringe fixture, award-nominated in 2008 for her two-hander with Kurt Braunohler,Double Down Hearts. Ifthose showsfound Schaal kooking on gas, about as wilfully dotty and insubstantial as you’d ever wish comedy to be, the intervening two decades seem to have changed her not a jot.The Legend of Crystal Shell, her two-hander with John Roberts, casts the comic actor as a half-woman, half-horse, overcoming a lifetime of shame to deliver a performance of Tchaikovsky’s Swan Lake for tonight’s audience. It plays as if written by a primary schoolchild high on pick’n’mix, and is endearing and nonplussing in equal measure.It begins with Schaal confined to a cardboard refrigerator-cum-horsebox, shyly announcing herself to the crowd. She emerges, to recount her origin story, as the progeny of her mum’s unlikely tryst with a stallion called Shimmer. We meet her friend Arnold the (suspiciously dormant) mouse. She reads non sequitur poems and tries to catch fairies in a net.View image in fullscreenHorsing about … Kristen Schaal and John Roberts.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianA flightier confection it would be hard to imagine, and my patience was fraying with it until – at the blast of a trumpet – Crystal’s long-lost dad makes an appearance. That multiplies the cast, at least, if not the significance, as this wannabe unicorn starts singing about the malfunctioning healing powers of his “teeny tiny horn”.So what does all this horsing about amount to? They’re both compelling performers: Schaal the otherworldly womanchild, Roberts her Fonz-alike father. There’s something almost audacious in the randomness of the play’s narrative development, as if they’d set themselves the challenge of accepting every first idea, however arbitrarily it advances the plot. There are hints too, if tenuous, that Crystal’s late blooming may be a metaphor for the menopause. If so, it sheds little light, but plenty of sparkle, as Schaal’s alter ego grows her own twinkling uni-horn and puts a life of meekness behind her. There’s nothing meek about Schaal’s comedy, whose take-it-as-you-find-it idiosyncracy is easy to admire and, usually, to indulge.At Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh until 16 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Kristen SchaalComedy (Stage)Edinburgh festivalTheatreComedy (Culture)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Vile statues, writhing liquorice and kids marooned online: Edinburgh art festival review | Art | The Guardian
description: From queer narratives to secret histories, this year celebrates the underground and the unheralded. Our writer uncovers so many stories, he feels like Columbo
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: From queer narratives to secret histories, this year celebrates the underground and the unheralded. Our writer uncovers so many stories, he feels like Columbo
Content: Making connections … The Cloud, 2026, by Eva Rothschild.Photograph: Ruth Clark/courtesy the artist/Modern Art/The Modern Institute/Toby Webster Ltd, GlasgowView image in fullscreenMaking connections … The Cloud, 2026, by Eva Rothschild.Photograph: Ruth Clark/courtesy the artist/Modern Art/The Modern Institute/Toby Webster Ltd, GlasgowArtReviewVile statues, writhing liquorice and kids marooned online: Edinburgh art festival reviewVarious venues, EdinburghFrom queer narratives to secret histories, this year celebrates the underground and the unheralded. Our writer uncovers so many stories, he feels like ColumboEddy FrankelFri 14 Aug 2026 09.31 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 09.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy the time you’re done with Edinburgh art festival you’ll have uncovered so many hidden stories you’ll feel like Columbo. We’re talking queer narratives, secret histories, undiscovered archives: the whole festival is a celebration of the underground and unheralded. You can’t walk into a gallery without learning about some subcultural genius or longlost creative you’ve never heard of. That’s not a bad MO for a city-wide art festival.But EAF is also a big, unwieldy, confusing thing. There are curated displays, satellite exhibitions, performances, off-site projects, and it’s impossible to figure out how any of it fits together. You’ve just got to follow your nose and hope you sniff out something you like. And you’d better like photography, because there’s a lot of it here.View image in fullscreenEdinburgh everyone should see … Craigmillar School, 1994, by Sandra George.Photograph: courtesy Craigmillar Now © Sandra George EstateThe whole thing starts with US photographerDel LaGrace Volcano, whose images of queer nightlife in 1980s London are great: intimate, confrontational, erotic, totally defiant, as are the images of lesbian goths draping themselves over tombstones in Edinburgh graveyards. They’re insights into properly underground, subcultural life in the 1980s and 90s. Plenty of the photos aren’t all that good, but this feels like an artist who should be gathering a lot more attention, dealing with themes that have been all over the art and museum world recently.When it comes to untold stories, that ofSandra George(1957-2013) is worth telling. She was a black photographer and photojournalist who documented life on the margins of inner city Edinburgh. Like a lot of people in EAF, she never showed her work publicly in her lifetime, and was only discovered after her death in 2013.From her unique perspective as a semi-outsider, she documented communities in the city’s impoverished Craigmillar area. She captured protests and action groups operating out of living rooms and town halls; people living in hostels and housing schemes, skinheads, labourers, Hare Krishnas, Indians, Jamaicans, white and black. She appears throughout her show at CityArtGallery in self-portraits, often with her young son. There are kids everywhere, always playing and laughing, often in desperately bleak places. This might be work about Edinburgh, but it deserves to be seen far outside the city’s confines.Jill Edelstein, at Stills Gallery, also started out as a photojournalist, but took a different approach to George. Her polished images of Robert Rauschenberg, James Baldwin and Nelson Mandela don’t do a lot for me, although she does have a series about wild swimming that may find a different audience.Scottish photographerWendy McMurdo’s show at the Scottish National Portrait Gallery is quietly unsettling. For decades she’s been photographing children playing. But the results aren’t joyful visions of childhood: they’re disquieting portraits of a shifting society trying to make sense of rapid technological innovation. The kids play on computers and tablets, but the technology has been digitally removed, leaving behind isolated figures interacting with nothing. These are kids drifting into online worlds, and at risk of being lost in them for ever.View image in fullscreenThe Somnambulist, 1995, by Wendy McMurdo.Photograph: © Wendy McMurdo, all rights reserved, DACS 2026/courtesy Patricia Fleming Gallery, GlasgowWhen it’s not photography, EAF trades in pretty hard-edged contemporary art. Irish sculptorEva Rothschildhas taken over Fruitmarket with a disparate exhibition that feels like someone saved a collection of modernist sculpture from a skip. In the space downstairs, it’s all hyper-referential, full of riffs on Brancusi and Hepworth. Some of it is figurative, some abstract. Some of it is soft, some hard. It’s a lot of things, but none of them good.The work upstairs is way better, the palette reduced down to black and primary colours. She’s used rubber hoses like giant bits of liquorice and coiled, squiggled and squirmed them around metal frames. There’s a pile of half-graffitied concrete blocks you can climb, a glossy black geometric tower that reaches towards the ceiling. It’s like Memphis Group aesthetics gone goth and left to rot in the street. I love it, but I’m not sure how the art downstairs fails to work so well.A strange ritual from some dystopian future has been built into the vaulted Georgian spaces of Talbot Rice Gallery byAnne Hardy. The floor is covered in breeze blocks and markings in dirt, the lights flicker, the sound of rain fills the gallery. Figures made of bronze and wood stand before you, draped in hooded jackets. The handout talks about vibrations, energy, AI, weather systems in Texas. It’s mind-meltingly indecipherable. So what’s left is more of a vibe: a sense of human spirituality, survival and endurance in the bleak near-future. I’d be lying if I said I had any of this figured out, but its immersiveness and delicacy works well, although it is way too knowingly obtuse.View image in fullscreenKnowingly obtuse … The Beginning and the End by Anne Hardy.Photograph: © Anne HardyRichard Maguireat Collective Gallery at the top of Calton Hill suffers a similar fate, where the strength of the ideas – looking at representations of race and homosexuality across south Asian and British histories – is let down by some wispy, barely contextualised lumps and scrawls.Nearby,Emii Alrai’s huge, fractured monument overlooking the city is meant to reference Sumerian deities, standing in opposition to the National Monument of Scotland a few metres away. It feels like something almost ancient, broken, a relic in progress. But up close it’s a pretty shonky looking thing.If contemporary artists and institutions want to tell hidden stories, I think they have a duty – to viewers and to their subjects – to tell them clearly. Which is whatJamie Fitzpatrickat Edinburgh Printmakers has done. His show is the result of spending way too long thinking about the statues that sit on plinths all around the cities of the UK and realising that we’re all being constantly loomed over by war criminals, land barons and slavers.View image in fullscreenSubtle, strange … Out of the Swim by Frank Walter.Photograph: Andy Keate/Frank WalterA figure in a Georgian wig grins menacingly at you as you enter, a red plasticine smile plastered across his face. He’s on the verge of tumbling and collapsing into a messy pile, as is the skeletal figure behind him, all bared teeth and lumpen features. They’re inspired by the statues you see around Edinburgh, their vileness amplified to better reflect the kinds of men we publicly memorialise. The whole thing is like someone let the Muppets loose on some clay. It’s brilliantly gloopy, messy, cartoonish, chaotic and satirical.The group show atIngleby Galleryis good, too. It’s all centred on Frank Walter (1926-2009), an Antiguan painter, writer, poet and polymath, who died having never shown any of the thousands of paintings and drawings he amassed over his lifetime. His work is small, subtle, strange. He paints on ripped cardboard and fading paper; he depicts rainbows and stars and smiling faces, dancing women and strange trees that bend and twist at weird angles. His works are flanked by some giants of contemporary painting – a big Rose Wylie vision of young tulips, a gorgeous Lynette Yiadom-Boakye portrait of a kneeling figure – but it’s all eclipsed by his weird little paintings.Over among the horses and goats of Jupiter Artland, young Northern Irish artistSgàire Woodhas set about mashing together pop culture symbolism and the visual language of heraldry. The result is a gallery filled with shields, drums and birds covered in sequins and pink fur. It feels like a show that’s come too early in their career, but what it lacks in finesse, editing and finish, it makes up for in an overabundance of ideas.Another largely undiscovered artist,Sadao Hasegawa(1945-1999), really ramps up the eroticism with an eye-popping display of throbbing members and gushing penetration at Custom Lane. Most of the Japanese illustrator’s work, you guessed it, stayed unpublished and unseen in his lifetime. And that’s a shame because they’re amazing images: either soft-focus portraiture or a violent fusion of Japanese mythology and hardcore porn-filled naked figures writhing and brandishing katanas while fighting off giant spiders.There are lots of good shows here and plenty of bad ones, too. The whole thing could do with some more ambition, some bigger names, some starrier attractions. And it’s all a bit worthy and lecture-y, like you’re getting told off in every gallery you enter. “You’ve never heard of this previously undiscovered marginalised artist? You bastard!”Basically, EAF is too big and complex, with too many moving parts and collaborations and clashing ideas to really make sense. But maybe not everything has to make sense – maybe sometimes a city can just be filled with interesting, fun, diverse art, with loads of hidden stories and undiscovered narratives, and we can all go home happy. I did.Various venues, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustExplore more on these topicsArtEdinburgh festival 2026InstallationPaintingSculpturePhotographyEdinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Midsummer! review – Suri Noelle sparkles in a frisky Dream at the Edinburgh fringe | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: A lusty adaptation by Avenue Q’s co-creator is performed with verve by Katie Holmes and Tom Cruise’s daughter and her fellow students
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: A lusty adaptation by Avenue Q’s co-creator is performed with verve by Katie Holmes and Tom Cruise’s daughter and her fellow students
Content: Teenage energy … from left: Moyo Ifafore, Rusty Daniel, Celia Evans, Christian Trimmingham, Logan Yao and Suri Noelle in Midsummer!Photograph: Mackenzie BreedenView image in fullscreenTeenage energy … from left: Moyo Ifafore, Rusty Daniel, Celia Evans, Christian Trimmingham, Logan Yao and Suri Noelle in Midsummer!Photograph: Mackenzie BreedenEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewMidsummer! review – Suri Noelle sparkles in a frisky Dream at the Edinburgh fringeAssembly @ St Andrew Square, EdinburghA lusty adaptation by Avenue Q’s co-creator is performed with verve by Katie Holmes and Tom Cruise’s daughter and her fellow studentsChris WiegandFri 14 Aug 2026 07.03 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 16.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNot every undergraduate Shakespeare show at the Edinburgh fringemakes headlinesbut this one brings stardust by association. Suri Noelle, the 20-year-old daughter of Tom Cruise and Katie Holmes, appears with her fellow drama students from Pittsburgh’s Carnegie Mellon University. However, it’s a bit of an event regardless – the UK premiere of a “modern translation” of A Midsummer Night’s Dream adapted by Jeff Whitty, a Tony award-winner for the riotous Avenue Q.That show,newly returned to the West End, is populated by some horny puppets and Whitty’s Dream is similarly frisky. Often more lustful than lovestruck, Noelle’s Helena prowls after Demetrius (Logan Yao) on all fours, Puck (Eli Strain) bares his nipples during the “up and down” speech and when Titania (Siahvash Marshall) instructs the fairies to show Bottom some courtesies, it fuels an orgy.View image in fullscreenRunning rings … Midsummer! at Assembly, Edinburgh.Photograph: Mackenzie BreedenThe show has a teenage energy – the lovers are described as “bright young things” – but this is not a total rewrite like the high-school Taming of the Shrew,10 Things I Hate About You. Whitty retains many of Shakespeare’s speeches but tweaks certain lines to elucidate meaning. For example, in the opening scene, Theseus’s “earthlier happy is the rose distill’d” becomes “happier is the rose plucked for perfume”. Most alterations work just about seamlessly but there are also colloquial additions: Theseus tells the protesting Hermia “let’s put a pin in it” while Bottom later jarringly declares himself “jonesing for a bale of hay”. Most audaciously, yet effectively, Whitty takes a line from Shakespeare and fuses it into a new couplet with words of his own, as he does with Hippolyta’s jibes at Quince.Kim Weild’s production takes full advantage of this Spiegeltent-style venue’s mirrored interior, with the characters literally running rings around each other. (Strain’s elfin Puck adds the odd forward roll and plié.) Zhuang Kang’s design includes woodcut-style forests and factories, a nod to industrial Pittsburgh which – though the setting is still spoken of as Athens – informs themes of class and social status with the arrival of the rude mechanicals. Bri Johnson’s elegant costumes include some magnificent millinery and a dash of tartan.View image in fullscreenLike a dream … Midsummer! at Assembly, Edinburgh.Photograph: Mackenzie BreedenIn a heatwave, the climate disorder of the “forgeries of jealousy” speech should really burn through but it’s lukewarm and the play’s darker undercurrent is missing. Bottom’s transformation is also not staged to full effect, though there’s a shiny ass’s head to match the play’s metallic imagery.As for Noelle, she sparkles in the comedy throughout as well as in the despair of Helena’s Act 1 Scene 1 monologue, imploringly offered with wide eyes to the front row. Elsewhere, Celia Evans is a wonderfully cowardly lion, Rusty Daniel’s Pyramus makes a bid for the world’s longest death scene and even Moyo Ifafore’s Quince falls for Bottom. The cast’s delivery is crisp, the energy unflagging throughout 90 minutes – bookended by folk songs – that go like a dream.AtAssembly @ St Andrew Square, Edinburgh, until 19 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreA Midsummer Night's DreamEdinburgh festivalComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Boys Don’t Dance review – jump back to the 80s to celebrate the power of pop | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: A sunny mashup of music accompanies choreographer Marc Brew’s feelgood coming-of-age story
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: A sunny mashup of music accompanies choreographer Marc Brew’s feelgood coming-of-age story
Content: Boys Don't Dance.Photograph: Brian HartleyView image in fullscreenBoys Don't Dance.Photograph: Brian HartleyEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewBoys Don’t Dance review – jump back to the 80s to celebrate the power of popAssembly @ Dance Base, EdinburghA sunny mashup of music accompanies choreographer Marc Brew’s feelgood coming-of-age storyLyndsey WinshipFri 14 Aug 2026 12.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMarc Brew made the acclaimed showAn Accident/A Lifein 2024, with choreographer Sidi Larbi Cherkaoui, about the car accident that left him paralysed below the waist aged 20. Brew went on to be a successful dancer and choreographer, performing using a wheelchair, and Brew’s latest piece returns to autobiographical territory. This time the focus is on the young Marc – or dancer Ross Malloy as a proxy – growing up in rural Australia, surrounded by football fans and sheep, and told repeatedly that boys don’t dance.What the show does really well is capture Malloy’s character’s absolute joy in dancing, how totally innate it is, the rhythm in his blood as he’s throwing himself into the routine from Footloose, or dancing along to a nostalgia-fest of songs and video clips from Culture Club, Wham! and cartoon pop star Jem, to the theme from Wonder Woman or jingles for Gillette. We get a sunny mix of disco, jazz, acro-moves and fizzing energy, with BMX tricks thrown in. It’s a reminder of the power of pop music, and also of the boredom and freedom of an 80s childhood. When his mum is out, Malloy dresses up in her clothes and performs, but this thing he desires is also torturing him, as does living in a place where he has to hide his true self.View image in fullscreenRemembering and reconciling … Piotr Iwanicki in Boys Don’t Dance.Photograph: Brian HartleyChampion wheelchair Latin dancer Piotr Iwanicki plays the grownup Brew, remembering his past and reconciling with it, and he and Malloy find some synergy and inventive moves together. The staging is simple but nicely done, video designer Jamie Wardrop’s backdrop of animated line drawings creates the neighbourhood, and monochrome turns to neon as Brew finds his real freedom in the big city.Yeehaw! Bring on the tap-dancing cowgirls! How the Edinburgh Military Tattoo suddenly got coolRead moreIt’s engaging storytelling, warm and feelgood, and with a brilliant soundtrack (especially for viewers of the appropriate vintage). Boys Don’tDancewas created with eight to 13-year-olds in mind, so it’s not the most complex dramatically, emotionally or choreographically – and their parents might get more out of the cultural references – but it’s a really sweet show.AtAssembly @ Dance Base, Edinburgh,until 23 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalFestivalsDanceChildren's theatreTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I felt so inspired’: Guardian readers on trying Homer’s epics after seeing The Odyssey | The Odyssey | The Guardian
description: Readers describe how Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster has ignited or reawakened their interest in classical texts
Author: Alfie Packham
Headline: Readers describe how Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster has ignited or reawakened their interest in classical texts
Content: Charlize Theron as the nymph Calypso and Matt Damon as Odysseus in Christopher Nolan’s film version of The Odyssey.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyView image in fullscreenCharlize Theron as the nymph Calypso and Matt Damon as Odysseus in Christopher Nolan’s film version of The Odyssey.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyThe Odyssey‘I felt so inspired’: Guardian readers on trying Homer’s epics after seeing The OdysseyReaders describe how Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster has ignited or reawakened their interest in classical literatureAlfie PackhamandJane ClintonFri 14 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“I’m having a classics summer this year,” says Tommy Maddinson, 26, from London. He’s been inspired by Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey to delve into the subject, which has involved cinema trips, visits to the British Museum, and reading Homer’s epic before the film’s release. “I managed to finish it the day before. Since then I’ve been reading a few other classical texts and commentaries …”Maddinson is not alone. Thanks to the popularity of Nolan’s film, poetry sales in the UK are on courseto reach a record highthis year after surpassing £8m during the first 30 weeks of 2026 – an increase of 13.3% on the same period last year, according to the market researchers NielsenIQ.Robert Zoellner, 70, had never read any of the Greek classics because of a “fear” of poetry translations being pretentious and unreadable. “After seeingThe Odyssey, I decided to try again,” he says. “I saw on Kindle that Emily Wilson’s translations were available. I found out that if I ignored the fact that it was written in verse and just read it as if it were a normal text, I was really enjoying it.It’s not just Homer: the new generation of poets enjoying epic successRead more“I read The Iliad before The Odyssey since it sounds like the proper progression. Agamemnon and Achilles are at each other’s throats, and that’s fun to read about.”Kerry Lecomber, 56, from Suffolk, has seen The Odyssey three times and says it has “really stoked” her love “of all things ancient Greece”.“I had a place to study classics at age 18 at Leeds University, but it was 1988, and I was far too busy raving and I didn’t get the grades. I’ve always retained a keen interest in the subject. I’ve just started Emily Wilson’s translation of The Odyssey, which my daughter, who studied ancient history at A-level, bought me recently for my birthday.”She adds: “I’m now looking into finally doing a degree in classics via the Open University. I’ll have to do it part-time while I work full-time, but I know how much I’ll enjoy it.”A similar trend can be seen in the US, where print sales of The Odyssey across all editions areup 76% so far this year, according to Circana BookScan figures. Emily Wilson’s translation, published by WW Norton, is the bestselling edition.“I actually watched the film because of all the criticism,” says Kaylee Brent, 32, from Montana, referring toWilson’s recent critique of the film. The classicist, whose 2017 translation of The Odysseywas cited by Christopher Nolan in early publicityfor his adaptation of the poem, said the film “has nothing convincing to say” and “lacks psychological, emotional, political and ethical depth”, adding: “Its narrative structure is gimmicky. The writing is abysmal. None of the characters has convincing motivation for their actions or words.”However, Wilson acknowledged the film’s impact in “bringing audiences back to cinemas” and increasing cultural awareness of ancient Greek literature.It’s not just the Odyssey effect: poetry is booming because it’s the only language for these times of violence and chaos | Charlotte HigginsRead moreBrent says: “I hadn’t much been into Greek literature except some required readings as a teen, but it was really the back-and-forth critiques and interpretations of Nolan’s interpretation that convinced me I needed to read The Odyssey and The Iliad. Now I’m even getting into the weeds of translation arguments and having the time of my life.”Emily Hughes, 33, a charity fundraiser from Cheltenham, says that after seeing the film she “wanted to explore the female characters more”. Before the film came out, she reread The Odyssey (the Emily Wilson translation), which she “really enjoyed”.“Coming out of the cinema, I felt so inspired by how epic it was and wanted to read it again,” she says.“In my local bookshop, they had a table of books to read if you’ve seen The Odyssey and wanted more,” she says. “I decided to pick up Claire North’s Ithaca, which explores more of what Odysseus’ wife, Penelope, might have been experiencing during his 20 years away. It’s told from the perspective of the goddess Hera, and explores a kingdom ruled by the old, infirm and, most importantly, by women, during such a time. It’s brilliant, and I immediately ordered the next two books in the series after finishing it.”Emily regretted not studying classics at sixth form, so she is making up for lost time. “I had already read a few different Greek myth retellings like The Song of Achilles and Circe by Madeline Miller, but the film really reignited my interest in reading more,” she adds. “I am definitely going to keep collecting more retellings, especially from the perspective of female characters or figures. I’ve got Costanza Casati’s Clytemnestra on my list next.”Explore more on these topicsThe OdysseyPoetryHomerChristopher NolanClassicsClassics and ancient historyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Iris Murdoch artworks from secret room go on display – including self-portrait | Iris Murdoch | The Guardian
description: Second world war paintings and sketches show novelist ‘engaging with her world in a new light’
Author: Donna Ferguson
Headline: Second world war paintings and sketches show novelist ‘engaging with her world in a new light’
Content: Detail from Iris Murdoch self-portrait from 1941.Photograph: Iris Murdoch/Miles LeesonView image in fullscreenDetail from Iris Murdoch self-portrait from 1941.Photograph: Iris Murdoch/Miles LeesonIris MurdochIris Murdoch artworks from secret room go on display – including self-portraitSecond world war paintings and sketches show novelist ‘engaging with her world in a new light’Donna FergusonFri 14 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor decades, they lay in a secret room in her attic gathering dust. Now, newly discovered artworks by the Booker prize-winning authorIris Murdoch– including the only self-portrait she is known to have painted, four surrealist landscape paintings and three sketches of female nudes – will go on display for the first time on Friday.The artworks were created at the start of the second world war when Murdoch was a student at Oxford. They expose her early interest in surrealism and fascination with the naked female form.Until now, Murdoch was only known to have created three paintings in her lifetime.In total, more than 80 new artworks by the novelist were discovered last year at Murdoch’s former home in north Oxford by Dr Miles Leeson, director of the Iris Murdoch Research Centre at the University of Chichester.He was invited by the executors of Murdoch’s estate to explore 30 Charlbury Road after the death of Audi Bayley, the second wife of Murdoch’s late husband, John Bayley, who lived there until 2024.Murdoch, who died in 1999 and was known to be a hoarder, had stashed the paintings and sketches in a secret room in her attic. The door was hidden behind a large bookcase. “It was inaccessible,” Leeson said. “It was like an inner sanctum.”He suspects no one had been inside the room for decades and that only Murdoch and her husband were aware of its existence.“I don’t think Audi knew about it,” he said. “I don’t think anybody knew about it … there were a lot of personal effects and items in there. Really private stuff.”Murdoch had realised she was bisexual at 15 and the drawings reveal her fascination with the naked female form, shortly before she embarked on her first known physical relationship with a woman. “There is a sexual frisson in the drawings of female nudes,” Leeson said. “Also the yearning that one feels in these life drawings, these nudes, comes through in her early poetry that is dedicated to women that she desired.”View image in fullscreenOne of Murdoch’s female nudes.Photograph: Iris Murdoch/Miles LeesonIn 2016, after Audi Bayley invited him round for tea, Leeson became the first person in at least a decade to enter the main, more exposed part of the attic. There, hediscovered 600 of Murdoch’s unpublished poems, including many lesbian love poems, buried in a chest.Last year, in the hidden room, as well as the signed and dated paintings and nude drawings, Leeson found 20 surrealist watercolours, two pencil and watercolour drawings of Murdoch’s parents and more than 50 pencil and pen sketches in two sketchbooks.“These artworks show her engaging with her world in a new light, displaying a new aspect of Murdoch that was hitherto hidden,” Leeson said. “Artworks and artists are everywhere in her fictional work, and she designs ‘scenes’ in her philosophy as well. Murdoch is a visual artist in all the mediums she was working in, and these newly discovered paintings lend more evidence to this.”View image in fullscreenA Murdoch surreal landscape painting.Photograph: Iris Murdoch/Miles LeesonTwenty-five of the newly discovered works, including the self-portrait and the surrealist landscape paintings, will be on display for the first timeat the University of Chichester Libraryuntil 10 December, as part of an exhibition, Iris Murdoch Amongst the Artists – the first ever devoted to Murdoch as an artist.It will feature all the major artworks Murdoch is known to have painted during her life, alongside works by British artists who designed her book covers, such as Reynolds Stone and Tom Phillips.The self-portrait is dated 7 January 1941, revealing how Murdoch saw herself at the age of 21. “It’s a portrait of somebody who’s clearly a deep and expressive thinker,” Leeson said.The newly discovered surrealist works date from 1939 to 1941, a formative and intensely intellectual period of Murdoch’s life, Leeson said. “These paintings were produced during a really heady time at Oxford, when she was a member of the Communist party, involved in student politics and the student newspaper … and of course, it’s the early years of the second world war, which is reflected in the surrealist landscapes.”The paintings, which appear to be influenced by the art of Salvador Dalí and Pablo Picasso, communicated a feeling of despair, anxiety and destruction, he added. “There’s a sense of the breakdown of society, of what’s keeping the centre together. I think she’s trying to say something deeply profound and philosophical about the state of Britain at the time, about the destruction of European culture … She’s capturing the mood of the nation on these canvases.”He believes she was drawn to the surrealist movement and turned to painting as an experiment. “She’s writing poetry, she’s beginning to write fiction and she’s trying out different art forms and finding out who she is as an artist … it’s all part of one great artistic mind trying to work out where her talents lie.”There were strong links between these formative works and her later literary masterpieces, Leeson said. “The Black Prince is a work of late modernism in which reality becomes skewed, and in her Booker prize-winning novel The Sea, The Sea, the main character, Charles Arrowby, tries to escape reality and lives within his own mind, and is completely self-absorbed,” he said.“I think some of Murdoch’s surrealist paintings are asking us to look at reality in a different way and to think about the essentials of the human condition. They add another layer of complexity and interest to the story of Iris Murdoch and how we now consider her in the 21st century.”Explore more on these topicsIris MurdochPaintingArtExhibitionsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nicole Kidman opens up about divorce from Keith Urban – and ‘throwing my career away’ for Tom Cruise | Nicole Kidman | The Guardian
description: Actor, 59, reflects on high-profile marriages in Vogue interview, saying she felt ‘deeply vulnerable’ after split from Urban
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: Actor, 59, reflects on high-profile marriages in Vogue interview, saying she felt ‘deeply vulnerable’ after split from Urban
Content: Nicole Kidman said of her life: ‘You make all these plans and you have all these ideas of what it’s all going to be like and then it’s… not.’Photograph: Marechal Aurore/Abaca/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenNicole Kidman said of her life: ‘You make all these plans and you have all these ideas of what it’s all going to be like and then it’s… not.’Photograph: Marechal Aurore/Abaca/ShutterstockNicole KidmanNicole Kidman opens up about divorce from Keith Urban – and ‘throwing my career away’ for Tom CruiseActor, 59, reflects on high-profile marriages in Vogue interview, saying she felt ‘deeply vulnerable’ after split from UrbanSian CainFri 14 Aug 2026 00.32 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 12.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNicole Kidman has opened up about her divorce from Keith Urban and reflected on her marriage to Tom Cruise, saying she was warned being his wife would overshadow her career.Ina new interview with Vogue, the 59-year-old actor spoke about going through two divorces under intense media scrutiny: with Cruise, who she married in 1990 and divorced in 2001, and musician Urban, who she married in 2006.Kidman filed for divorce from Urban in September 2025citing marital difficulties and irreconcilable differences, with the separation finalised out of court by January.‘We laced Nicole into her corset and her rib broke again’: Moulin Rouge at 25 – an oral history by cast and crewRead moreKidman said her second divorce had been a difficult period in her life, adding: “But at the same time I’m like, ‘OK, I didn’t expect this. I had a different view of what my life was going to be, but this is what it is now.’ You make all these plans and you have all these ideas of what it’s all going to be like and then it’s … not. You have to adjust. You adapt. The future, it’s completely unknown to me right now.”Asked if it had also been a “scary” time, Kidman said: “There was a point where I was very fearful and deeply vulnerable, which is exposing. And then at the same time [I’m] going: ‘Well, I can either really not confront it and just curl up, or I can just go forward with an enormous amount of hope.’”Asked if her split from Cruise had been “useful” for weathering the scrutiny around her second divorce, Kidman said: “It’s all new. Every time!”View image in fullscreenTom Cruise and Nicole Kidman at the premiere of his film Jerry Maguire in Rome, 1997.Photograph: Maurizio Brambatti/PAOf her marriage to Cruise, who she married when she was 23 and he was 28, she said, “Suddenly I was 22, 23 years old and I had this huge movie star husband. But it just seemed completely natural. We just fell madly in love and it was that simple. I remember people saying to me, ‘OK, well this is really going to affect your career’. I’m like, ‘I don’t care. I’m in love. I want to be married.’“And then I was his wife and they were like, ‘See, we told you.’ I’m like, ‘So what? I wasn’t meant to marry the man I love? Of course I’ll throw my career away. I don’t care.’”In the Vogue interview, Kidman also revealed she sometimes goes dancing in disguise, saying: “I’ll put on glasses. Sometimes I’ll wear a wig to hide, a little dark wig, and then I can just dance. As long as I’m surrounded by people – like, I take people with me – then I’m fine. I need it.”Explore more on these topicsNicole KidmanTom CruisenewsShareReuse this content

title: Post your questions for Robert Carlyle | Robert Carlyle | The Guardian
description: Bond villain, Begbie, male stripper … the Trainspotting and Full Monty star has played everyone from Sherlock Holmes to Rumpelstiltskin. As his latest directorial project premieres in Edinburgh, he is here to answer your questions
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: Bond villain, Begbie, male stripper … the Trainspotting and Full Monty star has played everyone from Sherlock Holmes to Rumpelstiltskin. As his latest directorial project premieres in Edinburgh, he is here to answer your questions
Content: Can he still drive a double-decker? … Robert Carlyle.Photograph: Alana Paterson/The ObserverView image in fullscreenCan he still drive a double-decker? … Robert Carlyle.Photograph: Alana Paterson/The ObserverFilm & Music reader interviewRobert CarlylePost your questions for Robert CarlyleBond villain, Begbie, male stripper … the Trainspotting and Full Monty star has played everyone from Sherlock Holmes to Rumpelstiltskin. As his latest directorial project premieres in Edinburgh, he is here to answer your questionsRich PelleyFri 14 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 08.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou’ll know Robert Carlyle for many things – getting his kit off inThe Full Monty, being skewered through the heart with a plutonium rod as Bond villain Renard in The World Is Not Enough, playing Sherlock Holmes in Watson, joining Line of Duty as a gruff specialist firearms officer, and appearing opposite David Tennant and Toby Jones in ITV’s The Hack.He also appeared as Adolf Hitler in Hitler: The Rise of Evil and (uncredited) as John Lennon in Yesterday; as a cannibalistic soldier in Ravenous; Rumplestiltskin in Once Upon a Time; and the British prime minister in Cobra. But it’s hard to ever fully dissociate him from the fantastic moustache he sports as violent, pint-swilling psychopath Francis Begbie inTrainspotting– a moustache that is now, unbelievably, 30 years old and heading back to cinemas in a new 4K restoration from 21 August.But for the purposes of our next readers’ interview, we are also interested in Carlyle behind the camera. More than a decade after directing and starring in 2015 black comedy The Legend of Barney Thomson, alongside Emma Thompson, Ray Winstone and Ashley Jensen, he has returned to the director’s chair with a new short film, Three – a darkly funny, increasingly unsettling three-hander about sex, class, power and three people trying to work out exactly who is using whom. The film has its European premiere at the Edinburgh international film festival on Friday and screens again on Sunday.So, what to ask him? Does Begbie’s moustache deserve its own 30th-anniversary interview? Has playing Sherlock Holmes made him any better at Cluedo? Can he still drive a double-decker bus, like he does inKen Loach’s Carla’s Song? What happened to his Saturday Tunes, where he used to recommend new bands every week on Twitter? Did he have the two teeth put back in that he had removed to bring Begbie back for T2 Trainspotting? And what does it feel like to stomp through the countryside as a giant, as he does inthe video for Oasis’s Little By Little?Post your questions below by 6pm on Wednesday 19 August and we’ll print his answers as part of our readers’ interview series.Threescreens as part of the Edinburgh international film festival’s Out of Competition Shorts at 2pm on Friday 14 August at Cameo and at 2pm on Sunday 16 August at Cineworld.Explore more on these topicsRobert CarlyleFilm & Music reader interviewLine of DutyTrainspottingEdinburgh film festivalDramaFestivalsTelevisioncalloutShareReuse this content

title: ‘It opens up doors and minds’: inside Sydney’s tattoo convention | Tattoos | The Guardian
description: While some of the event’s 5,000 attenders arrive sporting full bodysuits and ready to compete, others are gearing up for their first tattoo
Author: Mike Hohnen
Headline: While some of the event’s 5,000 attenders arrive sporting full bodysuits and ready to compete, others are gearing up for their first tattoo
Content: Will gets his first tattoo by artist Ben HastingsTattoos‘It opens up doors and minds’: inside Sydney’s tattoo conventionWhile some of the event’s 5,000 attenders arrive sporting full bodysuits and ready to compete, others are gearing up for their first tattooMike Hohnenwith photography byBlake Sharp-WigginsFri 14 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 11.02 EDTShareAt theSydneytattoo convention, the city’s historic town hall fills with the buzz of tattoo machines, the comforting aroma of hospital-grade sanitiser and the timeless tunes of Linkin Park.Convention founder and managing director of Thirteen Feet Tattoo studios, Katie Bailey, says it wasn’t easy to secure the 137-year-old venue. When she pitched it to Sydney council for their first event four years ago, “at first they were nervous about it, they had people everywhere checking in on us, but after that first event, they thought it was amazing. Tattooing and town hall just go together.”View image in fullscreen‘This will never be replicated elsewhere,’ says co-organiser Rhys GordonView image in fullscreen‘The power to make a choice for yourself is pretty big,’ Gordon says. ‘It’s a big step to change your body and express yourself – this is me, this is what I want to look like’Roughly 700 artists applied for the convention, but only 180 were approved to display their work for a crowd of 5,000 visitors. Many artists have filled their weekend’s schedule well in advance while other stalls have left space in their schedule for walk-ins. As well as seminars, documentaries, talks and a nail-biting, machete-juggling performance from the world’s most tattooed man, Lucky Diamond Rich, much of the event revolves around the competitions, held at the end of each day.View image in fullscreenAttenders stand on stage before judging kicks off for day two’s competition. The convention offers a free entry day for anyone with a bodysuit of artView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreen“It’s a platform to legitimise tattooing, which is becoming much more mainstream,” says co-organiser Rhys Gordon. “It opens up doors and minds,” making the world of tattooing more accessible to the uninitiated – like Sydney local Will, who is attending the convention to get his first tattoo.As the stencil of a soaring American traditional eagle is placed across Will’s torso, he describes the situation as “a bit overwhelming … but I’ll get it done”. His artist, Ben Hastings from Sydney studio Tattoo Rosies supports his canvas – “he’s got this, he’s in the zone”. Not only did the piece get finished, William’s inaugural ink won the tattoo of the day competition.View image in fullscreenWill (right) gets the stencil for his tattoo applied by his artist, Ben HastingsView image in fullscreenWill’s debut tattoo with lines and shading going onOrganisers put a strong emphasis on diversity among the stalls, and sought tattooists from regional towns. Artist Duane James, from Higherground tattoo studio in Kurrajong, spends the day working on a marathon thigh piece for Dasha, a tattoo devotee from Sydney’s northern beaches. “Being fully tattooed, it’s nice being among people that all share a common interest, it’s like I’m among my people,” she says. “It’s been wonderful.”Tattoo artists at work at Sydney Tattoo Convention“We’ll absolutely get it finished today,” James promises. The pair are committed.View image in fullscreenFeaturing two floors of tattoo artists and other stalls, the top floor of town hall becomes an observation deckView image in fullscreenA client sits for a custom script tattoo on her backView image in fullscreenTattoo artist Flex wins the best head competition for her recently completed black ornamental head piece. ‘For me, it doesn’t matter if it’s a little love heart or whatever, it changes who you are. It just feels like it should always have been there’Laura has travelled from Hobart to go under the needle of artist Anna Rose. Rose and fellow artist Twitch spend much of the weekend collaborating on a leg sleeve for Laura.“Anna and I have built a bit of a rapport over the time that we’ve done a few tattoos together,” Laura says. “There’s a lot of trust involved in this now – from both directions. I have a lot of faith in Anna and I know her work. We were just throwing around ideas but I knew coming into this that I was going to love whatever she was going to do.”View image in fullscreenAnna Rose and Twitch work on a collaborative tattoo for Laura, who has travelled to the event from Hobart. The piece wins the best collaboration competition on SundayView image in fullscreenJohnie Evans, from Halfway House tattoo studio, polishes up one of his worksView image in fullscreenA tattoo artist and their client work through a mammoth thigh pieceTestament to fostering a close relationship between artist and canvas, Laura’s piece wins the best collaboration competition.Shell, winner of perhaps the most-entered competition, best back piece, proudly displays a massive traditional American eagle entangled with a traditional Japanese dragon, “a duality that represents my own taste and style”, she says. Both a tattoo artist and canvas, Shell beams at the opportunities to fan out at the convention. “I’m wanting to see what the other back pieces look like! I wanted to see what I was up against, because I know a lot of people have amazing back pieces.”View image in fullscreenChelsea gets a tattoo from Manny. The pair first collaborated on a small ornamental piece for Chelsea’s sternum, which has since blossomed into a larger artwork. ‘It feels like there’s nobody else here, just me and my artist. I’m comfortable. I love it here. I’m in my element,’ Chelsea saysView image in fullscreenWinner of best back tattoo, tattoo artist Shell, with her piece by William Brown from Tattoo RosiesView image in fullscreenCo-organiser Rhys Gordon works the crowd while the judges for the best leg sleeve competition take notesBut the convention is not all about competition.Thirty-year veteran of the industry Ichi Hatano, visiting from Japan, and his canvas Hugh are slowly chipping away on a traditional Japanese back piece. “I’ve been going to Japan to see him since about 2022,” says Hugh. “I go over a couple of times a year”. They are in no rush to finish. “It’s a very slow process, but it’s always worth it,” he says.View image in fullscreenJapanese artist Ichi Hatano, one of the few international artists invited to attend the convention, works on Hugh’s back pieceView image in fullscreenA tattoo station with ink pots ready to goView image in fullscreenPauly, who booked a hotel for three nights so he could complete his back piece from artist Troy Inkman, takes a break from his session

title: The hill I will die on: Questions can go unanswered. Stop pulling out your phone | Helene Rosenthal | The Guardian
description: I don’t care what the capital of Uzbekistan is. I want to trade celebrity gossip and hear how your marriage counselling is going, says Helene Rosenthal, a writer based in New York City
Author: Helene Rosenthal
Headline: I don’t care what the capital of Uzbekistan is. I want to trade celebrity gossip and hear how your marriage counselling is going, says Helene Rosenthal, a writer based in New York City
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onMobile phonesThe hill I will die on: Questions can go unanswered. Stop pulling out your phoneHelene RosenthalI don’t care what the capital of Uzbekistan is. I want to trade celebrity gossip and hear how your marriage counselling is goingFri 14 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 12.59 EDTShareIt’s been a long, dreary winter. I am at dinner with a group of friends when someone wonders aloud when the first day of summer is. Lizzie insists it’s 21 June, Cleo is equally sure it’s 1 June. Sylvie says she is willing to bet her covetedThe Row flip-flopson Cleo’s answer. The social rewards from “arguing” over this far outweigh knowing a trivial piece of information that no one at the table will remember. And yet, we can’t help ourselves.Invariably, someone pulls out their phone, does a not-so-quick search online, and then declares, as though she has uncovered something truly revelatory, the first day of the astronomical summer is on thesummer solstice, 21 June. Whereas 1 June is when the meteorological summer begins.Turns out nobody cares. The obligatory “hmmmm” travels around the table as everyone looks at their watches. There’s a shift in the social dynamic. Lizzie says something about an early-morning root canal. The person with the phone becomes the self-appointed “expert” at the table. What started out as a fun, casual evening with friends has become a teaching moment.The night is over. Someone asks for the check.Should you send that midnight text? 11 essential rules for phone etiquetteRead moreAlternatively, here’s what could have happened: a somewhat raucous argument over who is right. Lizzie standing up and swearing she knows the exact date because of a late-June “welcome to summer” party where she was making out with a hottie and accidentally leaned against the air conditioning off/on switch, turning the room into a sauna. Everyone ended up in their undies. “It was one of the best nights of my life, I’d never forget it,” Lizzie blurts out with pride. We’ve all learned something – but not about the start of summer, whenever that is.Suffice to say, smartphones are a buzz kill. Researchers at theUniversity of Texashave shown that even having your mobile phone at the table, powered down and turned over, affects your ability to connect. Let that sink in: even when your phone is off, your brain is still distracted by it.There’s also something called theGoogle effect, where we’ve become so accustomed to retrieving information easily and quickly that we don’t bother retaining it. We rarely remember these Googled titbits, and yet we allow them to turn a perfectly good night into our dullest university lecture.The next time you are out with friends and a burning question comes up, forget about checking with Google. Ask your friends. Even if they don’t know the answer, it’s OK. The point is to keep talking. While we still know how.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHelene Rosenthal lives in New York City and writes about families, friendships and relationshipsExplore more on these topicsMobile phonesThe hill I will die onFriendshipcommentShareReuse this content

title: The best electric toothbrushes in the UK for every budget – tested | Health & wellbeing | The Guardian
description: We put 31 electric toothbrushes to the test, from oscillating Oral-B models to sustainable brands like Suri, to find the best for cleaning power and value for money
Author: Alan Martin
Headline: We put 31 electric toothbrushes to the test, from oscillating Oral-B models to sustainable brands like Suri, to find the best for cleaning power and value for money
Content: View image in fullscreenThe Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterHealth & wellbeingReviewThe best electric toothbrushes in the UK for every budget – testedWe put 31 electric toothbrushes to the test, from oscillating Oral-B models to sustainable brands like Suri, to find the best for cleaning power and value for moneyHow to make your toothbrush last longerAlan MartinFri 14 Aug 2026 09.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you grew up using a conventional toothbrush – essentially a stick with bristles on the end – you may be surprised to learn just how long the electric toothbrush has been around. The first was designed in the late 1930s, but that model was a long way from the sleek, feature-packed and Bluetooth-enabled beasts you can buy today.There are now dozens of ultra-advanced versions on the market, but which ones are worth your cash? To help answer that question, my teeth have become figurative guinea pigs. Over the past 20 months, I’ve put 31 electric toothbrushes from the likes of Oral-B, Philips, Suri, Ordo, Silk’n and Foreo through their paces to separate the best from the rest. Here are my conclusions.At a glanceBest electric toothbrush overallLaifenWave Pro£99.99 at AmazonBest budget electric toothbrushOdontaPowerPlus£29.99 at AmazonMost intuitive all-rounderSpotlightSonic Pro£64.99 at AmazonBest electric toothbrush for sustainabilitySuriCore 1.0£65 at SuriBest premium electric toothbrushPhilipsSonicare Smart 9400£199.99 at John LewisBest oscillating toothbrushOral-BiO3£65 at BootsThe best water flossers, tested: seven models for that dentist-clean feelingRead moreWhy you should trust meAs well as having the physical qualities required to test electric toothbrushes (my own teeth and a reliable toothpaste budget), I’ve been testing electronics – phones, drones and almost everything in between – for more than a decade.Also – and I’ll put this delicately to prevent you from closing the page in justified disgust – as someone who has to wear a retainer every night after Invisalign treatment, the toothbrushes weren’t short of nasties to clean during testing. They’ve seen things, man.How I testedView image in fullscreen‘I appeared to undergo a Damascene conversion to good oral hygiene.’Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianI doubt many people include the four minutes spent brushing their teeth as a highlight of even the most tedious day, so spare a thought for the months when it has become my life’s obsessive focus. Fortunately, and purely by chance, my first test coincided with a dentist’s visit in which I appeared to have undergone a Damascene conversion to good oral hygiene, so it did have its upside.Anyway, the process was actually pretty simple: brush, brush and brush again, taking note of mouthfeel, grip, cleanliness, the features that appealed and those little things that made me irrationally grumpy. I used plaque-disclosing tablets, which turn your teeth a charming shade of pink and blue to reveal areas where plaque resides. Even the cheapest brushes did a good job of removing the blue, though, even if they didn’tfeelas clean, so this test proved unhelpful.Ultimately, while each of the 31 brushes I tested was leagues ahead of manual toothbrushes, I ordered them based on performance, features, feel, stamina and – perhaps most importantly, given how close the final results were – value for money.A quick note on that: toothbrush recommended retail prices (RRPs) are often what you’d call “aspirational”. They’re frequently on offer, and even £500 models regularly go on sale for less than half price. It’s worth clicking through and checking what today’s price is on the off-chance.The best electric toothbrushes in 2026View image in fullscreenA dental hygiene lineup of some of the toothbrushes tested.Photograph: Alan Martin/The GuardianBest electric toothbrush overall:Laifen Wave ProLaifenWave Profrom£99.99€139.99 (about £120) at Laifen£99.99 at AmazonWhat we lovePowerful and effective; two types of brushingWhat we don’t loveSlippery handle; you may feel more dribblyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian€139.99 (about £120) at Laifen£99.99 at AmazonMost toothbrushes use either vibrations (sonic) or physical movements (oscillating) to move the bristles to dislodge plaque. The Laifen Wave Pro does both in tandem and with the most power and customisation of any brush I’ve tested – without breaking the bank. This innovation sees it ably dislodge not only plaque from teeth, but also the excellent Spotlight Sonic Pro from first place on this list.Why we love itWhat that means in practice is that the head vibrates faster than most of the brushes here, with speeds of up to 66,000 brush strokes per minute (BPM), while the neck twists left and right up to 60 degrees to replicate the sweeping gestures you’d make with a traditional mechanical toothbrush.This left my mouth feeling cleaner than ever, although the default settings might not suit everyone. Thankfully, the app lets you customise any of the three modes – daily, deep and custom – with controls for vibration intensity, oscillation range and speed, giving you plenty of combinations to experiment with.Once it’s set to your liking, you don’t have to use the app at all, but you can dive in to view a report on whether you’re brushing enough or pushing too hard (although the pressure sensor will alert you to that in real-time).It’s a shame that …its oscillations may make you more dribbly than using a standard sonic brush, and its wireless charging may be inconvenient while travelling – although any wireless charger seemed to work for me. Thetranslucent versionI tested was also a little slippery in the hand.Type:sonic/oscillating hybridModes:two built-in (daily and deep), with customisations in appPower:66,000 BPMPressure sensor:yesBattery life:70 daysApp:yesReplacement head cost:£26.99 for sixLaifenWave Profrom£99.99€139.99 (about £120) at Laifen£99.99 at AmazonWhat we lovePowerful and effective; two types of brushingWhat we don’t loveSlippery handle; you may feel more dribblyBest budget electric toothbrush:Odonta PowerPlusOdontaPowerPlus£29.99£29.99 at AmazonWhat we loveGood-value brush; more sustainable bristlesWhat we don’t loveAt this price? Very littleView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£29.99 at AmazonOdonta only launched in April 2026, but its debut PowerPlus toothbrush has swept in to take the best-value crown, undercutting the price of the previous occupant – the £64.99Icy Bear Next-Generation sonic toothbrush– by more than half.Why we love itAt £29.99, the brush is exceptional value. It’s by far the cheapest I’ve tested to contain a pressure sensor and packs a solid 42,000 BPM across five cleaning modes.It’s IPX7 water-resistant, and battery life is listed at a solid three weeks. To top it up, you simply place it in its wireless charging cradle. The heads aren’t recyclable, but the bristles are made from Nylon 1010 – a bio-based polyamide derived from castor oil, rather than the fossil fuels used for traditional bristles.Also in Odonta’s range isthe PowerLite. This toothbrush comes in at the same £29.99 price, but features a more compact design and a longer 60-day battery life. Note that it lacks a pressure sensor, has a simple USB-C port for charging, and maxes out at 40,000 BPM across its five modes, however.It’s a shame that …it’s difficult to read which mode you’re using when in use.Type:sonicModes:five (white, clean, sensitive, massage, polish)Power:42,000 BPMPressure sensor:yesBattery life:about three weeksApp:noReplacement head cost:£14.99 for fourOdontaPowerPlus£29.99£29.99 at AmazonWhat we loveGood-value brush; more sustainable bristlesWhat we don’t loveAt this price? Very littleMost intuitive all-rounder:Spotlight Sonic ProSpotlightSonic Profrom£64.99£99.99 at Spotlight£64.99 at AmazonWhat we loveA great all-rounder; a super clean at a fair priceWhat we don’t loveThe different modes aren’t labelled on the brushView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£99.99 at Spotlight£64.99 at AmazonThis was our top pick overall until the Laifen, above, arrived. The Spotlight Sonic Pro is a great all-rounder, with excellent features and a price that doesn’t verge on ridiculous. Founded by two sibling dentists, Spotlight has only three electric toothbrushes for adults at the moment, and the Pro model tested here delivers on every metric that counts.Why we love itFirst, the Sonic Pro performs an impressive clean. Its four modes range from 30,000 (gentle) to 50,000 (polish) BPM. While not completely necessary for a healthy mouth, such speeds help provide that “fresh from the hygienist” feeling, when your teeth are crying out for a thorough clean after a day of mainlining soft drinks.It also packs a pressure sensor to make sure you’re not brushing too hard and potentially damaging your gums, and there are four lights just below the head to show how far you are into your two-minute brushing cycle.Flip the heads over and you’ll find a tongue cleaner, and it also comes with a travel case.
