This doesn’t charge the brush, but the magnetic USB-C charging base is pretty compact, and a single charge can last up to 70 days, which is above average for an electric toothbrush. Even at the higher speeds I was using it at, it didn’t show any signs of slowing down during the testing period, so that feels accurate.If you can do without the pressure sensor, progress lights, tongue cleaner and polish setting, you’re likely to be just as happy with thenon-Pro version(£64.99) and can save a few quid.It’s a shame that …modes aren’t labelled on the brush itself, even if you can easily feel the difference.Type:sonicModes: four (gentle, clean, white and polish)Power: 50,000 BPMPressure sensor:yesBattery life: up to 70 daysApp: noReplacement head cost:£29.99 for threeSpotlightSonic Profrom£64.99£99.99 at Spotlight£64.99 at AmazonWhat we loveA great all-rounder; a super clean at a fair priceWhat we don’t loveThe different modes aren’t labelled on the brushBest electric toothbrush for sustainability:Suri Core 1.0SuriCore 1.0from£65£65 at Suri£65 at AmazonWhat we loveCheaper, with less kitWhat we don’t loveFeels underpowered compared to rivalsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£65 at Suri£65 at AmazonTheSuri 2.0(or Suri Pro 2.0 as it’s been renamed) previously occupied this slot. But the cheaper Core 1.0 outdoes the previous sustainability champ by ditching the charging case, which contains a lithium-ion battery, and it does so at a substantial discount too.Why we love itOne of the key drawbacks of the Suri Pro 2.0 is that sustainability comes at a financial cost. The brush was £105 when it was released in 2025, and although you can buy the model without the case for £85, that’s still a significant outlay – even if the recyclable cornstarch and castor oil brush heads make it kinder to the planet than most.The Core 1.0 is £65, and makes cuts in the right places. Gone is the bundled case, the battery is 100mAh smaller, and the aluminium body is replaced with a bio-circular plastic made from waste cooking oil. These are minor cuts, and crucially it retains a pressure sensor, wireless charging and the recyclable heads of its pricier sibling.It’s not all good news. It’s incompatible with the charging case, meaning you can’t upgrade later, and the power has dropped from an already weak 30,000 BPM to 28,000 BPM. Some may favour the original for the UV-C-light cleaning case, but if sustainability is your main motivator, the Core 1.0 has plenty of appeal.It’s a shame that …it’s even less powerful than the Suri Pro 2.0, with a motor that manages just 28,000 BPM.Type:sonicModes:two (clean and polish)Power:up to 28,000 BPMPressure sensor:yesBattery life:up to four weeksApp:noReplacement head cost:£14.99 for three(or £8.98 for two every six months)To find out more,read our full Suri Core 1.0 toothbrush reviewSuriCore 1.0from£65£65 at Suri£65 at AmazonWhat we loveCheaper, with less kitWhat we don’t loveFeels underpowered compared to rivalsBest premium electric toothbrush:Philips Sonicare Smart 9400PhilipsSonicare Smart 9400from£199.99£199.99 at John Lewis£199.99 at AmazonWhat we loveMost powerful brush tested; a clever glass chargerWhat we don’t loveHave you seen the price tag?View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£199.99 at John Lewis£199.99 at AmazonIf you have a toothbrush budget most people could only dream of, then the Philips Sonicare Smart 9400 is the model to go for. I also tested theDiamondClean 9900, which retails for £60 more than the 9400’s current price, but I actually prefer the way this one charges.Why we love itWhen I took the Sonicare 9400 out of the box, I thought they’d packed the wrong charger. It turns out that the handy rinse glass in the boxishow it charges. You rest the charging puck underneath it, and the toothbrush charges through the glass. What a time to be alive.With a BPM of up to 62,000, it’s the joint most powerful sonic brush I tested (tying with the aforementioned DiamondClean 9900), and you can really feel the results after use. It has four modes – clean (with three intensities), deep clean, gum health and white – and feels comfortable in the hand. It even comes with a charging case, if you don’t want to take the magical glass charger on the road.You can track your brushing habits via its excellent app; however, unlike with the DiamondClean 9900, where it’s the only way to cycle between modes, you don’t have to use it. If you do, though, you’ll receive guidance on your brushing, showing areas you’ve missed with the option to spend a bit longer on them if needed. It can be connected with Apple Health for iPhone data nerds, and it’ll even automatically reorder brush heads for you if you want, so you’re never caught short.It’s a shame that …it misses out on the sensitive mode of the DiamondClean 9900, so those with tooth pain may want to look elsewhere. Battery life is also rather stingy, thanks to the Bluetooth.Type:sonicModes:four (clean, deep clean+, gum health and white+)Power: 62,000 BPMPressure sensor:yesBattery life: up to 14 daysApp: yesReplacement head cost:from £15.09 for twoPhilipsSonicare Smart 9400from£199.99£199.99 at John Lewis£199.99 at AmazonWhat we loveMost powerful brush tested; a clever glass chargerWhat we don’t loveHave you seen the price tag?Best oscillating toothbrush:Oral-B iO3Oral-BiO3from£65£65 at Boots£75 at AmazonWhat we loveWell-priced; best pressure sensor I testedWhat we don’t lovePricey head replacements (even when discounted)View image in fullscreen£65 at Boots£75 at AmazonThis oscillating toothbrush (which moves bristles in a circular motion, rather than vibrating like most other brushes here – see the buying guide below for more information) isn’t technically the best one you can buy, as you can probably tell from the fact that Oral-B’s iO line goes all the way up to the iO10. But because they all use the same motor and brush, and thus offer similar performance, this is the one I recommend: it jettisons unnecessary extras (like a connected app and screen) in order to simply deliver the features you need for a great clean.Why we love itIt boasts three modes – daily clean, sensitive and whiten – and its round heads are small enough to get into tight areas. Most importantly, its pressure sensor won’t only tell you when you’re applying too much pressure, but also when you’re applying too little, via an easy-to-understand white/green/red lighting system in a ring at the top of the handle.While it has fewer modes than the higher-numbered iOs, it delivers the same dentist-fresh-feeling performance, while retailing for a fraction of their optimistic RRPs.It’s a shame that …at £15 for two,replacement headsare a touch on the pricey side. And, like all the Oral-B brushes I tested, it made me oddly dribbly during brushing, so stay near the sink.Type:oscillatingModes:three (daily clean, whitening and sensitive)Power: not disclosedPressure sensor:yesBattery life: up to 18 daysApp: noReplacement head cost:£15 for twoOral-BiO3from£65£65 at Boots£75 at AmazonWhat we loveWell-priced; best pressure sensor I testedWhat we don’t lovePricey head replacements (even when discounted)The best of the restCoulax C8CoulaxC8£19.99£19.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIncredible price; seven replacement heads includedWhat we don’t loveSome user reviews question its reliabilityView image in fullscreen£19.99 at AmazonBest for:if money is tightI thought the cheap and cheerfulOdonta PowerPluswould be the most affordable model on test, but this Amazon bestseller comes with a surprising number of features.For just over £15, you get a toothbrush with five settings, up to 40,000 BPM and eight(!) brush heads in the box. While my mouth didn’t feel as fresh as with more expensive models, bluntly, it didn’t feel like a quarter of the performance for a quarter of the price.It didn’t make the final cut because …while I had no issues with my test unit, Amazon’s AI analysis of its customer reviews found that “some customers report that it turns on randomly, doesn’t charge, and doesn’t retain any charge”. So there may be an element of getting what you pay for.Type:sonic;modes:five (white, clean, sensitive, polish and massage);power: 40,000 BPM;pressure sensor:no;battery life: up to 120 days;app: no;replacement head cost:£16.74 for 10CoulaxC8£19.99£19.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIncredible price; seven replacement heads includedWhat we don’t loveSome user reviews question its reliabilityForeo Issa 4ForeoIssa 4from£89£89 at Boots£89 at ForeoWhat we loveBattery life; familiar feel for manual brushersWhat we don’t loveTeeth didn’t feel as clean as traditional rivalsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£89 at Boots£89 at ForeoBest for:sensitive teethThe Foreo Issa 3 previously sat in this spot on the list. Does that mean that the Issa 4 is a huge leap forward? Not really, but if smartphone-makers can get away with perfunctory updates, then why can’t toothbrush manufacturers?More importantly, the Issa 3 has been retired, and there’s still nothing else quite like Foreo’s take on dental hygiene. Unlike every other toothbrush here, you use the Issa 4 like a manual brush, rubbing it against your teeth, rather than letting it glide over them. And unlike its rivals, it lasts a full year on a single charge.So, what’s changed? Rather than having to jump between 16 intensities as you did with the Issa 3, there are now three buttons to toggle between the default deep clean, sensitive and whitening modes, although the top setting remains as powerful as before. The new (and sadly compulsory) app lets you fine-tune power and running time for each mode, and there’s a “find my brush” button for people who unaccountably manage to misplace their toothbrushes in presumably palatial bathrooms.The heads still only need replacing once every six months because of the medical-grade silicone and PBT polymer bristles, which Foreo believes are up to 10,000 times more hygienic than their nylon equivalents.The manual motion and somewhat underpowered motor make this a great choice for newcomers to electric toothbrushes and those with sensitive teeth, especially with the new dedicated Sensitive button. But for me, it doesn’t provide that squeaky clean feel that regular sonic or oscillating brushes provide.It didn’t make the final cut because …it may be more effective than manual brushing, but it doesn’t feel like it’s as effective as other brushes at cutting through plaque.Type:sonic hybrid;modes:three (deep clean, sensitive and whitening);power: 11,000 BPM;pressure sensor:no;battery life: up to 365 days;app: yes;replacement head cost:£24.99 for oneForeoIssa 4from£89£89 at Boots£89 at ForeoWhat we loveBattery life; familiar feel for manual brushersWhat we don’t loveTeeth didn’t feel as clean as traditional rivalsOrdo Sonic EdgeOrdoSonic Edgefrom£14.99£15 at Argos£14.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIncredible price; recyclable heads; colour choicesWhat we don’t loveVery basic; unable to stand on rounded baseView image in fullscreen£15 at Argos£14.99 at AmazonBest for:recyclable heads on a budgetA bargain toothbrush from a well-known, reputable brand. What’s the catch? There are some, as I’ll get on to in a moment, but this is an utter bargain of a toothbrush for the most part. It hits a decent 36,000 BPM, and the USB-C chargeable battery will go for six weeks.Ordo fully embraces the chunky charm of its plastic design, and it comes in a range of bright colours. Best of all, it uses the same heads as other Ordo brushes, meaningthe company will recycle them free of charge.That said, there are some obvious compromises. It’s a basic, no-frills package with no case and just a single head in the box, and you can forget about a pressure sensor or multiple modes (although there is a built-in timer to tell you when to move to the next section).There are also some questionable design decisions, such as the rounded base that makes it impossible to stand upright, and the high-pitched noise it makes in use, which my partner found immensely irritating. On top of that, Ordo’s heads have a silicone bit in the middle of the bristles for polishing: it divides opinion, but you can put me firmly on Team No Thank You.It didn’t make the final cut because …it can feel a little too no-frills at times.Type:sonic;modes:one;power:36,000 BPM;pressure sensor:no;battery life:up to six weeks;app:no;replacement head cost:£5 eachOrdoSonic Edgefrom£14.99£15 at Argos£14.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIncredible price; recyclable heads; colour choicesWhat we don’t loveVery basic; unable to stand on rounded baseOral-B iO9Oral-BiO9from£154£200 at Boots£154 at AmazonWhat we loveThe most fully featured toothbrush you can buyWhat we don’t loveIt’s the definition of pricey overkillView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£200 at Boots£154 at AmazonBest for:if money is no objectWith a crazy £500 RRP, you may wonder what kind of black magic the Oral-B iO9 offers your daily brush. The answer is lots, but not enough to justify its price.It comes with a whopping seven cleaning modes (daily clean, sensitive, gum care, intense, whiten, super sensitive and tongue clean), a colour screen to cycle through them, and built-in 3D teeth tracking that can detect 16 mouth zones to indicate how your technique is in the connected app. It charges quickly, too – just three hours via the magnetic charging stand or the bundled snazzy charging case and proprietary cable with a plug.There is a middle ground between this and the recommended iO3 above, with theOral-B iO6offering a black-and-white screen and a connected app, albeit with slower charging, a non-charging case, weaker position tracking and fewer modes. If an app is important to you, but your money-to-sense ratio is still intact,that’s probably the one to go for.It didn’t make the final cut because …at RRP, it costs half a grand! You could buy 38 Coulax C8s for that.Type:oscillating;modes:seven (daily clean, sensitive, gum care, intense, whiten, super sensitive, tongue clean);power: not disclosed;pressure sensor:yes;battery life: up to 14 days;app: yes;replacement head cost:£15 for twoOral-BiO9from£154£200 at Boots£154 at AmazonWhat we loveThe most fully featured toothbrush you can buyWhat we don’t loveIt’s the definition of pricey overkillSilk’n SonicYouSilk’nSonicYoufrom£61.99£61.99 at Currys£67.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIncredible battery life for a sonic toothbrushWhat we don’t loveMore powerful options are availableView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£61.99 at Currys£67.99 at AmazonBest for:battery lifeToothbrush battery life varies wildly because it depends on a host of factors: how often you brush, how long you spend doing so, and which modes you use. As such, plenty of people may find that manufacturers inadvertently (or, cynically, advertently) oversell their stamina.Still, if battery life is the be-all and end-all for you, you should give the Silk’n SonicYou a look. The manufacturer suggests you’ll get up to 300 days’ use if you use the sensitive (30,000 strokes a minute) setting twice a day for a total of four minutes. That’s not as good as the Foreo, and it’d obviously go down faster if you brush more often, for longer, or use the 37,000-stroke-a-minute whitening mode – but given most of the toothbrushes I was testing were rated in the 14- to 90-day area, it’s still a stamina champion. It certainly didn’t need charging while I was using it.Infrequent charging can be a curse if you’re dealing with a bespoke charger that you can’t find when the time comes, but thankfully you just need to pop open the base and connect a common-or-garden USB-C cable to top it up.It didn’t make the final cut because …battery life is often directly linked to the power of the brush, and while 37,000 BPM is nothing to be sneezed at, you can get more power if you’re prepared to charge more often.Type:sonic;modes:three (sensitive, clean and white);power: 37,000 BPM;Pressure sensor:no;battery life: up to 300 days;app: no;replacement head cost:£19 for twoSilk’nSonicYoufrom£61.99£61.99 at Currys£67.99 at AmazonWhat we loveIncredible battery life for a sonic toothbrushWhat we don’t loveMore powerful options are availableWhites Beaconsfield sonic LED toothbrushWhites BeaconsfieldSonic LED toothbrushfrom£99.99£99.99 at Whites Beaconsfield£99.99 at AmazonWhat we loveOffers whitening with your regular brushWhat we don’t loveThe whitening blue light hits battery life hardView image in fullscreen£99.99 at Whites Beaconsfield£99.99 at AmazonBest for:whiteningWhile many toothbrushes (including this one) have a built-in whitening setting that adds time or alternates speeds to remove surface stains, the Whites Beaconsfield sonic LED toothbrush – with its terrifying picture of a toothy strawberry on the box – goes the extra mile by including blue-light whitening technology. The company says this can whiten teeth by an average of 2.5 shades in three days.A week’s use did indeed appear to make my teethslightlylighter in before-and-after shots, although you shouldn’t expect miracles. All the same, combining this with whitening toothpaste and other products could really make a difference in the long run.It didn’t make the final cut because …other toothbrushes offer a cleaner-feeling mouth. And that blue light makes for a shorter, two-week battery life.Type:sonic;modes: four (clean, white, polish and gum care);power: 39,600 RPM (revolutions per minute, vibration frequency);pressure sensor:no;battery life: 15 days;app: no;replacement head cost:£12.49 for twoWhites BeaconsfieldSonic LED toothbrushfrom£99.99£99.99 at Whites Beaconsfield£99.99 at AmazonWhat we loveOffers whitening with your regular brushWhat we don’t loveThe whitening blue light hits battery life hardPhilips OnePhilipsOnefrom£14.49£14.49 at Holland & Barrett£15.99 at SuperdrugWhat we loveAs compact as electric toothbrushes getWhat we don’t love13,000 movements a minute is extremely lowView image in fullscreen£14.49 at Holland & Barrett£15.99 at SuperdrugBest for:travelWhile most electric toothbrushes include a travel case for hygiene (and to prevent them from buzzing in your bag), you might not want to take an expensive electric toothbrush with you everywhere – especially if it has its own bespoke charger.The Philips One is cheap, cheerful and compact, and it will last for 90 days with a single AAA battery. You can also geta version with a built-in batterythat’s chargeable via USB-C, but you’ll get only 30 days out of that.It didn’t make the final cut because …13,000 movements a minute is fine for a few days’ travelling, but you’ll want more power for day-to-day brushing.Type:sonic;modes:one;power: 13,000 BPM;pressure sensor:no;battery life: up to 90 days (AAA) or 30 days (USB);app: no;replacement head cost:£9.99 for twoPhilipsOnefrom£14.49£14.49 at Holland & Barrett£15.99 at SuperdrugWhat we loveAs compact as electric toothbrushes getWhat we don’t love13,000 movements a minute is extremely lowSoocas Neos IISoocasNeos II£129.99£129.99 at AmazonWhat we loveA space-saver: toothbrush and flosser in oneWhat we don’t loveYou can get better brushes and water flossersView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£129.99 at AmazonBest for:2-in-1 water flossingWith cabinet space at a premium, what if you could combine an electric toothbrush and water flosser in one? That’s the question quite ably answered by the Soocas Neos II, with its built-in water tank, which fires jets of water out of a small hole in the middle of the brush head once a two-minute brushing timer has elapsed.With three brushing levels going up to a maximum of 34,400 BPM, it offers a solid if unspectacular brushing “main course”, slightly let down by the lack of a pressure sensor. The water flossing “dessert” is introduced gently too, with short but powerful bursts, rather than a steady stream filling your mouth with water. As a way of ensuring you don’t neglect flossing, it’s hard to beat.That said, this space-saving design does come at a cost compared to getting two dedicated devices, the main one being that this isn’t thebest water flosseryou can buy. Without tapered tips to aim at the edge of your teeth, it feels a little inexact, plus, to keep it (relatively) slim, the water tank is just 50ml. For context, the largest tank on a cordless model I tested in the roundup was 400ml, and the smallest was 200ml.The £130 price is competitive when you consider it’s doing the work of two devices, but you may well decide that you’d be better off getting a couple of standalone products for a bit more cash.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s a jack of two trades, but a master of none.Type:sonic with water flosser;modes:three (gentle, medium, strong);power:34,400 BPM;pressure sensor:no;battery life:30 days;app:no;replacement head cost:£24.99 for twoSoocasNeos II£129.99£129.99 at AmazonWhat we loveA space-saver: toothbrush and flosser in oneWhat we don’t loveYou can get better brushes and water flossersTao Clean Umma DiamondTao CleanUmma Diamondfrom£128.77£199 at Tao Clean£128.77 at AmazonWhat we loveAn elegant system for cleaning and chargingWhat we don’t loveNot the most powerful; takes up a lot of spaceView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Alan Martin/The Guardian£199 at Tao Clean£128.77 at AmazonBest for: the hygiene-consciousDoes the idea of a toothbrush head exposed to all sorts of bathroom nasties give you the heebie-jeebies? Personally, it doesn’t bother me in the slightest, but for those with hygiene concerns, California-based brand Tao Clean has an answer.The Tao Clean Umma Diamond looks slightly odd, as if it’s a “pregnant toothbrush” – and not because there’s a baby brush inside. This design means that, when not in use, it can be placed upside down in a plastic triangular dock. Not only does this charge the toothbrush, but it also air dries the head while hitting it with UV-C light for four minutes, starting 12 minutes after docking, then 12 hours later and then every 24 hours until it’s used again. This, TAO Clean says, will deal with all kinds of hard-to-spell bacteria fromStaphylococcus aureustoPseudomonas aeruginosa.At full price, itcosts an eyebrow-raising £199. At the time of writing, however, doing a quiz on site takes it down to a more reasonable £99.50 with extra whitening brush heads and a portable battery-powered sanitiser for when you’re away from home. There’s also a lifetime warranty, although you must register within 90 days and cover shipping to the US yourself. Normal wear and tear and the battery itself aren’t covered, either.It has drawbacks. There are only two modes, which reach a maximum speed of 40,000 BPM: respectable, but some way short of the best toothbrushes here. More seriously, not everyone will have the space for a huge cleaning/charging dock, no matter how convenient it is in principle. The UV-C charging case bundled with theSuri Pro 2.0is far more practical for most people.It didn’t make the final cut because …it takes up a lot of space.Type:sonic;modes:two (super clean, sensitive clean);power:40,000 BPM;pressure sensor:no;battery life:two to three weeks;app:no;replacement head cost:£24.95 for two(20% off on subscription)Tao CleanUmma Diamondfrom£128.77£199 at Tao Clean£128.77 at AmazonWhat we loveAn elegant system for cleaning and chargingWhat we don’t loveNot the most powerful; takes up a lot of spaceWhat you need to knowAre electric toothbrushes better than manual ones?Generally speaking, yes. Without them, “it’s harder to get the same result”, says Caitlin Miller, head of hygiene and therapy at Bupa Dental Care UK. “To get the same level of cleaning found with an electric toothbrush, you’d have to spend a lot longer than two minutes brushing with a manual.”The reasons are threefold, she explains: manual dexterity; people being more likely to use their expensive electric device properly; and sheer power.“You don’t have to really do anything with it, and it does a better job,” Miller says. “That’s not to say that they suit everybody. There are people who can do a perfectly good job with a manual toothbrush, but for most of my patients, I will see improvements when people go on to an electric toothbrush.”How do you use an electric toothbrush?“You want to hold your toothbrush at a 45-degree angle – half on the gum, half on the tooth. You should just be holding it horizontally, sweeping across the tooth and gum margins,” says Miller, adding that you should move slowly, allocating a couple of seconds for each tooth.“You don’t move it up and down, you don’t need to move it round and round. That’s the beauty of the electric toothbrush: you can be pretty lazy with it, and it still does a good job.”But a common mistake is to press too hard, which is why some of the brushes in our guide come with pressure sensors – something actively recommended by Miller. “If you’ve got too much pressure, you’re essentially dampening the vibrations and bristles.”How often do you need to charge an electric toothbrush?This varies hugely between toothbrushes, and depends on how often you brush and the settings you use. The only certainty is that you need to charge them more often than a manual toothbrush – which is to say “at all”.According to Miller, plenty of patients fall back on inferior manual brushing because of this. “The number of people who say, ‘Oh, I do have an electric toothbrush, but I always forget to charge it, and then it takes three days, so I just use my manual toothbrush,’” she laments. “Keeping it charged is quite important.”The good news is that batteries now tend to be lithium-ion, meaning they charge quickly, and they last a decent amount of time, too.The ones I tested had manufacturer-quoted battery lives of between 14 and 365 days, which is an enormous gulf. Plenty of factors play into this, including power, connectivity and the size of the battery itself, but it’s also worth bearing in mind how this is measured. Generally, a manufacturer counts a day as four minutes of brushing over two sessions, but it might be more or less, so read the small print.You may instinctively be drawn to brushes with longer battery ratings, but convenience is also a factor. A proprietary charger might be more of a faff than a USB-C one, or a charging dock that sits neatly on the sink, especially if months go between charges and you forget where your cable lives.You may also want to charge more often than required. Anecdotally, I can easily feel the difference in strength between a toothbrush approaching the end of its battery and the same model fresh off the charger.How often do you need to replace your toothbrush head?As for replacing the heads, Miller suggests you do this every three months – or earlier if it looks splayed or frayed – because its cleaning performance will suffer. “You can see it under a microscope: it gets really worn on top.”Beyond an electric toothbrush, Miller stresses the importance of cleaning between the teeth, and she has a clear order of preference: interdental brushes, then floss and finallywater flossers.“If I’ve got patients who won’t use anything often, if I can get them on a water flosser, then that’s better than nothing,” she says.The different types of electric toothbrush: oscillating vs sonic toothbrushesThere are two main types of toothbrushes on the market: oscillating and sonic. “They work differently, but they’re both doing a similar sort of thing,” says Miller.In short, an oscillating toothbrush moves the bristles back and forth in a circular motion, while sonic brushes use vibrations to move the bristles in two directions to loosen plaque. The latter is measured in brush movements per minute (BPM), and my selection was rated between 11,000 and 66,000 BPM. Miller says some of her clients find the sonic brushes a bit “ticklish” at first, but this is something you can get used to.As metrics go, BPM is a bit like the number of megapixels in a camera: a useful pointer about performance, but higher doesn’t automatically mean better. There are a number of other factors at play in cleaning performance, including the design of bristles and the user’s own brushing method.As for whether you should favour oscillating or sonic, asystematic review and meta-analysis of 38 comparison studiespublished in the International Journal of Dental Hygiene found a “small but clinically relevant advantage” for oscillating brushes. But it added that it’s “unlikely that dental care professionals in routine examination would be able to detect [the] small differences” between the two. But you don’t necessarily have to choose between the two. Our current champion, theLaifen Wave Pro, includes both oscillating and sonic action to effectively remove plaque.What should I do with my old electric toothbrush?If it’s still working, you might consider passing it on to a friend or family member who’s still using a manual toothbrush.Don’t include used heads, obviously. Old models can also enjoy a second life scrubbing between tiles or cleaning grubby cat chins (a nightmare retirement for the heads, but maybe no worse than rubbing against sticky teeth and gums).Still, while you cantake steps to make your toothbrush last longer, eventually it will need replacing. It’s important not to put broken electric toothbrushes in regular household waste, asbatteries are an environmental hazard. Instead, look for an e-waste bin if your council has one, or consider recycling points in shops such asBootsandCurrys. You can find a list of local options on theRecycle Your Electricals website.Can I get a two-in-one electric toothbrush and water flosser?A few options exist, such as the Soocas Neos II in the list above. But while you’ll save space and the tediousness of having to charge two devices rather than one, there are drawbacks.Firstly, cordless water flossers are bigger than toothbrushes, as they have a reservoir for the water. As I wrote in my guide to thebest water flossers, they look a bit like pregnant electric toothbrushes, making them less comfortable to hold for extended periods and slightly more bulky for trips.On top of that, because 2-in-1 devices try to replicate the shape of toothbrushes a little more, water capacity suffers compared with dedicated flossers. The Soocas unit above has a capacity of just 50ml – a quarter of the size of the smallest flosser in my guide.Another issue is accuracy. Rather than having tapered tips for careful direction, the water comes out of a hole nestled between the bristles of the toothbrush head. This takes some getting used to, and even then feels less accurate than aiming a thin nozzle that can be placed up against the gaps between your teeth.In short, you pay a price for minimalism and, as is often the case with 2-in-1 devices of all stripes, you may feel they end up doing neither task as well as dedicated versions.For more:How I tested 20 electric toothbrushes (and became a toothbrushing pro)How to make your toothbrush last longer – and keep it out of landfillSuri Core 1.0 electric toothbrush review: this new budget model is still sustainable – and the one I’d buyAlan Martin is awriterwhohas been putting products –including phones, gaming devices and wearables – through their paces formore than a decade. Although hewouldn’t call teeth brushing a hobby, it’s something he’s been doing for decades with a degree of aptitude that haslargelysatisfieddentistsThe article was originally published on 29 December 2024. Reviews published in the Filter may be periodically updated to reflect new products and at the editor’s discretion. The date of an article’s most recent update can be found in the timestamp at the top of the page. This article was amended on 14 August 2026; the Suri Core 1.0, Tao Clean Umma Diamond and Soocas Neos II were added after testing, one toothbrush was removed, more information was added to the buying guide, and prices were updated throughout.Explore more on these topicsHealth & wellbeingThe FilterHygienefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Iceberg, romaine, kale: which salad greens are healthiest? | Well actually | The Guardian
description: If you’re trying to meet your daily serving of 2.5 cups of vegetables, you might have some questions
Author: Adrienne Matei
Headline: If you’re trying to meet your daily serving of 2.5 cups of vegetables, you might have some questions
Content: Bok choy and kale are among the nutrient-rich greens you can add to a salad.Photograph: Anastasiya Mihailovna/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBok choy and kale are among the nutrient-rich greens you can add to a salad.Photograph: Anastasiya Mihailovna/Getty ImagesWell actuallyIceberg, romaine, kale: which salad greens are healthiest?If you’re trying to meet your daily serving of 2.5 cups of vegetables, you might have some questionsAdrienne MateiFri 14 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 12.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you want to eat lettuce, that no longer just means iceberg. In our bountiful age, there are many options: romaine, red-leaf lettuce, butter lettuce, beet greens, bok choy, bitter radicchio, every developmental stage of arugula.Sometimes, it’s simply up to preference. But if you’re trying to meet your daily serving of2.5 cupsof vegetables – or you’re rethinking your salad choices amid theUS cyclospora outbreak, you might have some questions about which greens to go with.Are salad greens nutritious?Health authoritieswidely agreethat a diet high in nutrient-dense fruits and vegetables is associated with reduced chronic disease risk. But which greens are giving you the most nutritional bang for your buck?“Nutrient density”, defined as the “nutrients per calorie” of a food, can be a factor when shopping for produce, notesJamie Mok, a Los Angeles–based registered dietitian nutritionist.In 2014, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention released astudyattempting to help people better understand nutrient density via a ranking system that declaredwatercressa powerhouse champion, with 17 nutrients per calorie – almost twice the nutrient density askale.View image in fullscreenThe CDC recently declared watercress a nutrient powerhouse.Photograph: haoliang/Getty Images“Watercress is rich in vitamin K, vitamin C, minerals like calcium, manganese, copper and lots of phytochemicals, which are beneficial compounds that we find in plants,” says Mok, who grew up eating watercress in Chinese soups her mother made. “It’s a very light, delicate flavor.”This doesn’t mean you should opt for watercress and ban other greens from your crisper. While watercress grabbed the CDC’s top spot, many other cruciferous greens, like green or Napa cabbage, kale or arugula, boast similar, substantial health benefits.“Cruciferous vegetables contain a group of compounds called glucosinolates,” as well as vitamin C, vitamin K and fiber, explains Mok. “These are sulfur-containing compounds that have antioxidant activity.” Researchers believe glucosinolatessupportcancer-prevention.Rather than focusing on only the most nutrient-dense greens, experts advise prioritizing variety. Even the fruits and veggies that scoredloweron the CDC’s ranking, such as blackberries, leeks and sweet potatoes, offer their own substantial health benefits – they simply don’t have the breadth of nutrients cruciferous veggies pack per calorie.Beans, beans, the magical fruit: how healthy are they really?Read more“I don’t encourage people to focus on finding one ‘best’ leafy green,” says Dr Nina Cherie Franklin, a research scientist and health coach who goes by “That Salad Lady”. “Eating a variety is almost always the better approach. Spinach, kale, watercress, romaine, arugula, chard, collards, mustard greens, turnip greens and dandelion greens all bring something different to the bowl.”For instance, one cup of shredded cabbage willnetyou about 2g of fiber and 28mg of vitamin C, but no vitamin A. A cup of spinachcontains1g of fiber, 9mg of vitamin C and 16mcg of vitamin A.That means easy staples that include various vegetables are a good option, including boxed mesclun mix, which contains different leafy greens, such as mustard greens, arugula and different lettuces, notes Mok.Are darker green vegetables more nutritious than lighter green ones?Many people believe that darker greens are healthier than lighter ones. Experts say that in terms of nutritional content, this is true – the rich hunter green of kale trumps the pallid hues of iceberg lettuce.“Darker green vegetables are generally richer in nutrients, especially phytonutrients,” a kind of bioactive antioxidant-like compound, says Franklin.But you don’t have to chuck your head of iceberg. “Lighter greens are far from nutritionally empty,” Franklin adds. “Romaine, butter lettuce, endive and other lettuces still provide vitamins, fiber, hydration and beneficial plant compounds.”Is it healthier to eat greens cooked or raw?Some of the nutrients in greens are fat soluble – “particularly vitamins A, E and K”, says Mok. Adding healthy fats like avocado, olive oil or eggs to salad greens can help your body absorb their nutrition. “Sauteing them with a healthy fat like olive oil can help improve the absorption” of these important compounds too, says Mok.Cooking also reduces the volume of greens, making it easier to eat larger quantities; two cups of raw leafy vegetables are the equivalent of a 1-cup vegetable serving.When eating iron-heavy greens like spinach, Mok recommends pairing them with foods rich in vitamin C, which helps with iron absorption. Citrus, bell peppers and tomatoes are some good options, she says.What’s the best way to avoid getting sick while eating greens?Heating to about 160F (71C) can make greens safer to consume, particularly if you’re concerned about risks posed by microorganisms likecyclospora,Ecolior salmonella.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“Washing raw produce can reduce dirt and some contamination, but no home-washing method can guarantee the removal of every organism,” says Franklin. “Cooking is more effective at reducing the risk of foodborne illness.”If you simply must have a salad, clean your greens thoroughly. “For raw greens, the basics matter,” Franklin says. “Wash your hands and preparation surfaces, discard damaged leaves, rinse loose greens thoroughly under running water and dry them with a clean cloth, paper towel or a salad spinner.”Why are greens so susceptible to contamination?Up to9%of foodborne illnesses caused by pathogens in the US are linked to leafy greens. This looks like an estimated2.3millnesses annually, costing the nation more than $5bn to address, according to research from the Ohio State University.When it comes to waterborne pathogens likecyclosporiasis, the physical attributes of leaves make them susceptible to harboring disease, says Kristin Krokowski, a commercial horticulture educator at the University of Wisconsin–Madison.Graphic with three lines of text that say, in bold, ‘Well Actually’, then ‘Read more on living a good life in a complex world,’ then a pinkish-lavender pill-shaped button with white letters that say ‘More from this section’The leaves of leafy green vegetables are bumpy, says Krokowski: “There’s lots of little places for the cyclospora to attach, and the fact that they’re heads – multiple layers of leaves – allows for space in between the leaves. So water isn’t evaporating quickly, and there’s more places to hide.”The nooks and crannies of leafy greens also provide hiding places for the pathogensEcoli,norovirusand salmonella, though these can also spread through the use of tools like cutters, or during harvest, transport or storage.How much nutrition do greens lose sitting in the fridge?It’s one thing to stock up on leafy greens at the store, and another thing to actually eat them in a timely manner; we’ve all felt guilt over limp lettuce and slimy mesclun.Researchhas found that some nutrients, likefolateand vitamin C, can decrease when stored. But the good news is most vitamins and minerals, as well as fiber, remain stable in produce for days or weeks in the fridge.“When stored properly, whole leafy greens can remain fresh for one to two weeks, depending on the variety and their condition,” says Franklin.View image in fullscreenStoring fruits and veggies in reusable cotton produce bags can work to preserve the freshness of greens because they allow some airflow without trapping too much moisture.Photograph: Anikona/Getty Images“There is no single point at which greens suddenly stop being nutritious,” she adds. How quickly nutrient loss happens “depends on factors such as how fresh greens were when purchased, how they were handled, and the temperature, humidity and moisture conditions in the refrigerator”.“Cutting, bruising or otherwise damaging the leaves can also shorten their useful life,” she says.Franklin says reusable cotton produce bags can work to preserve the freshness of greens because they allow some airflow without trapping too much moisture. “A regular plastic bag can also work when used properly,” she says. She recommends placing a slightly damp paper towel inside the plastic bag to help “manage humidity without allowing the greens to become soggy”.You can also place a paper towel inside a plastic clamshell, then flip the box upside down –a methodthat can keep spinach crisp and odorless for up to two weeks.“For whole, unprocessed greens that you’re not planning to use right away, I generally recommend storing them unwashed,” says Franklin. This is because washing introduces moisture, which can accelerate spoilage.Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyFoodHealthSaladfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cocktail of the week: Whiteley’s at Six Senses’ strawberry & basil margarita – recipe | Cocktails | The Guardian

Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A vibrant and playful twist on the classic cocktail, with a bright, citrus kick and a subtle herbal note
Content: Whiteley’s strawberry and basil margarita.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.View image in fullscreenWhiteley’s strawberry and basil margarita.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.The good mixerCocktailsCocktail of the week: Whiteley’s at Six Senses’ strawberry & basil margarita – recipeA vibrant and playful twist on the classic cocktail, with a bright, citrus kick and a subtle herbal noteAdrian Gonzalez ParrondoFri 14 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFresh, vibrant and full of summer character, this is a playful twist on the classic. It’s juicy and refreshing, with a bright, citrus kick and a subtle, herbal note that keeps things light and balanced. It also works very well with non-alcoholic tequila. If you like, double the syrup quantities, because it’s delicious drizzled over pancakes or diluted with sparkling water for a refreshing, summery drink.Strawberry and basil margaritaServes1For the strawberry syrup (for 6 serves)75g fresh strawberries, hulled and chopped75ml agave syrupFor the drink50ml tequila– just use your favourite (we useThe Lost Explorer Tequila Blanco)Juice of1lime25mlstrawberry syrup(see above and method)2 basil leavesFirst, make the syrup. Put the chopped strawberries and agave in a blender and blitz smooth. Fine strain into a clean jar, then seal and store in the fridge, where it’ll keep for about a fortnight.To build the drink, put everything in a shaker filled with ice, add a basil leaf, seal and shake hard. Strain into a rocks glass filled with fresh ice, garnish with the second basil leaf and serve.Adrian Gonzalez Parrondo, director of bars,Six Senses, London W2Explore more on these topicsCocktailsThe good mixerSpiritsFoodSummer food and drinkFruitHerbs and spicesMexican food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Helen Goh’s recipe for frozen Eton mess with plum, coconut and raspberry | Dessert | The Guardian
description: The classic British dessert, but with a frozen twist, captures all of the charm of the original with a welcome chill for summer
Author: Helen Goh
Headline: The classic British dessert, but with a frozen twist, captures all of the charm of the original with a welcome chill for summer
Content: Helen Goh’s frozen Eton mess with plum, coconut and raspberry.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.View image in fullscreenHelen Goh’s frozen Eton mess with plum, coconut and raspberry.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.The sweet spotDessertHelen Goh’s recipe for frozen Eton mess with plum, coconut and raspberryThe classic British dessert, but with a frozen twist, captures all of the charm of the original with a welcome chill for summerHelen GohFri 14 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIlove the glorious unruliness of Eton mess, all billowy cream, crushed meringue and tumbling fruit. This frozen version captures all of that charm but in a sliceable, make-ahead dessert that’s perfect for August entertaining. The fruit can even be cooked a day in advance, leaving little more to do than whip everything together before freezing. Thanks to the condensed milk, the cream freezes surprisingly softly, while the meringue keeps its gentle chew and the toasted coconut adds a welcome crunch and nuttiness. Late summer plums bring a lovely tartness that balances the sweetness beautifully, though apricots, peaches and nectarines would also work well.Frozen Eton mess with plum, coconut and raspberryWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep10 minCook40 minFreeze8 hr+Serves8For the fruit400g red plums(about 5 medium fruit), stoned and quartered40g caster sugar2 tsp lemon juice1 pinch fine sea salt120g raspberries, plus a few extra to decorateFor the ice-cream150g coconut condensed milk, or regular condensed milk250ml double cream1 tsp vanilla extract½ tsp fine sea salt120g shop-bought meringues, roughly broken50g toasted coconut chips, plus 15g extra to decorateStart by cooking the fruit, as it needs to cool completely before being folded into the ice-cream. Put the plums, sugar, lemon juice and salt in a medium pan on a medium heat. Cover partially with a lid and leave to cook gently for about 10 minutes, until the plums soften and collapse. Add the raspberries, stir gently for about a minute, just until they begin to soften, then take off the heat.Strain the fruit through a fine-mesh sieve set over a bowl, reserving both the fruit and its juices separately. Return the juices to the pan and simmer on a medium-high heat for three to five minutes, until reduced to a lightly syrupy consistency. Pour into a small jug and leave both the syrup and the fruit to cool completely.Line a 20cm x 10cm loaf tin with baking paper, leaving plenty of overhang on all sides. Put the condensed milk, cream, vanilla and salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment. Whisk on medium-high until the mixture holds firm peaks. Fold in the broken meringues and toasted coconut chips, until evenly incorporated, then add the cooled fruit. Fold gently a few times, just so the fruit remains in generous ripples, rather than becoming fully incorporated.Spoon the mix into the lined tin and smooth out the surface with a spatula. Tap the tin firmly on a work surface a few times to knock out any air pockets, then fold the paper overhang over the top and freeze overnight, or for at least eight hours.To serve, briefly wrap the outside of the tin with a hot, damp tea towel, then use the paper overhang to lift the ice-cream on to a platter. Spoon over the reserved fruit syrup, scatter with the extra toasted coconut and decorate with a few extra raspberries. Slice thickly and serve immediately with any remaining syrup alongside.Explore more on these topicsDessertThe sweet spotFoodSnacksFruitSummer food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Can antihistamines really help with PMDD and menopausal symptoms? | Well actually | The Guardian
description: Debilitating symptoms lead some to try over-the-counter medications Allegra and Pepcid due to a social media trend
Author: Sarah Sloat
Headline: Debilitating symptoms lead some to try over-the-counter medications Allegra and Pepcid due to a social media trend
Content: Here’s what experts say about the science behind the antihistamine hack.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHere’s what experts say about the science behind the antihistamine hack.Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesWell actuallyCan antihistamines really help with PMDD and menopausal symptoms?Debilitating symptoms lead some to try over-the-counter medications Allegra and Pepcid due to a social media trendSarah SloatFri 14 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePremenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD) and menopause can come with debilitating symptoms, like intense emotional changes and exhaustion.All over social media, women are claiming that a simple hack has helped enormously: a combination of two over-the-counter medications, both antihistamines – typically, the name brands Pepcid AC and Allegra.Almost all women experience symptoms during the dramatic transition to menopause, but only asmall portionreceive helpful treatment. Similarly, those with PMDD also contend withdramatic effects, and can have an evenharder timereceiving effective care.“When people are suffering from bothersome symptoms, and the strategies offered to them don’t seem to help, it makes sense for them to look elsewhere,” says Dr Alison Huang, a professor and director of the Women’sHealthClinical Research Center at the University of California, San Francisco.The antihistamine hack seems so simple. Is there science to back it up? Here’s what experts say.What are histamines and antihistamines?Histamine is a chemical the immune system releases; it has other functions but is primarily known for triggering allergy symptoms.There are four types ofhistamine receptorsin the body. Two are relevant here: H1 and H2. When activated, H1 receptors are responsible for many classic allergy symptoms, such as itchiness and sneezing. H1 antihistamines, like Allegra, block these receptors and reduce the severity of symptoms.Famotidine is an H2 blockermedication;Pepcidis one of the most common brands. H2 receptors are mainly in stomach cells. When these are activated, it can lead to issues like increased stomach acid secretion, flushing and headache.Can antihistamines help with perimenopause?Experts say there are plausible reasons to think histamine and perimenopause might be connected, but there’s not enough good evidence to prove histamine is a significant cause of perimenopausal symptoms like brain fog, anxiety and hot flashes.During perimenopause, ovaries produce fluctuating levels of a form of estrogen called estradiol. Estradiol can stimulate mast cells, which are responsible for releasing histamine.This is why allergy symptoms can flare up during menstrual cycles and perimenopause, says Dr Amy Voedisch, a clinical associate professor of obstetrics and gynecology at the Stanford University school of medicine.How do I know when I’ve hit perimenopause?Read moreDespite this known link between female sex hormones and histamine, it doesn’t prove that perimenopausal symptoms – as opposed to allergy symptoms – are related to histamine. The current expert consensus is that perimenopausal symptoms are not histamine-driven, says Huang.Regardless, the thinking behind the online trend is that if histamines do make these perimenopausal symptoms worse, then taking medications that block histamine receptors will in turn improve the symptoms, explains Voedisch.There areanecdotal reportsof women who, after being prescribed Allegra or Pepcid for hives or reflux, noticed improvements in their hot flashes.H1 and H2 antihistamines are also used as afirst-line treatmentfor a condition called mast cell activation syndrome, which is related to the body releasing excessive amounts ofhistamineand other inflammatory chemicals.This use may have inspired people to experiment with the same combination to address hormonal symptoms, theorizes Jessica Peters, a clinical psychologist and associate professor at Brown University, and member of the International Association of Premenstrual Disorders (IAPMD)clinical advisory board.Graphic with three lines of text that say, in bold, ‘Well Actually’, then ‘Read more on living a good life in a complex world,’ then a pinkish-lavender pill-shaped button with white letters that say ‘More from this section’Ultimately, “we do not have enough information” to know whether histamines can worsen perimenopausal symptoms, says Voedisch.There are very few studies on the subject. For example, a 1976papersuggests that how the body makes, stores, releases and breaks down histamine can fluctuate across the menstrual cycle and may be linked to estrogen. Limitedresearchon rodents suggests histamine can affect the parts of the brain involved in anxiety and stress, raising questions about whether it could influence mood-related symptoms. More recent research on links among menstrual cycle changes, symptom severity and the immune system has been mixed; somereport associationsandsome doesn’t.Confounding the situation further is the fact that “symptoms that can be associated with elevated histamine levels can mimic perimenopausal symptoms”, says Voedisch. These crossover symptoms include hot flashes, sleep disruptions and anxiety.Can antihistamines help with PMDD?Women have been trying to useantihistaminesto alleviate PMDD symptoms for about a year, says Jennifer Gordon, an associate professor and director of the Reproductive Mental Health Research Unit at the University of Regina, who is also on the IAPMD clinical advisory board.But in its May 2026position statement, IAPMD noted that “there is insufficient evidence to conclude that histamine tolerance, mast cell activation, or related immune mechanisms are a primary cause of [pre-menstrual disorders]”.That said, Gordon “wouldn’t be surprised” if histamine and immune system processes potentially play a role in PMDD symptoms for some individuals. Still, there’s a need for much more research on the topic, as well as on PMDD and hormone sensitivity more broadly.Antihistamines could be helpful for “at least a subset of people with PMDD”, says Peters, but scientific evidence is lacking.Critically, even if a potential treatment for PMDD works for one individual, it probably will not work for all, says Peters. The causes of PMDD are still being untangled, and there could be many mechanisms at play.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We don’t yet have a sense of what someone should expect in terms of how much it helps and how often,” says Peters. “I have heard from many patients who say they don’t get any benefit.”Are there any risks?When it comes to perimenopause, Voedisch doesn’t think trying the Allegra-Pepcid combination “is an unreasonable thing for people to do, especially if other things haven’t worked”.Anyone trying out a new medication should run it by their care provider to make sure there is no potential negative interaction with any other medications they use. If there’s no potential risk, then it’s probably safe enough for individuals to experiment with the antihistamine-Pepcid combination, says Gordon.Gordon also emphasizes that there are otherevidence-based treatmentsfor people seeking PMDD relief – more on this below.PMDD is ruining my life. What can I do?Read moreIt’s possible the combination leads to “some indirect benefit”, explains Huang. For example, antihistamines often make people feel drowsy. If you have deeper sleep after using antihistamines, perhaps hot flashes won’t wake you up during the night, and your mood could be better the next day, she says. Relatedly, one 2025papernotes that off-label use of sedative antihistamines is an option for managing some PMDD sleep disturbances.But antihistamines could actually worsen some menopausal symptoms, says Huang. For instance, drowsiness can make it more difficult to think clearly and be experienced as brain fog. Long-term use of Pepcid may also affect the absorption of vitamins and nutrients, she adds.What other treatments can help with perimenopause symptoms?Hormonetherapycan ease menopausal symptoms, but some don’t choose this route. This is down to preference or being in a medical group not advised to use hormonal therapies, such as individuals with a personal history of breast cancer, or of blood clot or stroke, says Voedisch.The Allegra-Pepcid combination hasappealed to peoplelooking for non-hormonal relief. But there are other non-hormonal options, says Voedisch. For example, the FDA-approved medicationsVeozahandLynkuettreathot flashes.Some medications aren’t approved for menopausal symptoms, but are used off-label. These include gabapentin and SSRIs (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors), which can be helpful for hot flashes, anxiety and mood. Clinical hypnosis can also reduce the severity and impact of perimenopausal symptoms, says Voedisch.Non-hormonal treatments, however, tend to be more expensive, says Huang, and insurance is less likely to cover them. While she doubts the effectiveness of the Allegra-Pepcid combination, she says it’s “understandable that people turn to things that they can get easily, quickly and less expensively”.“A lot of problems that come up in the menopausal field come from assuming all women are cut from the same cloth,” says Huang. “This is a field that continues to need to grow.”What treatments can help with PMDD symptoms?There are medical, therapeutic and lifestyle interventions for PMDD. TheIAPMDoffers free resources for understanding these options.SSRIs are one option, says Peters. These can work differently in a PMDD population than in other patient groups, she explains, often beating a placebo within 24 hours instead ofweeks. For some,it’s effectiveto only take these antidepressants during the luteal phase, which appeals to patients who don’t want to use SSRIs full-time because of potentialside-effects, like changes in weight or sexual desire, she explains.‘Why do I feel crappy?’: women are learning about their luteal phases - and Maha is weaponizing itRead morePatients have described SSRIs’ function as similar to taking an Advil, says Peters: “It usually helps with the intense irritability and reactivity that are some of the most common and impairing symptoms of PMDD.”Hormonal contraceptives, cognitive behavioral therapy andcertain diet changes, like limiting caffeine and alcohol, can also be helpful.With any PMDD treatment, Peters recommends tracking symptoms. This provides information about efficacy and can reveal patterns, such as when symptoms are most severe and if they change month to month.“If the scientific data isn’t there, something else will fill the void,” says Voedisch. “Women want and deserve to have answers.”Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyMenopauseMenstruationHealthWomen (Life and style)Women (Society)Health & wellbeingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A long hot summer of copy, paste on social media’: why everything is kinda chic now  | Fashion | The Guardian
description: The latest online craze reveals how quickly personal expression can be absorbed into a homogenised feed and exploited by brands
Author: Chloe Mac Donnell
Headline: The latest online craze reveals how quickly personal expression can be absorbed into a homogenised feed and exploited by brands
Content: Kinda chic … Amber Brookes Instagram.Photograph: Amber Brookes @amberbrookesdiary/Amber Brookes InstagramKinda chic … Amber Brookes Instagram.Photograph: Amber Brookes @amberbrookesdiary/Amber Brookes InstagramFashion Statement newsletterFashion‘A long hot summer of copy, paste on social media’: why everything is kinda chic nowThe latest craze on Instagram reveals how quickly personal expression can be absorbed into a homogenised feed and exploited by brandsChloe Mac DonnellFri 14 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 04.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor those looking for the defining social media trend of summer 2026, it’s time to call off the search party.A new phrase is dominating algorithms and entering the English lexicon.It goes roughly like this: a carousel of images or a video overlaid with a pale yellow font that reads: “Kinda chic to” followed by an image of a look or trend that the average user doesn’t consider traditionally chic.The images are usually a mirror selfie ora fancy cup of matcha– but the trends vary. This morning alone I have seen posts spanning everything from “kinda chic to repeat outfits” to“kinda chic to always have a trip booked”to “kinda chic to be overdressed” to “kinda chic to bake a quiche,” (to be fair it did look like a very nice quiche).Similar to 2024’s “brat” takeover and last summer’s“very demure, very mindful”craze, the phrase “kinda chic” has quickly become ubiquitous. But unlike its predecessors, the catalyst is harder to track down. Some point to plus-size influencerMariaBeginsas one of its earliest instigators due to using the format in April for a series of body positivity posts. “Kinda chic posting myself online despite the hate comments I receive,” reads one.Take a pic … Matcha chic.Photograph: Annabel Morris @belsbookcase/Belsbookcase InstagramAccording to Google Trends, searches for the term are up 5000% while on last check the hashtag has amassed over 60k posts on Instagram. On TikTok, posts which suggest it’s “kinda chic to do it alone and scared” in reference to solo backpacking trip have amassed hundreds of thousands of likes. The posts can be aspirational or relatable, and that’s the point: its mass appeal lies in the fact, that there is a post for everyone.It is often used as a humblebrag which, depending on the viewer’s circumstances, can be either inspiring or irritating. “Kinda chic to call the Upper East side home,” posts one user from their balcony overlooking the city. “Kinda chic to make all your big decisions in the bath” proclaims another post featuring a gorgeous outdoor tub setup. “Kinda chic to book the spontaneous trip” states another accompanied with a hotel room overlooking the Eiffel Tower.The Berlin-based fashion editor and influencer Brenda Weischerrefers to itas “template slop” pointing that due to its widespread use it is now “an unoriginal idea”.“I have never seen Instagram so homogenous,” agrees Bella Younger, a social media consultant who says we’re going to endure “a long hot summer of copy, paste on social media.”Lit chic … reading is cool.Photograph: Annabel Morris @belsbookcase/Belsbookcase InstagramDespite this, the trend prevails, particularly among the rich and famous. Drew Barrymore declared it “kinda chic to be in your 50s”, accompanied by a selfie taken in her car. Reese Witherspoon posed with Lauren Dern captioning it “kinda chic to cheer on other women” while Ashley Graham used an image of her on the Victoria’s Secret catwalk to describe it as “kinda chic to know cellulite never held you back”.Brands have been quick to hop on the bandwagon too. The retailer Boots posted it was “kinda chic to reapply your SPF” over an image of various SPF products it stocks. “Kinda chic to sell a foldable sock hanger by the wine”, posted Aldi while the airline Virgin Atlantic declared it “kinda chic to book a flight with no annual leave left.”Surely, at any moment Andy Burnham is going to post that it is “kinda chic to push for devolution”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFashion StatementStyle, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solvedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSo what is driving its rise? Just as core became a replacement for trend (think “cottagecore”, or“goblincore”, plus, who could forget the OGs – “normcore” and “dadcore”), the word chic has become all encompassing. The definition is now so diluted it can be used to describe anything. Perhaps, it is chic that is in the eye of the beholder.In fashion circles, it’s a word that is rarely used now – for precisely these reasons. Last year Vogue declared it dead. “RIP “Chic” – the word has finally lost all meaning”read the headline. In the 2017 drama Phantom Thread, Daniel Day-Lewis who plays a fictional British designer takes great offence to use of the word. “Chic! Whoever invented that ought to be spanked in public,” he shouts. “I don’t even know what that word means! What is that word? Fucking chic! They should be hung, drawn, and quartered.”And yet social media algorithms reward this type of repetitive content. “Instead of being creative, people are borrowing proven ‘hooks’ and formats that they know will perform,” explains Younger. “We are now all talking about how homogenous it is [social media] but it has become very difficult to get content that doesn’t fit strict parameters seen at all,” she adds.“I don’t know how this started but it’s annoying as heck. It’s chic to not be annoying as heck,” reads one comment in aReddit forumdedicated to talking about how infuriating the trend is.Younger suggests to get out of the cycle a month long Instagram ban should be implemented. “Then we can all come back with some original thoughts” she says. Kinda chic?To read the complete version of this newsletter – complete with this week’s trending topics in The Measure and your wardrobe dilemmas solved –subscribe to receive Fashion Statementin your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFashionFashion Statement newsletternewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Experience: I found my long-lost twin aged 49 | Family | The Guardian
description: The joy, disbelief and shock of discovering I had a brother the same age as me came with a million questions. How were we separated and why?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The joy, disbelief and shock of discovering I had a brother the same age as me came with a million questions. How were we separated and why?
Content: ‘As a child, I wasn’t curious about my adoption’: Chantal Doecke at Onkaparinga River in Adelaide.Photograph: Carrie Jones/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘As a child, I wasn’t curious about my adoption’: Chantal Doecke at Onkaparinga River in Adelaide.Photograph: Carrie Jones/The GuardianExperienceFamilyExperience: I found my long-lost twin aged 49The joy, disbelief and shock of discovering I had a brother the same age as me came with a million questions. How were we separated and why?Chantal DoeckeFri 14 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 12.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1975, my parents saw an advert in their local Australian newspaper. With the Vietnam war coming to an end, thousands of orphaned children were being evacuated. As part of the American-led Operation Babylift, the Australian government was looking for families who would adopt them. My parents decided to do it.I arrived in Adelaide in April in a shoebox. I was so tiny that my umbilical cord was still attached. My parents knew that the document they were given, with a January birthday and the name Le Thi Ha, couldn’t be mine. But with the chaos of the evacuation there was no way to find out more.Despite my parents divorcing when I was two, I had a happy childhood. I had an older sister, who’d been adopted at five, three brothers and parents who loved me. As a child, I wasn’t curious about my adoption. Even if I had been, Mum didn’t have any answers. She’d been told that my birth parents were probably dead, and if I’d stayed in Vietnam I’d have died, too. My teenage years were harder. I was the target of racial slurs and tried to hide my Asian heritage, becoming heavily tattooed and dying my hair.Having my daughter Jade in 1995, the first person I knew that I had a biological connection with, changed everything. I’d stare at her for hours, unable to comprehend that this baby was from my blood. I’d look in the mirror and think: “Jade looks like me, but who did I look like?” Those questions only grew as I had my sons and second daughter.double quotation markI could barely tear my eyes away from Glenn, constantly reaching out to touch him and remind myself he was realIn 2004, Mum and I took our first trip to Vietnam. I was surrounded by people who looked like me. I veered from joy at the connections I felt to depression at the endless unanswered questions. In 2015,a group of Operation Babylift evacuees from across the world met in Vietnam. We were offered the chance to take a DNA test, and I was excited at the possibility of finding biological relatives. Seeing 12 cousins listed on my results felt monumental. But they weren’t interested in our connection.In early 2024, I saw that a TV show was helping people solve family mysteries. Claire, the producer I spoke to, sent me a new DNA test, but the show then lost its funding. Months later in July, I remembered I hadn’t seen my test results. I asked my daughter Brooklyn to log in. She said, “Mum, you’ve got a brother.” There was the name “Glenn” and beside it “brother”. I began rocking back and forth, shouting, “Oh my God.” I couldn’t believe this was real. I searched on Facebook and saw a face so like mine, I was speechless. Frantically scrolling, I found a post about his birthday. Seeing both his age and the fact he’d been born in April, the month I arrived in Australia as a newborn, I froze. He wasn’t just my brother; he was my twin.The joy, disbelief and shock came with a million questions. How were we separated and why? How was it possible to be 49 and discover I had a twin who lived a 2.5-hour flight away in Brisbane? I messaged Claire, who said she could reach out to him. Waiting for news was torturous. I jumped every time the phone rang.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionExperience: we found a baby on the subway – now he’s our 26-year-old sonRead moreIn November, he finally called. We spoke for two and a half hours. I was the one to tell him we were twins, which he found as incredible as I did. Two months later, shaking with nerves, I went to meet him. Then I was in his arms, sobbing, and didn’t want to let him go. We’d shared a womb and were finally reunited. In those two days, I could barely tear my eyes away from Glenn, constantly reaching out to touch him and remind myself he was real. In the weeks that followed, we messaged and spoke often, but then our communication slowly dropped away. His wife reassured me that he was just trying to process it all.I’m angry that no one has taken responsibility for our separation from our parents. I don’t know what the future holds. I’ve learned that reunions don’t always lead to a neat happy ever after. But I’ve also discovered how strong and persistent I am. Last year, I gave a speech at the Department of Home Affairs for Refugee Week. It was cathartic to share my story. I want other adoptees to know they matter. We all deserve to be heard.As told to Kate GrahamDo you have an experience to share?
