title: Why is Drake barking like a dog? Six things you need to know about the rapper’s midlife pivot | Drake | The Guardian
description: There’s a lot to unpack as this proud son of Toronto closes in on 40 – from his gambling to his very public dates. Here goes!
Author: Elle Hunt
Headline: There’s a lot to unpack as this proud son of Toronto closes in on 40 – from his gambling to his very public dates. Here goes!
Content: Composite: Guardian Design; Simone Joyner/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design; Simone Joyner/Getty ImagesCelebrity crib sheetDrakeWhy is Drake barking like a dog? Six things you need to know about the rapper’s midlife pivotThere’s a lot to unpack as this proud son of Toronto closes in on 40 – from his gambling to his very public dates. Here goes!Elle HuntFri 14 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 11.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEven if you can only name a handful of rappers,Drakeis probably one of them. Not so many years ago, he was among the planet’s biggest celebrities, named in the same breath as Taylor Swift and Beyoncé and breaking chart records set by the Beatles. Many of his dozens of hit singles – Work, One Dance, Hotline Bling and God’s Plan – were ubiquitous, among the last truly crossover radio hits.Drake is still landing chart spots (if not critical acclaim), but now it’s his foray intothe “creator economy”that’s raising eyebrows –shilling for a crypto casino,fraternising with manosphereinfluencers and, just last weekend, live-streaming dates with OnlyFans models. So what’s this all about? Is Toronto’s once-golden boy having a midlife crisis – or is it a media-savvy pivot? Here’s how Drake got caught up in the “creator economy”.1. He’s live-streaming his ‘dates’View image in fullscreenWith Lily Phillips during the ‘20-v-1’ dating show.Photograph: YouTube/NELKOn Saturday, Drake appeared as the eligible bachelor on a speed-dating show on the live-streaming platform Kick, the online home to many controversial internet celebrities such asthe “looksmaxxer” Clavicular. Though the “20-v-1 challenge” is an established format (named for the women-to-men ratio), Drake is by far the biggest name to have ever taken part. This particular broadcast played out like a Bad Place Blind Dates, over three desultory hours. Twenty women, mostly performers on the adult platform OnlyFans, competed for Drake’s affections along with cash prizes, holidays and Hermès bags in bawdy challenges such as “Wife, Pipe, Bestie”. (You may know it as “Kiss, Marry, Kill”.) Among them was Lily Phillips, the Briton notorious for a 2024 stunt in which she attempted to have sex with 100 men in 24 hours. The chosen lucky lady was a cosplay creator and “goth baddie”named Pinkchyu, who requested, as her prize, that Drake buy her mother a house and also bark like a dog. He agreed to both.Complex reportedhe was “like a poodle”. Rest easy, Cilla Black: you were not cut out for this world.2. He’s partnered with a gambling companyView image in fullscreenThat ‘drone’ video.Photograph: YouTubeDrake’s participation came as part of a broader partnership with Australian crypto-gambling platform Stake, which backs Kick.According to the Financial Times, Drake was an early adopter of the platform, betting with bitcoin, and became a brand ambassador in 2022, in a deal reportedly worth $100m a year. Now the rapper drives traffic by live-streaming himself gambling, giving away money and performing social-media-friendly stunts. Last year,a video of Drake apparently beingbothered by a drone at his Sydney penthouse went viral before many users clocked that it was a staged ad. Last month,a video was“clipped” from a stream, showing Drake saying “Oh my God” 70 times after a big win. Drake’s golden deal with the gambling company has drawn scrutiny: an investigation byBloomberg Businessweekfound that the rapper saw four times as much success playing Stake’s slot machines as the average person (according to Bloomberg’s methodology, which is disputed by Stake). He’salso been accusedin a class action lawsuit of using the platform to inflate streams of his songs, although a federaljudge has paused the lawsuit, stating the plaintiffs must first complete arbitration.3. Finally, he has some new friendsView image in fullscreenWith Adin Ross on YouTube.Photograph: YouTube/Adin LiveDrake is still making music, and even swamping the charts, having put outthreealbums back in May– but his priorities have been shifting for a while. In 2023, he rapped: “My youngins richer than you rappers and they all stream.” Lately he’s been running with the new-gen influencers Adin Ross and Kai Cenat, twentysomethings with millions of followers. Drake has even been trying to ingratiate himself with thenextnew gen, delivering an(prerecorded) address and free merchto Cenat’s Streamer University bootcamp last month.4. … but is he on his worst behaviour?View image in fullscreenHeadlining the Wireless festival in London, in 2025.Photograph: Simone Joyner/Getty ImagesDrake has always been corny, cringe and perhaps too comfortable with self-deprecation. Now, some say his flirtations with content are bringing out the worst of those tendencies, shifting his public persona and potentially tarnishing his legacy. In GQ,Josiah Gogarty noted thatDrake’s fraternising with streamers has him increasingly skirting the online manosphere, noting that the speed-dating “meat market” was also hosted by Kyle Forgeard, from theTrump-supportingNelk Boysgang of YouTubers. Drake himself can seem to provoke people online, Gogarty argued, pointing to his “whiny, almost incel-coded” posts, such as an Instagram list of “reasons why I’m single … I care too deeply.” Having previously penned a “joyful women’s-empowerment anthem” (per the New Yorker!) in Nice For What, and declared himself aCertified Lover Boy, Drake’s latest hit is called Janice, STFU.By way of apology, in June, he threw some “Janice-only parties”, with government ID a requirement of entry. As Gogarty wondered: “Is Drake a better rage baiter than rapper now?”5. He will soon turn 40View image in fullscreenKendrick Lamar performs at halftime during last year’s Super Bowl.Photograph: Gregory Shamus/Getty ImagesSome have drawn a link between Drake’s recent activities – participating in online “challenges”, hanging out with twentysomethings, gambling, gaming and degrading himself in front of young women – with his looming milestone birthday. Vulture declared of the live-dating stream:“This is Drake’s midlife crisis.”The past few years have not been kind to October’s Very Own (setting aside its co-founder’s vast fame and fortune, of course). The last time Drake was central to the cultural conversation was early 2024,and his highly public feud with Kendrick Lamar. Lamar was not only widely deemed the victor with his record-breaking, Grammy-winning diss track Not Like Us – but took his victory lap at the Super Bowl,leading seemingly theentire stadium in a rap that accuses Drake of being a paedophile. To be very clear, Drakehas denied this.6. Grimly, he might be ahead of the gameView image in fullscreenAt an NBA match between the Toronto Raptors and the Golden State Warriors in Toronto last year.Photograph: Cole Burston/Getty ImagesThose of us who had time for the old Drake might be bewildered by his evolution, if not already long checked out. But he’s likely being driven by the changing cultural tides. The monoculture by which he became a household nameis mostly gone, receding in memory with millennials’ youth, while younger audiences don’t draw the same distinctions between streamers and celebrities, or social-media stunts and “authentic” entertainment. Just as you may know someone valiantly experimenting with the front-facing camera on Instagram, traditional stars not yet close to retirement are feeling the pressure to adapt. (See Timothée Chalamet’s#sponcon for the prediction market Kalshi.) Drake’s pivot to influencer mode is arguably one of his most savvy, investing his celebrity in growing economies and platforms seeking mainstream respectability, and reinventing himself with younger generations. Rather than going through a midlife crisis, Drake may be once again ahead of the curve.Explore more on these topicsDrakeCelebrity crib sheetRapCelebrityKendrick LamarGamblingInternetfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Creating mounds in your garden can take it to another level | Gardening advice | The Guardian
description: From creating informal boundaries to providing a place for kids to play, these tiny mountains of topsoil offer a world of possibilities
Author: Alice Vincent
Headline: From creating informal boundaries to providing a place for kids to play, these tiny mountains of topsoil offer a world of possibilities
Content: A pleasing garden mound designed by Nic Howard.Photograph: GAP Photos/John GloverView image in fullscreenA pleasing garden mound designed by Nic Howard.Photograph: GAP Photos/John GloverGardening adviceCreating mounds in your garden can take it to another levelFrom creating informal boundaries to providing a place for kids to play, these tiny mountains of topsoil offer a world of possibilitiesAlice VincentFri 14 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 08.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSo, the works have begun. The scorched scrubland that was the garden is now a large pile of earth and – excitingly – a big old hole for the rainwater harvesting tank that I hope is going to help us navigate these increasingly dry summers and wet winters.More on that once it’s in. For now, though, the matter of soil. So much of it! Soil everywhere! I am determined to send as little of it off in a skip as possible. And what do you do with mounds of earth? You make mounds.Among the notable mounds I have admired (and there have been many) are those made of crushed substrate in the walled garden at Knepp in West Sussex. When the rewilding estate’s custodian was showing me around, she said head gardener Charlie Harpur and his team demolished an outbuilding and had it deposited in its entirety on the croquet lawn.double quotation markI want the surprise and intrigue that make the best gardens, and that requires a level of partitionWhat could have been carted off in a skip became a mesmerising dry garden planting base. We visited on the hottest day last summer and it was a golden, shimmering mass of swaying colour and umbellifers, its undulating landscape providing habitats for all sorts of insect life.I have neither an outbuilding to demolish nor a croquet lawn to deposit it on, but I will be making mounds in our (far more modest) garden. It is a classic long and skinny urban plot, and I’m depriving my children of the biggest lawn possible because we live near a park and, well, the garden isn’t just for them. Instead, I want to create the kind of surprise and intrigue that makes the best gardens, and that requires a level of partition.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI used to be intimidated by roses. But they are not as high-maintenance as you thinkRead moreI’m thinking of some mounds at the far end of the plot: a couple around where the compost pile will be, and then another one or two towards the end, where I’m planning wilder, looser planting where the kids can run amok (I’m not a total monster).If you’re not unearthing a load of soil,hugelkulturis the ancient practice of building mounds from decaying wood, mulch, rotting branches and twigs, followed by topsoil and plants. Start by removing any turf, which you can then layer upside down on top of the wooden base before mulching – it compacts the materials and speeds up the decay necessary to boost soil nutrition.Once you’ve got your mound in place, plant it as you would a flowerbed, thinking about repetition, structure and a variety of heights, colours and textures.Mounds can be good for creating privacy without the infrastructure of a more formal boundary: trees and shrubs can be planted alongside smaller perennials and ground cover, extending your planting space up as well as out.Explore more on these topicsGardening adviceGardensfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘What’s happened to us? Where did we get lost?’ Zimbabwe reckons with the reality of violence against women | Global development | The Guardian
description: The deaths of a Bulawayo mother and her daughters spark calls for an urgent action on gender-based violence
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The deaths of a Bulawayo mother and her daughters spark calls for an urgent action on gender-based violence
Content: Mourners at the funeral in Bulawayo of Zandile Khumalo Tshuma and her daughters, Nala and Natalie, on 4 August.Photograph: AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenMourners at the funeral in Bulawayo of Zandile Khumalo Tshuma and her daughters, Nala and Natalie, on 4 August.Photograph: AFP/GettyGlobal development‘What’s happened to us? Where did we get lost?’ Zimbabwe reckons with the reality of violence against womenThe deaths of a Bulawayo mother and her daughters spark calls for an urgent action on gender-based violenceSupported byAbout this contentTendai Marima in BulawayoFri 14 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe three white coffins were draped in white lace and topped with small sprays of flowers. The mourners who filled a Bulawayo church last week to pay their respects to Zandile Tshuma and her daughters, Natalie, 15, and Nala, five, had not engaged in the usual tradition of first viewing the dead at their home: the bodies of this family had travelled all the way from England to reach their final resting place at Luveve cemetery on the edge of Zimbabwe’s second city, in Matabeleland.While the deaths attracted few news reports in the UK, in Zimbabwe and South Africa, the tragic case hasreignited concern over the region’s high rates of femicide. Many commentators on TV and social media expressed shock that a well-educated woman with a successful career abroad seemed as vulnerable to familial violence as a poorer woman in a southern African township.Tshuma’s elderly parents were at the gravesides. The father, in a blue suit and clutching a wooden cane, and her mother, in the black-and-white uniform of her church’s elders, sat in silence. Never Mpofu, 44, a neighbour, was taught at primary school by Tshuma’s mother. He says he was saddened by the violent way the family had been killed.View image in fullscreenZandile Tshuma, with her daughters Nala, 5, and Natalie, 15. Their bodies were found in their home in Great Denham, Bedfordshire, in July.Photograph: Bedfordshire police/PATshuma, a 42-year-old financial data analyst, Natalie, an avid computer science student and budding sportswoman, and Nala, described as a bubbly little girl, were all found dead at their home in Britain on 6 July.Bedfordshire police have said that “work is now underway” to have a British-Zimbabwean man returned to the UK from SouthAfricain connection with the murders. “Zandile never really said if there were problems,” Mpofu says. “Whenever she came home, she was happy to see her family, but now we can see the monsters are out here.”At the funeral service, Theophilus Khumalo, an uncle, says the family is deeply hurt by the killings and he hopes they will find justice.“We will allow the law to take its course. We will not be drawn into anger or bitterness; we will not allow this tragedy to define us. Instead, we choose to honour their memory with grace, unity and unwavering faith in God’s justice,” he adds.Each day, an estimated137 women and girls around the world are killedby someone they know. Femicide – defined by the United Nations as an “intentional killing with a gender-related motivation” – is driven by discrimination and inequality.View image in fullscreenMourners attend the funeral of Zandile Tshuma and her daughters Natalie and Nala in Bulawayo.Photograph: Zinyange Auntony/AFP/GettyZimbabwe does not keep specific data on femicides, but according to governmentstatistics, nearly 40% of Zimbabwean women aged 15 to 49 have experienced physical violence and an estimated 12% to 25% of them have been sexually assaulted.Musasa, a local organisation set up to help survivors of gender-based violence (GBV), reported more than 30,000 GBV incidents in 2024, while the Zimbabwean police recorded nearly 19,000 cases. Much of the abuse happens inside the home. During Covid lockdowns, GBVrose by 60%.Judith Ncube, minister of state for provincial affairs, says she is deeply concerned as southern Matabeleland, which borders Bulawayo, has the highest rates of intimate partner violence in the country.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |MonthlySign up toHer StageHear directly from incredible women from around the world on the issues that matter most to them – from the climate crisis to the arts to sportEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenMourners wearing memorial ribbons in Bulawayo.Photograph: Zinyange Auntony/AFP/Getty“In the region of Matabeleland, it’s as if we take the silver medal. What has gone wrong, what’s happened to us, where did we get lost? In marriage, not everything is smooth, but it shouldn’t lead to death and a home of fear,” she says.Ncube has called for an urgent debate about domestic violence and suggests launching home-care programmes for community elders to contact families to discuss problems.“Something has gone wrong in our social fabric: we no longer have aunts and uncles who are go-betweens in marriages,” she says. “We need to capacitate caregivers to be professional and sit down with our young people and talk. We have pastors that can help, too.”Samkeliso Tshuma, founder of the Zimbabwean advocacy group The Girls Table, says there is a critical need to educate people about domestic violence.“It’s heartbreaking,” she says. “We need to use social media to raise awareness of what intimate partner violence does to a community, to a society and the families that we are building.“We need people to renew their minds, because as long we have people who still think that there is a reason for a man to abuse a woman, then we have a long way to go,” she says.Bulawayo’s courts are only too familiar with femicide cases. In July, a43-year-old church elderwas charged with murdering his wife with an axe then attacking the couple’s children with a metal rod in the city’s suburb of Nkulumane.View image in fullscreenPallbearers uncover a coffin during the funeral of Zandile Khumalo and her daughters in Bulawayo.Photograph: Zinyange Auntony/AFP/Getty ImagesA study in Zimbabwe carried out by the Swedish International Development Agency (SIDA) and the United Nations put the direct and indirect costs of gender-based violence at up to $2bn, taking into account the cost of injury, trauma and death, multiplied by the loss of productivity and of young girls dropping out of school due to violence.Miranda Tabifor, the representative in Zimbabwe of the UN Population Fund (UNFPA), calls on the government to invest more in addressing domestic violence because of the far-reaching costs to the state.The cost to the government to “address issues of psychosocial support [and] the social scars that continue to haunt the survivors of gender-based violence” Tabifor puts at more than $1bn, but she warns that the government will continue to lose up to 3.8% of its $57bn GDP if the violence continues to be unaddressed.“We should all unite,” she says. “Every woman, every girl in Zimbabwe has to live a life free from violence, not just because it is their right but because it is the right thing to do.”Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentZimbabweFemicideAfricaDomestic violencefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We feared we’d all be drowned’: the Indian floods that killed more than 100 and left thousands homeless | Global development | The Guardian
description: More than 2,600 villages have been flooded in Assam this year, in a climate disaster made worse by uncontrolled deforestation and mining in the region
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: More than 2,600 villages have been flooded in Assam this year, in a climate disaster made worse by uncontrolled deforestation and mining in the region
Content: People in Jorhat, Assam, wade through floodwaters with animals and belongings salvaged after flooding in late July.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople in Jorhat, Assam, wade through floodwaters with animals and belongings salvaged after flooding in late July.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesGlobal development‘We feared we’d all be drowned’: the Indian floods that killed more than 100 and left thousands homelessMore than 2,600 villages have been flooded in Assam this year, in a climate disaster made worse by uncontrolled deforestation and mining in the regionSupported byAbout this contentMaitreyee Boruah in Guwahati, AssamFri 14 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was a normal July morning in the Indian state of Assam. After finishing her chores and eating breakfast, Gitali Phukon, a resident of the town of Gaurisagar, left her home to buy groceries. After two days of rainfall that had made the unpaved roads muddy and slippery, the sun was shining.But less than an hour later, she returned home to a nightmare: the Mitong River, which runs through the town, was overflowing and water was gushing through the streets.“I could not believe my eyes. The water came with great force. It quickly rose to waist level,” she says. She had seen the surrounding paddy fields flood in the past, but never before on this scale.As evening approached, flood waters entered most of the homes in her neighbourhood. The rain resumed, and darkness descended. Standing on her veranda with a candlestick in her hand, Phukon watched as her neighbours moved to their rooftops or the elevated highway to escape the rising water.View image in fullscreenGitali Phukon in flood water outside her house on 28 July, a week after the village was flooded.Photograph: Gitali Phukon/The Migration StoryThey waved at each other, signalling they had survived. No one slept that night. “We feared we would all be drowned,” she says. Along with mosquito bites, they had endured a foul smell emanating from the flood waters.The next morning, the situation worsened. Most villages in Assam depend on wells. “People were thirsty; they were crying for water. But there was no water to drink as the groundwater was contaminated,” says Phukon.“Thankfully, I had some stored water, and I shared that with my neighbours,” says Phukon. People ate biscuits and puffed rice for at least three days until the water started to recede.People in the Sivasagar district of Assam, as well the neighbouring districts of Charaideo and Jorhat on the southern bank of the mighty Brahmaputra River, reported similar experiences.The Sivasagar village of Nepalikhuti, about 60 miles west of Gaurisagar, lies in ruins. As far as the eye can see, there is thick mud and silt. Drowned cars, dead cows and the broken walls of a house demonstrate the scale of the calamity. There is no sign of any cattle, goats or other livestock, the main means of support for the residents.At least 10 people from the village of 3,000 people have died, and many remain missing. Villagers say they have seen several unidentified dead bodies floating on the Dikhou River.Assam, in the far northeastern corner of India, is one of the most flood-prone regions in the country. About 40% of its land is vulnerable to inundation from the Brahmaputra and Barak rivers and other smaller rivers, and it sees at least two or three major floods annually.According toofficial figures, about 2,690 villages in 25 districts have been flooded this year, affecting more than 1 million people. As of 11 August, 101 people have lost their lives. The death toll is likely to rise, officials fear.In 2025, the death toll due to floods and landslides was 36. The year before, when all 35 districts of the state were affected by floods, at least 110 people died.View image in fullscreenThick mud and flood water, dotted with drowned cars or dead cows, cover much of Assam’s Sivasagar district.Photograph: Anadolu/GettyAccording to Partha Jyoti Das, a specialist in water and climate hazards with the environmental organisation Aaranyak, the current disaster was inevitable. The climate crisis has led to heavier rainfall, and changes to the landscape made flooding more likely.“It’s a much-abused landscape, turning into a burial ground,” he says. Had it been just flood waters, the damage would have been less, but the rain brought with it debris, mud, silt and soil from the hills of Nagaland.“These areas have seen mining and quarrying, both legal and illegal, for several years. From coal, sand or boulder mining, everything happens in these places. The whole landscape has been changed by large-scale deforestation, encroachment and excavation,” he says.By 11 August, flood waters had receded in several villages, leaving behind heavy layers of mud and silt. However, low-lying areas of Sivasagar, Jorhat and Charaideo districts are still flooded, including the well-known Jokaichuk paddy field, a vast stretch of agricultural land shaped like ajokai, or bamboo fishing tool, near Gaurisagar.View image in fullscreenJorhat, in Assam, after heavy monsoon rains on 22 July.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty“The floods have ruined 95% of the farmland across Sivasagar,” says Himadrijyoti Dutta, who works with farmers in the district through his non-profit organisation, Krishak Nyas, and has been visiting different villages to provide relief materials.“The flood waters have washed away all the hard work and financial investments of the farmers. They have all been left poorer and desperate.”Kalyan Das, a geography professor at Guwahati’s Cotton University, says the latest disaster will trigger a wave of migration. “Assam is already witnessing a serious crisis of out-migration of people from every block. There are many factors – primarily land degradation – making farming unsustainable,” he says.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEmployment-driven migration from Assam rose from 16.3% in 1991 to 24.4% by 2011, according to a2022 study. In rural areas, floods and soil erosion were the primary causes, the study said. “The latest floods have destroyed homes and agricultural fields. The villagers will be forced to migrate in search of livelihood opportunities,” Das says.Eight years ago, Mintu Hazarika, 30, left Kosumari village in Sivasagar district for the IT hub of Bengaluru (formerly known as Bangalore). He earns 25,000 rupees (£195) a month by working double shifts as a security guard in Bengaluru’s Marathahalli suburb and sends half his earnings home.“My father is a farmer, so is my elder brother,” says Hazarika. “They tend paddy fields, but it is not financially viable. So they also work as daily wage earners in nearby urban areas to supplement the household income.On 22 July, Hazarika received a call from his father. He was told that the floods had destroyed their family’s two-hectare paddy field. “I don’t know how my family is going to survive. My elder brother is planning to come to Bengaluru to find work. There are already so many men from Sivasagar and other parts of Assam working in Bengaluru,” he says.View image in fullscreenRelief supplies being distributed from a truck on 4 August 4 in Sivasagar district.Photograph: Ritesh Shukla/Getty ImagesBitupan Raidongia, district president of Sivasagar for the Bharatiya Janata party, the ruling party in Assam, says the authorities are providing support for affected communities. “Our government is doing its best to rescue marooned people. We are also reaching out to affected families by providing them with food items, clothes and other essentials.”Sivasagar’s district commissioner, Mridul Yadav, adds that the local administration was making a coordinated effort to address the flood situation. “Various departments are working together on rescue, relief distribution, and damage assessment. Health camps, essential medicines, drinking water, livestock fodder and relief kits are being provided. Several relief camps remain operational to support affected families and restore essential services,” he adds.But the authorities’ response has been criticised as too little, too late. In avideo that went viral, the Assam-based singer Nilotpal Bora said thousands more people would have died were it not for the intervention of local charities and individuals.“You people [the government] had a delayed response in reaching out to the affected people. If common people had not distributed relief, at least 3,000 people from flooded areas would have died because of hunger and thirst,” he said in response to a comment from Assam’s chief minister, Himanta Biswa Sarma, that“the situation was under control”, and the public should not raise money to help flood victims.Meanwhile, local groups and people are doing what they can to help. About 40 bikers from One Northeast Motorcycle Club are travelling to affected areas to distribute food, clothing, sanitary items, candles, matchboxes and other essentials. “It’s a heartbreaking sight,” says the club’s founder, Chow Sureng Rajkonwar.View image in fullscreenA girl and her grandfather travel on a raft through flood waters in Sivasagar district.Photograph: Biju Boro/AFP/Getty Images“Hundreds of people across villages have become homeless. Their homes were destroyed and flattened to the ground. Those that remain are filled withpolokh[alluvial silt or sediment left behind by flood waters]. All their belongings were destroyed or washed away with the water. It will take months to rebuild those houses,” he says, adding that people are living in tents made of plastic sheets and tarpaulins on roads or higher ground near their villages.Phukon was one of the luckier ones. Although the water level was more than 1.5 metres (5ft) high in her courtyard, it did not enter her house, which is built on higher ground.For almost a week now, she has been providing relief aid to flood victims after getting distress calls from family, friends and acquaintances. “I decided to leave my home and reach out to people who need food, clothing, and other essentials. Everyone I know has been affected by floods.”Maitreyee Boruah is a contributor tothe Migration Story, where this story was first publishedExplore more on these topicsGlobal developmentIndiaSouth and central AsiaClimate crisisExtreme weatherRiversMigration and developmentfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tell us: have you struggled to find work later in your career? | Unemployment | The Guardian
description: We’re interested in hearing from people who have found themselves unexpectedly out of work in midlife and have struggled to get another job despite years of professional experience
Author: Guardian community team
Headline: We’re interested in hearing from people who have found themselves unexpectedly out of work in midlife and have struggled to get another job despite years of professional experience
Content: The number of people aged 50 to 64 receiving out-of-work benefits has reached 2.15 million, according to recent analysis.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe number of people aged 50 to 64 receiving out-of-work benefits has reached 2.15 million, according to recent analysis.Photograph: Linda Nylind/The GuardianUnemploymentTell us: have you struggled to find work later in your career?We’re interested in hearing from people who have found themselves unexpectedly out of work in midlife and have struggled to get another job despite years of professional experienceGuardian community teamFri 14 Aug 2026 04.22 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 05.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor many people in their 50s and 60s, losing a job can be the start of a long and unexpected struggle to get back into work. Despite years – or even decades – of professional experience, some say they areapplying for hundreds of roles without success, while others have had to take lower-paid work or claim benefits to make ends meet.The number of people aged 50 to 64 receiving out-of-work benefits has reached 2.15 million,according to recent analysis by the Centre for Social Justice.
