Two days earlier he told Palestinians the army would remove the settlers, but soldiers retreated from confrontation with the group.Instead they forced one of the Palestinian families out of their home, saying they needed it as a base for the unsuccessful military operation against the settlers.View image in fullscreenIsraeli settlers re-established Ganim on 13 August 2026, starting with two dozen prefabricated homes.Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPAOne of the homes is owned by a US citizen, and US ambassador Mike Huckabee described the Israelis besieging it as terrorists, and said he had requested the Israeli police and army act to remove them.Huckabee, who supports the settlement movement’s vision of establishing a “Greater Israel” on land seized from Palestinians and neighbouring countries, said the militants in Qusra represent a “very small minority” of the settler movement.State and settler violence has driven a surge in displacement of Palestinian communities in the past three years.Since October 2023, Israel has forcibly displaced 64 entire Palestinian communities and parts of 15 additional communities, affecting nearly 5,000 people, according to data from Israeli rights group B’tselem.On Friday Israeli gunmen opened fire at a group of unarmed Israeli and Palestinian activists as they attempted to peacefully reclaim Palestinian land seized by settlers in Beit Sahour, just outside Jerusalem. A Catholic bishop and journalists covering the event were also targeted by the attackers.Israeli settlers had put a large Star of David and Israeli flags on the roof an old, dilapidated house, owned by Palestinians, just 500 metres from a Palestinian family home.View image in fullscreenThousands of residential units under construction in the Giv’at Ze’ev settlement in the West Bank, near Jerusalem and Ramallah, 6 August 2026.Photograph: Debbie Hill/UPI/ShutterstockMia Biran, from the groupCombatants for Peace, said: “They are all the time threatened by the settlers. We were about a hundred activists, our goal was to clean the area, plant some trees, to show presence and to stand with the residents who are very scared. We were on private Palestinian land.”A few minutes after they started work, the group heard gunfire from the settler outpost and were forced to take cover. One gunman moved close to the group, opened fire in the air and aimed the gun at activists, in an attack videoed by the group.He was later joined by three or four others. “We screamed in Hebrew ‘do not fire’ and then they understood there are Israelis among the crowd,” Biran said.“I called the police to tell them we are threatened by settlers, the activists who were at the roof saw there was a military Jeep all the time in the area who did nothing.”After they withdrew from the area, settlers visited the nearby Palestinian home and threatened to burn it down, she added. Settlers regularly launch arson attacks on Palestinian homes. One such attack in 2015 killed a baby and his parents, orphaning their only surviving son.Quique Kierszenbaum and Sufian Taha contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsWest BankIsraelPalestineMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Benjamin Netanyahu describes UK as ‘first Islamic republic to get a nuclear weapon’ | Benjamin Netanyahu | The Guardian
description: Israeli PM criticised by political rival for attacking an international ally and overseeing ‘horrific diplomatic failure’
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Israeli PM criticised by political rival for attacking an international ally and overseeing ‘horrific diplomatic failure’
Content: The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, is hoping to be reelected when his country goes to the polls later this year.Photograph: Ronen Zvulun/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenThe Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, is hoping to be reelected when his country goes to the polls later this year.Photograph: Ronen Zvulun/AFP/GettyBenjamin NetanyahuBenjamin Netanyahu describes UK as ‘first Islamic republic to get a nuclear weapon’Israeli PM criticised by political rival for attacking an international ally and overseeing ‘horrific diplomatic failure’Emma Graham-Harrisonin Jerusalem andRowena MasonFri 14 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTFirst published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 07.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Israeli prime minister,Benjamin Netanyahu, called the UK “the Islamic republic of Britain” in a podcast interview, where he also described the country as the “first Islamic republic to get a nuclear weapon”.His comments, made during an interview for Israel’s army radio, played into a common far-right Islamophobic trope about Britain’s small Muslim population.Netanyahu praised positive coverage of Israel by the journalist Randolph Churchill, the son of former prime minister Winston Churchill, over half a century ago, then said: “Go find that in today’s Britain, in what is called the Islamic republic of Britain.”Rather than challenge Netanyahu’s comments, the host questioned whether he is unfairly singling out the UK, asking: “Isn’t all of Europe is like that?”Netanyahu replies by doubling down. “Yes, but you know someone said the first Islamic republic with nuclear weapons will be the Islamic republic of Britain.”Pakistan, officially the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, has had a nuclear arsenal since the 1990s.Relations between the UK and Israel have been increasingly strained in recent months, especially since Andy Burnham took over in No 10. Shortly before becoming prime minister, heapologised for Labour’s initial response to Israel’s military action in Gaza, saying the party “didn’t get it right” and needed to “do better” under his leadership, signalling a significant shift in the UK’s approach to the Middle East.In July, he said he would “do more to put pressure on the Israeli government”, including through further sanctions on individuals and entities, as well as a potential ban on the trade of goods with illegal settlements.View image in fullscreenThe US vice-president JD Vance suggested the UK could become an ‘Islamist country’ in 2024.Photograph: Alex Wong/GettyThe US vice-president, JD Vance, maderemarkssimilar to Netanyahu’s commentsduring the 2024 presidential campaign, saying the UK could become the first “truly Islamist country that will get a nuclear weapon”.London’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, has also been a frequent target of racialised attacks from rightwing leaders abroad,includingDonald Trump, seeking to gain political advantage from Islamophobic lies.Israeli troops force families from homes amid settler terror campaign in West BankRead moreMuslim leaders in the UK have said that hate crimes targeting their community arehitting new levelsamid a rise in far-right rhetoric and growing support for anti-immigrant political parties.Avi Dabush, who is running for the Knesset with Israel’s opposition Democrats party, attacked Netanyahu for mocking a critical ally at a time when Israel faces unprecedented global isolation. “That’s what happens when there’s a horrific diplomatic failure, and an inability to rally countries in the world in favour of our interests,” he said in a social media post.Leading themost far-right government in Israel’s history, Netanyahu has alienated traditional allies while aligning with far-right figures, including some with a history of antisemitism.The British Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office said: “These comments are completely unacceptable and we have raised them with the Israeli government.”The Prime Minister’s Office did not respond to requests for comment on whether Netanyahu’s statement represented the official position of the Israeli government.Get in touchContact us about this storyThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreExplore more on these topicsBenjamin NetanyahuIsraelThe far rightIslamophobiaAndy BurnhamSadiq KhanJD VancenewsShareReuse this content

title: Jason Arday, professor at centre of Cambridge plagiarism row, found dead  | Jason Arday | The Guardian
description: Academic was pronounced dead at his home in south London after police called to address after 3pm on Friday
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Academic was pronounced dead at his home in south London after police called to address after 3pm on Friday
Content: Jason Arday was appointed as professor of sociology of education at Cambridge in 2023, and was the university’s youngest black professor.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJason Arday was appointed as professor of sociology of education at Cambridge in 2023, and was the university’s youngest black professor.Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The GuardianJason ArdayJason Arday, professor at centre of Cambridge plagiarism row, found deadAcademic was pronounced dead at his home in south London after police called to address after 3pm on FridayRichard AdamsandVikram DoddFri 14 Aug 2026 18.10 EDTFirst published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 15.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJason Arday, the academic whoresigned last week as a professor at the University of Cambridge, has been found dead at his home in south London.The Metropolitan police said officers were called to Arday’s address by theLondonambulance service after 3pm on Friday.A spokesperson for the Met said: “A 41-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene. His next of kin have been informed and are being supported by officers.“At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious. The case is being investigated by officers from the Met’s central south command unit. A file will be prepared for the coroner.”The body was believed to be that of Arday. At this stage, police are understood not to believe anyone else was involved in the death.London ambulance service was the first emergency service at the scene. The person discovered inside the home was found unresponsive.Arday’s family said in a statement: “Jason was subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for more than three years since he accepted the role of professor at Cambridge University by those who would leave no stone unturned in their quest to undermine him.“The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone.“We are in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son.“We won’t comment further at this point beyond asking the press to leave us alone now, and to stop the campaign of harassment which has been waged against Jason and his family for too long.”The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, said: “I’m devastated for the family and friends ofJason Arday. He faced an unacceptable public hounding and campaign of abuse. I know many Londoners will be angry and upset this evening.“Jason Arday was the victim of a pernicious public shaming that other people in his position simply wouldn’t have faced. His death was a tragedy, but once again it should be a wake-up call for all of us.”Arday was appointed professor of sociology of education at Cambridge in 2023, and was the university’s youngest-ever black professor. But he resigned last week afteraccusations of plagiarismandinconsistencies in statements about his career and achievements.In a statement announcing his resignation, Arday said: “It is with profound sadness that I write to resign, with immediate effect, from my position at theUniversity of Cambridgeand Jesus College.“When I accepted the extraordinary honour of becoming professor of sociology at Cambridge, it was, without question, the greatest professional privilege of my life.”Arday said he had been driven to resign because the “relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love”.Prof Deborah Prentice, Cambridge’s vice-chancellor, said in a statement: “We are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news. Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday’s family and friends at this incredibly difficult time.”Durham University, where Arday worked between 2019 and 2021, said: “We are shocked and terribly sad to learn of the death of Jason Arday.“He is remembered at Durham as a kind and warm person who actively sought to promote opportunities for PhD students. We want to express our deepest sympathy to his family who are in our thoughts.”Arday’s rise to a prestigious professorial chair was remarkable. Arday said he had been nonverbal until the age of 11, requiring extensive speech and language therapy, as well as being illiterate until 18.That life story contributed to him being made a torchbearer for the 2012 London Olympics flame.After leaving school, Arday went on to further study before completing a doctorate in education at Liverpool John Moores University in 2015. That was followed by a string of academic posts culminating in a professorship at the University of Glasgow and a professorial chair at Cambridge.Arday was initially accused of plagiarising another academic’s work for his PhD thesis. But he denied the accusations, and an investigation by Liverpool John Moores University earlier this year upheld its decision to award him a PhD.But other elements of his life story were increasingly questioned, including claims of prodigious money-raising for charity and feats of long-distance running.He was also challenged about whether he was nonverbal as a child.However those claims meant little in the world of academia. After initially defending Arday as the victim of a smear campaign, as further questions arose about his academic career, the university began to temper its support.On 5 August Cambridge announced it would hold an internal inquiry after it said it received “new information” about his academic qualifications and honorary appointments, as well as what it described as “a number of ongoing complaints regarding academic misconduct”. Jesus College, of which he was a member, said it would also hold an inquiry.But while Cambridge said Arday would remain in post and continue to receive support, Arday immediately announced his resignation.At the end of last week Glasgow University said it would also investigate Arday’s academic credentials.The controversy has stirred considerable anger within Cambridge’s academic community, both between Arday’s supporters and those who said the university had erred in appointing him to such a prestigious position.After resisting calls from senior staff for an independent inquiry, earlier this week Prentice backed down, saying she recognised the “anger and anxiety around this damaging and difficult case”.She described it as an aberration that should not be used to cast aspersions on the abilities of its staff of colour.Arday’s memoir, entitled Great and Unfortunate Things, was published this week in the US by an imprint of Simon & Schuster, with UK publication scheduled for later this month. Simon & Schuster has been contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsJason ArdayLondonEnglandUniversity of CambridgeUniversitiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham announces £65m for drought-hit farmers after Labour pressure | Farming | The Guardian
description: PM steps up climate response with measures including better water access and support for building farm reservoirs
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: PM steps up climate response with measures including better water access and support for building farm reservoirs
Content: Sweetcorn on a farm near London. The south-east of England is experiencing an exceptionally hot run of weather.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreenSweetcorn on a farm near London. The south-east of England is experiencing an exceptionally hot run of weather.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAFarmingBurnham announces £65m for drought-hit farmers after Labour pressurePM steps up climate response with measures including better water access and support for building farm reservoirsAletha AduPolitical correspondentFri 14 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 18.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFarmers must not carry the risks of the climate crisis alone,Andy Burnhamhas said, as he announced £65m of funding to help them manage the devastating drought.The prime minister is stepping up his response to the immediate climate crisis after facing a backlash from his own MPs and Labour’s grassrootsfor not addressing the climate crisisdespite wildfires tearing through Britain and a drought affecting food producers. Labour MPs argued Burnham had taken too long to talk about the climate crisis and had not made it a priority.Some farmers have had to harvest their crops early, while others are seeinglow-quality produce and low yields. Most of the £65m will go to the sustainable farming incentive (SFI), which pays farmers in England to support nature. Officials have said this extra £50m will bring the total SFI budget to £290m, with extra money prioritised for areas of greatest need during the drought.Burnhamchaired a Cobra meeting on extreme heat, wildfires and drought this week. Downing Street is seeking to establish a cross-government response to the drought, bringing together action on farming, water and infrastructure, including more flexibility for food producers. Farmers who are paid to look after nature on parts of their land and are usually barred from cutting or grazing it until later in the year are now able to do so where grass is scarce, without losing payments.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and the West Midlands mayor, Richard Parker (third from right), met fire service staff in Stourbridge on FridayPhotograph: Peter Byrne/AFP/Getty ImagesFarmers will also get £15m in support for building on-farm reservoirs to provide supplies during future dry summers.However, campaigners have warned this £15m is reallocated money from existing funds and will only fund a “fraction” of reservoirs needed.They will get improved access to water through simpler arrangements around how much they can take from the environment and changes to the speed at which licences are given, making it easier for farmers to use water where it is most needed.Burnham is to visit a farm in the south-west of England on Saturday and is expected to say:“I am meeting with farmers here in the south-west who brought in the earliest harvest of their working lives and watched the yield come in well down on what it should be. Lower income, higher costs and no rain in the forecast. I understand the worry that comes with that.“The ability to grow our own food is national security and I will treat it that way. So we are acting now: more money into farm support, help to get reservoirs built and easier access to water when it is scarce.“This is the third drought in five years. Farmers are at the sharp end of a changing climate and they should not be carrying that risk alone.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘Let’s see what he can do’: will Burnham bring Barnsley voters back to Labour?Read moreAs MPs urged Burnham to speed up the rate at which new reservoirs are built, given five have “exceptionally low” levels at present, officials announced their support of nine new reservoirs being developed.Speaking after visiting the scene ofa fire in Stourbridge in the West Midlandson Friday, Burnham said: “We have to face up to the changing climate. I think we need a different debate about that. There’s no point denying where we are. We need to face up to it. We need more clean energy. We need to see that transition accelerate. Those are all of the issues that are right now in discussion.“But the Cobra meeting earlier this week, I think, has enabled us to mobilise resources today to individuals, to communities, and to our fire and rescue services, and we’re very, very grateful to them.”Gavin Lane, the president of the Country Land and Business Association, said: “This is a welcome and pragmatic movebut little more than a temporary fix.“The announcement that government will make it easier to build on-farm reservoirs is a positive step, but the £15m made available will fund a fraction of the reservoirs we need. This needs to become a sustained programme, with planning and abstraction lined up in support.“The vast bulk of the cost of building on-farm reservoirs will still fall on farmers, who are already facing record costs as well as absorbing new tax burdens.”Explore more on these topicsFarmingDroughtClimate crisisAndy BurnhamLabourWaternewsShareReuse this content

title: Emergency alert warning of wildfire risk sent to phones in England and Wales  | Wildfires | The Guardian
description: People urged not to light barbecues, campfires or anything else that could spark fire during period of extreme heat
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: People urged not to light barbecues, campfires or anything else that could spark fire during period of extreme heat
Content: A UK government alert seen in Welsh on an iPhone warning of the risk of wildfires on 14 August 2026 in Cardiff, Wales.Photograph: Matthew Horwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA UK government alert seen in Welsh on an iPhone warning of the risk of wildfires on 14 August 2026 in Cardiff, Wales.Photograph: Matthew Horwood/Getty ImagesWildfiresEmergency alert warning of wildfire risk sent to phones in England and WalesPeople urged not to light barbecues, campfires or anything else that could spark fire during period of extreme heatAletha AduPolitical correspondentFri 14 Aug 2026 15.19 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 17.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMillions of people acrossEnglandand Wales received an emergency alert to their phones on Friday as the government warned against activities that could start fires.The deputy prime minister, Louise Haigh, said it was the most extensive use to date of the emergency alert system, with phones beaming a siren noise about 7pm, with the warning: “There is a serious risk of wildfires nationally.”People have been urged not to light barbecues, campfires, fireworks or anything else that could spark a blaze while the wildfire risk remains high. They have also been urged to call 999 immediately if they spot a fire.‘It’s due to climate’: the people of Stourbridge on the town’s wildfiresRead moreAndy Burnham spent time in Stourbridge in the West Midlands on Friday afterhomes were destroyed and residents were left injuredby a series of fires. The prime minister warned that Britain “is a tinderbox right now” with the public set for a “difficult weekend”.He announced atemporary national ban on the sale of disposable barbecuesto be enforced immediately. The ban will remain in place as long as the risk of wildfires remains high.The military was called in to assist stretched emergency services in southWales. About 100 personnel were deployed with about 100 more due to arrive on Friday evening, distributing water and providing logistical support.It has been a record year of wildfires in England and Wales: the number so far this year has passed the 1,017 recorded in 2025. Fire services have declared 11 major incidents in a 24-hour period starting on Thursday.Haigh said: “In response to the continued risk proposed by wildfires, the government has taken the decision to issue an emergency alert to England and Wales.“This is the most extensive use of the UK’s emergency alert system in response to an active incident, and reflects the seriousness with which the government is acting to safeguard people and property.“During this period of extreme heat, we are asking people to take simple steps to limit the risk of further fires.“By following the safety guidance, everyone can play their part in protecting local communities and supporting our frontline services who are working around the clock to keep people safe.“The government will continue to provide every assistance to communities being impacted by these fires, including the deployment of 100 additional military personnel in major incident areas.”Explore more on these topicsWildfiresExtreme heatEnglandWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham criticised for EV and North Sea approach amid climate crisis | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: Cut in electric vehicle sales targets could add millions of tonnes of CO<sub>2</sub> to emissions in UK, say green campaigners
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: Cut in electric vehicle sales targets could add millions of tonnes of CO2 to emissions in UK, say green campaigners
Content: The UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, speaks to staff during a visit to the Met Office weather and climate service in Exeter on Friday.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, speaks to staff during a visit to the Met Office weather and climate service in Exeter on Friday.Photograph: Finnbarr Webster/AFP/Getty ImagesClimate crisisBurnham criticised for EV and North Sea approach amid climate crisisCut in electric vehicle sales targets could add millions of tonnes of CO2to emissions in UK, say green campaignersJasper Jolly,Rowena MasonandMatthew TaylorFri 14 Aug 2026 14.51 EDTFirst published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 09.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has been criticised for moving to cut electric vehicle (EV) sales targets and accept North Sea drilling at a time of devastating wildfires caused by the climate emergency.The prime minister for the first time acknowledged on Friday that the climate crisis was behind hundreds of wildfires that have ripped across the parts of the UK.The scale of the disaster has prompted the government to bring in the military, ban the sale of disposable barbecuesand activate the national alert system to issue safety advice to people across England and Wales in areas at risk on Friday night.However, Burnham was also accused of failing to take the push for net zero seriously enough, as the government took steps towards watering down EV targets on the same day.View image in fullscreenSeveral homes in Stourbridge in the West Midlands were destroyed as a result of wildfires this week.Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/Getty ImagesThe government on Friday launched a consultation on cutting the target for new EVs to as little as 50% of all new cars in 2030, down from 80% under existing rules, in proposals that could add millions of tonnes a year to the UK’s carbon dioxide emissions.The consultation will include several options, including leaving the headline target unchanged, or cutting it to 70%, 60% or 50%.In a video from the West Midlands, where homes have been destroyed and dozens of people injured, Burnham appeared to acknowledge the seriousness of the climate crisis. “We cannot accept this as the new normal,” he said. “This isn’t happening in isolation.“Much of England and Wales is in drought and we are in another period of extreme heat. Farmers are watching crops fail and firefighters have faced hundreds of wildfires in a matter of weeks. This is what climate change looks like, here and now.”View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham and the West Midlands mayor, Richard Parker, right, with the West Midlands chief fire officer, Simon Tuhill, during a visit to Stourbridge on Friday.Photograph: Peter Byrne/ReutersBut in a broadcast interview, he alsodefended his “pragmatic” approach on extracting oil and gasfrom the North Sea. His government will shortly have to decide whether to allow new drilling at the Rosebank and Jackdaw fields, with a consultation on the former closing on Monday.Environmental groups have said permitting extraction at the fields should be inconceivable after five heatwaves this summer, with Greenpeace saying it was a “Rubicon that he must not cross”.The decision to consider weakening one of the UK’s key climate policies on EVs was announced hours after the country recorded itshottest day of the year so far– and the fifth hottest ever – after five heatwaves that scientists have said are almost certainly worsened by global heating caused by carbon emissions.Fire services said 19homes were destroyed, 200 hectares (500 acres) burnt and dozens of people sent to hospital in the West Midlands, the UK’s traditional automotive centre, in grassfires that may have been worsened by drought.‘It’s due to climate’: the people of Stourbridge on the town’s wildfiresRead moreSpeaking from Stourbridge, Burnham said it was necessary to bring in a temporary ban on disposable barbecues from Friday, asking retailers to withdraw them from sale.“Please think about the situation we are in,” he said. “Britain is a tinderbox right now. Setting a fire in any outdoor setting is a risk to people’s homes and other people’s lives.”The prime minister also revealed he planned to commission firefighting planes to combat the spread of wildfires and appointed a new fire minister, as he made the case that country had to “face up” to the “changing climate”.Environmental groups largely welcomed Burnham’s words on the climateafter 50 organisations earlier criticised him in a letterfor failing to mention it following a Cobra meeting on the heatwave earlier this week.Hannah Martin, the co-director of Green New Deal Rising which coordinated Friday’s letter, said: “Finally Andy Burnham has said the words ‘climate change’ as prime minister and acknowledged the cause of the wildfires, drought and extreme heat that is raging across the country. Now he needs to put policies in place to deal with the scale of the crisis.“That means saying no to new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea … it also means ramping up new investment in renewable energy and climate jobs, doubling down on insulating homes and improving public transport, and making sure our homes, hospitals, schools and emergency services are properly equipped to deal with extreme weather caused by climate change.”Extreme heat: why our cities can’t cope | OpinionSam Keely from the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU) thinktank also urged Burnham not to row back on the government’s commitment for the rollout of electric vehicles.Keely said: “At the same time as the prime minister was speaking, the government launched itsconsultationon watering down the zero emissions vehicle mandate.“Getting more EVs on the road is one of the single most important policies for cutting UK emissions and will also insulate more British motorists from paying more at the petrol pump as a result of volatile oil prices, saving billions of pounds on the British driving bill.”Electric car sales have soared by 29% in the UK this year, but the automotive industry has said the sales targets, known as the zero emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate, are putting too much pressure on manufacturers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThey say the mandate forces them to sell electric cars at discounts and have threatened job losses or even UK factory closures if the rules do not change.The government said it needed the targets to “remain pro-business and grounded in the real world”.Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, said: “It’s right we keep targets under review to ensure they’re practical and back British industry. The end goal hasn’t changed – but we need to take business with us on the journey.”The changes arestrongly opposed by climate campaignersand by the electric car charging industry, which has plans to spend billions of pounds to install charge points across the country.View image in fullscreenThe electric car charging industry has plans to spend billions of pounds installing charge points across the UK.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThe switch to EVs is expected to be the single biggest contributor to cutting UK carbon pollution in the next decade, according to the government’sClimate Change Committee.Under the existing rules, carmakers need to sell an increasing proportion of pure electric cars every year or face fines. The targets tighten from 33% this year to 80% in 2030. The sale of new petrol and diesel cars is then to be banned from 2035.Ami McCarthy, the Greenpeace UK head of politics, said weakening the rules would be “a wrong turn for drivers, energy security, our climate and the economy”.Milk, wine, salad: how your food will be affected by the summer of heatRead moreShe added: “Both the Iran war and this summer’s extreme weather have shown once again why we’re better off cutting our dependence on fossil fuels.“This mandate is one of the most powerful policies we have to bring down planet-heating emissions, which is the only way to stop more deadly heatwaves in future.“Burnham can’t fulfil his promise of tackling the cost of living crisis and reindustrialising Britain without the green economy. So why put on the brakes now?”It would be the second time that Labour has watered down the targets after itlast year added loopholescalled “flexibilities” to the original rules. The loopholes allowed more plug-in hybrid EVs, which combine a polluting petrol engine with a smaller battery, to count towards the mandate, as well as permitting carmakers to catch up with more battery car sales in later years.Extending the flexibilities to 2034 will also be considered in the consultation, which will run until 23 October. Van sales targets are also likely to be changed.The most extreme change proposed, cutting the headline rate to 50%, could reduce electric car sales by as much as 5.8m, according to analysis by the ECIU. It added that the changes would make the 2035 ban much harder to achieve, with some carmakersalready lobbying for it to be delayed.Colin Walker, the ECIU head of transport, said: “Proposing to water down the UK’s biggest climate policy the day after temperatures hit 38C, and a summer of heat and drought that risks the UK having its worst ever harvest, may seem strange to the increasing number of people concerned by images of homes on fire, and the security and affordability of the food we eat.”Mike Hawes, the chief executive of the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders lobby group, said: “The automotive industry is fully committed to a zero-emission future, investing billions in new technologies, products and incentives.“However, with the ZEV mandate conceived under vastly different conditions, this welcome review is a timely opportunity to adjust the transition so it works for all.”Explore more on these topicsClimate crisisAndy BurnhamElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsAutomotive industryAutomotive emissionsGreenhouse gas emissionsEthical and green livingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Madonna will not be playing Glastonbury in 2027, Emily Eavis says | Glastonbury festival | The Guardian
description: Festival organiser says she has booked next year’s headliners but would not say if Taylor Swift is among them
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Festival organiser says she has booked next year’s headliners but would not say if Taylor Swift is among them
Content: Rumours of a Glastonbury set began when Madonna told Graham Norton she had something ‘big’ planned in the UK next year.Photograph: NDZ/Star Max/GC ImagesView image in fullscreenRumours of a Glastonbury set began when Madonna told Graham Norton she had something ‘big’ planned in the UK next year.Photograph: NDZ/Star Max/GC ImagesGlastonbury festivalMadonna will not be playing Glastonbury in 2027, Emily Eavis saysFestival organiser says she has booked next year’s headliners but would not say if Taylor Swift is among themNadeem BadshahFri 14 Aug 2026 14.38 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 16.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMadonna will not be performing at next year’s Glastonbury, the festival’s organiser, Emily Eavis, has said.The singer, who has the most top 10 singles in UK chart history of any female artist, has never featured at Britain’s biggest music festival.Eavis said Glastonbury had booked all its headliners for June 2027. Asked about the lineup and speculation that the Queen of Pop would make her debut at the event in Somerset, Eavis told BBC Radio 4’s PM programme: “No, it’s definitely not Madonna, I’ll tell you that.”She added: “But we have got three [other] headliners and we’re very excited about it – it’s all coming together really well.”When asked about the possibility of a performance fromTaylor Swift, Eavis laughed and said she did not want to discuss the lineup any further.Speculation about Madonna, 67, appearing at Glastonbury began in June when the singer suggested to theBBC talkshow host Graham Nortonthat she was planning “something bigger” in the UK next summer.Eavis said: “Pretty much 95% of the stories [about Glastonbury] you read are not true, and rumours are pretty much always wrong.“But the good news is that we’ve got our headliners and we’re cracking on, and we just can’t wait to get back.”Last year’sGlastonbury festivalwas headlined by the 1975, Neil Young and Olivia Rodrigo, with Rod Stewart in the legend slot.On Friday, it was confirmed that Madonna’s collaboration with Kylie Minogue, Love Sensation, debuted at No 8 on the singles chart, becoming Madonna’s highest-charting UK song in 17 years.Love Sensation is the second single from Madonna’s latest album, Confessions II, and a remixed version features the Australian singer.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMadonna’s last highest-charting single was Celebration in 2009. Her latest track has become her 65th UK top 10 single, spanning four decades since the 1980s.Only two artists have achieved more UK Top 10 singles: Elvis Presley with 76 and Cliff Richard with 68.Last month, Madonna performedduring the half-time show at the Fifa men’s World Cup final in New York between Spain and Argentina.Explore more on these topicsGlastonbury festivalMadonnaFestivalsMusic festivalsTaylor SwiftnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump downplays concerns about sailors onboard USS Abraham Lincoln amid record deployment | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: President said nine months at sea ‘not nearly long enough’ even as families call for attention to mental health crisis
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: President said nine months at sea ‘not nearly long enough’ even as families call for attention to mental health crisis
Content: The USS Abraham Lincoln has been supporting the US war against Iran.Photograph: Abaca/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe USS Abraham Lincoln has been supporting the US war against Iran.Photograph: Abaca/ShutterstockDonald TrumpTrump downplays concerns about sailors onboard USS Abraham Lincoln amid record deploymentPresident said nine months at sea ‘not nearly long enough’ even as families call for attention to mental health crisisMarina DunbarandJoseph GedeonFri 14 Aug 2026 18.12 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has downplayed concerns about US sailors enduring a record-setting deployment of nearly nine months onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln on Friday, saying the deployment was “not nearly long enough” as concerns mount over mental health and supply issues onboard the aircraft carrier.The US president made the comments during a brief exchange with reporters before flying toNew Yorkfor an event highlighting falling violent crime rates across the US.“That ship is moving right now, or very shortly, and it’s being replaced with another very similar ship,” Trump said when asked about the lengthy deployment. When asked by reporters whether family members were worried about the situation, the president claimed: “No, they’re not.”The Lincoln has been supporting the US war against Iran, and several Democratic lawmakers are pressing the Pentagon for accountability over conditions onboard the carrier. The defense secretary,Pete Hegseth, on Thursday said those conditions had been “completely misrepresented”.Trump orders Pentagon to redesign US aircraft carrier to use steam catapults to launch jetsRead moreMilitary families and US Congress members have called attention to the intensifying mental health crisis for those onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, as its 5,000 sailors and marines endure a record-breaking deployment at sea tied to the war with Iran.The scrutiny comes as the navy hasreimposed a blockadeon Iranian ports in the crucial strait of Hormuz, even as hostilities between the US and Iran have calmed in recent weeks. The Trump administration has offered no clarity on how it intends to wind down the war, while Hegseth has suggested the US military can maintain the blockage of Iranian ports “indefinitely”.Another aircraft carrier, the USS George Washington, left port in Da Nang, Vietnam, last week and is expected to replace the Lincoln, one of two aircraft carriers currently deployed in the Middle East.Two leading specialist military papers, theNavy TimesandStars and Stripes, reported that there have been multiple attempts by sailors tojump overboardas poor conditions and mental stresses on the Lincoln reach a breaking point in its ninth month at sea.One sailor succeeded in early August, a US official confirmed. “The sailor was quickly recovered by an air wing search and rescue helicopter, treated by Abraham Lincoln’s medical department, and transferred off ship for follow-on care.”Worried families expressed their concerns about loved ones onboard the Lincoln at an emotional town hall meeting with navy leaders in San Diego last week, Stars and Stripes reported. One spouse among the 200 or so family members said that her husband had texted her that day saying “he hopes he doesn’t wake up tomorrow”.The US navy said it has “not observed an increase in suicidal ideations or attempts aboard the ship”, but declined to provide data, citing operational security and patient privacy concerns.The Lincoln is “operating in a highly contested environment where traditional supply hubs in the Middle East were disrupted by combat actions”, the US official said, adding that navy leaders had “prioritized mission-critical supplies: first food, then hygiene items, then mail”.“Current reports from the ship confirm continuous access to clean water, functional [air conditioning], and healthy meal options,” the official claimed.In astatementreleased on Friday, Hung Cao, the acting secretary of the navy, similarly downplayed the reports, saying that “sailors and marines are expected to dig deep” and accused the media of “trying to paint our warriors as victims”.The statement acknowledged that a “small number” of mental health cases were “treated with no loss of life”, and added that “there is no question our young men and women have been pushed to their limits”.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpUS militaryPete HegsethUS politicsTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Devastating’: bulldozers plough through Big Bend national park as Trump’s border work pushes ahead | Texas | The Guardian
description: Heavy machinery seen operating in famous Santa Elena Canyon amid outcry over new wall infrastructure in beloved Texas park
Author: Roque Planas
Headline: Heavy machinery seen operating in famous Santa Elena Canyon amid outcry over new wall infrastructure in beloved Texas park
Content: Tensions have run high since the Trump administration announced plans to erect new border security infrastructure.Photograph: Hannah GentilesView image in fullscreenTensions have run high since the Trump administration announced plans to erect new border security infrastructure.Photograph: Hannah GentilesTexas‘Devastating’: bulldozers plough through Big Bend national park as Trump’s border work pushes aheadHeavy machinery seen operating in famous Santa Elena Canyon amid outcry over new wall infrastructure in beloved Texas parkRoque PlanasFri 14 Aug 2026 15.27 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 16.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBulldozers have begun plowing up ground at the mouth of Big Bend national park’s famed Santa Elena Canyon as part of the Trump administration’s multibillion-dollar“smart wall” expansionon the US-Mexico border, according to new footage taken by activists who have been monitoring the site.Tensions have run high since theTrump administrationannounced plans to erect new border security infrastructure in the roughly 500-mile Big Bend region of south-west Texas, which includes the Lone Star State’s largest and most-visited national park.Since last week, activists have shared video footage that appeared to show heavy machinery laying the groundwork for newborder infrastructure that US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) did not announce and initially denied was happening. By Thursday, photographer Natalie Newmancaptured video footageof bulldozers plowing earth at the mouth of the Santa Elena Canyon, a frequently visited stretch of the Rio Grande flanked by 1,500ft cliffs.“It’s just devastating,” said Laiken Jordahl, a public lands advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity. “They’re bulldozing a brand new road through the most beloved stretch of the park.”Bulldozer in Big Bend National ParkBig Bend national park is a vast, 800,000-acre (325,000-hectare) expanse of Chihuahuan desert punctuated by the Chisos mountain range and bordered by the Rio Grande River. Local businesses, river guides and political leaders from both parties have decried the administration’s plans to mar the wilderness in the name of border security – not least because the region sees so few unlawful crossings.Immigration authoritiesmade between 100 and 125 arrests annuallyin 2023 and 2024 within the park’s boundaries, according to the park’s former superintendent, Bob Krumenaker, who now leads the advocacy groupKeep Big Bend Wild. Those numbers almost certainly dropped last year, as unlawful crossings plunged across the US-Mexico border after Trump retook office and began a broad immigration crackdown in January 2025.View image in fullscreenA person protesting against the building of a wall at the Big Bend national park.Photograph: Hannah GentilesBut CBP has looked to the park as a site for new security installations ever since the Republican-dominated Congress threw a whopping $46.5bn for border wall expansion into the “big, beautiful” spending bill that Trump signed into law on 4 July last year.Over the following months, the Trump administration’s plans for Big Bend constantly shifted. CBP first signaled in February that it planned to erect a 30ft steel bollard wall across an area that is naturally obstructed by steep cliffs. Facing a sharp backlash from park users and locals, CBP walked those plans back, eventuallypublishing a more limited planof about 200 miles of new patrol roads and four sections of non-contiguous vehicle barriers measuring about 6ft tall and totaling 17 miles. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS)waived dozensof federal environmental and cultural protection laws to speed construction along.Opponents first began filming bulldozers clearing dirt and plowing into trees and brush last week, marking what they described as the beginning of construction of a new road and probably one of the four vehicle barriers that CBP has contracted to build. Big Bend national park’s press office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Big Bend National Park border wall constructionAt first, CBP publicly denied that the bulldozers had anything to do with its construction plans, issuing a statement last week that instead said the agency was regrading roads damaged by heavy rains. John Mennell, a CBP spokesperson, later backtracked, tellingSF Gatethe bulldozers were turning up ground to assess the soil for construction. This week, Rodney Scott, the CBP commissioner, said more barriers and roads were needed to keep the park “free from fear of cartel activity”. Scott said the bulldozers were doing prep work for planned roads and vehicle barriers,but that construction had not started.“What people are seeing right now is survey and design work – NOT construction of a wall through the park,” Scott said. “We are working to preserve the landscape and protect the access visitors and local businesses depend on.”But opponents of the Big Bend border wall expansion say the bulldozers are clearly breaking new ground.“They are obscuring what they are doing,” said Krumenaker, the park’s former superintendent. “They refuse to tell people what the complete plan is.”View image in fullscreenRally outside Santa Elena Canyon on 12 August 2026 in Big Bend national park, Texas.Photograph: Hannah GentilesThe construction activity has continued to draw broad condemnation from local politicians of both parties. Democrats in Congress have repeatedly lambasted plans to degrade the wilderness of Big Bend in the name of border security, citing the low number of unlawful crossings and widespread public opposition.But despite the unpopularity of the border barrier expansion through the state’s public land crown jewel, the most prominent Texas Republicans have largely kept their mouths shut. Governor Greg Abbott’s press secretary, Andrew Mahaleris, said in March that rugged regions such as Big Bend were “great opportunities to deploy technology to aid in securing the border”, but has shied away from commenting on CBP’s more controversial construction plans. Ken Paxton, the state attorney general, who is currently running for a US Senate seat, hasalso kept silent.John Cornyn, an outgoing US senator, however,penned a letterto Markwayne Mullin, the US homeland security secretary, last week asking him to halt construction in order to spend more time hearing from locals and community leaders.Southwest Valley Contractors of New Mexicosecured a $1.7bn contractin May to construct border security infrastructure in the area that includes the park.View image in fullscreenRally outside Santa Elena Canyon on 12 August 2026 in Big Bend national park, Texas.Photograph: Hannah GentilesBilly Miller, a river guide with the Friends of the Ruidosa Church, and the Center for Biological Diversity are currently suing the DHS, the parent agency of CBP, contending that waiving dozens of federal laws to expedite construction violated due process and other constitutional rights. The DHS had agreed in June to provide at least 30 days’ notice before “commencement of any ground disturbing activities in Big Bend Ranch State Park or Big Bend National Park”.“They’ve shown time and time again that we have absolutely no reason to trust them,” Jordahl said. He remains concerned that CBP’s plans will not stop at vehicle barriers.“They issued this contract back when they were still planning to build a wall,” Jordahl said. “They have the money they need to build a whole border wall through the national park.”This article was co-published withPublic Domain, an investigative newsroom covering public lands, theinteriordepartment and wildlife.Explore more on these topicsTexasTrump administrationUS immigrationNational parksUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: US Forest Service chief reportedly pressed staff for more support for wildfire near his ranch | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Michael Boren requested more aircraft for 7-acre Cabin Creek fire, some of which were diverted from other fires
Author: Anna Betts
Headline: Michael Boren requested more aircraft for 7-acre Cabin Creek fire, some of which were diverted from other fires
Content: Michael Boren during a confirmation hearing on Capitol Hill on 3 June 2025 in Washington DC.Photograph: Alex Wong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMichael Boren during a confirmation hearing on Capitol Hill on 3 June 2025 in Washington DC.Photograph: Alex Wong/Getty ImagesTrump administrationUS Forest Service chief reportedly pressed staff for more support for wildfire near his ranchMichael Boren requested more aircraft for 7-acre Cabin Creek fire, some of which were diverted from other firesAnna BettsFri 14 Aug 2026 15.01 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 16.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Boren, the US undersecretary of agriculture for natural resources and environment who oversees the US Forest Service, reportedly pressed agency staff last month to deploy more aircraft to a 7-acre (2.8-hectare) fire that was burning near his Idaho ranch, according to a Washington Postreporton Friday.TheCabin Creek firein Idaho began on about 12 July as a result of anunattended campfire, and spread across several acres in Idaho’sSawtooth national forest. By 15 July, the forest service said that the fire was100% contained.In the Post report, a forest service official who spoke on the condition of anonymity, told the outlet that Boren, whom the Post reports owns a 480-acre ranch in the Sawtooth national recreation area, contacted forest service officials at the regional and national levels multiple times while the fire was burning, questioning why more aircraft were not being used to fight the blaze.Six current and former forest service officials told the newspaper that the response was greater than is typical for a fire of its size that posed no significant threat to life or property.View image in fullscreenThe Cabin Creek fire in Idaho.Photograph: US forest service - Sawtooth national forestThe Post said it also reviewed communications sent during the response to the fire, which it said corroborated that Boren personally contactedforest service staff about the fire. The Post also conducted an analysis of flight paths, which it said revealed that there were about nine aircraft, including helicopters, air tankers and tactical planes, responding to the blaze on 12 July.According to the analysis and two agency officials who spoke to the newspaper, at least some aircraft were diverted from efforts to contain other fires inIdaho.A USDA spokesperson issued a statement on Friday, saying: “Mike Boren is expected to have regular contact with the agencies he oversees. The fact that a senior government official would be monitoring and communicating with other government officials about an event he oversees is a non-story. Under Secretary Boren did report a fire that was near property he owns, just as one would hope any citizen in an area under threats from wildfires would do. However, at no point did he pressure leadership or order more resources to fight this or any other fire.”Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationWildfiresIdahoUS wildfiresUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: US firms that kept DEI policies despite ‘go woke, go broke’ threats thrived  | DEI policies | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Companies that kept policies did just as well financially, even after Trump’s executive order, as those that didn’t
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: Exclusive: Companies that kept policies did just as well financially, even after Trump’s executive order, as those that didn’t
Content: ‘In the days after the executive orders were signed, companies that kept their DEI policies actually performed better on the stock market than those that didn’t.’Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘In the days after the executive orders were signed, companies that kept their DEI policies actually performed better on the stock market than those that didn’t.’Composite: The Guardian/Getty ImagesDEI policiesUS firms that kept DEI policies despite ‘go woke, go broke’ threats thrivedExclusive: Companies that kept policies did just as well financially, even after Trump’s executive order, as those that didn’tGaya GuptaFri 14 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 14.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleConservative backlash was supposed to put an end to the diversity, inclusion and equity (DEI) movement as companies were warned “go woke, go broke”.In January 2025,Donald Trumpdelivered a death knell, ending DEI within the federal government withexecutive ordersand threatening to target companies that still supported it. Companies including Google, Goldman Sachs, McDonald’s and Walmart that had embraced DEI years earlier fell into line and announced an end to their policies.Butnew researchpublished on Friday and shared exclusively with the Guardian found that companies that resisted the pressure and kept their DEI practices, including Costco, Apple and Delta Air Lines, performed just as well as their competitors who pulled back.For the research, Jacob Grumbach, an associate professor at at the University of California at Berkeley’s Goldman School of Public Policy, analyzed how S&P 500 companies fared after Trump’s January executive order. He used what economists define as “abnormal returns” – the difference between how a stock was expected to perform versus how it actually performed – to isolate the impact of a company’s DEI decision.What he found was the firms that kept theirDEI policiesor voted down anti-DEI shareholder resolutions did just as well financially, even after Trump’s executive order, as firms that didn’t. In the days after the executive orders were signed, companies that kept their DEI policies actually performed better on the stock market than those that didn’t.Chart of companies’ stock performance after Trump’s anti-DEI executive orderWhether or not DEI benefits a company’s bottom line can depend on its consumers. Grumbach noted companies that publicly stood firm on their DEI policies might have known they could weather a political storm. Apple, for example, may have known it could maintain its DEI efforts in a way that Tractor Supply, another prominent company that pulled back its policies, could not.The“go woke, go broke” movementfound its power in 2023, when a series of conservative backlashes against companies gained momentum. Bud Light sales dropped following a conservative boycott after the beer company featured the transgender influencer Dylan Mulvaney. Target became an embodiment of its name after fury erupted over its pride month merchandise.Ron DeSantis, the Florida governor, embarked on a prolonged fight with Disney after the company vocally opposed the state’s “don’t say gay” bill. “Cracker Barrel has fallen,” a conservative group wrote after the restaurant chain celebrated pride month on social media.Then, also in 2023, the US supreme court ruled that race-conscious admissions policies in higher education wereunconstitutional, opening the floodgates for legal challenges against DEI policies in other places, including the workplace.“That really created a lot of fear and panic in corporate America and is what led to a lot of the pullbacks around DEI,” said David Glasgow, executive director of the Meltzer Center for Diversity, Inclusion and Belonging at New York University’s law school. “When Trump came into office for the second time, that just poured fuel on an already raging fire.”After Trump’s executive orders, companies had to weigh the risks. Many quietly scrapped the DEI promises they had made after the murder of George Floyd and the racial reckoning it inspired. Some ended up facing a reverse backlash: the Twin Cities Pride paradedroppedTarget, which is based in Minneapolis, as a sponsor after the company withdrew some of its DEI policies.But the reality of this pullback was probably different from what was seen in the headlines, Glasgow said. Of the many companies he spoke to, most “made adjustments to their diversity principles on account of legal and regulatory environments”.“Often what’s going on is something more in the messy middle, where they’re sticking with some things, deleting others and then reframing or rebranding some,” Glasgow said.While there was “no perfect way” to measure whether a firm was pulling back its DEI policies, Grumbach kept track of company policies by analyzing news coverage, pulling anti-DEI shareholder proposals and keeping track of the proposals’ votes, and using data from an activist group calledDEI Watch, which maintains a tracker of companies.“No matter how we measure DEI in companies, we find the same answer,” he said: holding on to DEI promises ultimately had no impact on financial performance.Grumbach said the implications go beyond DEI and illustrates how organizations fare after resisting authoritarian policies.“What happens when you don’t comply with that executive branch pressure in a moment of great fear in these civil society organizations?” Grumbach said. “This shows that large US corporations really do have leeway and the ability to sort of do noncompliance to executive branch pressure and end up fine.”Explore more on these topicsDEI policiesTrump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: BBC seeks to subpoena Trump children and son-in-law over defamation lawsuit | BBC | The Guardian
description: Network wants to serve Jared Kushner, Ivanka Trump and Donald Trump Jr after president sues over January 6 documentary
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: Network wants to serve Jared Kushner, Ivanka Trump and Donald Trump Jr after president sues over January 6 documentary
Content: From left, Jared Kushner, Ivanka Trump and Donald Trump Jr at the inauguration of Donald Trump in Washington DC on 20 January 2025.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/EPAView image in fullscreenFrom left, Jared Kushner, Ivanka Trump and Donald Trump Jr at the inauguration of Donald Trump in Washington DC on 20 January 2025.Photograph: Chip Somodevilla/EPABBCBBC seeks to subpoena Trump children and son-in-law over defamation lawsuitNetwork wants to serve Jared Kushner, Ivanka Trump and Donald Trump Jr after president sues over January 6 documentaryGaya GuptaFri 14 Aug 2026 17.05 EDTFirst published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 17.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe BBC is trying to subpoena Donald Trump’s children as it builds its defense against the president’s defamation lawsuit centered on a documentary on the January 6 insurrection.In a motion filed on Friday, the BBC sought authorization to serve Trump’s two eldest children,Donald Trump Jrand Ivanka Trump, and son-in-law Jared Kushner, with subpoenas for testimony and their records on the events of 6 January 2021.TheBBC, its lawyers wrote in court documents, is entitled to discover Trump’s “intention behind the speech and anything that bears on the impression his audience could have reasonably obtained in listening to the speech”, which includes whether Trump “gave it intentionally or otherwise; the breadth of the audience of the message and impression; and the extent of any resulting injury or harm”.Trump filed the lawsuit against the BBC in December over scenes in the 2024 BBC documentary Trump, A Second Chance?. It argued that the BBC spliced scenes from Trump’s 6 January 2021 speech so that it appeared Trump directly urged his supporters to attack the US Capitol building.Trump’s children and son-in-law have, “without question”, knowledge of several incidents that day, BBC’s lawyers wrote, , including when Trump sought to convince former vice-president Mike Pence to refuse certifying the results of the 2020 election. The BBC also said that Kushner allegedly helped to draft a statement for Trump that would have condemned the use of violence at the Capitol.The British broadcaster had been unable to previously serve Trump’s children and son-in-law with subpoenas because they are protected by the US Secret Service as members of the sitting president’s immediate family, according to the court documents. The BBC had tried previously to serveIvanka Trumpand her husband, Kushner, at their home in Florida but were blocked by law enforcement officials.Trump’s legal team did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Last week, a federal judge granted Trump’s request to block the BBC from accessingfinancial recordsafter Trump’s lawyers said they would amend the lawsuit to focus specifically on the reputational damages rather than business impacts. Another judge had previously ruled that Trump would have to start handing over records that would have provided details on the hundreds of businesses owned by Trump’s family trust.Trump recentlyclaimedthat the BBC used artificial intelligence to alter his speech, which the network has denied. While the BBC has apologized for the editing, it has maintained that Trump lacks the grounds for a defamation lawsuit.The BBC is being represented by the law firm Ballard Spahr, which has also defended several publications facing lawsuits from Trump and his allies, including the New York Times and the Associated Press. It is one of several media organizations that Trump has targeted after they published critical reporting of him. The Wall Street Journal is also facing a $10bn lawsuit for its reporting on Trump’s alleged contributions to Jeffrey Epstein’s birthday book, and several journalists at the New York Times were subpoenaed over an article detailing security concerns with the Air Force One presidential jet.Explore more on these topicsBBCDonald TrumpUS Capitol attackDocumentary filmsEuropeJared KushnerIvanka TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Europe’s top clubs threatened Club World Cup boycott before Fifa plan collapsed | Fifa | The Guardian
description: Europe’s leading clubs threatened not to participate in future Club World Cups unless Gianni Infantino withdrew his Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme, issuing their ultimatum hours before the plan was scrapped
Author: Nick Ames
Headline: Europe’s leading clubs threatened not to participate in future Club World Cups unless Gianni Infantino withdrew his Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme, issuing their ultimatum hours before the plan was scrapped
Content: Nasser al-Khelaifi (right), chair of European Football Clubs, and the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, pictured together in 2025.Photograph: Fabrizio Corradetti/APView image in fullscreenNasser al-Khelaifi (right), chair of European Football Clubs, and the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, pictured together in 2025.Photograph: Fabrizio Corradetti/APFifaEurope’s top clubs threatened Club World Cup boycott before Fifa plan collapsedUltimatum issued hours before plan was scrappedEuropean Football Clubs demanded Infantino back downExclusive byNick AmesFri 14 Aug 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 18.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEurope’s leading clubs threatened not to participate in future Club World Cups unlessGianni Infantinowithdrew his Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme, issuing their ultimatum hours before the plan was scrapped.In a letter to the Fifa secretary general, Mattias Grafström, the influential European Football Clubs (EFC) group warned that its cooperation with future tournaments would hinge on Infantino backing down. It said the threat would hold unless a joint venture between EFC and Fifa – a framework for which has already been agreed – is completed before television rights can be sold for the 2028 Women’sClub World Cup.Continental clash: where world football stands on Fifa and Infantino – explainedRead moreThe letter, dated 31 July and signed by the EFC chief executive, Charlie Marshall, said Infantino’s actions could constitute a “substantial breach” of the bodies’ existing memorandum of understanding (MoU) and suggested this could be grounds for its termination. It floated the idea that EFC and its clubs may push back against the international match calendar and its player release rules, which are crucial to ensuring national team tournaments can function. Infantinoshelved the privately backed Football Forward Enterprise (FFE)in the early hours of 1 August after widespread condemnation.Fundamental to EFC’s complaints was the impression FFE would bring all broadcasting, commercial and sponsorship rights under its own umbrella. The letter askedFifato confirm this and said it would take decisive action if these elements were not included in the long-proposed joint venture, whose creation is enshrined in the MoU and intended to involve managing the commercial side of global club competitions. It witheringly wrote that the tie-in had, “unlike the FFE proposal, made no meaningful progress over the past year”. EFC already has a similar joint venture with Uefa, named UC3, which was launched in 2025.A potentially incendiary section read: “Unless a fully operational Fifa-EFC CWC joint venture, with exclusive authority over, among other things, all commercial and operational matters, is established well ahead of the women’s 2028 Fifa CWC rights cycle, EFC will not support – and its member clubs will not participate in – any future edition, including the women’s and men’s 2028 and 2029 Fifa CWC.”In theory the threat still holds although Fifa, in a response to EFC’s letter since Infantino climbed down, is understood to have promised a swift meeting to keep the joint venture on track. EFC’s position followed concerns raised by a vast number of clubs around Europe, who were angered by the lack of consultation around the design of FFE. One major European club expressed concerns in its own letter saying it would support EFC in any “firmer collective action” if necessary and called for “more rigorous and transparent governance processes”.Any European withdrawal from Club World Cups would in practice mean those tournaments could not run. EFC and Fifa operated last year’s Club World Cup, the first to take place with 32 teams, using a short-term prototype for any future joint venture. No hosts have yet been announced for the new-look Women’s Club World Cup or the next edition of the men’s tournament in 2029.View image in fullscreenChelsea won the Club World Cup in July 2025 by beating Paris Saint-Germain in the final.Photograph: Chris Brunskill/Fantasista/Getty ImagesEFC’s letter also raised the continuing delay,first reported in February, in distributing £185m of solidarity money to clubs that did not participate in the Club World Cup. Transparency over the event’s financial performance was also requested.“We ask that you urgently share the final surplus revenue generated by the 2025 Fifa WC, together with a full profit and loss statement, so that all revenues, expenses and costs can be properly assessed in line with our partnership in this competition,” it said. “The absence of information on this matter, as with the lack of a solution on CWC solidarity for over a year, is also of serious concern and disappointment to EFC and our member clubs.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt is understood there is increasing optimism that this issue is on the verge of resolution, although a notional average £50,000 windfall for every global top-flight club, if the pot was divided equally, pales in comparison with the £84m reward long since banked by last year’s winners, Chelsea.Referring to clubs releasing players for international duty, EFC continued: “Our memorandum of understanding, set to expire on 30 December 2030, includes EFC’s and its member clubs’ acceptance of the international match calendar and the release rules. Both are directly relevant for Fifa’s non-European member associations and to any value FFE may have.” It said Fifa’s apparent commercial vision for FFE constituted a “serious breach of trust” and warned the MoU could be jeopardised.The letter demonstrates the extraordinary level of leverage EFC, which is chaired by the Paris Saint-Germain president, Nasser al-Khelaifi, can claim over Fifa and its increasing influence on football’s future. The organisation, set up in 2008 as a lobby group for clubs around the continent, now has well over 800 members although only a minority hold full voting rights. Some stakeholders elsewhere in football’s ecosystem have expressed fears about the level of power it has assumed. A separate representative body,the Union of European Clubs, was created in 2023 to represent smaller sides but is not recognised by Uefa.One potential consequence of EFC’s discussions with Fifa could, in the medium term, be its expansion into a group representing clubs around the world. More immediately, last month’s letter demanded that Fifa deliver on a previous promise to fully integrate Al-Khelaifi into the Fifa council, which is purportedly its main decision-making body.Explore more on these topicsFifaClub World CupGianni InfantinoEuropean club footballFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: NFL preseason storylines: are the Rams inevitable and will the Pats survive scandal? | NFL | The Guardian
description: With the Hall of Fame game done, and the second round of preseason games underway, let’s look at the storylines that could dominate the coming weeks
Author: Doug Farrar
Headline: With the Hall of Fame game done, and the second round of preseason games underway, let’s look at the storylines that could dominate the coming weeks
Content: Justin Herbert, Myles Garrett and Mike Vrabel will be in the spotlight this season.Composite: AP; The Boston Globe/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJustin Herbert, Myles Garrett and Mike Vrabel will be in the spotlight this season.Composite: AP; The Boston Globe/Getty ImagesNFLNFL preseason storylines: are the Rams inevitable and will the Pats survive scandal?With the Hall of Fame game done, and the second round of preseason games underway, let’s look at the storylines that could dominate the coming weeksDoug FarrarFri 14 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCan the Seahawks run it forward?Winning the Super Bowl back in February puts theSeattle Seahawksin line to become the 10th team, and the ninth franchise, to repeat as champions (the Pittsburgh Steelers went back-to-back twice in the 1970s). While a lot of Super Bowl winners experience massive drains of coaching and playing talent after clinching the title, these Seahawks are left in pretty good shape.Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III signed with the Kansas City Chiefs, and pass-rusher Boye Mafe is now with the Cincinnati Bengals, but the champs return 21 of their 22 starters from the Super Bowl team (Mafe wasn’t technically a starter).Offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak was tabbed by the Las Vegas Raiders to become their new head coach. The Seahawks replaced Kubiak with former San Francisco 49ers run game coordinator & tight ends coach Brian Fleury, who has said that he’ll keep most of Kubiak’s passing concepts, with some different wrinkles in the run game. First-round pick Jadarian Price seems to have everything it takes to replace Walker. Price wasn’t the lead running back at Notre Dame only because third overall pick Jeramiyah Love was the star of the show, but Love recently told me thatPrice can do everything he can do… and in some cases, better.The Seahawks have the right head coach to run it back in Mike Macdonald,because as he told me over the summer, it’s all about running it forward instead. That proactive mindset could make all the difference when navigating the NFC West – the NFL’s toughest division – on the way back to the biggest game.Will the Rams’ all-in approach pay off?Seattle’s most formidable opponent last season wasn’t theNew England Patriotsteam they beat in the Super Bowl; it was the Los Angeles Rams team they played three times, going 2-1 with a total score differential of 88-85 in Seattle’s favor. That included the Seahawks’ 31-27 NFC Championship game win, and everyone in the Seahawks’ building knew that it had been their toughest test.What did that loss do to the Rams? It encouraged them to pony up for shorter-term success. Cornerback was the team’s biggest problem last season, so they traded for Trent McDuffie, and then signed Jaylen Watson, McDuffie’s Chiefs teammate, to solidify things. Then, they traded outstanding pass-rusher Jared Verse, a first-round pick, and additional draft compensation to the Cleveland Browns for Myles Garrett,one of the most productive pass rushers in history.The 30-year-old Garrett is coming off a 2025 campaign in whichhe tied the NFL’s single-season sack record, and he did so with very little help. Now, Garrett joins a defensive line that was already great before he showed up, and may soon include the legendary Aaron Donald, who is considering ending his two-year retirement by the promise of playing with a fellowall-time demolition expert.Snead and McVay have never had a problem going all-in like this before – they’ve done so in trades for Stafford and defensive back Jalen Ramsey in the past – and those moves helped the Rams win the Super Bowl at the end of the 2021 season. As long as the 38-year-old Stafford can stay healthy, and the Rams don’t need to rely on their shaky quarterback depth chart, pushing the chips in could pay off once again.Can Mike McDaniel unleash Justin Herbert?Every year, it seems that preseason prognosticators want to stick their chests out and declare that this is the Los Angeles Chargers’ year. The Chargers are a flashy franchise with quarterback Justin Herbert and talent all along the roster, but it’s been a struggle to align Herbert with the kind of coaching and schematic wizardry that could bring everything out of his rare athletic gifts.From Joe Lombardi to Kellen Moore to Greg Roman, the Chargers’ offensive coordinators seemed to be more interested in making sure Herbert was as mistake-proof as possible at the expense of explosive plays – which are the primary currency in theNFLtoday.I spoke with Chargers head coach Jim Harbaugh right after he got the job, and he spoke of the “awesome responsibility” of coaching someone as talented as Herbert. As a former NFL quarterback himself, Harbaugh knows of what he speaks.Which is where new Chargers OC and former Miami Dolphins head coach Mike McDaniel comes in. Through his four seasons in Miami, McDaniel proved to be all about those explosive plays, and his schematic marriage with Herbert could pay rare dividends. It’s a boon for McDaniel as well, who was restricted in what he could do with the Dolphins, because Tua Tagovailoa was his primary quarterback, and Herbert is physically in a different universe.So maybe this is the year that all those filled with hope for the Chargers actually have something to crow about.View image in fullscreenJosh Allen is still looking for his first NFL title.Photograph: Adrian Kraus/APCan Jim Leonhard take the Bills over the top (finally)?As the Buffalo Bills’ head coach from 2017-2025, Sean McDermott compiled a 98-50 regular-season record that was among the best in the NFL –only the Kansas City Chiefs had more regular-season wins in that timeframe, with 106. But the Chiefs also won a bunch of Super Bowls, something McDermott’s Bills never achieved.
