So, the Bills fired McDermott in large part because of his 8-8 postseason record, and replaced him with offensive coordinator Joe Brady.But the big news in Buffalo, and the thing that could finally take Josh Allen’s team over the top, is the hire of new defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard. The former Wisconsin defensive coordinator has long been regarded as one of the finest defensive minds at any level of football. If you go back and watch any of Leonhard’s Wisconsin defenses through the 2022 season, you’ll see a lot of the line stunts and coverage switches that have becomede rigueurin the NFL today, and it’s why those in the know believe thatLeonhard is ahead of the game schematically, and a future NFL head coach.Like the Cowboys, the 2025 Bills were a bit under-coached – the talent didn’t match the results. Leonhard’s ascent could well mirror the Bills’ rise to Super Bowl team.Can the Patriots stave off regression and internal drama?The Patriots don’t just have to deal with the threat of regression after enjoyingone of the league’s easiest schedules in 2025; they also have to contend with the scandalMike Vrabel got caught up in this offseason. We are not here to cast aspersions on Vrabel’s dedication to his job; some things are more important. But if the 2026 Patriots get off to a slow start, and they fail to replicate last season’s secret sauce, things could snowball in a hurry.The Patriots did do a lot in the offseason to improve – the additions of receivers AJ Brown and Romeo Doubs give quarterback (and 2025 NFL MVP candidate) Drake Maye better targets than he’s ever had before. But there are slippery slopes to navigate for the reigning AFC champs.Can the Cowboys bring their defense up to par?The 2025 Dallas Cowboys defense, “constructed” by defensive coordinator Matt Eberflus, allowed the sixth-most pointsany team has allowed in NFL history(511). But the team still had a 7-9-1 record, because the offense, led by quarterback Dak Prescott, was so good. Eberflus and his outmoded concepts are out now, replaced by former Philadelphia Eagles passing game coordinator & defensive backs coach Christian Parker. The 34-year-old Parker comes from the Vic Fangio school of defense, with the Eagles’ brilliant DC as the tone-setter for about half the NFL. You should see offshoots of that everywhere in Big D. From the defensive line to the secondary, these Cowboys have the talent to win on defense, and with that top-tier offense already in hand, they could be more competitive than they’ve been in recent years.Now, it will be about using that personnel the right way. Those in the building are already raving about Parker’s knack for doing what he does.“To be a great defensive coordinator, you have to have confidence and swagger, and that’s two things he has,” new defensive lineman Rashan Gary recently said of Parker. “And the players now have to back up his swagger and his confidence.”The Cowboys had three straight 12-5 seasons from 2021-2023 under Mike McCarthy, and they won a grand total of one playoff game in that span. Now, head coach Brian Schottenheimer hopes that Parker’s addition can bring even more value to a franchise that has beenfar more valuable financiallythan in a competitive sense in recent years.Can the Texans bring their offense up to par?Texas’s other NFL team has no such issues on defense. The Houston Texans may have had the NFL’s most formidable defensive unit last season –they ranked second in FTN’s opponent-adjusted metricsbehind only the Seahawks – and if you wanted to lobby for Houston as the league’s best overall, nobody would blink.It was the offense, and specifically quarterback CJ Stroud, who struggled to keep up. Stroud was the NFL’s offensive rookie of the year in 2023, and it looked for all the world that he would be the league’s next great signal-caller. But a combination of offensive line issues, receiver injuries, and Stroud’s own issues in development, came home to roost. It didn’t show up as much in the regular season, as the Texans managed a 12-5 record and Stroud was generally good enough when healthy. But when the Texans faced the Patriots in the divisional round of the postseason, Stroud fell apart with a four-interception game that showed just how far he had fallen. Stroud’s two-game playoff performancewas perhaps the worst in recent NFL history.Now, the Texans have refurbished the offensive line with veterans Wyatt Teller and Braden Smith, and they selected Georgia Tech’s Keylan Rutledge in the first round of the draft. They signed former Chicago Bears and Detroit Lions running back David Montgomery, and they hope that speed receiver Tank Dell has fully recovered fromthe gruesome knee injury he suffered in December 2024.If Stroud can elevate the offense to a better place, the Texans are as Super Bowl-compliant as anybody. If not? Questions will abound as to the future.Explore more on these topicsNFLNew England PatriotsLos Angeles ChargersSeattle SeahawksLos Angeles RamsUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Struggling Venus Williams suffers 14th straight defeat in Cincinnati rout | Tennis | The Guardian
description: World No 615 falls to Emilia Arango in 66 minutes, while Stefanos Tsitsipas advances and Grigor Dimitrov lets a 4-1 final-set lead slip
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: World No 615 falls to Emilia Arango in 66 minutes, while Stefanos Tsitsipas advances and Grigor Dimitrov lets a 4-1 final-set lead slip
Content: Venus Williams of the United States plays a forehand during her match against Emilia Arango of Colombia  on Friday at the Cincinnati Open.Photograph: Dylan Buell/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenVenus Williams of the United States plays a forehand during her match against Emilia Arango of Colombia  on Friday at the Cincinnati Open.Photograph: Dylan Buell/Getty ImagesTennisStruggling Venus Williams suffers 14th straight defeat in Cincinnati routSeven-time major champion beaten 6-2, 6-2Williams, 46, loses 11th match of the seasonTsitsipas advances as Dimitrov squanders leadGuardian sportand agenciesFri 14 Aug 2026 16.27 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 16.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleColombian Emilia Arango handedVenus Williamsa 14th straight loss dating to July of last year, defeating the fading seven-time grand slam champion who is currently ranked 615th in 66 minutes by 6-2, 6-2 at the ATP-WTA Cincinnati Masters.The 46-year-old Williams was given a wild card entry at an event where she reached a semi-final a dozen years ago. She has played and lost 11 times this season while competing on organizer free entries.Iga Swiatek takes swing at critics after ending title drought in CincinnatiRead moreCzech Sara Bejlek allowed compatriot and 2016 titleholder Karolina Pliskova only two games in a first-round 6-0, 6-2 rout.With 64 seeds in the men’s and women’s draw of the last major warm-up prior to the 30 August US Open only going into action from Saturday, interest focused on the fate of 2017 winner Grigor Dimitrov and 2022 runner-up Stefanos Tsitsipas.The popular Dimitrov was unable to hold onto a 4-1 lead in the third set against Argentine Sebastian Baez, exiting in the first round 1-6, 6-3, 6-4 as he lost the last five games of the encounter.The 35-year-old Dimitrov, his ranking down to 138 and playing on a wild card, was bidding for his first Cincinnati victory in five years.Baez goes on to next play American Learner Tien, a semi-finalist this week in Montreal.Tsitsipas, a one-time world number three now standing 49th after a months-long slump in form, got past Valentin Royer of France 7-6 (7/4), 7-5 after struggling somewhat to close out the victory, which sent him into a match with second seed Felix Auger-Aliassime.The Greek led a set and 5-2 but was broken as he served for victory, with Royer saving two match points on the way to 5-all.Tsitsipas managed a late break two games later on his sixth match point to advance in two hours.“I’m trying to come to the net as much as possible,” Tsitsipas said. “Whenever a ball is short I try to capture it inside the baseline. That’s where I shined the most.“I felt confidence running through my veins. My offensive strategy helped me today, my composure was excellent.”Tsitsipas admitted he was tested at the end as he tried to close out against Royer, and found himself stalling as he missed conversion on winning chances.“It was nerve-wracking at the end with those match points I was not able to capture,” the Greek said. “It would have been easy to get tight.“I had to remind myself to stay loose and play aggressive. If I was going to miss, at least I knew I had done the right thing.”Tsitsipas, now several months into his coaching split with his father, has lifted his ranking to 49th after coming through qualifying at the Montreal Masters, where he lost in the second round.Hubert Hurkacz, a 2023 semi-finalist, advanced 6-2, 6-4 over qualifying lucky loser Sho Shimabukuro while Italian Matteo Berrettini defeated Thomas Droguet 3-6, 6-2, 6-4, playing only his second match since Wimbledon due to injury.Explore more on these topicsTennisVenus WilliamsUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s dismal Patriot Games were the Hunger Games ordered off Temu | US sports | The Guardian
description: Monkey bars, gawky teenagers and a presidential cameo, all nationally televised by ABC, combined for the most leaden hour of America’s 250th birthday summer
Author: Aaron Timms
Headline: Monkey bars, gawky teenagers and a presidential cameo, all nationally televised by ABC, combined for the most leaden hour of America’s 250th birthday summer
Content: US president Donald Trump attended the Patriot Games final on Tuesday at Spire Academy in Geneva, Ohio.Photograph: Kylie Cooper/ReutersView image in fullscreenUS president Donald Trump attended the Patriot Games final on Tuesday at Spire Academy in Geneva, Ohio.Photograph: Kylie Cooper/ReutersUS sportsTrump’s dismal Patriot Games were the Hunger Games ordered off TemuMonkey bars, gawky teenagers and a presidential cameo – all given a prime-time showcase by ABC – combined for the most leaden hour of America’s 250th birthday summerAaron TimmsFri 14 Aug 2026 10.16 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 10.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCulturally, it’s been a tough few months for Donald Trump. The UFC nighthe held at the White Housefor his birthday got lost amid the froth and excitement of the World Cup. The Great American State Fair on the Washington DC National Mallwas a dud. The president’s jokes at the White House Correspondents’ Dinnerall bombed. Could the Patriot Games, a nationwide competition to find the American schoolchildren most adept at traversing a set of monkey bars, help rescue the summer?Patriot Games: Trump’s ‘freedom finale’ to celebrate 250 is … a school sports dayRead moreLast night we got our answer: no. A one-hour prime-time special brought us the best of the Patriot Games, and in a crowded field it managed to offer some of the most leaden TV of the American semiquincentennial. Freedom 250, the White House-backed non-profit that hosted the UFC fight at the White House and the Great American State Fair, produced the event, and put up the $125,000 in college scholarship winnings that went to each winner on the boys’ and girls’ side of the competition. The final round of the Gamesactually took place earlier this week, at a sports training facility outside Cleveland, Ohio. Last night we just got the best bits, and judging by what that amounted to, we should all be thankful we never had to endure the other bits. This was Trumpworld’s answer to the Hunger Games, but it’s unlikely there will be much clamor for a sequel. The patriots may be hungry for more, but the rest of us? Eh.The climax of this hour-long trudge was its final quarter, in which the four most athletically talented schoolchildren in the (Maga-aligned) nation faced off to see who could negotiate the “Patriot Course”, a gladiatorial obstacle course featuring ropes, hoops, kettle bells, something called “the freedom gate”, the monkey bars of “American traverse”, and a final climb up “patriot’s peak”, fastest. But to get thereABCput us through 45 minutes of highlights from the Games’ qualifying rounds, a test of spectator endurance every bit as trying as anything inflicted on the competition’s collection of awkward 15-year-olds. To a soundtrack of rap-rock and screeching eagles, we watched as various high schoolers – “one male and one female from every state and some tribal nations and territories”, as the broadcast put it, and almost all of them white – tested themselves on the medicine ball toss, the agility shuttle, the 55m hurdles, and the flexed arm hang. “What a way to start!” exclaimed co-host Matt Barrie as various gawky teens shuffled and huffed before a sparse crowd of other teenagers. “84.72 for Bridget,” added, without context, his on-air colleague Laura Rutledge.View image in fullscreenTrump watches a girl compete in the kettle bell portion of the Patriot Course during Tuesday’s final.Photograph: Kylie Cooper/ReutersView image in fullscreenTeenage athletes march before Trump’s arrival.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/APThe kids next had to prove themselves in various dork sports (my term) – dodgeball, kickball, and the like. Then came the Varsity Circuit (please respect the capital letters), Operation Endurance Course (“You like to see these different athletes step up and crush the monkey bars”), and the tug of war, a contest so powerfully traditional it resisted upper-case Trumpification. Finally: Victory Hoops, an arcade-style basketball shootout game. “It’s been one of the best experiences of my life,” announced a young woman over slow-motion footage of her shooting a miniature basketball at a hoop three feet away. From the living rooms of red America, you could almost hear the sigh of relief that greeted these words: the kids are alright.And finally, at the end of all that, it was on to the main event: an interview with the president himself! “Coming up, a conversation with President Donald J Trump,” Rutledge announced, over footage of TrumpHitler salutingwaving to a crowd of smiling young patriots. Flanked by ESPN talk-show hostPat McAfee, who then promptly disappeared from the broadcast, the big dog entered the arena – a dark coliseum lit up by neon lights and sparklers to resemble adrone racing course– to approach his own test of agility: a two-minute interview with Rutledge in which she asked, “How have you found the Patriot Games?” The president paused. A hush descended on the crowd. “Well I love Ohio,” he responded. The crowd erupted. Patriotism in action! And then came the Trumpian coup de grâce. “This has been as exciting as anything, I got here and I didn’t know what to expect,” he added, taking a snide little dig at a competition his own administration created.View image in fullscreenThe Patriot Games brought together ‘one male and one female from every state and some tribal nations and territories’.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/APThe finals, in the end, were a disappointment: both winners, Kennadi Fuhrman and Rockwell Myers (even the names at the Patriot Games had to project a powerful air of all-American excellence), strolled to victory after their opponents fell while attempting to cross American traverse. No matter what happens from here – to Trump, to America, to the world – we now all know to never, ever underestimate American traverse. On the victory dais, the final patriots thanked God, Trump presented them with their trophies (small, probably bought off Temu) and their checks (big, $125,000). The winners celebrated as the president smiled and clapped and pointed at no one in particular, and this hour of endurance, agility, strength, and dime-store Maga theatrics came to an abrupt end.It was all very Hitler Youth. But as a TV spectacle, these Patriot Games did have one virtue that set them apart from the endless flotsam of 250th birthday kitsch that has crammed our screens this summer: they were, at the very least, brief.Explore more on these topicsUS sportsABCDonald TrumpOhiofeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Not going to be an issue’: Mikel Arteta relaxed about Arsenal contract situation | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: The Arsenal manager, whose current deal expires at the end of the new season, said of his future: ‘They don’t have to worry about that, I want to be here’
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: The Arsenal manager, whose current deal expires at the end of the new season, said of his future: ‘They don’t have to worry about that, I want to be here’
Content: Mikel Arteta’s Arsenal will play Manchester City in the Community Shield on Sunday.Photograph: Marc Atkins/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMikel Arteta’s Arsenal will play Manchester City in the Community Shield on Sunday.Photograph: Marc Atkins/Getty ImagesArsenal‘Not going to be an issue’: Mikel Arteta relaxed about Arsenal contract situationManager’s deal expires at end of the new season‘They don’t have to worry … I want to be here’Ed AaronsFri 14 Aug 2026 17.30 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 17.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMikel Arteta has said he is relaxed about his Arsenal contract expiring at the end of the new season and believes his side will need to be better than last year to defend their title successfully.The Premier League champions will face Enzo Maresca’s Manchester City in the Community Shield in Cardiff on Sunday and are heavy favourites to win back-to-back league titles for the first time since the 1930s. The departure of Pep Guardiola from their traditional rivals City means Arteta is now the Premier League’s longest-serving manager, with the Spaniard having joined in December 2019.Arsenal open talks with Bayer Leverkusen over deal for Jarell QuansahRead moreHe signed a three-year contract extension in September 2024 afterArsenalfinished as runners-up to City and had been expected to agree a new deal over the summer that would make him one of the highest-paid managers in the world. Arteta acknowledged on Friday that his priorities have been elsewhere this summer as he attempts to strengthen his squad before the new season but reassured supporters that he is fully committed to the club.“They don’t have to worry about any of that, because I want to be here. I am extremely happy. I feel very grateful to work with the people that I work with and when we have the possibility, we will resolve that. And that’s it,” he said.Asked if he expects talks over a new contract to continue after the transfer window, Arteta added: “There is always another priority, I think. And that’s the way we have been treating it, I think because everybody feels comfortable that the time on the contract is not going to be an issue. I think because my will, certainly, is to be here and I am very happy here. My feeling from the club is the same one. That is why everyone is doing things in a really organic way.”Arsenal have opened negotiations with Bayer Leverkusenover a move for Jarell Quansahas they seek cover for William Saliba and Jurriën Timber, while they are still in the market for another attacker if they can offload Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus. After missing out on Vinícius Júnior when the Brazil forward opted to sign a new deal with Real Madrid, Arteta defended Arsenal’s strategy this summer and is hoping that they can still add to their squad.“I am really happy with the squad, the players that I have and I am really happy with the ambition of the club. There is zero question about that. We have shown that in the manner we have tried to act,” he said.“But I think we need to do it our own way. We have super strengths and we have other areas we need to be very conscious [of] because we don’t have the elements or the structure that other clubs have. We need to do it our way. We are always on it that way and we will do what we believe is the right thing to do. To have the best possibility to compete in every competition that’s for sure.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionArteta added: “We’re going to prepare to elevate our level, expecting that the rest will do the same. That’s traditionally what happened in the league in the last few years, and that’s the way we have planned the season, and the way we want to evolve the team.”Explore more on these topicsArsenalMikel ArtetanewsShareReuse this content

title: Superb Summer McIntosh bounces back with 400m medley gold at Pan Pacs | Summer McIntosh | The Guardian
description: The Canadian rebounded from defeat in the 200m freestyle to win the 400m medley, while Australia held off Katie Ledecky in the 4x200m relay
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Canadian rebounded from defeat in the 200m freestyle to win the 400m medley, while Australia held off Katie Ledecky in the 4x200m relay
Content: Summer McIntosh of Canada competes in the women's 400m IM on day two of the Pan Pacific swimming championships in Irvine, California.Photograph: Sean M Haffey/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSummer McIntosh of Canada competes in the women's 400m IM on day two of the Pan Pacific swimming championships in Irvine, California.Photograph: Sean M Haffey/Getty ImagesSummer McIntoshSuperb Summer McIntosh bounces back with 400m medley gold at Pan PacsCanadian wins in championship-record timeAustralia hold off Ledecky and US in 4x200 relayUS swimmers claim six golds on second nightAgenciesFri 14 Aug 2026 01.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSummer McIntosh of Canada led all the way in winning the 400m individual medley at the Pan Pacific Championships on Thursday night, bouncing backafter a runner-up finish in the 200 freestyle.Australia led all but 150 meters of the women’s 4x200 freestyle relay, with the team of Inez Miller, Lani Pallister, Hannah Casey and Milla Jansen winning in 7min 42.40sec to lower the country’s championship mark of 7:44.12 set at the 2018 Pan Pacs.Swim hero Katie Ledecky extends 16-year winning streak  in 1500m with Pan Pacs goldRead moreKatie Ledecky swam the anchor leg for the US, but couldn’t overhaul Jansen although she got within a body length in the closing meters. Erin Gemmell, Anna Peplowski, Rylee Erisman and Ledecky took silver in 7:43.10, also going under the old championship mark.“I’ve kind of struggled with the 200 individually from a flat start over the last couple years, but I always know I’ll have something in me for the relay and I’ll pull out a good split,” Ledecky said. “I love swimming that anchor leg.”McIntosh helped Canada earn the relay bronze.The US team of Luke Hobson, Aaron Shackell, Patrick Sammon and Gabriel Jett won the men’s 4 x 200 free relay in a championship record of 6:59.37. The Americans led the entire race, with Jett’s explosive turn off the final wall helping him hold off a charging Sam Short of Australia on the anchor leg.“I just kind of poured everything on,” Jett said. “I swim with my eyes closed, so I didn’t know where I was.”McIntosh briefly dipped under her own world-record pace early in the 400 IM. McIntosh finished in a championship record time of 4min 28.01sec after qualifying second-quickest for the eight-woman final at the outdoor pool.McIntosh was disappointed with her time in the 200 free after losing to Pallister of Australia on opening night of the four-day international meet.“Just trying to forget about it,” McIntosh said.Jenna Forrester of Australia was second in 4min 31.50sec. Agostina Hein, an 18-year-old from Argentina, took bronze after coming into the final with the fastest time in preliminaries.Meg Harris of Australia surprised herself with a victory in the women’s 100 freestyle from lane six. She touched in 52.60sec, beating American Gretchen Walsh, who was second in 52.78 after being 0.01sec under world-record pace at the turn. Olivia Wunsch of Australia was third.American Simone Manuel, the 2016 Olympic champion, finished fourth.The US went 1-2 in the men’s 100. Jack Alexy won in 47.14, lowering his championship-record time of 47.40 from the preliminaries. Teammate Patrick Sammon was second at 47.62. Guilherme Caribe of Brazil was third.American McKenzie Siroky won the 100 breaststroke for her first international medal. She outdueled Tang Qianting of China down the stretch to touch first in 1min 5.32sec. Tang was second in 1min 5.46sec.The US swept the 50 backstroke events.View image in fullscreenMeg Harris of Australia celebrates after winning the women's 100m freestyle final over USA’s Gretchen Walsh.Photograph: Maddie Meyer/Getty ImagesQuintin McCarty won the men’s race in 24.51sec, lowering the championship record set by Isaac Cooper of Australia in the prelims. Cooper took silver.Katharine Berkoff won the women’s race in a career-best 26.90sec, bettering her championship mark set in the prelims. Teammate Regan Smith was second in 27.14.American Van Mathias earned his third medal of the meet, winning the 100 breaststroke in 58.02sec, lowering his championship record from the prelims. He took silver in the 50 butterfly and gold in the world record-setting 4x100 mixed medley relay Wednesday.The men’s 400 IM was won by Tomoyuki Matsushita of Japan in 4:06.75. His time erased American Ryan Lochte’s championship mark of 4:07.59 set at the 2010 Pan Pacs, also in Irvine.“Next time I come back to the US, I’m going to get gold again,” a smiling Matsushita said through a translator.American Carson Foster was second.Explore more on these topicsSummer McIntoshSwimmingKatie LedeckyUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: Ben Shelton prevails in all-American final to retain Canadian Open title | Tennis | The Guardian
description: The 23-year-old became the fourth man this century to win back-to-back Canadian Open titles with a 6-3, 7-6 (4) victory in Montreal
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The 23-year-old became the fourth man this century to win back-to-back Canadian Open titles with a 6-3, 7-6 (4) victory in Montreal
Content: Ben Shelton reacts after seeing off fellow American Brandon Nakashima in Thursday’s Canadian Open final.Photograph: Yannick Legare/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBen Shelton reacts after seeing off fellow American Brandon Nakashima in Thursday’s Canadian Open final.Photograph: Yannick Legare/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockTennisBen Shelton prevails in all-American final to retain Canadian Open titleAmerican wins second straight Masters 1000 titleShelton improves to 6-0 against fellow AmericanNorrie advances as Draper falls in CincinnatiAgenciesThu 13 Aug 2026 23.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBen Shelton broke onto the scene by winning his first-ever ATP Masters 1000 championship a year ago in Toronto.He earned his second crown at that level ⁠by successfully defending his Canadian title on Thursday, defeating fellow American Brandon Nakashima 6-3, 7-6 (4) to win the National Bank Open in Montreal.It was the fourth time this century a ⁠male player won the ⁠Canadian title back-to-back. Rafael ​Nadal was the most recent to do so in 2018-19. Andy Murray (2009-10) and Novak Djokovic (2011-12) accomplished the feat previously.“For me to play the way that I ⁠played this week to go through this draw speaks to the work I have been putting in,” Shelton said. “It also speaks to my mental toughness, my ability to focus through everything that was ⁠going on this week.“In winning his fourth tournament of the season (Dallas, Munich and Stuttgart), fifth-seeded Shelton collected 22 winners and committed ​12 unforced errors. Nakashima, seeded 28th, had 19 winners and ‌21 unforced errors.Nakashima fell to ‌0-6 against Shelton and was denied his first Masters 1000 title. His only tournament win on the tour came in ‌2022 in San Diego.Shelton rolled to a win in the opening set in 33 minutes. Neither player faced a break point through the first six games before Shelton broke for a 4-3 lead and then got another break to seal the set.Serving also dominated the second set of the 1-hour, 27-minute match, with neither player producing a break-point opportunity. The tiebreaker also was controlled by the servers. Shelton finally won a point on Nakashima’s serve for a 4-2 lead ‌in the tiebreaker, and he closed out the match on Nakashima’s serve, too.Cincinnati OpenRain interrupted play on the first day of the tournament, but it didn’t stop Great Britain’s Cameron Norrie, who ​downed Croatia’s Dino Prizmic 3-6, 6-1, 6-4 in Mason, Ohio.Norrie withstood a 25-14 disadvantage on winners, rallying from a first-set loss to take control in the second set. Norrie converted two of three break points in the set and took advantage of seven unforced errors by Prizmic. He then broke Prizmic’s serve in the seventh game of the third set to move in front for good.Norrie ⁠might find the going tougher in the second round, where he faces top-seeded Alexander ​Zverev of Germany.Another early winner Thursday ​was Spain’s Martin Landaluce, who shook off ​a six-match losing streak to down Britain’sJack Draper6-3, 7-5. Draper, a former world No 4 ​player, couldn’t find traction against ‌the younger Landaluce, who ​had fewer winners (33-21) but almost ​half the number of Draper’s unforced errors (47-24).“I think the important thing today was believing in my shots, believing in my game,” Landaluce said. “I did some big misses at times but that’s OK, because it is how I enjoy playing.“Other winners included Germany’s Jan-Lennard Struff, Argentina’s Thiago Agustin Tirante, Canada’s Denis Shapovalov, Serbia’s Miomir Kecmanovic and Argentina’s Mariano Navone. France’s Terence Atmane advanced when Hungary’s Marton Fucsovics ‌retired.Explore more on these topicsTennisJack DraperUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: How will the three promoted teams fare in the Premier League? | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Sunderland and Leeds defied the odds and stayed up last season. Will Coventry, Hull and Ipswich continue the trend?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Sunderland and Leeds defied the odds and stayed up last season. Will Coventry, Hull and Ipswich continue the trend?
Content: Ryan Giles celebrates Hull’s promotion; Coventry players look steely; Marcelino Núñez shone for Ipswich after leaving Norwich (clockwise from top left).Composite: Getty, Rex FeaturesView image in fullscreenRyan Giles celebrates Hull’s promotion; Coventry players look steely; Marcelino Núñez shone for Ipswich after leaving Norwich (clockwise from top left).Composite: Getty, Rex FeaturesGuardian Sport NetworkPremier LeagueHow will the three promoted teams fare in the Premier League?Sunderland and Leeds defied the odds and stayed up last season. Will Coventry, Hull and Ipswich continue the trend?ByWhoScoredHarry PatersonFri 14 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 07.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCoventryA quarter of a century after their last appearance in thePremier League– following financial ruin, ground-sharing in Northampton and Birmingham and even a spell in League Two – Coventry have finally completed their comeback story. But the bunting has been packed away and they now face the daunting task of proving they belong in the top flight.Frank Lampard is not starting from scratch. Coventry’s success last season was a collective effort and a product of smart recruitment over the past few years. The result was a side that overwhelmed the Championship with a fearless front-footed approach without relying on a single scorer. Seven Coventry players scored seven or more league goals.They led the division for shots on target; they ranked second for big chances created, touches in the opposition’s final third and touches in the penalty area; and they produced direct attacking speed and passes-per-sequence numbers comparable to those of some of the Premier League’s most direct sides, including Brentford and Bournemouth.The title was wrapped up with three games to spare; they conceded the fewest goals in the division (45 in 46 games); and their 97-goal haul was the fourth highest in a 46-game Championship season, behind only Fulham in 2021–22, Bournemouth in 2014–15 and Reading in 2005–06. Given the success Fulham and Bournemouth have enjoyed in recent years, Coventry will hope that proves a good omen.Continuity is going to be central to their hopes of survival. They are not following in the footsteps of Sunderland,who spent about £155m last summer. Coventry’s net spend was about £3.5m last summer and just 17% of minutes on the pitch last season went to newcomers. Their best business in the transfer window was holding on to players such as Jack Rudoni and Milan van Ewijk, who were attracting interest from top-flight clubs.View image in fullscreenCoventry’s captain, Matt Grimes, and manager, Frank Lampard enjoy the Championship parade. Now comes the hard part.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersThey have not gone wild this summer but they have invested. Coventry have signed the centre-back Aurèle Amenda from Eintracht Frankfurt, the winger Loum Tchaouna from Burnley, and the midfielderCaleb Yirenkyi from Nordsjællandwhile also securing permanent deals for Frank Onyeka andCarl Rushworth, who were on loan at the club last season. They have also brought back the former favourite Gustavo Hamer after his spell at Sheffield United.Lampard’s biggest challenge will be adapting a style built to dominate in the Championship into one capable of surviving the Premier League. Their direct, attacking approach will be riskier against opponents who possess the pace, quality and tactical sophistication to punish a rushed pass or a risky vertical ball.Coventry will not have the same territorial control or volume of chances they enjoyed last season either – they need players who can get them up the pitch. Haji Wright’s pace and ability to attack space should be valuable, but Ellis Simms, who tends to thrive attacking the penalty area, will need service.HullThe fact Hull are playing in the Premier League this season borders on miraculous. This is a side that survived relegation to League One on goal difference the season before last, entered 2025-26 under a transfer embargo, scraped into the playoffs by beating Norwich on the final day of the season, and scored a stoppage-time winner in the playoff final. No one backed them in their pre-season predictions and yet, under the guidance of the relatively unknown Sergej Jakirovic in his first season in charge, they defied the statistics.If matches in the Championship last season had been decided by expected goals, Hull would have finished second bottom. The glaringly obvious problem was at the back. They conceded 66 goals, giving them the fourth worst defensive record in the Championship. Looking back at the last 15 teams to be promoted to the Premier League, only Southampton (who conceded 63 goals when they were promoted in 2023-24) have come close to that tally and they went on to concede 86 goals in the top flight, finishing rock bottom with just 12 points.As if that weren’t bad enough, Hull were lucky to not concede more: opponents failed to convert 10 opportunities where they had at least a 50% chance of scoring according to xG – the most of any side in the league. Hull simply have to improve as fortune does not tend to stick around long when you’re in the Premier League.There are some reasons for optimism, though. Their form against the top teams in away matches was impressive. They conceded just eight goals in their matches at the teams in the top 10; they did not concede in either of their games against Coventry; and they didn’t concede in any of their playoff matches.View image in fullscreenHull City players celebrate reaching the Premier League with a victory parade.Photograph: Bruce Rollinson/PAJakirovic showed an impressive knack of switching tactics depending on whom his side faced or how a game was evolving. His switch from their usual 4-2-3-1 formation to a back three with wingbacks in the second leg of their playoff tie against Millwall was perhaps the most telling example of this succeeding as they caught Millwall by surprise, winning 2-0 at the Den. If continuity is the key word in Coventry’s fight for survival then chaos seems to be Hull’s. You don’t really know what to expect from them. The striker Oli McBurnie pointed this out last season: “It’s probably hard to gameplan against us, because we play so many different ways against different teams.”As well as their unpredictability, this team have heart. They defied all expectations to reach the top, overcoming a relegation battle, a transfer embargo and statistical odds. Jakirovic put their success down to the bond they have forged. “It was like a puzzle,” he said. “Maybe it was the best that it happened like this. This group of players became even closer. They had to stick together and help each other.” As Robert Earnshaw, who played for Derby in their disastrous 2007-08 campaign, has warned: “You can relegate yourself based on how you think. It was almost as if everyone gave up. It was 20 games to go and it was like: ‘We’re never going to do it.’” This Hull side have fight and that should count for something.IpswichTwo years ago Ipswich entered the Premier League as one of football’s feelgood stories. After they had had 22 years away from the top flight, Kieran McKenna took them back through back-to-back promotions, turning a squad largely built for League One into Championship contenders. The 2023-24 campaign was fuelled by fearless, attacking football, late goals and a sense of togetherness, with Ipswich finishing second behind Leicester and becoming the first side in 12 years to climb from League One to the Premier League in successive seasons.McKenna’s side had an established core who had grown together and exceeded expectations but they were small fish in a very big pond, and the Premier League quickly exposed the gulf in quality. Ipswich won just four games, conceded 82 times and finished 19th with 22 points. Their immediate return to the top flight, fuelled by Premier League experience and parachute payments, means this is a very different promotion story – less about underdogs defying expectations and more about a club that is aiming to belong in this league.Their recruitment in 2024 suggested they had one eye on a return to the second tier. They brought in leading Championship players who had potential but were not proven at the top: Omari Hutchinson, Jack Clarke, Liam Delap, Dara O’Shea and Jacob Greaves. The club’s CEO, Mark Ashton, says they have to be “a bit braver” this time around. Rather than focusing on potential, they want to sign battle-ready, established top-flight performers.Championship angst: why the sense of rejuvenation in EFL is not universalRead moreFlorentino Luís and Sasa Lukic bring the physicality and ball-winning presence the midfield lacked in 2024-25, while Issa Diop adds Premier League experience at the back. At the other end, with no Ipswich player scoring more than 10 non-penalty goals last season, Emersonn gives them a physically imposing striker, while Daizen Maeda and Abdul Fatawu add running power and intensity. Crucially, a lot of these players have Premier League experience and, with O’Shea, Clarke, Greaves and Jaden Philogene remaining from the season they went down, this is a side that look more ambitious and ready to compete.Their defence also looks far more equipped for the top flight. They had the second best defensive record in the Championship last season, keeping 17 clean sheets and conceding just 47 goals (10 fewer goals than when they were promoted in 2023-24). This is not the chaotic and entertaining side that got them to the Premier League two years ago, but a more patient team that know how to be pragmatic and aggressive.The biggest negative is the departure of the man who guided them back to the Premier League, withMcKenna stepping away from football. Gary O’Neil, his replacement, has experienced Premier League relegation battles with Bournemouth and Wolves but it will be difficult to replace the identity, relationships and collective belief McKenna spent five years building through three promotions in four years, and 105 wins in 222 games. O’Neil is inheriting a more expensive and talented side than Ipswich had two years ago, but he will have to hit the ground running and help a host of new players to adapt quickly.This is an article byWhoScoredExplore more on these topicsPremier LeagueGuardian Sport NetworkCoventry CityHull CityIpswich TownfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Liverpool owner FSG seals £1.65bn sale of 30% stake to consortium including Jeff Bezos | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: Liverpool’s owner has confirmed the sale of 30% of the club to a consortium including Amit Bhatia, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin
Author: Andy Hunter
Headline: Liverpool’s owner has confirmed the sale of 30% of the club to a consortium including Amit Bhatia, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin
Content: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos is the third richest man in the world but FSG will remain in operational control at Anfield.Composite: ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAmazon founder Jeff Bezos is the third richest man in the world but FSG will remain in operational control at Anfield.Composite: ShutterstockLiverpoolLiverpool owner FSG seals £1.65bn sale of 30% stake to consortium including Jeff BezosConfirmed deal values club as a whole at £5.5bnAmit Bhatia will become club’s new vice-chairmanAndy HunterFri 14 Aug 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 16.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLiverpool’s owner,Fenway Sports Group, has confirmed it has agreed the sale of 30% of the club to a consortium including Amit Bhatia, the Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and the Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin. The deal is understood to be worth £1.65bn, valuing Liverpool at £5.5bn, and will see Bhatia become the club’s new vice-chair on an expanded board.Bhatia, the son-in-law of Indian steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, initiated and led talks with FSG on behalf of the 1892 Holdings consortium, a reference to Liverpool’s founding year. The former co-owner of Queens Park Rangers has received financial backing from the Mittal Family Trust, the K5 Sports fund, of which Bezos is the lead investor, and EE Capital, the family office of Elaine and Eduardo Saverin.Arsenal in talks over Quansah; transfer news; Giuliani slams Infantino’s critics: football – liveRead moreElaine Saverin, wife of Eduardo, and Bryan Baum, co-founder and managing partner of K5 Global, will also join the Liverpool board. Bezos is considered a passive investor and will not have a seat on the board.Despite the involvement of Bezos, the third richest man in the world with $272bn (£201bn), Eduardo Saverin, worth an estimated $33bn and the Mittal family, worth around $17bn, FSG will remain in operational control of Liverpool as well as majority owners. 1892 Holdings’ investment remains subject to regulatory approval, which could take up to 90 days, and will have no impact on Liverpool’s transfer budget or strategy for this summer. There is also no change to the leadership or day-to-day running of Liverpool.FSG insist the deal is not part of an exit strategy from a club they acquired in 2010 for £300m after the near-ruinous ownership of Tom Hicks and George Gillett. The transaction does not compel FSG to sell more of the club to 1892 at a future date, or include obligations for 1892 to increase their stake, but it does give Bhatia’s consortium options to purchase more of Liverpool should the majority owners eventually decide to sell.It is the makeup of Bhatia’s consortium, rather than any financial need, that FSG claim attracted them to the British-Indian businessman’s proposal. The FSG leadership team of principal owner John W Henry, chair Tom Werner and president Mike Gordon have spent almost a year getting to know Bhatia and believe the deal will create further opportunities for Liverpool in global business, technology and investment, including in the important markets of India and Asia.View image in fullscreenThe sale will have no impact on Liverpool’s transfer budget or strategy for this summer.Photograph: News Images/NurPhoto/ShutterstockGordon, who has resumed a more hands-on role at Liverpool following the departure of Michael Edwards as chief executive of football at FSG, said: “Liverpool has always been built by thinking beyond one season and making decisions with the club’s long-term interests in mind. That approach continues to attract interest from respected investors and business leaders around the world.“As we considered this opportunity, it became clear that Amit and the consortium shared our long-term philosophy and appreciation for what makes Liverpool special. Their experience and perspective will complement the strong foundation already in place, and we look forward to working together.”With Premier League and Uefa financial regulations linking a club’s spending to turnover, the new investment will not have an immediate benefit for head coach Andoni Iraola and his Liverpool team. However, the commercial opportunities presented by the involvement of Bezos, Bhatia and Saverin will enable the Anfield club to grow their annual revenue significantly. Liverpool’s annual revenue increased to a record £703m in the year ending May 2025.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSpeaking on behalf of 1892 Holdings, Bhatia said: “We are incredibly proud to be investing in Liverpool Football Club and to be doing so alongside FSG. We have the utmost respect and admiration for FSG as owners and for everything they have achieved at Anfield.“To be welcomed as a partner in a club of this stature is a huge privilege. We are making this investment because we believe deeply in Liverpool and its leadership, and we look forward to supporting the club’s continued success for years to come.”Bhatia was involved in QPR for almost 19 years and took on numerous roles, from chair of the club to chair of the club’s community trust, until transferring his shareholding in July. He is likely to have a more visible presence at Anfield than fellow members of his consortium or FSG.Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolFenway Sports GroupJeff BezosFinancesBusinessnewsShareReuse this content

title: Raúl Jiménez’s injury-time penalty salvages point for Wolves against Blackburn | Championship | The Guardian
description: Wolves drew 2-2 against Blackburn in the Championship season opener after Raúl Jiménez scored a spot-kick deep in stoppage time
Author: Peter Lansley
Headline: Wolves drew 2-2 against Blackburn in the Championship season opener after Raúl Jiménez scored a spot-kick deep in stoppage time
Content: Raúl Jiménez slots home his penalty for Wolves in stoppage time.Photograph: Brett Patzke/WWFC/Wolves/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRaúl Jiménez slots home his penalty for Wolves in stoppage time.Photograph: Brett Patzke/WWFC/Wolves/Getty ImagesChampionshipRaúl Jiménez’s injury-time penalty salvages point for Wolves against BlackburnPeter Lansleyat MolineuxFri 14 Aug 2026 17.21 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 19.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRaúl Jiménez marked his return to Wolves with the stoppage-time equaliser that saved them from an embarrassing start to their return to the Championship. The Mexico striker, whoscored against Englandduring the World Cup, came off the bench to convert a penalty given for handball by Ryan Alebiosu that would have had VAR questioning whether the defender was in the area when Jackson Tchatchoua’s cross struck his arm.One minor consolation from Wolves’ relegation is that the video assistant referee is no longer their problem. Jiménez, who had bought scarves for all supporters in the South Bank in gratitude for their welcome home, tucked away his first goal in this second spell for the club he graced during their recent heyday before leaving for Fulham.Wolves 2-2 Blackburn: Championship opener – liveRead more“He’s an important striker,” César Peixoto, Wolves’ new head coach said. “He lives for scoring and making goals. Raúl is a key player for us. He helped the team inside and outside the pitch but we have to go slowly with him because he is 35 years old and comes back from the World Cup. We want him to stay good and scoring for us is good for him and for the team.”Goals from Sean McLoughlin and Andri Gudjohnsen allowed Blackburn to provide Wolves with a reality check after Marshall Munetsi had scored early. Confidence is a fragile commodity and, after their decision to replace Rob Edwards with a manager with no experience of English football, the Wolves board know that their supporters’ patience is thin. Leading Gil Vicente to sixth place in the Portuguese first division does not make Peixoto a guaranteed winner.Conceding the equaliser, through Jiménez’s first goal for Wolves in 1,311 days, denied unfancied Blackburn a deserved victory after Wolves lost their shape. Tony Mowbray, their head coach, felt the penalty decision was harsh. “I’ve just been shown an angle by my analyst where he [Alebiosu] is outside the box; another angle I’m told shows he’s just inside the box. I just felt like more and more decisions were starting to sway their way,” the former West Brom manager said. “It’s harsh to take because I don’t think they deserved that second goal.”Molineux was awash with fading golden sunlight and rising optimism at kick-off. A summer that started with such a surprising managerial departure was promising to end with renewed faith in the team’s direction of travel, until Peixoto’s admired high press came unstuck as his team started to “play with their hearts more than their heads”.View image in fullscreenMarshall Munetsi (right) celebrates scoring Woves’ first goal with Fer López.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAThe Blackburn defence had split generously to allow Munetsi a clean run through on to Fer López’s sumptuous pass. The left-footed finish from the Zimbabwean, himself coming back to Molineux after a loan at Paris FC, strengthened the feelgood factor.Peixoto’s tactics do currently lead to gaps on transition. Blackburn, who have not done so much in the transfer market to suggest they should aim higher than last season’s 20th place, got behind Wolves on several occasions. It was no great surprise when, from Ryoya Morishita’s superb right-wing cross, McLoughlin headed beyond Dan Bentley to equalise.Some of Wolves’ best business this summer has been bringing players back to Molineux. While Jiménez started the night on the bench, after a late start to pre-season following his impressive World Cup for Mexico, López was the classiest player on view. Back from a loan at Celta Vigo, he has been invited to make the No 10 position his own, and the Spaniard nearly regained Wolves the lead only to curl his shot wide.View image in fullscreenBlackburn’s Andri Gudjohnsen gives his side a 2-1 lead early in the second half.Photograph: Simon Davies/ProSports/ShutterstockBlackburn continued to benefit from Wolves’ soft centre however. Oladapo Afolayan’s shot needed tipping over by Bentley before the right winger again got space down Wolves’ left – where David Møller Wolfe, in for the injured Hugo Bueno, showed he is still not match fit after his World Cup endeavours with Norway – to cross for Gudjohnsen to turn in Rovers’ second goal. “The team lost some organisation and played with their heart rather than their head and brains,” Peixoto said. “It’s a lesson for us in the future, we need to stay with mental stability for the 90 minutes.”By the hour mark, the South Bank were swirling their Jiménez scarves above their heads and chanting “Si Señor” in honour of the veteran striker who was such an esteemed figure at Molineux for five of the club’s best years in modern times. Before his horrific head injury, he was the pivotal attacking player as Nuno Espírito Santo’s team reached the later stages of the FA Cup and Europa League. The scene was set for the Mexican. Could he deliver? Si, señor.Explore more on these topicsChampionshipWolverhampton WanderersBlackburn Roversmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Chelsea expect Enzo Fernández to stay after Manchester City opt not to meet deadline | Manchester City | The Guardian
description: Manchester City did not make a £120m bid for Enzo Fernández before Chelsea’s 5pm deadline on Friday but Enzo Maresca still expects a busy end to the transfer window
Author: Will Unwin
Headline: Manchester City did not make a £120m bid for Enzo Fernández before Chelsea’s 5pm deadline on Friday but Enzo Maresca still expects a busy end to the transfer window
Content: Enzo Fernández during a training session at Cobham on Friday.Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEnzo Fernández during a training session at Cobham on Friday.Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesManchester CityChelsea expect Enzo Fernández to stay after Manchester City opt not to meet deadlineCity could maintain interest despite lack of bidMaresca expecting busy end to transfer windowWill UnwinFri 14 Aug 2026 12.58 EDTFirst published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 07.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester City did not make a £120m bid for Enzo Fernández beforeChelsea’s 5pm deadlineon Friday but Enzo Maresca still expects a busy end to the transfer window, as the club seek incomings and outgoings. Chelsea, meanwhile, now expect the Argentina midfielder to stay at Stamford Bridge.Maresca takes charge of City for the first time in a major match on Sunday against Arsenal in Cardiff in the Community Shield but is a long way from finalising the squad he will have for the season. Fernández, who played under Maresca atChelsea, remains a target for City, who could still test the water despite missing the deadline.Arsenal open talks with Bayer Leverkusen over deal for Jarell QuansahRead more“For sure there are things we need to do, how many I don’t know, can be one, can be two, depends also if players want to leave, so we can see,” Maresca said on Friday, having suggested City would not agree to Chelsea’s demands. “It’s 48 hours for the final, my first final in this club, I would like to win my first trophy, so my focus isn’t on players that can leave or players that can arrive, my focus is on the game.”City have rejected two bids from Barcelona for Rodri but anticipate a third, and are expected to sell Tijjani Reijnders in the coming days. They are also in the market for reinforcements as they aim to challenge on four fronts. City are close to signing the 18-year-old Morocco internationalAyyoub Bouaddi from Lillebut are willing to bring in others.Rodri, who has a year remaining on his contract, returned to the club on Friday after his holiday which followed a triumphant World Cup, but Maresca would not be drawn on the midfielder’s immediate future with a third Barcelona offer expected.“The transfer window is open, we can buy players, we can sell players, anything can happen. I just saw Rodri now in the building, I gave him a big hug, he looks good, so we’ll see what happens.”Reijnders is set to join the Saudi Pro League side Al-Qadsiah after the two clubs agreed a £51m fee for the Dutchman, who moved to City last summer from Milan but wants more regular playing time.“They all work every day, they all do sessions every day and at the end of the week they all want to play a game,” Maresca said. “When they don’t play they struggle to understand or they struggle to see the reason why, and I can understand that after one season some of them would like to play a little bit more. It’s a normal situation.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJames Trafford has already been sold to Leeds, while Omar Marmoush, Rico Lewis and Savinho are others who spent much of Pep Guardiola’s final season on the periphery and could be sold.Explore more on these topicsManchester CityTransfer windowEnzo MarescaChelseanewsShareReuse this content

title: Arsenal open talks with Bayer Leverkusen over deal for Jarell Quansah | Arsenal | The Guardian
description: Arsenal have opened talks with Bayer Leverkusen over a move for Jarell Quansah as they seek cover for William Saliba and Jurriën Timber
Author: Ed Aarons
Headline: Arsenal have opened talks with Bayer Leverkusen over a move for Jarell Quansah as they seek cover for William Saliba and Jurriën Timber
Content: England's Jarell Quansah holds off Panama’s José Luis Rodríguez at the World Cup.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersView image in fullscreenEngland's Jarell Quansah holds off Panama’s José Luis Rodríguez at the World Cup.Photograph: Dylan Martinez/ReutersArsenalArsenal open talks with Bayer Leverkusen over deal for Jarell QuansahBundesliga club want at least €50m for England defenderGunners remain interested in Aston Villa’s Ezri KonsaEd AaronsFri 14 Aug 2026 06.40 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 14.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArsenal have opened talks withBayer Leverkusenover a move for Jarell Quansah as they intensify efforts to bring in cover for William Saliba and Jurriën Timber.The England defender, who left Liverpool last summerfor an initial £30mand was part of Thomas Tuchel’s World Cup squad, has been identified as an ideal replacement for the France and Netherlands defenders, who will miss the start of the new season due to injury. While Quansah’s preferred position is in central defence, he was also deployed at right-back by Tuchel at the World Cup and was sent off inthe last-16 victory over Mexico.Men’s transfer window summer 2026: all deals from Europe’s top five leaguesRead moreIt is understood that Leverkusen are reluctant to sell the Warrington-born 23-year-old, who signed a five-year deal when he left Anfield last July, and would want at least €50m (£43m).Arsenal– who saw a bid of £30m for Aston Villa’s Ezri Konsa rejected earlier in the window – are not thought to want to pay that much but now could test the German club’s resolve by submitting a similar offer. Liverpool had a €70m buyback option on Quansah but that has now expired.Arsenal are still believed to be interested in Konsa, who also filled in at right-back for England during the World Cup but is better known as a central defender. Villa value the 28-year-old at £60m.Mikel Artetasaid this weekthat Saliba’s back injury would take “some time to heal” and he was unsure about when he would be available again. Arsenal also have concerns over Timber, who pulled out of the Netherlands squad on the eve of the World Cup after failing to recover from a persistent groin injury that forced him to miss most of the run‑in last season.“Jurriën is progressing really well,” Arteta said after Arsenal’s friendly defeat by Borussia ­Dortmund last Sunday. “He’s on the pitch, he’s doing quite a lot right now, but it’s still weeks away. I cannot tell you how much.”Arsenal would still like to sign a new attacker before the end of the window and could allow Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus to depart in order to free up more funds. ­Galatasaray have offered £38m for Martinelli, although the Brazil ­forward has turned down a move to Turkey. Napoli have shown an ­interest in Jesus.Ethan Nwaneri could also be sold, with Milan, Fulham, RB Leipzig and Borussia Dortmund among those who have been linked with the 19-year-old.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe future of Myles Lewis-Skelly is unclear after he wasoffered to Chelsea and Manchester United this week. Arteta refused to address the rumours after he scored in the friendly against Como – managed by Cesc Fábregas – on Wednesday.“I’m not going to talk about speculation,” he said. “If there is speculation about our players, it’s a good sign. That means our players attract attention and are doing a good job.”Explore more on these topicsArsenalBayer LeverkusenEuropean club footballTransfer windownewsShareReuse this content

title: Rangers and the paradox of a painful exit that boosts their trophy chances | Soccer | The Guardian
description: In today’s Football Daily: Rangers book their spot in the Tin Pot playoffs
Author: Rob Smyth
Headline: In today’s Football Daily: Rangers book their spot in the Tin Pot playoffs
Content: Rangers booking their place in the Tin Pot playoffs, earlier.Photograph: Kirk O’Rourke/Rangers FC/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenRangers booking their place in the Tin Pot playoffs, earlier.Photograph: Kirk O’Rourke/Rangers FC/ShutterstockFootball Daily newsletterSoccerRangers and the paradox of a painful exit that boosts their trophy chancesSign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!Rob SmythFri 14 Aug 2026 10.48 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 11.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAND NOW FOR SOME PERSPECTIVEAll new managers want to hit the ground running. But landing with a dull thud has never been a barrier to future glory, certainly not at Ibrox. Take Graeme Souness, whose start as Rangers’ player-manager put the ‘pish’ in ‘inauspicious’. On his league debut, away to Hibs, he was sent off in the first half after a revenge attack on the wrong mullet. Rangers lost 2-1 and were beaten in the third game as well. Graeme out! Rangers won the League Cup and finished the season as champions for the first time in nine years.Dick Advocaat had a similarly awkward start in 1998. In his first game, played at Tranmere’s Prenton Park, Rangers went 3-0 down to Shelbourne in the first leg of their Big Vase tie. They went through comfortably in the end but lost the first league game a few days later.Dic-Advocaat out! Rangers had to settle for a domestic treble that season. Different times, when toys were played with for more than a few seconds before being launched from the pram with maximum force, followed a few seconds later by a handful of freshly sourced excreta. In 2026, alas, hot air and horse pucky are an acceptable substitute for reasonable discourse. And so, after failing to win any of his first four games as Rangers manager, Derek McInnes is “out of his depth” and a “dead man walking”.Que Sera, Sera? Eff that! Turns out the future is ours to see after four games, two of them in a competition Rangers had no chance of winning anyway. Football Daily hasn’t a clue if McInnes is up to the Brobdingnagian challenge of managing Rangers, one that most tea-timely newsletters don’t really understand. But we do know that a culture of self-fulfilling poppycock, where ostentatious negativity is football’s version of the fatberg and many people would rather be right than happy, is a stain on our daily bread.That said, what a roflcopter of a start! Given the events of last season, it was never going to be an equanimity-cultivating experience for a new Rangers manager to see Russell Martin’s start and lower it. Rangers have one point from two league games and are out of Bigger Vase after themost costly 1-1 drawagainst Polish opposition on British soil since Brian Clough called somebody a clown. Paradoxically, the aggregate defeat to Jagiellonia Bialystok – and subsequent drop into Tin Pot – has increased Rangers’ chances of winning a trophy under McInnes. Time will tell whether those chances have increased from 0.0000001% to 0.0000002%, from 9% to 9.4% or from some other figure to some other figure. Right now, the supercomputers know, and the bairns in the prams certainly don’t.LIVE ON BIG WEBSITEJoin Dominic Booth at 8pm BST for live updates on Wolves 2-0 Blackburn in the Championship opener.QUOTE OF THE DAY“If Gianni Infantino doesn’t get re-elected unanimously, then whoever voted against him needs to get their head examined” – Andrew Giuliani, the chief suit of the White House Task Force for the Geopolitics World Cup, emerges from Donald Trump’s fundament to give his view on the Fifa crisis. Alas, Giuliani’s interview with the Athletic didn’t take place atFour Seasons Total Landscaping.View image in fullscreenGianni Infantino doing loads of things that Andrew Giuliani approves of.Composite: Getty, Alamy, Reuters, ShutterstockFOOTBALL DAILY LETTERSdouble quotation markWhen I reflect on the lack of support for my very reasonable case from 1,057 people (Football Daily letters passim), I find consolation in the fact that I won letter o’the day, and none of them did. The Football Daily merch, when it arrives, will have pride of place in the trophy room at Cushion Towers” – Bob Cushion.double quotation markSo Arsenal are looking to spend €30m on Ezri Konsa as defensive cover. Meanwhile, the club I support, Exeter City, don’t have two brass farthings to rub together (ask your dad). Something wrong here” – Dave Hill.double quotation markI will admit to the occasional snigger, but today was the first time in a long time that I’ve actually laughed out loud at a joke in the Fiver – the one about Portugal and Euro 2028. It was a joke, wasn’t it?” – Bill Muskett.double quotation markThat 6ft 4in striker Brian Madjo has a very high ceiling is the most common sense, practical thing about modern football I’ve read in a long time” – Peter Oh.If you have any, please send letters tothe.boss@theguardian.com.Today’s letter o’ the day winner is … Peter Oh, who gets some Football Weekly merch. title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 10: Fulham | Premier League previews 2026-27 | The Guardian
description: With Marco Silva leaving after five years, can the club take advantage of the links their new coach, Álvaro Arbeloa, has with Real Madrid?
Author: John Brewin
Headline: With Marco Silva leaving after five years, can the club take advantage of the links their new coach, Álvaro Arbeloa, has with Real Madrid?
Content: César Palacios has previously worked with Fulham’s new manager Álvaro Arbeloa at Real Madrid. Photograph: Simon Dael/ShutterstockWith Marco Silva leaving after five years, can the club take advantage of the links their new coach, Álvaro Arbeloa, has with Real Madrid?ByJohn BrewinFri 14 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 10.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:15th (NB: this is not necessarily John Brewin’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:11thProspectsMarco Silva cutting the cord after five years by the river came as little surprise. If his time at Craven Cottage was successful in re-establishing Fulham as aPremier Leagueclub, he rarely concealed his ambitions to manage in European competition. He was frequently explicit in his disappointment that the club’s ownership did not meet him halfway by funding a stronger squad. Silva’s powers of rebadging and replenishing talent will be missed now that he has decamped to Benfica. Under him, Fulham played entertaining football, a collection of ugly ducklings showing their renewed worth for a club that, despite falling short of European qualification, looked upwards rather than downwards at the relegation battle. They were often a pleasure to watch, and ornery opposition for all-comers.Álvaro Arbeloa is a very different type of appointment, with far less experience than his predecessor in frontline coaching terms, even if he arrives with Real Madrid on his CV. His arrival, though, has opened up a working relationship with the Spanish aristos, Gonzalo García and César Palacios arriving to work with a coach who helped them through the ranks in Madrid. By little coincidence, all three share the same agency as their representatives. There have been links with Endrick and Thiago Pitarch, two further young Real jewels, leading to a sense ofFulhambecoming some form of Madrileño nursery, a Santiago Bernabéu on Thames. Should that play out, it would represent another sea change.Silva preferred to work with hard-bitten pros. A couple of his leading men, Raúl Jiménez and Harry Wilson, have departed. The latter played the best football of his career last season but, like his manager, got a better offer elsewhere, from Leeds. Fulham’s latest approach is to source young players and polish them up. Can they have the same successes as mid-tier peers such as Brentford, Brighton and Bournemouth, where the approach is far more data-driven? Will supporters be looking upwards rather than downwards? A previously enigmatic club just got more enigmatic.Past five seasonsOff-field pictureIn May, the club were runners-up at the football business awards, for stadium experience, as the Riverside Stand’s opulent hospitality completed its first full season in service. Fulham need the Riverside to deliver as a revenue stream, as financial results for the 2024-25 season showed a pre-tax loss for the year at £44.5m, and that was lowered by the sale of João Palhinha in July 2024. There has been no such windfall since. The Khan family ownership continues to back the club, its overall investment estimated at about £900m, with staff costs at 117% of turnover. Therein lies the reasoning behind Silva not receiving the backing he desired.Owner-fan relationshipThe most expensive season ticket at Craven Cottage comes in at £3,084 for access to the Riverside’s facilities, the highest in the Premier League. Shahid Khan and his son Tony, the vice-chair and director of football operations, are unpopular among committed supporters for price rises and pandering to tourism. Khan’s boat Kismet was named superyacht of the year in 2025, its main salon inspired by the Palace of Versailles, and can be chartered for more than $3m per week. Though the balance sheets confirm Khan’s outlay in funding a continued Premier League status, fans would prefer he recognised not everyone lives the high life.The managerWhere Silva had an unremarkable playing career, Arbeloa featured among the elite, a World Cup and Champions League winner. He also had the ear of Florentino Pérez, the perennial Real Madrid president asking him to replace Xabi Alonso mid-season in the 2025-26 campaign. That did not pan out and he took his first job away from Madrid, where he was a well-regarded youth coach, in south-west London. Khan Sr’s comment that Arbeloa “believes in giving young players a chance” is pertinent for Fulham’s change in direction. Crucially, as befitting traditions at Craven Cottage, the new man from Salamanca believes in open, attacking football, offering some continuity from Silva’s reign.Star signingView image in fullscreenGonzalo García surges forward during Fulham’s Costa del Sol Trophy match against Málaga.Photograph: Joaquin Corchero/AFP7/ShutterstockGonzalo García’s reputation was made by his performances at last summer’s Club World Cup, where he won the tournament’s Golden Boot. Comparisons were made to Raúl, a considerable accolade at the Bernabéu. Goals followed in the Champions League against Juventus and Borussia Dortmund but García eventually lost out to the star system of Vinícius Júnior and Kylian Mbappé. His reputation in Spain is as a hard worker off the ball, necessary for a Premier League player. Last season, Rodrigo Muniz’s injuries meant the old soldier Jiménez shouldered the burden at centre-forward. García is younger and fresher but the hype surrounding his arrival gives him much to live up to.Stat attackFulham had the oldest side in the Premier League last season, which may help explain why they had arguably the least intense press. Marco Silva’s side recorded the fewest high turnovers, which occur when a team recovers the ball to start a new open-play possession sequence in the final 40 metres of the pitch. Real Madrid are hardly known for being a high-pressing side but they comfortably outperformed Fulham on this metric. It will be fascinating to see how Arbeloa approaches this.StatSet for a breakthroughJonah Kusi-Asare’s arrival last summer from Bayern Munich is further mining of a super-club’s youth department. Bayern inserted a buy-back clause for a player they picked up from AIK. The Sweden Under-21s player has been compared to Alexander Isak, and made seven substitute appearances last season – without scoring – before an initial loan became a permanent move. At 6ft 5in he offers a different profile of striker to García. Hayden Mullins, the former under-21 coach now Newport manager, saw the best of Kusi-Asare last season, the 18-year-old scoring five goals in six matches.World Cup impactGarcía made his debut for Spain in a pre-World Cup friendly against Iraq but failed to make the eventual champions’ tournament squad. Antonee Robinson had a fine tournament for the USA until the co-hosts perished in the last 16 at the hands of a Belgium team featuring Timothy Castagne. Luc de Fougerolles, yet to play a Premier League game for Fulham, showed off teenage defensive talents in Canada’s run to the knockouts. To complete a successful quintet – saving the best till last? – Sander Berge had a fine tournament as Norway also reached the quarter-finals.Explore more on these topicsPremier League previews 2026-27FulhamPremier LeaguefeaturesShareReuse this content
