title: Audrey Werro holds off Britain’s Keely Hodgkinson to win European 800m gold | European Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: The Swiss runner set a 1:54.81sec championship best to win European 800m gold, ahead of Keely Hodgkinson in 1:55.01
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: The Swiss runner set a 1:54.81sec championship best to win European 800m gold, ahead of Keely Hodgkinson in 1:55.01
Content: Audrey Werro crosses the finish line to win gold in the women's 800m final at the European Athletics Championships.Photograph: Julian Finney/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAudrey Werro crosses the finish line to win gold in the women's 800m final at the European Athletics Championships.Photograph: Julian Finney/Getty ImagesEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsAudrey Werro holds off Britain’s Keely Hodgkinson to win European 800m goldSwiss runner sets 1:54.81sec championship bestFemke Broeders-Bol secures bronze in 1:55.54Sean Ingleat Alexander Stadium, BirminghamFri 14 Aug 2026 17.16 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 19.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Audrey Werro was a child, she was so painfully shy that her father told her she had to become a lion every time she raced. In a European women’s 800m final for the ages, she followed that advice to the letter.As the 22-year-old Swiss superstar came around the final bend, she could feel Britain’sKeely Hodgkinsonon her shoulder, waiting to strike. The Dutch flyer Femke Broeders-Bol was also close enough to dream too. But Werro was ready to flash her teeth.European Athletics Championships 2026: Werro holds off Hodgkinson for gold in 800m, Hughes takes silver in 200m – liveRead moreIt didn’t matter that she had been spiked by Broeders-Bol after 200m. Or that she had led the pack into the face of a swirling wind for most of the race. She didn’t succumb. She roared.The noise from the full house of 23,000 home fans was deafening as Hodgkinson tried to pass her on the outside. But the gap never closed. Instead Werro took gold in 1min 54.81sec – a time that broke a championship record that had stood since 1982.It left Hodgkinson looking mightily disappointed after running 1:55.01 to take silver, with Broeders-Bol claiming bronze. But the Olympic champion was also gracious in defeat after.“It doesn’t sting because I was beaten by a great athlete,” said Hodgkinson. “I think I put together a pretty good race. I don’t think I did anything wrong. The thing about the 800m is you have a million different ways of going in your head but I covered every move well. I just didn’t have enough.”There was a moment, though, that she did believe. “In that last 50, I thought I had it,” she said. “But she’s a strong athlete.” As for Werro, her smile told the story given that on Thursday lunchtime it appeared she was out of these Championships after being tripped in the semi-finals. “I am really happy with this medal after a crazy 24 hours,” she said. “When I was a child, my dad used to tell me I had to be a lion. So I decided to do a celebration with that when I crossed the line.”Before the final, Hodgkinson had asked the weather gods for no wind to help her bid for a third successive European title. But they had other ideas. It was whippy and blustery throughout.But that didn’t deter Werro, who went to the front early. And as the bell sounded with the clock showing 56.45, the big three began to stretch away. “Audrey wanted to take it on and, with that wind, I was happy to let her,” said Hodgkinson. “We’re all great athletes and I knew it was going to be close.”It was. And that allowed Hodgkinson to be philosophical after. “We’re all going to win some, lose some,” she said. “Shit happens. Audrey fell over yesterday. She’d made it back. I know what that took out of me a few weeks ago. So yeah, incredible for her. And yeah, life goes on. I’ll go back and train and just hope I get it next time.”View image in fullscreenAudrey Werro is all smiles after her 800m success.Photograph: Morgan Harlow/APThat may prove easier said than done given that Werro has run the third, fourth and ninth fastest times in history since June. But only a fool would write the British runner off.There was a second silver medal on the night for Britain in the form of Zharnel Hughes in the men’s 200m. Hughes ran a creditable 20.16, especially given that he has been battling a groin injury. However, he had no answer to the speed of Germany’s Owen Ansah, who powered to victory in 19.95. There was a rare dead heat for bronze between Italy’s Eseosa Fostine Desalu and Switzerland’s Timothé Mumenthaler, who both ran 20.26.However, Ansah’s gold medal was instantly controversial given that last week Germany’s National Anti-Doping Agency had recommended that he should receive a four-year suspension over a possible anti-doping violation.The German authorities claim that is because Ansah missed a test in July. Ansah disputes this. But Hughes will be upgraded to gold if Ansah is banned.Earlier in the night, some of Europe’s biggest stars also shone brightly. First Italy’s Nadia Battocletti added the European 10,000m title to her 5,000m crown with a devastating 28-second burst over the last 200m. Then Norway’s Karsten Warholm ran a championship record time of 46.63 to storm to gold in the men’s 400m hurdles.View image in fullscreenNadia Battocletti crosses the line to win the gold medal in the 10,000 metres final.Photograph: Sona Maleterova/Getty ImagesBut perhaps the sweetest moment of the night came when another Italian star, the high jumper Gianmarco Tamberi, asked the crowd to sing happy birthday to his one-year-old daughter, Camilla, after he leaped 2.32m to win gold. They duly obliged too.But there was little joy for Katarina Johnson-Thompson in the women’s heptathlon. The 33-year-old felt the effects of a calf niggle as she finished day one in 16th place with just 3,644 points – a long way behind the leader Adrianna Sulek-Schubert of Poland on 3,968.Explore more on these topicsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsKeely HodgkinsonAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: British cyclist Finlay Tarling, 19, dies in Volta a Portugal accident | Cycling | The Guardian
description: The British cyclist Finlay Tarling, a 19-year-old rider for the NSN Development Team, has died in a crash during the eighth stage of the Tour of Portugal
Author: Jeremy Whittle
Headline: The British cyclist Finlay Tarling, a 19-year-old rider for the NSN Development Team, has died in a crash during the eighth stage of the Tour of Portugal
Content: Finlay Tarling in action at the Tour of  Britain in 2025.Photograph: Huw Fairclough/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFinlay Tarling in action at the Tour of  Britain in 2025.Photograph: Huw Fairclough/Getty ImagesCyclingBritish cyclist Finlay Tarling, 19, dies in Volta a Portugal accidentTeenager involved in an accident in PortugalRider’s NSN Development Team ‘heartbroken’Jeremy WhittleFri 14 Aug 2026 13.42 EDTFirst published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 12.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFinlay Tarling, the younger brother of Netcompany Ineos rider, Josh Tarling, has been killed while racing in stage eight of the Volta a Portugal.Although the details are yet to be confirmed, reports in the Portugese and French media suggest that the 19-year-old Welsh rider was hit by a non-race vehicle travelling on the course in the opposite direction to the peloton.In a statement, the race organisation said: “The organisers of the Volta a Portugal em Bicicleta, Jogos Santa Casa, deeply regret to announce the death of British cyclist Finlay Tarling, from the NSN Development Team, following a serious accident that occurred during the eighth stage of the race, between Melgaço and Fafe.“At this time of profound sorrow, the organisers of the Volta a Portugal and the PortugueseCyclingFederation extend their deepest condolences to Finlay Tarling’s family, his teammates, the NSN Development Team, and all his friends and loved ones.”Tarling was a highly-rated young talent and time-trialling prospect and had placed third in the under-23 time trial at the British National Championships this summer.His NSN Development Team posted: “We are heartbroken to announce the passing of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal today.”“Fin was a much-loved member of our team but most importantly, he was a son, a brother, and a friend to so many. He will be deeply missed. Our deepest condolences go out to Fin’s parents Michael and Dawn, his brother Josh, and everyone who was lucky enough to call Fin a friend. Rest in peace, Fin.”Finlay Tarling’s progression had been through track and road racing. He joined the then Israel-Premier Tech Academy prior to 2025. He continued with the team after it was rebranded as the NSN Development Team for 2026, and, developing a reputation in European racing as a time trial specialist, finished 11th in the opening prologue stage of the Portugese race in Lisbon.The eighth stage, of 166.8 kilometres from Melgaco to Fafe, was neutralised with 23 kilometres to race, following Tarling’s death and the podium ceremony cancelled. His teammates rode together to the finish line in a show of solidarity.In a post on X, cycling’s governing body, the UCI, said it was “deeply saddened by the tragic death of British rider Finlay Tarling, who passed away following a serious accident during today’s eighth stage of the Volta a Portugal.”The Portugal prime minister Luís Montenegro also expressed his condolences to Tarling’s family and team, adding on X that the news of his death “leaves us deeply shaken.”Stephen Park CBE, the performance director for the Great Britain cycling team, said: “All of us at British Cycling are heartbroken to learn of the tragic passing of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal. Fin was a talented rider with a fantastic future ahead of him, a loyal teammate and an all-round brilliant young man.“Our deepest sympathies are with his parents and brother, Josh at this tragic time.”Explore more on these topicsCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Concern grows as British Athletics coach Leon Baptiste vanishes on trip to Morocco | European Athletics Championships | The Guardian
description: The coach and former international sprinter has not been seen for two months, with one former teammate calling the situation ‘very worrying’
Author: Sean Ingle
Headline: The coach and former international sprinter has not been seen for two months, with one former teammate calling the situation ‘very worrying’
Content: Leon Baptiste with a coaching award at 2023’s Sporting Equals ceremony. He won two golds at the 2010 Commonwealth Games.Photograph: John Phillips/Getty Images for Sporting EqualsView image in fullscreenLeon Baptiste with a coaching award at 2023’s Sporting Equals ceremony. He won two golds at the 2010 Commonwealth Games.Photograph: John Phillips/Getty Images for Sporting EqualsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsConcern grows as British Athletics coach Leon Baptiste vanishes on trip to MoroccoFormer international sprinter not seen for two monthsSituation ‘very worrying’, says former teammateSean IngleFri 14 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 18.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMystery surrounds a highly regarded BritishAthleticscoach who has not been heard from since visiting Morocco around two months ago.Leon Baptiste, 41, who coaches a number of elite athletes including the Paris Olympic 4x400m relay bronze medallist Charlie Dobson, is believed to have gone to Morocco for the weekend with some close friends for a stag do or golf trip.Seb Coe insists empty seats in Birmingham won’t harm London’s bid for 2029 worldsRead moreHowever, he has not been heard from since by his athletes or the UK Athletics officials who pay him as a Loughborough-based consultant, with messages to his phone not returned.UKA have declined to comment, citing confidentiality. The Guardian spoke to a former British teammate of Baptiste, who said: “He was a very calm and sensible chap, in my experience. No one knows what has happened. It is very worrying.”Dobson has struggled with injuries in Baptiste’s absence and failed to make it out of the 400m semi-finals at the European championships in Birmingham earlier this week.After finishing fourth in his semi-final in a time of 45.18sec, over a second outside his personal best of 44.14 set last year, Dobson alluded to the situation when he said it had been “an interesting eight weeks”.He also said he had been struggling with some injury niggles that had contributed to his withdrawal from the recent Commonwealth Games. He did not compete in the heats of the men’s 4x400m on Friday morning and it remains to be seen if he returns to the track for Sunday evening’s final.In the meantime UKA staff have stepped in to help Dobson and the rest of Baptiste’s group, with former European 400m champion and relays coach Martyn Rooney taking Dobson under his wing.Baptiste was a talented sprinter who won 200m and 4x100m relay gold at the 2010 Commonwealth Games in Delhi before being forced to retire aged 28 because of a serious knee issue.View image in fullscreenLeon Baptiste (left) wins the 200m final at the 2010 Commonwealth Games.Photograph: Suzanne Plunkett/ReutersSurgery resulted in him missing the London 2012 Olympics before he moved into coaching after deciding not to defend his Commonwealth titles at the 2014 Games in Glasgow.“As much as I am sprinting and progressing, my body has never fully recovered from my knee surgery,” he said that year. “My coach and I feel that Glasgow Commonwealth Games qualification is a tall order – so the time has come for my focus to move elsewhere.“The decision for an athlete to retire is never easy, but in essence the decision has been made for me.”The British Embassy in Rabat has been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsEuropean Athletics ChampionshipsAthleticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Arsenal in talks over Quansah; transfer news; Giuliani slams Infantino’s critics: football – as it happened | Championship | The Guardian
description: All latest from the football world, including a look ahead to the EFL season, transfer deals and some huge news at Liverpool
Author: Dominic Booth
Headline: All latest from the football world, including a look ahead to the EFL season, transfer deals and some huge news at Liverpool
Content: 12.02 EDTLiverpool confirm £1.65bn stake in club sold to consortium including BezosLiverpool’s owner, Fenway Sports Group, has confirmed it has agreed the sale of 30% of the club to a consortium including Amit Bhatia, the Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and the Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin. The deal is understood to be worth £1.65bn, valuing Liverpool at £5.5bn, and will see Bhatia become the club’s new vice-chair on an expanded board.Bhatia, the son-in-law of Indian steel magnate Lakshmi Mittal, initiated and led talks with FSG on behalf of the 1892 Holdings consortium, a reference to Liverpool’s founding year. The former co-owner of Queens Park Rangers has received financial backing from the Mittal Family Trust, the K5 Sports fund, of which Bezos is the lead investor, and EE Capital, the family office of Elaine and Eduardo Saverin.FSG president Mike Gordon said: “Liverpool has always been built by thinking beyond one season and making decisions with the club’s long-term interests in mind. That approach continues to attract interest from respected investors and business leaders around the world.”Here’s the full story from Andy Hunter:Liverpool owners seal £1.65bn sale of 30% stake to consortium that includes Jeff BezosRead moreLiverpool’s US owner John W. title: No 1 pick Fernando Mendoza throws for touchdown in Las Vegas Raiders preseason debut | Las Vegas Raiders | The Guardian
description: Top overall draft pick Fernando Mendoza threw a touchdown pass in his first Raiders preseason game on Thursday night
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Top overall draft pick Fernando Mendoza threw a touchdown pass in his first Raiders preseason game on Thursday night
Content: Las Vegas Raiders quarterback Fernando Mendoza throws against the Arizona Cardinals during the first half of Thursday’s preseason game.Photograph: John Locher/APView image in fullscreenLas Vegas Raiders quarterback Fernando Mendoza throws against the Arizona Cardinals during the first half of Thursday’s preseason game.Photograph: John Locher/APLas Vegas RaidersNo 1 pick Fernando Mendoza throws for touchdown in Las Vegas Raiders preseason debutHeisman winner finishes 10 of 16 for 97 yardsArizona beat Las Vegas 27-14 on Thursday nightLove rushes for 58 yards in Cardinals debutAgenciesThu 13 Aug 2026 23.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNo 1 draft pick Fernando Mendoza threw a touchdown pass in his preseason debut for the Las Vegas Raiders in a 27-14 loss to theArizona Cardinalson Thursday night.The Heisman Trophy winner led one touchdown drive for the Raiders (1-0) in four series – not including a kneel-down at the end of the first half – and finished 10 of 16 for 97 yards and a six-yard TD pass to Jack Bech.Mendoza became the first top overall draft selection to throw a touchdown pass in his first preseason game since 2018 when Cleveland’s Baker Mayfield had two against the New York Giants.Mendoza barely missed a second touchdown pass in the fourth quarter, throwing beyond the reach of Deven Thompkins. But Mendoza also was sharp at times, threading a 19-yard pass in the second quarter between three defenders to fellow rookie Malik Benson.The expected rematch of college football national championship quarterbacks didn’t happen because the Cardinals (1-1) decided not to play Carson Beck, who has sore ribs. Mendoza led Indiana to a 27-21 victory over Beck and Miami in the title game in January.Raiders pass rusher Maxx Crosby also did not play, which wasn’t completely unexpected after coach Klint Kubiak said Tuesday that his playing status was to be determined. Crosby, who underwent knee surgery in January, has participated in training camp.Teammate Jermod McCoy, who hasn’t played in nearly two years because of a torn ACL, played with the second-team defense at cornerback. He was the primary defender on two Cardinals touchdowns.Each team’s starting quarterback played one series, both resulting in touchdowns.Las Vegas’ Kirk Cousins was 5 of 6 for 50 yards and a 13-yard touchdown pass to Michael Mayer. Arizona’s Jacoby Brissett completed all five passes for 44 yards and a seven-yard TD to Marvin Harrison Jr.Brissett and former Raider Gardner Minshew combined to go 15 of 15 for 123 yards and three touchdowns in the first half to build a 21-14 lead. That string of completions extended 16 early in the second half before Minshew finally threw an incomplete pass on a rollout to the right.Rookie Jeremiyah Love, drafted third overall by the Cardinals, made his preseason debut and rushed for 58 yards on 11 carries.Explore more on these topicsLas Vegas RaidersNFLArizona CardinalsUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: As online dating goes into ‘salvage mode’, can AI solve all its problems? | Online dating | The Guardian
description: Dating apps such as Bumble forced to adapt as ‘swipe fatigue’ grows
Author: Amelia Hill
Headline: Dating apps such as Bumble forced to adapt as ‘swipe fatigue’ grows
Content: Bumble has abandoned its proposition that women make the first move, and is about to ditch the swipe. Photo posed by modelPhotograph: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBumble has abandoned its proposition that women make the first move, and is about to ditch the swipe. Photo posed by modelPhotograph: Getty ImagesOnline datingAs online dating goes into ‘salvage mode’, can AI solve all its problems?Dating apps such as Bumble forced to adapt as ‘swipe fatigue’ growsAmelia HillFri 14 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 12.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBumble was supposed to be different. When it launched in 2014, it offered women a simple proposition: if you matched with a man, you had to make the first move. The rule was meant to make online dating safer and less intimidating, while giving women control over who got to speak first.This week, Bumble abandoned it.The change follows the introduction of Opening Moves, which had already softened the original rule, and comes as Bumble prepares to abandon another defining feature: the swipe.The company says it is responding to changing user behaviour and wants to encourage more meaningful connections.But there is another way of reading the changes.Bumble was created to fix what many saw as Tinder’s chaotic and aggressive hookup culture by shifting the power dynamic entirely to women. Now it is dismantling those features. And it is not alone. Across the dating-app industry, the swipe-and-match model that transformed how people met is being quietly reworked while companies race to put artificial intelligence at the centre of whatever comes next.“Bumble is in salvage mode,” says Luke Brunning, a philosopher who studies the ethics of technology and relationships. “They’ve already reorganised, restructured and cut jobs in response to declining revenue. This risky, standout pivot suggests they’re wondering how, despite all that, to keep going.”The number of Bumble’s paying users fell sharply over the past year and its share price has been under sustained pressure. The company cut about 30% of its workforce this year.“It’s going to be fascinating to see whether they can weather it,” Brunning says. “But they’re not alone: a lot of the major players are also in salvage mode, trying to figure out how to position themselves in a market that is increasingly fed up with them.”Brunning’s research shows dating apps are now often used grudgingly, because people feel that they are necessary, rather than with the excitement that accompanied their rise.The online dating industry, estimated to be worth almost £10bn globally, is keenly aware of this. Its solution? To go full AI.Grindr – seen as a testbed for the wider industry – is transitioning into an “AI-first” platform. Tinder is testing Chemistry, an AI-powered system intended to reduce “swipe fatigue”. Bumble has been developing an AI matchmaking assistant called Bee.Other startups are dispensing with swiping altogether. London-based Fate describes itself as an “agentic AI dating app”: instead of browsing profiles, users are interviewed by an AI about what they want from relationships to find similarities with potential partners.So why aren’t we talking about being on the brink of a brave new world of dating apps, where AI will successfully sift the candidates to find our one true love? Why, instead, is the debate about whether the apps will even survive?Adam Peacock, a researcher of technology and intimacy, thinks the issue is that the industry is misreading what people are objecting to.“There’s a kind of emerging cultural backlash against allowing AI into our intimate lives as well as the additional concern that someone you’re talking to on these apps, is actually filtering the whole conversation through an AI concierge,” he says.Peacock says gen Z in particular are concerned as to whether dating apps are even being designed to make good connections between users but are, instead, opaquely tweaked to monetise the time users spend on the site. That, in a cynical twist, the apps are deliberately profiting from keeping people lonely.“The dating industry has turned intimacy into an enormous source of data,” Peacock says. “Dating apps can know where people live, what they look like, who they are attracted to, what they say to potential partners and, increasingly, how they behave.”Elsa Kugelberg, a philosopher who researches gender and relationships, says online dating has become too embedded in modern life to fail. But the first generation of dating apps – the era of the profile, the swipe, the match and the message – may be reaching its end.Peacock thinks the apps may evolve into something broader: “More of a social media, lifestyle product than a dedicated dating app.”But the question is whether any iteration of dating app will make the experience better, or whether the extra layers of AI will simply function as a temporary facade on an exhausted model.Brunning believes AI on dating apps doesn’t have to be like this. “There can be ways of trying to do digital better, that doesn’t involve giving people AI tools to talk to each other with,” he says.Better moderation, clearer policies, better ways of presenting yourself and more control over how the environment works could all improve online dating without handing more of it to machines, he says.The critical point is this, he says: “You can’t just take a product that’s out of favour, put AI on top of it and say: ‘OK, now we have a product that works.’”Explore more on these topicsOnline datingDatingAppsInternet safetyAI (artificial intelligence)featuresShareReuse this content

title: A Queensland man enjoyed soaring profits from a crypto trading app. Then his money started disappearing | Scams | The Guardian
description: The administrative work required to run an effective investment scam has been drastically cut by using merging technology
Author: Ima Caldwell
Headline: The administrative work required to run an effective investment scam has been drastically cut by using merging technology
Content: One Queensland man lost more than $166,000 to an investment scam constructed by AI.Photograph: Thomas Trutschel/Photothek/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOne Queensland man lost more than $166,000 to an investment scam constructed by AI.Photograph: Thomas Trutschel/Photothek/Getty ImagesScamsA Queensland man enjoyed soaring profits from a crypto trading app. Then his money started disappearingThe administrative work required to run an effective investment scam has been drastically cut by using merging technologyGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastIma CaldwellFri 14 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWithin days of clicking on an online ad for a cryptocurrency trading app, a 29-year-old Queensland man watched his dashboard soar with profits.Making investment gains was as simple as downloading the slick-looking app and browser extension linked to his crypto wallet. So he invested more.Then the losses began. Unauthorised transfers started flowing from his crypto wallet and soon he had lost more than $166,000.Frantic, he attempted to contact customer support, only to find the platform’s customer service team was a basic chatbot.It was only then he realised he had fallen victim to an investment scamconstructed by artificial intelligence.‘Scam ecosystems’Data fromScamwatchshows Australians have lost more than $45m to fraudulent investment schemes in 2026 so far, after over $160m in reported losses in 2025.Experts say AI is significantly cutting the administrative work required to run an effective investment scam, replacing cold calls and isolated phishing emails with entire “scam ecosystems”.Dr Marco Navone, an associate professor of finance at the University of Technology Sydney says traditional red flags no longer apply, meaning consumer can’t always recognise the “industrial-grade” deception.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“Criminal networks can now deploy hyper-realistic, localised media, fake news articles, synthetic reviews … at scale,” Navone says. “[Historically], your first suspicion came from a cheap webpage, or a company phone number that was a mobile number instead of a 1300.“All these small inconsistencies are now gone … this is especially the case when scammers target vulnerable parts of the population.”The Australian Federal Police say scammers can clone voices from a few seconds of audio, generate convincing deepfakes and send thousands of personalised messages based on a victim’s location and online history. AI-generated investment scams often offer access to a “financial adviser” with an Australian or English accent.Regulators can’t keep upWhile the Australian Securities and Investments Commission deactivated nearly 12,000 scam websites in 2025, scammers frequently bypass removal using “cloaking” technology to serve scams to targeted users while showing harmless content to moderators.Cybercrime groups now integrate AI into almost every operational phase, says Dr Andrew Childs, a criminology lecturer at Griffith University.“Offenders can construct an entire environment where each element verifies another,” he says.Digital platforms share responsibility, he says: “In these situations platforms aren’t being passive hosts.“They are actively recommending and distributing advertisements to audiences identified as likely to engage with them.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNavone says digital platforms should be held legally responsible and be mandated to verify Australian Financial Services (AFS) licensing before publishing investment ads.A 2026 report by the Australian Institute of criminology found that more than 49% of Australians worry about becoming victims of AI-related crime, with 43% identifying AI impersonation as a direct threat.Shifting defence to the financial systemAn AFP spokesperson acknowledged that fund recovery rates remain “incredibly low”, referring to a national scams prevention framework being developed. It will require banks, telecommunications providers and digital platforms to bolster AI scam detection.Experts are calling for more money monitoring, including mandatory confirmation-of-payee systems, forced settlement delays on high-risk transfers and stricter oversight of physical cryptocurrency ATMs.Navone says AI itself becomes a target for social engineering.“Over the coming years, we expect consumers and institutions to increasingly delegate financial decisions, portfolio management and trade execution to autonomous AI agents,” he says. “This introduces a dangerous new frontier: AI tools themselves becoming the targets of social engineering and financial scams.”How to spot an AI-generated investment scamAlways check that an investment provider holds an active AFS licence on theAsic register.If contacted about transferring funds, even by someone you know, call them back directly on the phone number you have for them.Navigate to investment platforms using an independent web search rather than clicking links in ads or messages. You should also check if there are any scam warnings in the search results.If compromised, freeze your bank accounts immediately, change all your passwords, and report it toScamwatchandpolice. Victims can contactIDCAREfor free national identity and cybercrime support.Explore more on these topicsScamsAI (artificial intelligence)Crime - AustraliaCryptocurrenciesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alien: Isolation 2 – another strong female protagonist stalked in a terrifying new world | Games | The Guardian
description: Creative Assembly could strike gold again with this follow-up to their fan-favourite, film-inspired game … if you’re brave enough to venture outdoors
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Creative Assembly could strike gold again with this follow-up to their fan-favourite, film-inspired game … if you’re brave enough to venture outdoors
Content: ‘The player and the alien are going to have to adapt to survive’ … Alien: Isolation 2.Photograph: SegaView image in fullscreen‘The player and the alien are going to have to adapt to survive’ … Alien: Isolation 2.Photograph: SegaSummer games previewsGamesAlien: Isolation 2 – another strong female protagonist stalked in a terrifying new worldCreative Assembly could strike gold again with this follow-up to their fan-favourite, film-inspired game … if you’re brave enough to venture outdoorsGraeme MasonFri 14 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlien: Isolationredefined Alien games on its release in 2014, bringing the original taut, haunted house theme of thefirst movieto fans who had mostly been fed action-packed shooters. Cowering under desks and inside lockers wasn’t a new thing; being hunted by an intelligent and lethal xenomorph that could spring down from a duct at any moment was.“I was thinking about what we could do for a sequel while we were still finishing the first game,” reveals Creative Assembly’s Alistair Hope, creative lead on Alien: Isolation and its sequel. “But we didn’t actually start the project until around the time of the 10th anniversary. We’ve seen the response grow over time, watching [Alien: Isolation] continue to find new players, even though it’s a relatively old game. And they’re surprised there isn’t a sequel.”Details are slight, but here’s what we know so far: a Weyland-Yutani survey team discovers a crashed vessel on a planet that resembles LV-426 crossed with a windswept forest. It’s a vessel that’ll appear familiar to fans of Alien: Isolation – it’s the part of Sevastopol that the duplicitous Marshal Waits jettisons from the station in the first game, with Amanda Ripley and the alien inside. Ripley escapes. The alien does not. Until now.“We were super proud of Amanda. She’s really important to the Alien: Isolation experience. But we wanted to tell a new story, in a new location, and to do that, it felt like we needed a new protagonist,” says Hope. That new character is Blake, although Hope is tight-lipped on any details beyond her employer, Weyland-Yutani. It seems likely, however, that this new lead, thrust into the dangerous world of the xenomorph, will follow the IP’s tradition of strong female characters.View image in fullscreen‘We’ve been effectively training it to hunt in the exterior’ … Alien: Isolation 2.Photograph: SegaA fascinating part ofAlien: Isolation 2will be how the alien reacts to its new environment. “The alien uses its senses to track you down, and it’s very effective in those interior spaces. So we’ve been effectively training it to hunt in the exterior. Those core survival skills that you needed in the first game will be the same – but the player and the alien are going to have to adapt to survive.” That’s not to say Alien: Isolation 2 won’t have plenty of claustrophobic interiors, creating a seesaw of emotions whether trapped inside or exposed outside. “We can play with that, and mess with it. It feels like a really exciting opportunity.”Carcass Clad: stifling tank combat promises tension, terror and surprising laughsRead moreTaking place months after the events of Alien: Isolation, the sequel will retain the low-fi sci-fi universe, leaning heavily once more on the first Alien movie. There’s a glimpse of a Working Joe in the trailer, suggesting that, once again, the alien might not be the only antagonist the player has to avoid. Could hostile humans enter the mix? Hope is guarded. “Alien: Isolation 2 absolutely is building on that core foundation that we established in the first [game],” he says. “And, yeah, we love that rock, paper, scissors setup and scenario.” Draw your own acid blood-spattered conclusions.Sevastopol, the decommissioned and slowly decaying space station of Alien: Isolation, became an evocative extra character in the original game. Creative Assembly appears well placed to repeat the trick with Alien: Isolation 2’s forbidding colony world, home to a remote Weyland-Yutani outpost, Kurosaki Station. Just don’t forget your umbrella.Alien: Isolation 2 is coming soon to PC, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S and Nintendo Switch 2.Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsAlienShooting gamesAction gamesAdventure gamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Donald Trump’s spying on leftwing groups recalls J Edgar Hoover’s Cointelpro | Kenneth Roth | The Guardian
description: The FBI from the 1950s to the 1970s tried to infiltrate and discredit leftist organizations. Trump seems to be repeating that sordid practice
Author: Kenneth Roth
Headline: The FBI from the 1950s to the 1970s tried to infiltrate and discredit leftist organizations. Trump seems to be repeating that sordid practice
Content: ‘This latest Trump abuse shows the importance of continuing to stand up to his lawless vision of his presidency.’Photograph: Alex Brandon/APView image in fullscreen‘This latest Trump abuse shows the importance of continuing to stand up to his lawless vision of his presidency.’Photograph: Alex Brandon/APOpinionTrump administrationDonald Trump’s spying on leftwing groups recalls J Edgar Hoover’s CointelproKenneth RothThe FBI from the 1950s to the 1970s tried to infiltrate and discredit leftist organizations. Trump seems to be repeating that sordid practiceFri 14 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 13.17 EDTShareIt is bad enough that the Trump administrationblockeda federal criminalinvestigationwhen an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent killed Renee Good as she was turning her carawayfrom him in Minneapolis the past January. Just before the shooting, Good and her partner had been observing andprotestingagainst ICE officers.Instead, it turns out the administration has beeninvestigatingprogressive and evenmainstreamgroups that have been involved in protests against Donald Trump’s sweeping deportations, according to newly released government documents.That Trump’s deportations have prompted widespread outrage is hardly surprising. The president arguably had an electoral mandate to secure the US-Mexican border butnotto raid workplaces and neighborhoods to deport undocumented immigrants.We are US civil rights lawyers. Trump’s policies have driven us to seek justice internationally | Thomas Becker and Antonio RomanucciRead moreMostsuch immigrants in the United States are now settled. They have been in the country for more than five years, and many have US-citizen children, work at regular jobs, pay taxes and are active members of their communities. Few Americans want their neighbors or work colleagues summarily deported.In January, Minnesota was a center of Trump’s deportation efforts. He deployed about3,000federal agents to this blue state to comb the streets in search of immigrants to deport. The public soon took to the streets in opposition, with some protesters using their phones to record detentions while others sounded thealarmthat Trump’s agents were in the vicinity.Yet rather than conduct an inquiry into the deportation agents’ often-unbridledviolence, the administration turned its prosecutorial sights on the protesters. In what it called “Operation Puppet Master”, it used its enormous investigative powers to pursue a vendetta against an array of groups that opposed its deportation agenda.Federal investigators justified the investigation by claiming that these groups might have provided help and money to theallegedly“violent opportunists and agitators” on the street. They also claimed that these groups provided “domestic terrorist financing”. This language parallels Trump’sdirectivelast September expanding the definition of domestic terrorism to include using violence or intimidation to obstruct the rule of law.Even if violence or other lawlessness occasionally broke out among the protesters, it is a huge leap to suggest that civic groups were criminally complicit. Federal conspiracy law is broad but not limitless. Itrequirestwo or more people to agree to commit a federal crime and for the accused to be a part of that agreement.It would hardly be surprising that various progressive groups banded together to monitor and oppose Trump’s deportations. But those activities are protected by the first amendment to the US constitution. They are completely lawful.For the Trump administration to transform coordinated protests into a criminalconspiracy, it would have to show that the targeted groups knew the protests wouldobstructfederal agents “by force, intimidation or threat” and that such criminality was a purpose of their coordination. That is an enormous stretch.double quotation markTrump’s criminal hounding of groups that oppose him shows no deference to the requirements of justiceThe role of federal prosecutor is powerful. A prosecutor can destroy a target’s life with the reputational sting and financial burden of a criminal prosecution. Before I joined Human Rights Watch, I served for more than four years in the 1980s as a federal prosecutor, mainly in New York City. My experience was that most federal prosecutors were aware of their power and tried to wield it in good faith.Trump’s criminal hounding of groups that oppose him shows no such deference to the requirements of justice.The first warning sign was that the Trump administration didn’t even use the justice department or its FBI, which traditionally pursue criminal investigations. Even though Trump hasdecimatedthe department, sparking the departure of many career officials who refused to be tainted bythe president’spersonal vendettas and politicized prosecutions, the administration chose instead to deploy the Department of Homeland Security.The DHS in turn issued administrative subpoenas, which donotrequire judicial authorization, and used other intrusive techniques to collect records and wire transfers from certain progressive groups going backthreeyears – long before the anti-deportation protests began. That suggests what prosecutors refer to as afishing expedition– the abuse of prosecutorial powers, in the absence of concrete evidence of wrongdoing, in the blind hope that something untoward might surface.Undercover federal investigators alsospiedon public meetings and even infiltrated group chats on Signal as activists discussed protests and their political opinions. Agentsrecordedlicense plate numbers to determine who was attending protest meetings.For example, at a 31 January meeting in a Minneapolis library, a homeland security undercover officerlistenedas supporters of a progressive climate group, the Sunrise Movement, discussed sit-ins, de-escalation tactics, and “having a police liaison and safety marshal present during events”. The agent at least had the honesty toreportback that the Sunrise Movement organization focused on “peaceful” protests.However, the Trump administration hascharged15 people with obstructing federal immigration operations in Minnesota using vehicles and other objects. The 94-page indictment does notallegeinjuries to specific ICE officers or serious violence, butassertsthat activists set up blockades around government buildings, threw chunks of ice at federal vehicles and “stalked” agents. Similar charges in parallel cases have already been dismissed or dropped at anunusually high rate.So far,noneof the groups under investigation has been criminally charged, but prosecutors showed a grand jury a PowerPointslideclaiming that 18 groups were part of a conspiracy to impede Trump’s deportation agents in Minnesota.The broad investigation brings back memories of a prior example of egregious federal misconduct targeting perceived leftist groups. Under the notorious J Edgar Hoover, the FBI from the 1950s to the 1970s conductedCointelproto infiltrate and discredit leftist organizations, especially those that promoted Black civil rights or opposed the Vietnam war. Exposure of these outrages led to majorreforms, which the Trump administration now seems determined to reverse.Many hope that the coming midterm elections in November will repudiate Trump’s lawlessness. Republicans are at risk of losing one or both houses of Congress. Yet this apparent abuse of criminal investigative powers reminds us that the presidency is powerful even without the legislative power of Congress.Fortunately, the judicial system has managed tohaltmuch of Trump’s deportation overreaching. Even grand juries, which traditionally show enormous deference to prosecutors, have beenrejectingrequests to bring charges. Moreover, while politicized federal prosecutors have ignored much of the misconduct by Trump’s deportation agents, some state prosecutors havetriedto pick up the ball.Yet much remains to be done as Trump seems determined to find ways toevadeeven adverse supreme court judgments. Exposure by journalists, protests by civic groups and outrage by the public are often the only tools we have.Responding to the Trump administration’s misconduct, Unidos MN, a human rights group in Minnesota,saidthat the government is “lashing out desperately in hopes of intimidating people and organizations that have shown the power of communities acting together”. This latest Trump abuse shows the importance of continuing to stand up to his lawless vision of his presidency.Kenneth Roth is a Guardian US columnist, a senior fellow at Yale University and a former executive director of Human Rights Watch. title: Donald Trump can’t beat Iran and Nigel Farage can only beat a bin. When it counts, these populists are just losers | Jonathan Freedland | The Guardian
description: The pattern in the US and Britain is clear. They serve up stunt after stunt to mask incompetence and the betrayal of all those who trusted them, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Author: Jonathan Freedland
Headline: The pattern in the US and Britain is clear. They serve up stunt after stunt to mask incompetence and the betrayal of all those who trusted them, says Guardian columnist Jonathan Freedland
Content: Nigel Farage at CPAC in London, July 2026, and Donald Trump at CPAC in Maryland, February 2025.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenNigel Farage at CPAC in London, July 2026, and Donald Trump at CPAC in Maryland, February 2025.Composite: Getty ImagesOpinionDonald TrumpDonald Trump can’t beat Iran and Nigel Farage can only beat a bin. When it counts, these populists are just losersJonathan FreedlandThe pattern in the US and Britain is clear. They serve up stunt after stunt to mask incompetence and the betrayal of all those who trusted themFri 14 Aug 2026 12.03 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 12.59 EDTShareIt’s a shame Nigel Farageducked the announcementof his victory in the Clacton byelection, which confirmed his return as MP for the seat he had needlessly resigned from just a few weeks earlier. You’d have thought he would have loved it. It was the culmination of a stunt, an exercise in politics as performance. It was a display animated by – and seeking to inflame – grievance, a million miles away from the hard, grinding work of tackling the problems that underlie those grievances. It was an attempt to deflect scrutiny, distract attention and evade responsibility. It was, in other words, everything nationalist populists like him excel at. Indeed, the only thing.Reform UK said Farage stayed away because Essex police had warned of a “credible threat” to his security, a claim swiftly denied by Essex police. (Add a flexible approach to the truth to that list of nationalist populists’ talents.) Still, it was a slightly odd claim to make. Recall Farage’s favoured explanation – there are others – for the undeclared £5m gift he received from the Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne, which prompted the very parliamentary investigation that so riled the Reform leader he felt compelled to quit his seat and seek a preemptive not guilty verdict from the people of Clacton: namely, that he needed the money to pay for private, enhanced security. It seems £5m was not quite enough to ensure the lucky recipient would be safe standing next to a man dressed as a bin.Unless, maybe, security was not the whole story. Farage also said he skipped the count because he didn’t want to be “demeaned and humiliated by nobodies”. Quite right. If Nigel Farage is to be demeaned and humiliated, it should be by people of standing. As it happens, he may get his wish. Now that he’s an MP again, the probe into the multiple financial questions that surround him, including over the undeclared support he received from the convicted fraudster George Cottrell,has resumed. A finding against him could necessitate yet another byelection, except this time the major parties will not repeat their boycott and he will have to do battle with opponents even more formidable than an aristocratic trash can.Naturally, Farage regards the likes of Count Binface and Baron von Thunderclap as beneath him, perhaps because it would be painful to admit the crucial thing they all have in common. To understand what that is, look no further than the man who is both Farage’s hero and the exemplar of nationalist populism.Ten years ago, less than five months after the Brexit referendum that represents Farage’s greatest triumph, Donald Trump rode a similar wave of US discontent with the status quo and did it in a similar way – by railing against an ill-defined establishment that had ruined everything. A vote for him would make it all better because, as Trump put it: “I alone can fix it.” In 2024, he was elected once again, on a similar promise.That victory proved Trump’s mastery of a certain strain of politics. His gift for seizing public attention, for channelling a society’s collective anxieties and for persuading people that a simple remedy is at hand, is unrivalled. While Farage plays the same tunes, Trump is the virtuoso.And yet, look at what happens once the carnival of the campaign is over and the governing begins. Trump’s record is disastrous. He was elected to tackle inflation, which he claimed was out of control under Joe Biden, butinflation is higher nowthan it was in November 2024, when he defeated his predecessor.Petrol prices, the indicator Trump repeatedly invoked on the stump in 2024, have leapt up. This, more than any other single factor, helps explain whyTrump’s approval ratingshave cratered, falling to just 34%.And yet Trump, whose appeal centred on his persona as a successful businessman – a persona that held, despite a career of failure and serial bankruptcy – is doing almost nothing to improve the economic fortunes of those who voted for him. I don’t mean that he’s trying to pull various policy levers and they’re not working. I mean he’s not trying. As Jonathan Swan, co-author of Regime Change, an eye-popping account of the first 15 months of this second Trump term,told me for the Politics Weekly Americapodcast: “He’s bored by economic policy.”Of course, those petrol prices did not rise all by themselves. What drove up the price of oil was the decision that seems set to define this presidency: the war on Iran that began on 28 February. It has proved a calamity. It has failed to achieve any of the admittedly shifting goals Trump declared for it: there has been no regime change in Tehran; Iran’s nuclear threat remains unchecked, while its nuclear ambition is now surely greater, if only to deter a repeat of that US-Israeli attack. And it has barely set back Iran’s conventional capability, judging by the regime’s continuing ability to strike its neighbours. As if all that were not bad enough, Trump has succeeded in making the Iranians stronger than they were on 27 February, by handing them an economic weapon of mass disruption, a chokehold on the global economy in the form of their control of thestrait of Hormuz.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMillions of US tax dollars sent to rightwing European thinktanks. Did any Trump supporters vote for that? | Arwa MahdawiRead moreTrump can do the performance, claiming to have “obliterated” the enemy one moment or to have made a breakthrough peace deal the next – but performance is all it is. While the Iranian missiles keep coming, the US military is fast running out of the munitions it needs either to intercept or hit back. Trump’s top general warned him of this danger from the start, but Trumpwaved away those objections, convinced that the war would be over quickly. Trump’s gut told him that Iran would go the way of Venezuela, that it would be fast and easy. His gut was wrong.It keeps happening the same way. Trump will announce an agreement with Iran or between Hamas and Israel, only for it rapidly to become clear thatno deal has been done. Trump lacks the patience for the long, painstaking, detailed work such diplomacy requires. He wants the sugar-rush of a social-media post or a headline. Put simply, he is a maestro of politics as it is now conducted, but he is useless at governing.In this, the nationalist populists who take their lead from Trump are no different. They are good at raging at how things are, but incapable of making them better. They can articulate resentment and exploit grievance, but they cannot cure the ills that fuel that unhappiness. This, ultimately, is what unites Farage with Trump and indeed with those 33 “nobodies” who fought the byelection in Clacton. They are all protest candidates. It’s just that some of them get elected.Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionNigel FarageUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: I’m a neuroscientist. Here’s why our brains need pop concerts | Bala Subramaniam | The Guardian
description: Attending a Nick Jonas show with my kids was an invitation to experience ‘collective effervescence’ – a healing, shared experience
Author: Bala Subramaniam
Headline: Attending a Nick Jonas show with my kids was an invitation to experience ‘collective effervescence’ – a healing, shared experience
Content: ‘Bizarrely, it was Nick Jonas (now an unlikely permanent fixture on my playlists) who reminded me of an obscure phrase coined by a 19th-century sociologist.’Photograph: David Becker/WireImageView image in fullscreen‘Bizarrely, it was Nick Jonas (now an unlikely permanent fixture on my playlists) who reminded me of an obscure phrase coined by a 19th-century sociologist.’Photograph: David Becker/WireImageOpinionMusicI’m a neuroscientist. Here’s why our brains need pop concertsBala SubramaniamAttending a Nick Jonas show with my kids was an invitation to ‘collective effervescence’. We need these shared experiences now more than everFri 14 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 13.30 EDTShareThree years ago, I agreed to accompany my children to a Nick Jonas concert. The appeal of the Jonas Brothers, and in this case only one of them, was unfamiliar territory.The concert happened to land on a particularly inconvenient day. As I sprinted out of the hospital, my mind was filled with the “what if’s” and “should haves” about our work that day.After lengthy negotiations with my daughter at the merchandise stand, we settled in as Nick Jonas began. I found myself surrounded by thousands of young people all singing the same songs, swaying to the same rhythm, and participating in the same moment.At first I felt like an impostor, as if I was attending a party I hadn’t been invited to. However, as the evening progressed, my thoughts of “me” shrank as I was absorbed into the intoxicating collective of the crowd.I was a whinger, a cynic, a misanthrope. Then I saw Harry Styles live – and I will never be the same againRead moreBizarrely, it was Nick Jonas (now an unlikely permanent fixture on my playlists) who reminded me of an obscure phrase coined by a 19th-century sociologist – Émile Durkheim’s “collective effervescence”. He was describing how individuals who are normally preoccupied with their personal concerns get swept up into a kind of electric, communal intensity.For “collective effervescence” to occur organically, bodies need to be present, in the same space, dancing to the same rhythm. The function, according to Durkheim, is to restore the social bonds and shared beliefs that are eroded by the drudgery of ordinary life.Such a state is a rare universal in human culture. Cave drawings displaying communal dancing, often around a fire, are found across centuries and continents.As a neuroscientist and practiced meditator, I’m familiar with the literature on ego dissolution. My own research on the Shambavi Mahamudra Kriya, an ancient yogic meditation practice, found that it reduces activity in the “default mode network” (DMN), the circuit in the brain that is responsible for planning, daydreaming and self-talking. Meditation is not alone in this; astronauts, big-wave surfers and skydivers all experience their egos melting away during an intense state of flow.We need this network. Without it, we couldn’t plan tonight’s dinner. Yet too much self-referential thought wears us out. Neuroimaging suggests that those with depression struggle to switch out of the DMN-heavy, rumination mode.We all need a break from ourselves sometimes. Nick Jonas showed me how “collective effervescence” could be the perfect circuit breaker.Synchronized dancing boostssocial closeness. Interestingly, some synchrony research suggests that shared dancing with “out-group members”, or those of a different age group, actuallyincreased the chances of real life cooperation.Here is where I believe concerts differ subtly from sports events or religious gatherings. Rhythm connects those who support different teams, and believe in different gods.In the west, we are crying out for more opportunities to experience this group fizz.A common sentiment is shared in the nightlife industry: “Phones killed the dancefloor.” This isn’t surprising. It’s hard to lose yourself in a crowd if you know you may find yourself again, getting ridiculed on a TikTok feed the next morning.The prehistoric ritual of ecstatic, synchronous dancing is being quietly eroded, and the modern mind is paying for it.The loneliness epidemic, compounded by the era of constant digital distraction and social comparison, is a serious public health risk. As the former US surgeon general Dr Vivek Murthy warned, lonelinesscarries comparable risksto that of smoking.I took up the ukulele after a chance encounter. It’s made me as happy as falling in love | Melanie TaitRead moreCovid-19 should have been our wake up call. The yearning for public, live music was deeper than many of us could have expected. We weren’t just robbed of the opportunity of seeing our favourite bands in the flesh. We were robbed of the collective effervescence that our nervous systems were built for.It’s time to make dancing sacred again. Sadhguru, the yogi who taught me how to meditate,appeared on stageat Romania’s 470,000-capacity electronic music festival Untold to speak on the need for greater global, collective consciousness. This unlikely crossover is not without precedent. The Indian spiritual leader Swami Satchidananda sat cross-legged on stage at the Woodstock opening ceremony in 1969; it became a pivotal moment in the hippie folklore of the 60s.We need to free dancefloors, concerts and festivals of their hedonistic connotations. Perhaps it’s time we assigned them the same “enriching” status as libraries and museums.The spaces that reliably produce collective belonging deserve to be treated as public health assets. The dancefloor, for all its apparent frivolity, may be doing more for community health than we have the measurement tools to capture. These spaces do something that no app, no algorithm and no prescription can replicate. They return us, briefly, to something primal, prehistoric and necessary. That is worth protecting.I have already arranged for my tickets to the next Nick Jonas concert, even though my teenagers’ tastes have changed. Thankfully, I still won’t have to attend alone.Bala Subramaniam, MD, MPH, is a Harvard Medical School professor of anesthesiology and director of the Sadhguru Center for a Conscious PlanetExplore more on these topicsMusicOpinionNeuroscienceClubbingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Karoline Leavitt leaves behind a legacy of lies. What’s next for the Trump aide? | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: The press secretary’s communication style made her eminently qualified for a role in this administration
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: The press secretary’s communication style made her eminently qualified for a role in this administration
Content: ‘As well as her flair for numbers, Leavitt will also be remembered as a consummate professional who remained dignified under pressure.’Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APView image in fullscreen‘As well as her flair for numbers, Leavitt will also be remembered as a consummate professional who remained dignified under pressure.’Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APOpinionTrump administrationKaroline Leavitt leaves behind a legacy of lies. What’s next for the Trump aide?Arwa MahdawiThe press secretary’s communication style made her eminently qualified for a role in this administrationFri 14 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 12.30 EDTShareKaroline Leavitt, 28, is leaving her demanding job as Donald Trump’s press secretaryto spend more timewith her two young children and her 60-year-old husband. According to apostby Trump On Truth Social, Leavitt will be departing her role at the end of the month and will serve as one of Trump’s “top outside advisors”.In other words: the official version of events is that Leavitt is resigning on her own terms for family reasons and not because Trump’s approval ratings are atrecord lowsand she’s a rat fleeing a sinking ship.But is the official version of events the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth? Don’t bother asking Leavitt – I’m not sure she knows much about the T-word. She may have been the youngest White House press secretary in history, but there’s no denying her communication style made her eminently qualified for a role in theTrump administration. I won’t muck about with euphemisms such asmisrepresentedorstated without evidenceormade false claims.Leavitt’s legacy in government was attacking Trump’s enemies and spouting lie after lie after lie.Being a lowly writer means I am held to far higher standards about what I can say than the departing press secretary or her boss, the president of the United States. Unlike Leavitt or Trump, I actually have to provide facts and evidence to back up my assertions. So here we go: here are a few fun facts about Leavitt’s tenure in public office.Karoline Leavitt: six key takeaways from 20 months as Trump’s press secretaryRead moreFirst, there’s her role in promoting lies about the economy. One of the most significant economic policies of Trump’s second term has been his global tariffs, which were initially extended even to volcanic islands inhabitedonly by penguins. During a press briefing in March 2025, Leavitttoldreporters that tariffs were a “tax cut for the American people”. Economists havesaidthis is nonsense. “Economists don’t agree on much, but we agree tariffs are taxes on consumers,” Tara Sinclair, a George Washington University economist told the fact-checking website Politifact. The non-partisanTax Foundationhas also run the numbers and said that in 2025, the Trump tariffs “amounted to an average tax increase of $1,000” per US household.But what’s $1,000, eh? It’s nothing to Trump, who made astaggering $2.2bnduring the first year of his second term in various questionable ways. One imagines it’s also not much to Leavitt, who earns just under $200,000 in her role and whose husband, Nicholas Riccio, manages what has beendescribed asa multimillion-dollar real estate business.And if you feel aggrieved about tariffs increasing the already sky-high cost of living, according to Leavitt, you should just work harder (or marry a real estate tycoon). “Some of these kids, and I call them kids because they are in their 20s and have never had real jobs, and they’re complaining things are expensive,” Fox News’Jesse Watters told Leavittlast month during a conversation about young Democratic party voters. “Yes, things are expensive when you don’t have a real job.” Leavitt agreed, adding that her generation had been raised with “silver spoons in their mouths, just getting everything handed to them”. That was un-American, she suggested, because this country “was built on meritocracy and hard work, pulling up your sleeves, pulling yourself up from your bootstraps”.It’s not just tariffs where Leavitt’s math seems to be off. In January 2025, the press secretary justified Trump’s order to freeze federal funding to the US Agency for International Development (USAID) by claiming it was wasting money.“[T]here was about to be 50m taxpayer dollars that went out the door to fund condoms in Gaza,”Leavittsaid. “That is a preposterous waste of taxpayer money. So that’s what this pause is focused on: being good stewards of tax dollars.”24:30Trump’s great plane escape | Politics Weekly AmericaTo be very clear: that condom claim was a lie. Documents shows that no condoms were sent anywhere in the Middle East, let alone to a place undergoing what many experts have termed a genocide. The US did, however, provide billions of taxpayer dollars to helpIsrael destroy Gaza, which has arguablyreducedbirths a lot faster than condoms would have. The dismantling of USAID, justified by Leavitt, has also increasedpregnancy complicationsand maternal death in poor countries. Astudy published in the Lancetjournal last year estimated that US funding cuts could result in more than 14 million deaths, including more than 4.5 million children under age five, by 2030. I guess, if you’re Leavitt, being “good stewards of tax dollars” means contributing to mass death and immiseration. Money well spent!As well as her flair for numbers, Leavitt will also be remembered as a consummate professional who remained dignified under pressure. Last October, for example, SV Dáte, Huffington Post’s senior White House correspondent,asked Leavittvia text message who had suggested Budapest for a meeting between Trump and Vladimir Putin to discuss Ukraine. Herresponse? “Your mom did.” When Dáte then asked if Leavitt thought that was funny, shereplied: “It’s funny to me that you actually consider yourself a journal [sic]. You are a far left hack who nobody takes seriously, including your colleagues in the media, they just don’t tell you that to your face. Stop texting me your disingenuous, biased, and bullshit questions.”That was a brief look at Leavitt’s past. What’s in store for her future? Despite her comments about her family, don’t expect her to go full tradwife. None of the ambitious women advancing the Trump administration’s anti-woman agenda want to devote their own lives to the domestic drudgery they extoll for others. They’ve got less privileged women to do the childcare and the cooking and the cleaning for them. No, rather than being a tradwife, one imagines Leavitt might end up with a nice little gig on Fox News orBari Weiss’s CBS. Or perhaps, like Sean Spicer, her predecessor under Trump 1.0, she might go the reality TV route and regale us all onDancing With the Stars. No doubt there will also be a “tell-all” book in her future in which, depending on which way the political winds are blowing, she’ll tell us all the things she thinks will rehabilitate her reputation.Will Trump’s next press secretary be a better liar than the first five?Read moreAnd, of course, for now there’s her new role as an “outside advisor”. I can’t tell you exactly what that entails but I can tell you that, going forward, communications with Trump and his outside advisers can apparently beconsidered privileged. On Monday, after Todd Blanche was sworn in as attorney general, the justice department’s office of legal counsel issued a 21-page opinion about the president’s “executive privilege” which protects communication between Trump and advisers whodon’t work for his administration. This makes a future Democrat-led investigation into the Trump administration a lot harder as his advisers – who will now include Leavitt – will not be able to be comprehensively questioned by Congress. Exactly the sort of move you’d expect from a president that Leavitt has called the “most transparent” in history.Best of luck, then, to Leavitt in her future endeavors. I’m sure she’ll roll up her designer sleeves, pull herself up by her bootstraps and find a way to make huge amounts of money. And best of luck to all of us. If there’s one thing that you can be sure about when it comes to the revolving door that isthe White House, it’s that no matter how bad the person leaving is, the replacement is always worse.Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsTrump administrationOpinionUS politicsRepublicanscommentShareReuse this content

title: Across the world authoritarians want to tell us what a ‘good life’ looks like. Here’s how liberals must respond | Alexandre Lefebvre | The Guardian
description: From Maga to Hungary’s Fidesz and Australia’s One Nation, politics is returning to its oldest question: what makes a life worth living? And liberalism needs a credible answer
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: From Maga to Hungary’s Fidesz and Australia’s One Nation, politics is returning to its oldest question: what makes a life worth living? And liberalism needs a credible answer
Content: ‘These leaders and movements promise to return the state to a core task that liberals are supposedly too embarrassed, weak or polite to perform,’ writes Alexandre Lefebvre.Photograph: Andrew Roth/Rex/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘These leaders and movements promise to return the state to a core task that liberals are supposedly too embarrassed, weak or polite to perform,’ writes Alexandre Lefebvre.Photograph: Andrew Roth/Rex/ShutterstockOpinionAustralian politicsAcross the world authoritarians want to tell us what a ‘good life’ looks like. Here’s how liberals must respondAlexandre LefebvreFrom Maga to Hungary’s Fidesz and Australia’s One Nation, politics is returning to its oldest question: what makes a life worth living? And liberalism needs a credible answerGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastFri 14 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 20.24 EDTShareThose of us who live in liberal democracies carry an image of what a decent state should do. It should protect rights, grow the economy, maintain order, uphold fairness and arbitrate disputes. But on life’s deepest questions – what makes a life worth living, and what sort of person one ought to become – it is meant to show restraint. The state should not privilege one vision of human flourishing, let alone promote it. That is for individuals, families and communities to decide. To borrow the Minnesota governor Tim Walz’sgolden ruleof politics: “Mind your own damn business!”Considerbirthrates. Across much of the wealthy world, they have fallen below replacement level. Fewer children mean fewer future workers, taxpayers and carers, and more pressure on pensions, health systems and aged care. Yet when liberal democracies encourage larger families, through baby bonuses or affordable childcare, they generally describe the goal as removing obstacles and expanding choice. Crucially, everyone should benefit: gay parents, straight parents, adoptive parents, biological parents, married parents, divorced parents – come one, come all.Earlier this year, I saw a different approach in Hungary. Hosted by athinktankaligned withViktor Orbán, I interviewed leading figures from his Fidesz party before its defeat in April’s election. For them, demographic decline was existential, not technical. The family was where people learned to be Hungarian and acquired the virtues of love and fidelity – values so important that they are named in the constitution Fidesz enacted. The family also connects national survival to personal flourishing. One leading defender of Fidesz told me, with startling bluntness, that women without children tended to be miserable and unfulfilled. This was no random digression. What I call a “good life state” honours certain ways of living as superior and uses public power and money to promote them. A liberal state, by contrast, helps people pursue the lives they choose and refuses to rank them.Pauline Hanson has knocked another brick out of our creaky political system. It’s not good for anybody | Peter GresteRead moreFidesz lost the election, but the model it helped popularise has not disappeared. Politics is returning to its oldest – and for many, most fundamental – question: who decides what makes a life worth living? From Maga and Fidesz to Modi’s India, Xi’s China, Israel’s governing right and Iran’s theocracy, leaders and movements are treating the good life as a public affair. Law, education, welfare, incentives, penalties and national narratives advance particular ideals of human flourishing. Some are religious and others secular, but they are substantive, specific and impossible for an entire citizenry to share.Liberals rightly find this abhorrent. Many of these regimes are already corrupt or repressive. Add the further mission of enforcing a vision of the good life and they become more frightening still.Yet liberals should not be surprised or refuse to see what is happening. The liberal belief that decent states must avoid prescriptive visions of the good is historically exceptional. For most of human history, the good life state has been the norm. Aristotle’s claim that politics aims not merely at life but at the good life is only the most famous formulation. Confucian and Islamic political traditions likewise made moral formation a public task. Seen this way, post-liberals are self-consciously pre-liberal. They promise to return the state to a core task that liberals are supposedly too embarrassed, weak or polite to perform.The mainstream liberal commentariat condemns these movements as simply bad. Their leaders want power, money and impunity, while their followers are ignorant, frightened or resentful – or so the thinking goes. Much of that may be true. But if liberals cannot see that these movements also hold out genuine human goods – belonging, purpose, family, faith and recognition, however cynically packaged – they will remain stunned by their appeal.Has this wave reached Australia? We have been resistant, not immune. Pauline Hanson and One Nation are already learning to surf it. Hanson’s call for a“monocultural” Australiais not just an immigration proposal. It is a claim about which identities and loyalties deserve public honour, reinforced by positions on family, gender and religion. One Nation has yet to produce anything as coherent or ambitious as Fidesz’s program. But the direction is recognisable: government should do more than protect choice; it should tell us what a proper Australian life looks like.What should the liberal answer be? Well, it can’t be to build a good life state of its own. That would sacrifice the freedom and pluralism it exists to protect. But neither can liberalism survive as a bloodless list of procedures and prohibitions. It needs anattractive moral and emotional visionof its own: fairness, freedom, irreverence and the adventure of living with difference. Those are not empty rules. They are elements of a common life worth loving. If liberals cannot say so – and make it credible in practice – authoritarians will make the good life state we hoped was past into our future.Alexandre Lefebvre is professor of politics and philosophy at the University of Sydney.
