title: The hill I will die on: Questions can go unanswered. Stop pulling out your phone | Helene Rosenthal | The Guardian
description: I don’t care what the capital of Uzbekistan is. I want to trade celebrity gossip and hear how your marriage counselling is going, says Helene Rosenthal, a writer based in New York City
Author: Helene Rosenthal
Headline: I don’t care what the capital of Uzbekistan is. I want to trade celebrity gossip and hear how your marriage counselling is going, says Helene Rosenthal, a writer based in New York City
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onMobile phonesThe hill I will die on: Questions can go unanswered. Stop pulling out your phoneHelene RosenthalI don’t care what the capital of Uzbekistan is. I want to trade celebrity gossip and hear how your marriage counselling is goingFri 14 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 12.59 EDTShareIt’s been a long, dreary winter. I am at dinner with a group of friends when someone wonders aloud when the first day of summer is. Lizzie insists it’s 21 June, Cleo is equally sure it’s 1 June. Sylvie says she is willing to bet her covetedThe Row flip-flopson Cleo’s answer. The social rewards from “arguing” over this far outweigh knowing a trivial piece of information that no one at the table will remember. And yet, we can’t help ourselves.Invariably, someone pulls out their phone, does a not-so-quick search online, and then declares, as though she has uncovered something truly revelatory, the first day of the astronomical summer is on thesummer solstice, 21 June. Whereas 1 June is when the meteorological summer begins.Turns out nobody cares. The obligatory “hmmmm” travels around the table as everyone looks at their watches. There’s a shift in the social dynamic. Lizzie says something about an early-morning root canal. The person with the phone becomes the self-appointed “expert” at the table. What started out as a fun, casual evening with friends has become a teaching moment.The night is over. Someone asks for the check.Should you send that midnight text? 11 essential rules for phone etiquetteRead moreAlternatively, here’s what could have happened: a somewhat raucous argument over who is right. Lizzie standing up and swearing she knows the exact date because of a late-June “welcome to summer” party where she was making out with a hottie and accidentally leaned against the air conditioning off/on switch, turning the room into a sauna. Everyone ended up in their undies. “It was one of the best nights of my life, I’d never forget it,” Lizzie blurts out with pride. We’ve all learned something – but not about the start of summer, whenever that is.Suffice to say, smartphones are a buzz kill. Researchers at theUniversity of Texashave shown that even having your mobile phone at the table, powered down and turned over, affects your ability to connect. Let that sink in: even when your phone is off, your brain is still distracted by it.There’s also something called theGoogle effect, where we’ve become so accustomed to retrieving information easily and quickly that we don’t bother retaining it. We rarely remember these Googled titbits, and yet we allow them to turn a perfectly good night into our dullest university lecture.The next time you are out with friends and a burning question comes up, forget about checking with Google. Ask your friends. Even if they don’t know the answer, it’s OK. The point is to keep talking. While we still know how.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHelene Rosenthal lives in New York City and writes about families, friendships and relationshipsExplore more on these topicsMobile phonesThe hill I will die onFriendshipcommentShareReuse this content

title: So Nigel Farage has beaten a man in a bin. But he’s in deep trouble, and he knows it | Owen Jones | The Guardian
description: The Reform leader claims vindication from the people, and it’s too early to write him off. But the problems he now faces may be more than he can bear, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Author: Owen Jones
Headline: The Reform leader claims vindication from the people, and it’s too early to write him off. But the problems he now faces may be more than he can bear, says Guardian columnist Owen Jones
Content: Count Binface celebrates his second-place finish at the Clacton byelection count, 14 August 2026.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenCount Binface celebrates his second-place finish at the Clacton byelection count, 14 August 2026.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAOpinionClacton byelection August 2026So Nigel Farage has beaten a man in a bin. But he’s in deep trouble, and he knows itOwen JonesThe Reform leader claims vindication from the people, and it’s too early to write him off. But the problems he now faces may be more than he can bearFri 14 Aug 2026 06.29 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 09.56 EDTShareNigel Farage is a rattled, embattled politician. Perhaps he feels buoyed up by securing slightly more votes in a byelection boycotted by all the main parties than he did in the general election two years ago. That was despite 10,000 fewer people turning out to vote. But there was never any question that he was going to win a byelection he called purely to deflect scrutiny of his undeclared £5m personal gift from a Thai-based crypto-billionaire and donations from a convicted fraudster.Farage chose Clacton as his parliamentary launchpad for a reason. It was here that his previous outfit, Ukip, secured its breakthrough in the byelection of 2014. It is one of the most pro-leave seats in Britain, whileElectoral Calculusestimates that almost no other constituency is this rightwing.When I visited, I found no shortage of voters who were defiant about Farage’s scandals. They saw no problem with a politician being showered with dosh by a foreign-based billionaire, arguing that Farage deserved it because he was a “nice man” and even suggesting he might invest it locally. They bought the narrative that the establishment was out to get their man, as if a millionaire ex-City broker who is a sometime friend of the US president is some plucky outsider.They are representative of about a fifth of the country who laud Farage as themainstream politician most hostile to immigration, and who are contemptuous of a Conservative party that failed even on its own terms in office. What should concern Farage, however, is thatmost Britons are more opposed to him than ever, and are determined to block him from power. That majority delivered victory to the Greens in February’s Gorton and Denton byelection, and to Andy Burnham in June’s Makerfield byelection.That the parody candidate Count Binface won more than a quarter of the vote in this ultra-rightwing heartland is a warning in itself. Yes, this “independent space warrior” secured plenty of media attention, but he had precious little ground game – that is, an army of volunteers to get out the vote. Many voters I spoke to hadn’t even heard of him. It seems plausible that some of those who made Count Binface the most successful joke candidate in history had previously voted not justLabour, Lib Dem or Green, but Conservative too.Farage refused to attend the official declaration of this election he chose to call. That suggests not just petulance and contempt for his own voters, but the insecurities of a jittery man.He claims Essex police had told himabout an “organised campaign to disrupt and degrade the result”, but the local force said there had been no “incidents or issues” related to the byelection and that attendance was up to candidates. And did Farage not claim that his £5m personal gift was needed to pay for his security?The explanation is probably more mundane. Being mocked on stage by a man in a bin does not exactly provide the optics of a heroic struggle against the establishment.What next for the Farage show? If he thought the byelection was an effective ruse to deflect from his money issues, reality caught up with him quickly. The parliamentary watchdog has nowreopened its investigationinto Farage’s gift and donations, and another byelection may be forced if there is an adverse ruling.But it is not just finances that have plunged Reform UK into crisis.Farage’s proud association with Donald Trump– toxic even to most Reform voters – has become an ever greater drag. Absorbing so many former Conservatives was surely another big error. The last government was bitterly rejected for a reason, not least by Farage’s own supporters, and filling Reform’s ranks with its former leading lights hardly helped the party’s anti-establishment pretences.And then there is the pivot to ever moretoxic rightwing politics, perhaps partly driven by pressure from the even further right Restore Britain, founded by the former Reform MP Rupert Lowe. Farage now talks of “anti-white discrimination” – rhetoric once confined to the ugliest reaches of the far right. His talk of “pure cold rage” after the conviction of Henry Nowak’s murder – just hours before riots over it – rightly disturbed many.Then there’s Zia Yusuf, his home affairs spokesperson, whose increasingly aggressive social media posts speak to Reform’s authoritarian underbelly. Yusuf repeatedly describes his opponents as “traitors” – his latest target was the Tory former defence secretary Ben Wallace – and threatens that an unspecific “reckoning is coming”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAll of this alarms most Britons, who have concluded that Reform must be kept from power and will vote tactically if needs be. Yet this is of scant comfort to the absurdly underscrutinised Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, because Reform’s hardened core shows no interest in returning to her camp. Rightwing Britain, then, is divided.It would be a mistake to write Farage off, however. We are in the midst of theAndy Burnhambounce. Voters are relieved to be rid of Keir Starmer, and for now Labour is tempting back some progressive voters who defected to the Greens. But Burnham has yet to be forced into many big decisions. Britain’s economic plight, its crisis-stricken public services and Burnham’s slowness to hike taxes on the booming rich could all come to a head in October’s budget. Disillusionment could swell, and Reform could benefit – unless, of course, Burnham calls a snap election first.But you have to ask whether Farage’s heart is really in this. Reports that he received his £5m gift after saying he would need“a million a year”to serve as an MP are telling. Here is a man who appears to enjoy the high life and feel parliamentary politics damages his earning potential. He seems increasingly riled by the sort of scrutiny he has long managed to avoid. Perhaps, after a pointless triumph over a bin, he may simply decide he has had enough.Owen Jones is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsClacton byelection August 2026OpinionNigel FarageByelectionsReform UKRestore BritainAndy BurnhamLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: How can we talk about this extreme weather now that it’s a battleground in the culture wars? | Andy Beckett | The Guardian
description: Weather forecasts once gave Britons something safe to chat about. Not any more, and that’s a problem for the experts – indeed, for all of us, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Author: Andy Beckett
Headline: Weather forecasts once gave Britons something safe to chat about. Not any more, and that’s a problem for the experts – indeed, for all of us, says Guardian columnist Andy Beckett
Content: Illustration: Nate Kitch/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Nate Kitch/The GuardianOpinionExtreme weatherHow can we talk about this extreme weather now that it’s a battleground in the culture wars?Andy BeckettWeather forecasts once gave Britons something safe to chat about. Not any more, and that’s a problem for the experts – indeed, for all of usFri 14 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 12.59 EDTShareIn this fragmented but supposedly mild country, watching and talking about the weather forecast is meant to be a reassuring, unifying activity. Collectively, we have created and maintained a national climate narrative of small disappointments and pleasures.The first weather forecaster to appear on British TV, George Cowling, made his debut on the BBC in January 1954, predicting that “tomorrow would be rather windy”, but “a good day to hang out the washing”. For most of the 72 years since, such brief, carefully calibrated broadcasts have provided people from Aberdeen to Penzance with practical information, small talk and minor grumbles about essentially the same situation: living in a country where the weather is constantly changing, in a paradoxically unchanging way.Yet like the traditional British climate, that common weather culture may now be evaporating. “Met Office considers issuing red ‘extreme heat warning’ across Britain while nation enjoys ‘incredible summer’,”said the headlineabove the forecast on the GB News website on Monday, caught between terror and delight at the latest heatwave. As the climate crisis has affected this country in more and more unmistakable but uneven ways, TV weather forecasters have increasingly struggled to find the right language to describe this transformation’s daily consequences. Their struggle influences and exemplifies that of many Britons to understand, and work out what we think about, the apparent end of the weather patterns we expected to shape our whole lives.Across all the British TV broadcasters, sometimes within the same bulletin, or even the same sentence, weather forecasters now present sunshine as welcome and oppressive; high temperatures as miraculous and unbearable; rain as an inconvenience and desperately needed; cloud cover as depressing and a relief. Tanned forecasters in sundresses, emphasising the positives for domestic holidaymakers of another record-breaking summer, alternate with grim-faced forecasters suggesting we are experiencing a weather apocalypse.Meanwhile, the wildly differing effects of the climate crisis on different areas, and from one season to another, are further fracturing Britain’s weather conversation into a babble of separate, sometimes conflicting discourses. This year, parts of the country have experienced such contrasting summers –wetter than usual in western Scotland, desert-like in southern England – that we can no longer say they share broadly the same northern European climate, as had been assumed for centuries. In an era of separatism and nationalism, another major binding element of the UK may be falling away.Beneath the relatively placid surface of our previous weather culture, there were always some tensions and contradictions. In a 2025 academic paper,British Heatwave Discourse (1985–2023): from Ice Cream to Armageddon?, Thijs van Dooremalen and Philip Smith analysed articles about heatwaves in the national press. They found that until 2000 positive and negative coverage coexisted in roughly equal quantities, “often in the same newspaper”. From 2000 to 2014, the balance shifted slowly towards the negative, as the climate crisis became a mainstream worry. Yet only from 2015 did an “Apocalyptic genre” of heatwave articles begin to become dominant; and a “Romantic genre” of celebratory coverage remains. In a country where many people still spend much of the year feeling cold, the idea of hot weather as a liberation is likely to linger, for some, for decades to come.For other Britons, heatwaves have become political flashpoints, their causes to be furiously contested, their existence even denied. During the record heat of 2022, “weather forecasters faced unprecedented levels of trolling”,the BBC reported, including “hundreds of abusive tweets or emails questioning their reports and telling them to ‘get a grip’… ‘it’s just summer’”. Some of these climate crisis deniers described advice on how to stay cool as “pandering to the ‘woke brigade’”, and accused the BBC and Met Office of “scaremongering” to help the then Conservative government impose unneeded green policies.This summer, some of these conspiratorial arguments have re-emerged. But with the Tories having in effect turned against net zero, joined by Reform UK, Restore Britain and most of the rightwing media, disagreeing with weather forecasters who express alarm about our changing climate has become more mainstream. Discussing the weather is no longer just small talk, but also a battlefield in the culture wars.No wonder forecasters often sound unsure or extremely cautious about what tone to adopt on air. In 2023, the BBC’s Tomasz Schafernaker gave a very carefulinterview to the Big Issue. “While our language remains largely the same,” he said, “we have adapted it to include references to climate change. We must be mindful that prolonged periods of sun and heat are not always good news … However, there are often areas in the UK where the weather is much more comfortable, [so] highlighting that it’s not ‘all bad’ is important. It’s a balance that we assess on a daily basis.”Yet three years on, his broadcasts have become less neutral. “The savage summer continues across Europe,” he said on the BBC weather website last Thursday afternoon. “It’s been excruciatingly hot …” On BBC One last Sunday evening, while giving this week’s UK forecast, he kept making gestures of helplessness and disbelief. It was like a weather bulletin from a dystopian drama.Such interventions no longer seem melodramatic. “The climate of the 20th century has now gone,” says Mike Kendon, a Met Office scientist and co-author ofState of the UK Climate in 2025, published last month. So far, this year’s weather has been more extreme. Even more than the heat, summer drought and winter floods, its key feature has been the weather getting stuck in one state for months – a characteristic of harsh continental climates, rather than the changeable one around which our society has been built. So it’s possible that next summer will feature relentless rain, not drought, and that other seasons will continue to stall as well, damaging the economy, everyday life and public health.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBritons are world famous for their weather stoicism. But this stoicism has been created by centuries of relatively minor weather discomforts and disasters. How the forecasters, and the rest of us, will react as the climate crisis intensifies – in our private behaviours and assumptions as well as our public lives – is a question we are only in the early stages of answering.Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsExtreme weatherOpinionExtreme heatUK weatherClimate scienceClimate crisisDroughtFloodingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Burnham won’t fix our prisons crisis until he dares to be honest with the public about crime | Polly Toynbee | The Guardian
description: Most crime figures have drastically fallen, but people don’t believe it. It’s no wonder when politicians whip up emotions and attempt to bend the law, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Author: Polly Toynbee
Headline: Most crime figures have drastically fallen, but people don’t believe it. It’s no wonder when politicians whip up emotions and attempt to bend the law, says Guardian columnist Polly Toynbee
Content: Prisoners being released from HMP Pentonville, London, 10 September 2024.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenPrisoners being released from HMP Pentonville, London, 10 September 2024.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAOpinionPrisons and probationBurnham won’t fix our prisons crisis until he dares to be honest with the public about crimePolly ToynbeeMost crime figures have drastically fallen, but people don’t believe it. It’s no wonder when politicians whip up emotions and attempt to bend the lawFri 14 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 05.11 EDTShareAn astounding change is happening to life in England and Wales that most people don’t know about, and when they are told they don’t believe it. Most crime, including violence, has fallen by aremarkable 90%over the past 30 years. Butonly 6%of people believe it, while61% think crime is going up. This great denial is the background cause of the prison overflow crisis, as politicians (of all parties) stir up voters to demand ever higher sentences as the imaginary cure to their imaginary soaring crime.Allwestern European countriesenjoy this same remarkable social improvement, with research over decades offering myriad reasons why: populations spending longer in education, CCTV, better security for cars and homes, and young people staying at home to play video games of fantasy crime instead of entertaining themselves with the real thing. Removingbrain-harming leadfrom petrol andabortionof unwanted foetuses at risk of future child neglect are other possible explanations.This generation inhabits a far less violent society, with many fewer homicides, thefts, burglaries and serious violent crimes, but also far less casual social violence in brawls and punch-ups. Older folk nostalgic for an orderly golden age when no one bothered locking their front door usually situate it just beyond their own memories, in their grandparents’ halcyon days. But radical social change leads to less acceptance of any violence. Online fraud and cybercrime are the ones that aresteeply rising, though they are committed by quite different criminals.The nature of violence has changed, too. Official statistics from the national crime survey for England and Wales show that 65% of violent crime incidentsresult in no injuryto the victim. (Though “no injury” can still mean people are seriously harmed by terrifying threats of violence or bysexual abuse and intimidation, of course.) There remains a dissonance between the way life is and the crime people fear.Single landmark horror cases – from the Moors murderers to Fred West andAxel Rudakubana– are seared for ever into the nation’s collective nightmares. Too often these freak incidents drive our sentencing policy. Five years after the trial of the 10-year-old killers of James Bulger, the 1998 Crime and Disorder Actabolished doli incapax– the requirement to prove that a child under 14 knew their act was morally wrong. The toughening of sentencing law time and again in response to public outrage at particular horrors, with no balancing context, is a root cause of overflowing prisons.It’s happening again in the case of two of those responsible for the heartrending death of PC Andrew Harper. Harper’s family, andevery chief constablein England and Wales, protested vigorously that they were due to be released under new rules after serving only half of their 13-year manslaughter sentences. The prime minister hasasked the justice secretaryto find a way to ensure the men stay inside: the law must be bent to this case. Harper’s Law, which in 2022 imposed life sentences for the killers of emergency workers, was introduced only as a result of their trial, so can’t be retrospectively applied. But anything singling out these men will be challenged in court. Blocking early release for all those imprisoned for manslaughter would fill too many cells: besides, that’s rough justice when some have sentences of one year, others for 24 years or life.The law is set by parliament for independent courts to apply, regardless of politics: look at Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump or Viktor Orbán for examples of those who break that democratic principle. We should be uneasy at our government declaring publicly that it is chasing after a way to bend laws to lock up two particular offenders.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWill Burnham fix our barbaric prisons – or cave to rightwing populism? The answer is a tragedy | Simon JenkinsRead moreDavid Gauke, a former justice secretary and lord chancellor, looks at Andy Burnham’s predicament with some sympathy but some frustration. Overcrowding, over-sentencing and under-building was Labour’s wretched inheritance and he was summoned by the new government in 2024 to find an answer to England and Wales’s bursting prisons. His excellent report describedsentence inflationand overuse of custody as unsustainable. He called for thesuspension of most sentencesof a year or less, which are proven to do no good. He advocated for more early release for good behaviour, rewarding engaging in education and work in prison, and for a boost to probation and community sentencing provision. In response to his report, early release in England and Wales was cut from 50% to 33% of sentence served.But, he says, “it was a mistake” for Burnham to start conceding early release exemptions for rape and child sex offences. “He has used up the spare capacity freed with these exemptions, opening the gates to other exemptions for heinous crimes.” Burnham is following Gauke’s recommendations to let more women out. “We supported deporting foreign offenders too, but it’s difficult: either countries won’t accept them, or they do but let them out, to great outrage.” He feels sorry for Burnham’s dilemma: “How easy for us ex-politicians to suggest liberal remedies,” he says. In power, he knows, politicians’ fear of public storms over exceptionally horrible crimes ratchets sentences ever upwards.Penal populism by all parties got us here, but even reducing sentences from now on would take years to empty cells. Gauke wonders why England and Wales are outliers, with lower crime now than some similar countries yet the highest incarceration rate in western Europe. “No, prison doesn’t make crime fall. Many countries with lower prison rates have even less crime.”The great question is how to convey true crime facts to a populace besieged by true crime stories, where gripping tales overwhelm mere statistics. Here’s a curiosity the government could begin with: though convinced of soaring crime everywhere else, people don’t in factfeel afraidin their own neighbourhoods. Their fears are roused by scabrously lying, vote-seeking politicians and timorous governments not daring to challenge crime untruths, while the hostile media terrify the living daylights out of everyone. At home, people do really know they are relatively safe. Just possibly, as Burnham confronts the prison emergency, he may be the first to dare start telling crime truths like these.Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsPrisons and probationOpinionCrimeLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: A critical mauling: Brian Logan on comedy critics being portrayed as horrible snobs | Stage | The Guardian
description: Two Edinburgh fringe shows feature savage send-ups of reviewers. Is this petty revenge or do they have a case? Our writer finds one ‘a hoot’ – and thinks the other let him off lightly
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Two Edinburgh fringe shows feature savage send-ups of reviewers. Is this petty revenge or do they have a case? Our writer finds one ‘a hoot’ – and thinks the other let him off lightly
Content: Poison pen … the critic in Andrew Doherty’s Reviewers Welcome … To Die!Photograph: PR handoutView image in fullscreenPoison pen … the critic in Andrew Doherty’s Reviewers Welcome … To Die!Photograph: PR handoutStageA critical mauling: Brian Logan on comedy critics being portrayed as horrible snobsTwo Edinburgh fringe shows feature savage send-ups of reviewers. Is this petty revenge or do they have a case? Our writer finds one ‘a hoot’ – and thinks the other let him off lightlyBrian LoganFri 14 Aug 2026 09.06 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 10.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNo one ever built a statue to a critic, they say – but plenty of art gets made about them. There wasWild Bore at the Traversea few Edinburgh fringes back, an eye-catching performance-art attack on the notion of critical authority. There was Tom Stoppard’s The Real Inspector Hound, Sheridan’s The Critic, and the 70s horror movie (later a play)Theatre of Blood, in which critics are subjected to gruesome murder at the hands of a deranged thesp. And while we’re talking unspeakable gore, one feature of Sarah Kane’s queasy play Cleansed, currently enjoying arevival, is that (in a wanton act of literary vengeance) its sadistic torturer antagonist is named after a theatre critic, Jack Tinker, who’d panned Kane’s work.Runts of the reviewing litter though we are, there’s even a sub-genre of art about comedy critics. The comic Russell Kane wrotea novelabout one who was unable to laugh. Ex-critic Charlotte Runcie wroteanotherabout a journo giving a woman a one-star review for her standup, then sleeping with her.double quotation mark‘Who wants to be a comedy critic?’ barks Riches, eyeballing the audience. I sink back into my seatSo there’s a precedent for the two shows on this year’s fringe that take comedy reviewing as their subject, one of them in direct response to so-so notices at last year’s festival. That show is Andrew Doherty’s Reviewers Welcome … to Die! It’s a folk-horror spoof about an up-himself critic obliged by demons to learn the error of his ways. It springs from Doherty’s dismay at receivinga three-star crit(“one of the three worst scores you can get!”) for his sophomore show Sad Gay Aids Play – after critical hosannahs greetedhis debut the year before.So where does Reviewers Welcome fall on the all-important five-star spectrum? Happily, given that this is not a review, I am under no obligation to rate his show, which characterises those in my profession as preening, nepotistic snobs, scorning the talent they purport to judge while nursing their own thwarted artistic delusions. “How sad, lonely and pathetic I am,” trills Doherty’s anti-hero Felix Chatelier, at least until popular and sexy playwriting genius “Andrew Doherty” shows up to shepherd our unlovely critic towards redemption. This happens at a fringe festival in the fictional Midlands town of Billington, a name that long-time readers of Guardian theatre reviews may recognise.View image in fullscreenClose to the bone? … Adam Riches, AKA Caliban Monroe, performs The Critic’s Way.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianAll of this unfolds in the spoof scary-movie style familiar from Doherty’s hit Gay Witch Sex Cult, another Wicker Man-ish affair pitting a dopey outsider against yokel locals and dark forces beyond everyone’s ken. Just as it trades in genre stereotype, so the show’s take on critics seldom outpaces cliche – although I did enjoy the closing gag about Chatelier’s constitutional inability to dole out that final, fifth star. But we critics get off lightly here, in that Reviewers Welcome is as much a mickey-take of thin-skinned artists bearing grudges as of those arbiters of taste who decorate or dismiss them with a swish of our pen.And now to the second show. When Adam Riches bounds on stage in character as eminent comedy critic Caliban Monroe, it looks like his show The Critic’s Way might land uncomfortably closer to the bone. Scottish accent? Replica Scottish football sportswear? Why do I feel like I’ve seen this (stylish, smooth-talking) guy before? But The Critic’s Way soon devolves into another of Riches’ familiar burlesques on swaggering but shallow masculinity (ah, so it can’t be me then) with strictly limited insight into Caliban’s critical calling. The persona makes Chatelier look multidimensional by comparison, as Riches loudly deplores comedians, claims to have invented star ratings and reads from his now-remaindered titular treatise on the art of what he calls “the ’tique”.double quotation markThere’s ridicule there (fair enough) but perhaps grudging affection tooThere’s little of the promised “razor-sharp satire”, although – like most of Riches’ uproarious interactive work – his show is never less than a hoot. “Who wants to be a comedy critic?” he barks, eyeballing the audience as I shrink in my seat. Inevitably, behind the arrogant veneer, Monroe is another “sad, lonely and pathetic” individual. The “voice of a veneration” no longer, he’s out of a job after a victim of his hatchet work hits back against one particularly indelicate review. You could just about read this as an exploration of a changing climate for criticism, in which speech is neurotically policed, and ideas like objective judgment and the single authoritative voice are both critically (as it were) out of fashion.Or you could enjoy Riches’ exuberant faux-workshop for what it is: a 50-minute piece of nonsense revelling in the archetype of the cultural snob, in love with his own supposed erudition, seething with resentment that to deploy it he must piggyback on the work of – shudder! – mere comedians.Considering these two shows together as a critique of the service we comedy reviewers render – well, there’s ridicule (fair enough) but perhaps grudging affection too. It’s probably a three-star review then for me and my counterparts – but I like to think it reads like a four.Andrew Doherty’s Reviewers Welcome … to Die!is Upstairs at Pleasant Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 August;Adam Riches’ The Critic’s Wayis at Cow Cafe at Underbelly, Cowgate, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustExplore more on these topicsStageComedy (Culture)Comedy (Stage)featuresShareReuse this content

title: ‘We get 200 tourists a day’: when your house becomes a TV star | Television | The Guardian
description: What’s it like to live on the set of a soap opera? Or above Ted Lasso’s favourite pub? The residents of the homes made famous by hit TV shows tell all
Author: Alexi Duggins
Headline: What’s it like to live on the set of a soap opera? Or above Ted Lasso’s favourite pub? The residents of the homes made famous by hit TV shows tell all
Content: ‘At any hour of the day or night, there are groups of visitors in front of the house taking flash photos’ …Sarah Jessica Parker filming at the apartment she’s helped to make famous.Photograph: Jose Perez/Bauer-Griffin/GC ImagesView image in fullscreen‘At any hour of the day or night, there are groups of visitors in front of the house taking flash photos’ …Sarah Jessica Parker filming at the apartment she’s helped to make famous.Photograph: Jose Perez/Bauer-Griffin/GC ImagesTelevision‘We get 200 tourists a day’: when your house becomes a TV starWhat’s it like to live on the set of a soap opera? Or above Ted Lasso’s favourite pub? The residents of the homes made famous by hit TV shows tell allAlexi DugginsFri 14 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHalf the world recognises the apartment that Carrie Bradshaw lives in. Or the New Jersey mansion where Tony Soprano ate, slept and obsessed over the ducks in his swimming pool. In the 1990s, if you asked a good chunk of the global population where Will Smith lived, they would instantly picture a huge, white abode in Bel Air.For the real people who call those places home, this can be an issue.“We had loads of problems with people just walking in during Covid,” says Kate Fox, who lives in a house that featured in British soapEmmerdale, for the years it was filmed entirely in her West Yorkshire village of Esholt. “Somebody actually came and just stuck their head through our front door. Maybe once a month you’ll get somebody opening the door or doing something inappropriate like peeking through your windows. People have no issues about completely invading your space – but you get used to it.”View image in fullscreenFenced off … Walter White’s Breaking Bad home in Albuquerque, New Mexico.Photograph: Raisa Macouzet/AlamyPublic intrusion is a common experience for the residents of TV-famous homes. In 2015, Vince Gilligan, the creator of Breaking Bad, had to urge fans to stop paying homage to his show – because they were recreating a scene where an entire pizza is thrown on to the roof of the house whose exterior was featured as Walter White’s bungalow. And last year, the owner of the apartment made famous by Sex and the City’s lead charactererected a gate outside itbecause “at any hour of the day or night, there are groups of visitors in front of the house taking flash photos, engaging in loud chatter, posting on social media, making TikTok videos or just celebrating the moment”. Eventually, the owners of the Breaking Bad house followed suit, erecting a 6ft iron fence – not that it stopped fans. “They still try to throw pizzas even though she’s got a gate, she’s got signage,” said Frank Sandoval, who runs Breaking Bad tours to the house in an RV. “They even try to climb the gate.”But not everyone treats the arrival of hordes of fans as a bad thing. “At first, I was confused why they would want to come in,” says Glenda Kenyon, whose place in Barry, south Wales, features in BBC sitcom Gavin and Stacey as the home of Stacey’s mum, Gwen. “I just said, no, sorry, I can’t do it. Then the second year I thought, no, I’ve got to change it, so I started opening up.”View image in fullscreen‘It has changed my life’ … Knock-off Nessa poses with Glenda Kenyon outside her home, which was made famous by British TV sitcom Gavin and Stacey.Photograph: Francesca Jones/The GuardianGlenda turned her home into a walk-in tribute to the show. It has a collection of memorabilia including fridge magnets, key rings, tea towels and “nearly every T-shirt you can buy”. She’s set up a photo opportunity in the kitchen with the frying pan Gwen uses to cook her infamous omelettes, as well as a face mask of the character visitors can put on. She even ended up partnering on tours with a coach firm, whose “Dave’s Coaches” bus regularly appeared in the show, and another run by Knock-off Nessa – who impersonates Ruth Jones’s character. Last year, she welcomed 168 busloads of people to her home, and it has given her a renewed purpose.“I was lonely before, so lonely,” says Glenda, who lives alone and has experienced depression. “It has changed my life, because before I was so quiet, and now I can open up. I’m a hell of a lot better than I used to be. When you’re meeting people, you’re not thinking about the depression. I had no friends before, and now I got everybody.”View image in fullscreenPutting Barry on the map … Knock-off Nessa with a group of tourists visiting Kenyon’s home in one of the Dave’s Coaches buses that featured in British sitcom Gavin and Stacey.Photograph: Francesca JonesHaving a home that’s famous for being on TV doesn’t just change the life of its owners. If the show is big enough, it can change an entire area – as a pocket of London’s Richmond found out after Ted Lasso was set there. The high-end jewellers and panama hat boutique that line the chi-chi alleyway of the soccer goof’s home are now joined by the Ted Lasso Store, featuring a recreated locker room decked out with a “Believe” poster, and a replica shirt for every player – available to purchase alongside a selection of mugs, scarves and snow globes. Over the road, an Italian restaurant attracts customers with a £5 “Eat like Ted” offer that entitles you to a box of Ted’s favourite shortbread biscuits.“I didn’t realise it would be such a big deal,” says Reece Kent – who lives above, and is the general manager of, The Prince’s Head pub – Lasso’s regular. “Before I started working here, I was like, OK, we might get a few tourists. But I get 150 to 200 a day. At first it was just people from America, but now it’s Germany, Australia, Japan. I had a couple from Jamaica the other day.”View image in fullscreenAnother round … Up to 200 fans a day visit The Prince’s Head pub, the setting of the fictional Crown & Anchor pub in Ted Lasso.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesRichmond is far from the only place this has happened to. Over 37 years, a suburb of Melbourne was thronged by more than a quarter of a million soap opera fans on bus tours, desperate to see the real-life cul-de-sac that moonlighted as Neighbours’ Ramsay Street – resulting in a security guard being permanently stationed there. Esholt had its share of soap fans, too, with regular coach tours turning up. But Richmond is still packed with fans – and the pub has transformed one table into a designated fan area, next to a big AFC Richmond logo, replica shirt and signed pictures of the cast. They’re now the end point of a Lasso tour, which leaves them regularly flooded by big groups of tourists wanting to see the non-existent dartboard that featured in the show, and fiercely competing to sit at the table where Lasso held chats with his footballing assistant coach Beard. There has been one unexpected consequence of it all for Kent, though: needing to convince fans that he didn’t inspire a character in the show, the similarly named Roy Kent.“A couple of weeks after I started, this tourist came in who’d seen my name on the website and had made all these connections that Roy Kent was based on me,” laughs Kent. “Luckily, after a while, they believed that it was actually based on Roy Keane. I would have loved to be Roy Keane, but I’m not.”View image in fullscreen‘I had a couple from Jamaica the other day’ …The Prince’s Head pub, the setting of the fictional Crown & Anchor pub in the ‘Ted Lasso’ Apple TV show.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesBeing confused with a star of the show isn’t the only strange side-effect of having a TV show filmed in your home. “The end of our house had a vet’s waiting room and surgery in when I was growing up,” says Fox, who spent a chunk of her childhood having to pick her way around cables and lights, and being instructed to be as quiet as possible during takes. Until, that is, Emmerdale moved production to a set, and decided to create a mock-up of Fox’s home as one of the highlights of the now-defunct Granada Studios tourist attraction. “So there was an exact copy of my front lounge in a studio. Me and my mum went a few years ago. It was just a bizarre, bizarre place to be.”Its effect on residents’ finances also doesn’t hurt. “When we were kids we sold tours of the house when my parents were out. We’d charge like 50p and let people have a look around,” says Fox. “I think the tourists liked getting a tour from a child. I never got any complaints!”View image in fullscreenSoap life … Kate Fox in Esholt, where Emmerdale was filmed.Photograph: Richard Saker/The ObserverThe owners of TV-famous homes who want to sell up also have very little to complain about. When the owners of Walter White’s Breaking Bad home eventually tired of fan attention, they sold it for $1.3m – reportedly to a streamer who intends to “treat it like a monument” – not bad compared to the $350-400,000 neighbouring homes are valued at. Esholt has attracted superfans “who have moved here specifically for the Emmerdale connection”, according to Fox. And two of the houses featured in Gavin and Stacey have been bought by superfans recently – one of which was sold very much as seen, because, they said, “To be able to own the original furniture was the cherry on top of the cake for us.”Having a house associated with TV stars can also work the other way round too. Fox’s family may no longer have their home if it weren’t for the relationship they struck up with an Emmerdale star.“At one point, Mum and Dad were at risk of losing the house to the council. Leah Bracknell [who played Zoe Tate] contacted the press and said: ‘You need to write about this,’” says Fox. “She’d appear in photos with them as well, and they did end up being allowed to buy the house off the council. We’ve still got all the press clippings now. She was really, really nice.”A number of the Ted Lasso stars also became fond of their filming locations. According to Kent, “they’d pop in on days they weren’t filming – for lunch or just a drink”, although Lasso himself wasn’t the main culprit. “Jason Sudeikis [who plays Lasso] only popped in once. I had Coach Beard in a couple of times. Dani Rojas was the main one – he’d have lunch and bring friends. They were lovely.”Despite getting to meet celebs, living somewhere TV famous isn’t for everyone. “People who moved here during filming or since, they really do struggle with the tourists – they think it’s so rude and shocking that people just walk into your house,” says Fox. But, ultimately, for some people, it brings a real sense of happiness – particularly if you’re a fan of the show.“I was over the moon when I first saw my house on telly. Every time I watch, I’m going: ‘That’s mine! That’s mine!’” says Glenda.“People tell me that I’ve put Barry on the map and I do feel like that’s true. I’ve had people from India, Africa, New Zealand, Swindon – you name it, I’ve had them. I’m very proud. I’ve done something in my life I can be happy about.”Explore more on these topicsTelevisionGavin & StaceySex and the CityAnd Just Like ThatEmmerdalefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Boys Don’t Dance review – jump back to the 80s to celebrate the power of pop | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: A sunny mashup of music accompanies choreographer Marc Brew’s feelgood coming-of-age story
Author: Lyndsey Winship
Headline: A sunny mashup of music accompanies choreographer Marc Brew’s feelgood coming-of-age story
Content: Boys Don't Dance.Photograph: Brian HartleyView image in fullscreenBoys Don't Dance.Photograph: Brian HartleyEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewBoys Don’t Dance review – jump back to the 80s to celebrate the power of popAssembly @ Dance Base, EdinburghA sunny mashup of music accompanies choreographer Marc Brew’s feelgood coming-of-age storyLyndsey WinshipFri 14 Aug 2026 12.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMarc Brew made the acclaimed showAn Accident/A Lifein 2024, with choreographer Sidi Larbi Cherkaoui, about the car accident that left him paralysed below the waist aged 20. Brew went on to be a successful dancer and choreographer, performing using a wheelchair, and Brew’s latest piece returns to autobiographical territory. This time the focus is on the young Marc – or dancer Ross Malloy as a proxy – growing up in rural Australia, surrounded by football fans and sheep, and told repeatedly that boys don’t dance.What the show does really well is capture Malloy’s character’s absolute joy in dancing, how totally innate it is, the rhythm in his blood as he’s throwing himself into the routine from Footloose, or dancing along to a nostalgia-fest of songs and video clips from Culture Club, Wham! and cartoon pop star Jem, to the theme from Wonder Woman or jingles for Gillette. We get a sunny mix of disco, jazz, acro-moves and fizzing energy, with BMX tricks thrown in. It’s a reminder of the power of pop music, and also of the boredom and freedom of an 80s childhood. When his mum is out, Malloy dresses up in her clothes and performs, but this thing he desires is also torturing him, as does living in a place where he has to hide his true self.View image in fullscreenRemembering and reconciling … Piotr Iwanicki in Boys Don’t Dance.Photograph: Brian HartleyChampion wheelchair Latin dancer Piotr Iwanicki plays the grownup Brew, remembering his past and reconciling with it, and he and Malloy find some synergy and inventive moves together. The staging is simple but nicely done, video designer Jamie Wardrop’s backdrop of animated line drawings creates the neighbourhood, and monochrome turns to neon as Brew finds his real freedom in the big city.Yeehaw! Bring on the tap-dancing cowgirls! How the Edinburgh Military Tattoo suddenly got coolRead moreIt’s engaging storytelling, warm and feelgood, and with a brilliant soundtrack (especially for viewers of the appropriate vintage). Boys Don’tDancewas created with eight to 13-year-olds in mind, so it’s not the most complex dramatically, emotionally or choreographically – and their parents might get more out of the cultural references – but it’s a really sweet show.AtAssembly @ Dance Base, Edinburgh,until 23 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalFestivalsDanceChildren's theatreTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Vile statues, writhing liquorice and kids marooned online: Edinburgh art festival review | Art | The Guardian
description: From queer narratives to secret histories, this year celebrates the underground and the unheralded. Our writer uncovers so many stories, he feels like Columbo
Author: Eddy Frankel
Headline: From queer narratives to secret histories, this year celebrates the underground and the unheralded. Our writer uncovers so many stories, he feels like Columbo
Content: Making connections … The Cloud, 2026, by Eva Rothschild.Photograph: Ruth Clark/courtesy the artist/Modern Art/The Modern Institute/Toby Webster Ltd, GlasgowView image in fullscreenMaking connections … The Cloud, 2026, by Eva Rothschild.Photograph: Ruth Clark/courtesy the artist/Modern Art/The Modern Institute/Toby Webster Ltd, GlasgowArtReviewVile statues, writhing liquorice and kids marooned online: Edinburgh art festival reviewVarious venues, EdinburghFrom queer narratives to secret histories, this year celebrates the underground and the unheralded. Our writer uncovers so many stories, he feels like ColumboEddy FrankelFri 14 Aug 2026 09.31 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 09.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy the time you’re done with Edinburgh art festival you’ll have uncovered so many hidden stories you’ll feel like Columbo. We’re talking queer narratives, secret histories, undiscovered archives: the whole festival is a celebration of the underground and unheralded. You can’t walk into a gallery without learning about some subcultural genius or longlost creative you’ve never heard of. That’s not a bad MO for a city-wide art festival.But EAF is also a big, unwieldy, confusing thing. There are curated displays, satellite exhibitions, performances, off-site projects, and it’s impossible to figure out how any of it fits together. You’ve just got to follow your nose and hope you sniff out something you like. And you’d better like photography, because there’s a lot of it here.View image in fullscreenEdinburgh everyone should see … Craigmillar School, 1994, by Sandra George.Photograph: courtesy Craigmillar Now © Sandra George EstateThe whole thing starts with US photographerDel LaGrace Volcano, whose images of queer nightlife in 1980s London are great: intimate, confrontational, erotic, totally defiant, as are the images of lesbian goths draping themselves over tombstones in Edinburgh graveyards. They’re insights into properly underground, subcultural life in the 1980s and 90s. Plenty of the photos aren’t all that good, but this feels like an artist who should be gathering a lot more attention, dealing with themes that have been all over the art and museum world recently.When it comes to untold stories, that ofSandra George(1957-2013) is worth telling. She was a black photographer and photojournalist who documented life on the margins of inner city Edinburgh. Like a lot of people in EAF, she never showed her work publicly in her lifetime, and was only discovered after her death in 2013.From her unique perspective as a semi-outsider, she documented communities in the city’s impoverished Craigmillar area. She captured protests and action groups operating out of living rooms and town halls; people living in hostels and housing schemes, skinheads, labourers, Hare Krishnas, Indians, Jamaicans, white and black. She appears throughout her show at CityArtGallery in self-portraits, often with her young son. There are kids everywhere, always playing and laughing, often in desperately bleak places. This might be work about Edinburgh, but it deserves to be seen far outside the city’s confines.Jill Edelstein, at Stills Gallery, also started out as a photojournalist, but took a different approach to George. Her polished images of Robert Rauschenberg, James Baldwin and Nelson Mandela don’t do a lot for me, although she does have a series about wild swimming that may find a different audience.Scottish photographerWendy McMurdo’s show at the Scottish National Portrait Gallery is quietly unsettling. For decades she’s been photographing children playing. But the results aren’t joyful visions of childhood: they’re disquieting portraits of a shifting society trying to make sense of rapid technological innovation. The kids play on computers and tablets, but the technology has been digitally removed, leaving behind isolated figures interacting with nothing. These are kids drifting into online worlds, and at risk of being lost in them for ever.View image in fullscreenThe Somnambulist, 1995, by Wendy McMurdo.Photograph: © Wendy McMurdo, all rights reserved, DACS 2026/courtesy Patricia Fleming Gallery, GlasgowWhen it’s not photography, EAF trades in pretty hard-edged contemporary art. Irish sculptorEva Rothschildhas taken over Fruitmarket with a disparate exhibition that feels like someone saved a collection of modernist sculpture from a skip. In the space downstairs, it’s all hyper-referential, full of riffs on Brancusi and Hepworth. Some of it is figurative, some abstract. Some of it is soft, some hard. It’s a lot of things, but none of them good.The work upstairs is way better, the palette reduced down to black and primary colours. She’s used rubber hoses like giant bits of liquorice and coiled, squiggled and squirmed them around metal frames. There’s a pile of half-graffitied concrete blocks you can climb, a glossy black geometric tower that reaches towards the ceiling. It’s like Memphis Group aesthetics gone goth and left to rot in the street. I love it, but I’m not sure how the art downstairs fails to work so well.A strange ritual from some dystopian future has been built into the vaulted Georgian spaces of Talbot Rice Gallery byAnne Hardy. The floor is covered in breeze blocks and markings in dirt, the lights flicker, the sound of rain fills the gallery. Figures made of bronze and wood stand before you, draped in hooded jackets. The handout talks about vibrations, energy, AI, weather systems in Texas. It’s mind-meltingly indecipherable. So what’s left is more of a vibe: a sense of human spirituality, survival and endurance in the bleak near-future. I’d be lying if I said I had any of this figured out, but its immersiveness and delicacy works well, although it is way too knowingly obtuse.View image in fullscreenKnowingly obtuse … The Beginning and the End by Anne Hardy.Photograph: © Anne HardyRichard Maguireat Collective Gallery at the top of Calton Hill suffers a similar fate, where the strength of the ideas – looking at representations of race and homosexuality across south Asian and British histories – is let down by some wispy, barely contextualised lumps and scrawls.Nearby,Emii Alrai’s huge, fractured monument overlooking the city is meant to reference Sumerian deities, standing in opposition to the National Monument of Scotland a few metres away. It feels like something almost ancient, broken, a relic in progress. But up close it’s a pretty shonky looking thing.If contemporary artists and institutions want to tell hidden stories, I think they have a duty – to viewers and to their subjects – to tell them clearly. Which is whatJamie Fitzpatrickat Edinburgh Printmakers has done. His show is the result of spending way too long thinking about the statues that sit on plinths all around the cities of the UK and realising that we’re all being constantly loomed over by war criminals, land barons and slavers.View image in fullscreenSubtle, strange … Out of the Swim by Frank Walter.Photograph: Andy Keate/Frank WalterA figure in a Georgian wig grins menacingly at you as you enter, a red plasticine smile plastered across his face. He’s on the verge of tumbling and collapsing into a messy pile, as is the skeletal figure behind him, all bared teeth and lumpen features. They’re inspired by the statues you see around Edinburgh, their vileness amplified to better reflect the kinds of men we publicly memorialise. The whole thing is like someone let the Muppets loose on some clay. It’s brilliantly gloopy, messy, cartoonish, chaotic and satirical.The group show atIngleby Galleryis good, too. It’s all centred on Frank Walter (1926-2009), an Antiguan painter, writer, poet and polymath, who died having never shown any of the thousands of paintings and drawings he amassed over his lifetime. His work is small, subtle, strange. He paints on ripped cardboard and fading paper; he depicts rainbows and stars and smiling faces, dancing women and strange trees that bend and twist at weird angles. His works are flanked by some giants of contemporary painting – a big Rose Wylie vision of young tulips, a gorgeous Lynette Yiadom-Boakye portrait of a kneeling figure – but it’s all eclipsed by his weird little paintings.Over among the horses and goats of Jupiter Artland, young Northern Irish artistSgàire Woodhas set about mashing together pop culture symbolism and the visual language of heraldry. The result is a gallery filled with shields, drums and birds covered in sequins and pink fur. It feels like a show that’s come too early in their career, but what it lacks in finesse, editing and finish, it makes up for in an overabundance of ideas.Another largely undiscovered artist,Sadao Hasegawa(1945-1999), really ramps up the eroticism with an eye-popping display of throbbing members and gushing penetration at Custom Lane. Most of the Japanese illustrator’s work, you guessed it, stayed unpublished and unseen in his lifetime. And that’s a shame because they’re amazing images: either soft-focus portraiture or a violent fusion of Japanese mythology and hardcore porn-filled naked figures writhing and brandishing katanas while fighting off giant spiders.There are lots of good shows here and plenty of bad ones, too. The whole thing could do with some more ambition, some bigger names, some starrier attractions. And it’s all a bit worthy and lecture-y, like you’re getting told off in every gallery you enter. “You’ve never heard of this previously undiscovered marginalised artist? You bastard!”Basically, EAF is too big and complex, with too many moving parts and collaborations and clashing ideas to really make sense. But maybe not everything has to make sense – maybe sometimes a city can just be filled with interesting, fun, diverse art, with loads of hidden stories and undiscovered narratives, and we can all go home happy. I did.Various venues, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustExplore more on these topicsArtEdinburgh festival 2026InstallationPaintingSculpturePhotographyEdinburgh festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Alien: Isolation 2 – another strong female protagonist stalked in a terrifying new world | Games | The Guardian
description: Creative Assembly could strike gold again with this follow-up to their fan-favourite, film-inspired game … if you’re brave enough to venture outdoors
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Creative Assembly could strike gold again with this follow-up to their fan-favourite, film-inspired game … if you’re brave enough to venture outdoors
Content: ‘The player and the alien are going to have to adapt to survive’ … Alien: Isolation 2.Photograph: SegaView image in fullscreen‘The player and the alien are going to have to adapt to survive’ … Alien: Isolation 2.Photograph: SegaSummer games previewsGamesAlien: Isolation 2 – another strong female protagonist stalked in a terrifying new worldCreative Assembly could strike gold again with this follow-up to their fan-favourite, film-inspired game … if you’re brave enough to venture outdoorsGraeme MasonFri 14 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 08.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlien: Isolationredefined Alien games on its release in 2014, bringing the original taut, haunted house theme of thefirst movieto fans who had mostly been fed action-packed shooters. Cowering under desks and inside lockers wasn’t a new thing; being hunted by an intelligent and lethal xenomorph that could spring down from a duct at any moment was.“I was thinking about what we could do for a sequel while we were still finishing the first game,” reveals Creative Assembly’s Alistair Hope, creative lead on Alien: Isolation and its sequel. “But we didn’t actually start the project until around the time of the 10th anniversary. We’ve seen the response grow over time, watching [Alien: Isolation] continue to find new players, even though it’s a relatively old game. And they’re surprised there isn’t a sequel.”Details are slight, but here’s what we know so far: a Weyland-Yutani survey team discovers a crashed vessel on a planet that resembles LV-426 crossed with a windswept forest. It’s a vessel that’ll appear familiar to fans of Alien: Isolation – it’s the part of Sevastopol that the duplicitous Marshal Waits jettisons from the station in the first game, with Amanda Ripley and the alien inside. Ripley escapes. The alien does not. Until now.“We were super proud of Amanda. She’s really important to the Alien: Isolation experience. But we wanted to tell a new story, in a new location, and to do that, it felt like we needed a new protagonist,” says Hope. That new character is Blake, although Hope is tight-lipped on any details beyond her employer, Weyland-Yutani. It seems likely, however, that this new lead, thrust into the dangerous world of the xenomorph, will follow the IP’s tradition of strong female characters.View image in fullscreen‘We’ve been effectively training it to hunt in the exterior’ … Alien: Isolation 2.Photograph: SegaA fascinating part ofAlien: Isolation 2will be how the alien reacts to its new environment. “The alien uses its senses to track you down, and it’s very effective in those interior spaces. So we’ve been effectively training it to hunt in the exterior. Those core survival skills that you needed in the first game will be the same – but the player and the alien are going to have to adapt to survive.” That’s not to say Alien: Isolation 2 won’t have plenty of claustrophobic interiors, creating a seesaw of emotions whether trapped inside or exposed outside. “We can play with that, and mess with it. It feels like a really exciting opportunity.”Carcass Clad: stifling tank combat promises tension, terror and surprising laughsRead moreTaking place months after the events of Alien: Isolation, the sequel will retain the low-fi sci-fi universe, leaning heavily once more on the first Alien movie. There’s a glimpse of a Working Joe in the trailer, suggesting that, once again, the alien might not be the only antagonist the player has to avoid. Could hostile humans enter the mix? Hope is guarded. “Alien: Isolation 2 absolutely is building on that core foundation that we established in the first [game],” he says. “And, yeah, we love that rock, paper, scissors setup and scenario.” Draw your own acid blood-spattered conclusions.Sevastopol, the decommissioned and slowly decaying space station of Alien: Isolation, became an evocative extra character in the original game. Creative Assembly appears well placed to repeat the trick with Alien: Isolation 2’s forbidding colony world, home to a remote Weyland-Yutani outpost, Kurosaki Station. Just don’t forget your umbrella.Alien: Isolation 2 is coming soon to PC, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S and Nintendo Switch 2.Explore more on these topicsGamesSummer games previewsAlienShooting gamesAction gamesAdventure gamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It was lonely being a young queer artist’: Sam Smith on finding health, happiness – and their hazel-eyed fiance | Sam Smith | The Guardian
description: On their new album, Smith is subverting their singer-songwriter roots to tell a queer love story. They talk about their shifting fanbase, the nasty undercurrents of fame – and finding sanctuary in New York City
Author: Juan A Ramírez
Headline: On their new album, Smith is subverting their singer-songwriter roots to tell a queer love story. They talk about their shifting fanbase, the nasty undercurrents of fame – and finding sanctuary in New York City
Content: ‘On Hazel Eyes, I wanted to capture the bloom of falling deeply in love’ … Sam Smith.Photograph: Collier SchorrView image in fullscreen‘On Hazel Eyes, I wanted to capture the bloom of falling deeply in love’ … Sam Smith.Photograph: Collier SchorrSam SmithInterview‘It was lonely being a young queer artist’: Sam Smith on finding health, happiness – and their hazel-eyed fianceJuan A RamírezOn their new album, Smith is subverting their singer-songwriter roots to tell a queer love story. They talk about their shifting fanbase, the nasty undercurrents of fame – and finding sanctuary in New York CityFri 14 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 05.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSam Smith logs on to our video call with the username “Lily of the Valley”, the May-born singer’s birth flower. It sets a serene tone. They’re in Guadalajara, Mexico, for the latest stop of a residency tour, titled To Be Free, in support of their fifth studio album. Instead of Smith’s usual jet-lagged arena itinerary, this lower-key excursion stops at smaller venues in only six cities and sheds the ostentatious theatricality of their last outing.On stage on their last tour, “I was flailing around on a massive gold bum and had, like, seven costume changes,” Smith says with a chuckle. It’s intimacy they’re after now, the ability to satisfy their “craving to look at people again”, which matches the romantic feeling of their fifth album, Hazel Eyes. But for Smith, whose genre-shifting stardom has been accompanied by harsh controversies, it’s also a chance to observe who’s still in their corner: “There’s some wonderful people that have stayed, but it’s a completely different room than it was with In the Lonely Hour,” their 2014 debut.View image in fullscreenSmith performs at the Castro theatre in San Francisco on their To Be Free tour.Photograph: Steve Jennings/Getty Images for Capitol RecordsSmith broke out at 20, as the featured vocalist on Disclosure’s massive 2012 hit Latch. That 2014 debut, featuring the mega-hit Stay With Me, heralded them as a soulful chart-topper, if one whose knack for heartbreak could verge on self-pity. It was good enough for Bond: in 2015, Smith sang the Spectre theme Writing’s on the Wall and won an Oscar. Their subsequent releases veered into a glossier pop sound and generally remained as successful. But since coming out as non-binary in 2017, the British singer has frequently been attacked and vilified by rightwing commentators. The peace that emanates from the 34-year-old during our call, and from this latest album, was largely achieved after relocating from the UK to New York three years ago to be with their fiance, the (hazel-eyed) designer Christian Cowan.“When I got here and was able to walk in the street and feel no judgment, I realised that I was very happy to have found a sanctuary in New York City as a queer person,” they say. Smith, who has been wearing “makeup and wild femme clothing from a very young age”, found that “tensions were a little high” after the 2023 release oftheir expressive last album, Gloria. “With a body like mine and the person that I am, it created a bit of a media storm.” (The videos for Unholy and I’m Not Here to Make Friends were accused of being oversexualised, with a rhetoric that felt transphobic to many observers.) “But I moved to New York for positive reasons. I wasn’t running away from anything.”After Gloria, Smith “was looking for safety and comfort in music”, something to capture “the bloom of falling deeply in love” and buoy their cross-continental move. They found it by downsizing their process. Simon Aldred, with whom Smith had co-written one song on their debut, had long told Smith to call whenever they were ready for a more intimate collaboration. For Hazel Eyes, Smith took him up on it.View image in fullscreen‘I was flailing around on a massive gold bum’ … Smith on stage in Berlin for the Gloria tour, 2023.Photograph: Frank Hoensch/RedfernsThe result is a more clear-eyed assessment of the reality of relationships than Smith’s lovelorn previous albums. They wrote the first half of what became the smoky opener, Everlasting Love, the night before meeting Cowan; the second half reflects on their three years together. It’s also Smith’s first time co-producing an album. “I’ve always been very hands on with my music, but I never felt like I could really put my name on the credit,” they say. “I’ve realised that I’m not just a singer and a songwriter, I’m an artist.” Hazel Eyes’ soundscape channels a dusky, 70s blend of blues and folk, R&B and outlaw country.The process was looser than Smith’s past experiences in more professional, structured writing rooms, where they felt that recording had to be done “completely sober and all had to happen between the hours of 10am and 5pm”. Hazel Eyes was written at all hours, thanks in part to their near-constant conversations with Aldred; Smith mentions tequila-tinged 1am studio sessions with the Dap-Kings, the late Sharon Jones’s band, as a high point: “It just felt so freeing, what music’s about.”These relaxed, more intimate collaborations scared Smith, who says they had operated as “a pop ho for a long time – in the best way. I loved it, and I will be that again, but every two, three records were written with a different group of people. It was like a speed-dating process of making music.”Watch the video for My Guy.Hazel Eyes is also a return to the singer-songwriter style of Smith’s debut. They don’t see it as a rehash, but a new angle on traditional songwriting tropes. “A song like My Guy, that lyric is so simple and one that maybe we’ve all heard before – ‘He’s mine, mine, mine, he’s my guy’ – but you haven’t heard it from a non-binary person who’s 34 years old in 2026. I was very interested in that type of lyric-writing for this album, to take the traditional and sing it through my lens and sing it freely.”It was only after the success of Unholy, their 2023 duet with Kim Petras, that Smith found the freedom to return to that classic sound. With its baroque electropop and panic-baiting live performances (at the Grammys, Smithsported a pair of devil hornsin a red-lit, fiery set), the global No 1 single earned them a Grammy – andcondemnation from conservatives. “When Unholy happened, I felt like I’d been fighting for that song for a long time,” says Smith – they had always wanted to top the US charts, having previously peaked there at No 2 with Stay With Me.Global competition is no longer a concern for Smith. “As a queer artist, I have different parameters and rules, so it’s just not a healthy way for me to think,” they say – that for any artist whose existence is, to some, contentious, fame is always rigged with a nasty undercurrent, no matter how quantifiable their success. Smith says they were at their “most depressed or creatively stunted” during that chase. With Hazel Eyes, they wanted to focus on emotional truth rather than “worrying about hooks, even though I love hooks”. They’ll return to that, says Smith, “but it’s my prerogative to choose when I want to use that tool”. This led to some “uncomfortable moments” with their label, with Smith having to say “I just wanted to keep the business out of the music”.View image in fullscreen‘I wanted to keep business out of the music’ … Smith.Photograph: Collier SchorrHazel Eyes was the first time Smith set a colour palette (“this brown, sepia filter”) and ethos to which every song must be upheld: a familiar guiding image, based on a lifelong affinity for rivers born out of a bucolic spot near their Cambridgeshire home town. Any ideas, sounds or lyrics, even the more urbane, New-York-inspired ones, would have to sound at home in that domesticated image in order to make it on to the record. They found that rigour liberating – it allowed Smith to lean into the maximalism of carrying through a single idea. “I like spilling over the sides,” they say. “There’s something for me in the imperfection of it that feels so pop.”It’s a point of pride for Smith to have reset their relationship with the public on their own terms. Becoming a celebrity at 20 meant that they quickly found an “incredibly traumatic” side to fame, “especially to a younger, queer brain, because it felt quite lonely at times within the industry”. For a few years, from 27, they shunned the “huge part of the job” that is constantly taking selfies with fans. Doing so allowed them to recover some semblance of privacy, but led to depression, “because I felt like I was upsetting people all day”.After a lot of therapy, they say, “I actually have started to find the happiness and the joy of meeting people. I’m a healthy person right now, so I’m able to juggle more. The trajectory of fame that I went through at such a young age, and trying to navigate my life as a gay person, then changing my pronouns – the weight of doing that so publicly in my 20s meant that I could juggle less.”Occasionally, there is a protective edge to Smith’s conversation, such as when they point out that they “juggled a lot, because I brought out four records and toured the world multiple times”. But it doesn’t feel confrontational; more demarcating well-defined boundaries and a hard-won ability to claim their achievements.Watch the video for Unholy.It’s true that controversy has hounded Smith from day one. They have never concealed their sexuality and have evolved almost entirely in the public eye, which has included some stumbles. In 2016, when collecting the Academy award for best original song for their Bond theme, they incorrectly claimed to be the first openly gay Oscar winner (that was John Schlesinger as best director of Midnight Cowboy, in 1970); shortly into the 2020 lockdown, they were ridiculed for sharing photosdepicting their “quarantine meltdown” that some felt to be tone deaf.Whatever anyone says, Smith’s sales and streaming figures put them in the echelons of Elton John and Freddie Mercury in terms of queer pop success stories, although Smith is cautious about placing themselves within that legacy. “George Michael was always a beautiful inspiration to me,” they say, but they’ve found a “deep comfort and understanding about the type of artist I am” from conversations withthe artist Anohni, with whom they’ve grown close, “because I am not like George Michael. I’m a femme queer and when it comes to that, and the people that came before me in the UK, it’s a different type of lineage.“What I’ve experienced as a queer femme artist on the global pop stage, I don’t think there’s others that I can compare my career to,” they continue. “I’ve learned to see that as a strength when, at times before, I just found that incredibly isolating. I’m trying not to compare or to look left and right in that sense any more.”Smith finds that, after a period of increased LGBTQ+ acceptance in the UK and abroad, the pendulum has swung back. “For trans people in the UK, it’s incredibly hard.” I ask if they ever find solace in the thought that history will probably only remember their successes: Michael’s cruising scandal, I point out, has been almost entirely vindicated on queer social media. Smith takes a beat to think.View image in fullscreenSmith at the Grammys in 2015, where they won four awards.Photograph: Frazer Harrison/Getty Images“I want to answer this honestly,” they say. “I’m encouraged sometimes, especially by straight people around me, to think of that. It doesn’t necessarily bring me comfort, because of the state of things. I think it’s important to be educated as a queer person, to know that things could get better, but things could also get worse in my lifetime, and we have to work hard for kindness and peace.” Two years ago, they established the Pink House foundation, a charity that will provide support for the LGBTQ+ community. It gives Smith a chance to “focus on the realities of situations and hope for a better future”, they say, more than focusing on their own legacy.But there’s at least one tribute to Smith’s life in New York. Julius’ is a gay bar in the city’s West Village with a history of community and rebellion. Alongside shots of icons such as Judy Garland and John Cameron Mitchell, some images of Smith line its walls. They were taken there by a friend, years ago. “I’m English, right? I love a pub.” It’s since become their favourite haunt; some of Hazel Eyes was written on the counter.‘Experimental, queer and kind of magical’: Sade and Sam Smith feature on 46-track album for trans rightsRead moreWith a self-effacing grin, they point out that those photos are “in the back” of the venue. Still, one is by the noted fashion photographer Alasdair McLellan. “I love Alasdair McLellan – so that’s just a slay.” The other is of Smith and Alicia Keys from a small performance they hosted at the bar for a 10th anniversary celebration of In the Lonely Hour. “It was such a beautiful, triumphant moment for me, as someone who was moving to New York, to get to sing with Alicia fucking Keys in this gay bar.” Smith beams. “If I could be part of the legacy of Julius’, that’s a legacy I’m proud to be a part of.”With all but their third album topping the UK charts (Love Goes peaked at No 2), there’s a confidence that, no matter what they release, Hazel Eyes will find an audience. “I’m a political artist, whether I want to be or not, so my audience is in flux at times,” Smith says. “I am singing for me, ultimately, and I’m singing to the sky and whoever hears it.”Hazel Eyes is released via Capitol on 21 AugustThis article was amended on 14 August 2026. Hazel Eyes is released via Capitol, not Polydor as previously stated.Explore more on these topicsSam SmithPop and rockLGBTQ+ rightsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Post your questions for Robert Carlyle | Robert Carlyle | The Guardian
description: Bond villain, Begbie, male stripper … the Trainspotting and Full Monty star has played everyone from Sherlock Holmes to Rumpelstiltskin. As his latest directorial project premieres in Edinburgh, he is here to answer your questions
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: Bond villain, Begbie, male stripper … the Trainspotting and Full Monty star has played everyone from Sherlock Holmes to Rumpelstiltskin. As his latest directorial project premieres in Edinburgh, he is here to answer your questions
Content: Can he still drive a double-decker? … Robert Carlyle.Photograph: Alana Paterson/The ObserverView image in fullscreenCan he still drive a double-decker? … Robert Carlyle.Photograph: Alana Paterson/The ObserverFilm & Music reader interviewRobert CarlylePost your questions for Robert CarlyleBond villain, Begbie, male stripper … the Trainspotting and Full Monty star has played everyone from Sherlock Holmes to Rumpelstiltskin.
