As his latest directorial project premieres in Edinburgh, he is here to answer your questionsRich PelleyFri 14 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 08.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou’ll know Robert Carlyle for many things – getting his kit off inThe Full Monty, being skewered through the heart with a plutonium rod as Bond villain Renard in The World Is Not Enough, playing Sherlock Holmes in Watson, joining Line of Duty as a gruff specialist firearms officer, and appearing opposite David Tennant and Toby Jones in ITV’s The Hack.He also appeared as Adolf Hitler in Hitler: The Rise of Evil and (uncredited) as John Lennon in Yesterday; as a cannibalistic soldier in Ravenous; Rumplestiltskin in Once Upon a Time; and the British prime minister in Cobra. But it’s hard to ever fully dissociate him from the fantastic moustache he sports as violent, pint-swilling psychopath Francis Begbie inTrainspotting– a moustache that is now, unbelievably, 30 years old and heading back to cinemas in a new 4K restoration from 21 August.But for the purposes of our next readers’ interview, we are also interested in Carlyle behind the camera. More than a decade after directing and starring in 2015 black comedy The Legend of Barney Thomson, alongside Emma Thompson, Ray Winstone and Ashley Jensen, he has returned to the director’s chair with a new short film, Three – a darkly funny, increasingly unsettling three-hander about sex, class, power and three people trying to work out exactly who is using whom. The film has its European premiere at the Edinburgh international film festival on Friday and screens again on Sunday.So, what to ask him? Does Begbie’s moustache deserve its own 30th-anniversary interview? Has playing Sherlock Holmes made him any better at Cluedo? Can he still drive a double-decker bus, like he does inKen Loach’s Carla’s Song? What happened to his Saturday Tunes, where he used to recommend new bands every week on Twitter? Did he have the two teeth put back in that he had removed to bring Begbie back for T2 Trainspotting? And what does it feel like to stomp through the countryside as a giant, as he does inthe video for Oasis’s Little By Little?Post your questions below by 6pm on Wednesday 19 August and we’ll print his answers as part of our readers’ interview series.Threescreens as part of the Edinburgh international film festival’s Out of Competition Shorts at 2pm on Friday 14 August at Cameo and at 2pm on Sunday 16 August at Cineworld.Explore more on these topicsRobert CarlyleFilm & Music reader interviewLine of DutyTrainspottingEdinburgh film festivalDramaFestivalsTelevisioncalloutShareReuse this content

title: How the mob took Hollywood: the story of organized crime and the movies  | Documentary | The Guardian
description: Hollywood Crime Story: The Mob Takes Over the Movies looks back at how criminals insinuated themselves in the film business
Author: Zach Vasquez
Headline: Hollywood Crime Story: The Mob Takes Over the Movies looks back at how criminals insinuated themselves in the film business
Content: A photograph used in Hollywood Crime Story: The Mob Takes Over the Movies.Photograph: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA photograph used in Hollywood Crime Story: The Mob Takes Over the Movies.Photograph: Getty ImagesDocumentaryHow the mob took Hollywood: the story of organized crime and the moviesHollywood Crime Story: The Mob Takes Over the Movies looks back at how criminals insinuated themselves in the film businessZach VasquezFri 14 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 16.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“From the foundation of Hollywood, organized crime is there.” So claims Tom Patterson, producer and director of new three-part documentary series, Hollywood Crime Story: The Mob Takes Over the Movies.American witchhunt: how the McCarthy blacklist annihilated the Hollywood leftRead moreOrganized crime’s connection to the film industry actually predates Tinseltown, being present for the foundation of the medium itself, when inventor Thomas Edison sicced his hired goons on competitors in an attempt to maintain total control over early motion picture technology. As covered in Hollywood Crime Story, this resulted in said competitors – mostly Jewish businessmen from the east coast – fleeing westward and establishing the town and studio system that would become synonymous with movies as we know them.That same period also begat the rise of organized crime syndicates on the other side of the country – The Outfit in Chicago, the mafia in New York – a result of the criminal economy created by Prohibition. It didn’t take long for the two worlds to collide. Combining archival footage with talking head interviews, Hollywood Crime Story charts the interdependent relationship between the mob and the movies from development of cinema through to the year 1990, when the dual releases of The Godfather Part III and Goodfellas, per Patterson, “put a nice cap on that era of Hollywood”.View image in fullscreenAl Capone in 1931.Photograph: APEpisode one covers the dawn of the motion picture through the 1960s, a period that saw the ascension of the Chicago kingpin Al Capone, who dispatches one of his underlings, Johnny Roselli, out west to explore new business opportunities. Roselli finds a Hollywood ripe for the picking, quickly establishing himself among its top stars and moguls, including and especially Harry Cohn, the vicious co-founder and president of Columbia Pictures. It was thanks to a half-million-dollar loan from Roselli that Cohn was able to buy out his partners at Columbia, thus giving the mob its first real stakes in one of the major studios.We learn about Capone’s short but lively trip to Hollywood and his initially antagonistic but ultimately positive reception to the loose biopic made about him in 1932, Scarface. We meet suave but volatile gangster Benjamin “Bugsy” Siegel, who moves to town and immediately starts rubbing shoulders with the industry elite; his underling and future replacement as head of vice in LA, the brutish Mickey Cohen, who got his start in crime at age nine when he held up a movie theater; Cohen’s abusive thug Johnny Stompanato, who dated movie star Lana Turner and was eventually stabbed to death by her teenage daughter; and the corrupt union officials whom the mob inserted as heads of the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees (IATSE) and the Teamsters. We get the startling tale of the bosses putting a hit out on the Screen Actors Guild president, James Cagney, when he wouldn’t hand his union over to them (his life only spared thanks to Scarface lead Paul Muni personally asking Capone to intervene) and a funny anecdote about Cohen robbing leading lady Betty Grable only for her to laugh it off when they reunite years later.Most of these violent characters meet violent ends, but nature abhors a vacuum, so it isn’t long before new shady figures take the reins. Episode two of Hollywood Crime Story is set between the late 60s and the early 80s. “Rather than disappearing after the fall of the studio system,” explains Patterson, “organized crime becomes more intertwined with Hollywood than ever, but in more mainstream-accepted ways.”View image in fullscreenLana Turner and Johnny Stompanato.Photograph: Getty ImagesIn one of the series’ best moments, one-time president of Universal Studios Tom Mount tells of attending a meeting presided over by director Alfred Hitchcock, super-agent Lew Wasserman (whose uber-powerful agency MCA rose to prominence with the direct backing of Capone), former mobster and Las Vegas mogul Mo Dalitz, and lawyer Sidney Korshak, one of if not the most powerful man in Hollywood thanks in no small part to his large mob clientele. Mount recalls listening to these men “carve out” parts of Hollywood for themselves.Wasserman and Korshack are two of the central figures in this middle chapter, as they were at the heart of a cadre made up of Jewish gangsters and businessmen known as the Supermob, or, alternatively, “the Kosher Nostra”. The Supermob ran every aspect of Hollywood, from casting to funding to unionizing – as well as off-the-books wheeling and dealing, such as negotiating the release of Frank Sinatra’s kidnapped son – but, as summed up by series narrator Jeff Rechner, “where the mob once used violence to exercise control, these new figures wield the boardroom as their weapon.”Their story leads directly to the creation of the most iconic mob movie of all time: The Godfather. Shepherded by Korshack protege and maverick president of Paramount Pictures Robert Evans, secretly funded in part by mafia and Vatican banker Michele Sindona, and given an unofficial greenlight by crime boss and Italian civil rights campaigner Joe Colombo (who’d be gunned down during a public speech while the film was in production), the huge success of The Godfather went on to reshape how both film-makers and criminals operated.“When The Godfather came out, mobsters were trying to keep it low-key,” says Patterson. “Then they see this grand, wonderful old school depiction and think, ‘I want to live like that.’ You start hearing stories of the gestures becoming bigger – the kissing the ring of the capo, the big weddings, the whispered meetings, the code names.”View image in fullscreenRobert Duvall and Marlon Brando in The Godfather.Photograph: Paramount/Kobal/ShutterstockAs with the rogue’s gallery from episode one, this renewed attention and heightened profile leads to tragedy for most of these individuals. But even as this second generation of shadowy powerbrokers are either dragged into the light or snuffed out for good, they manage to reshape the future of entertainment. Hollywood Crime Story argues: “In squeezing the life out of prestige film-making and transforming studio economics, Korshack and the Supermob may have unknowingly set the stage for the blockbuster age.”That age truly dawned in the next decade, alongside mainstream cinema’s disreputable sister industry: pornography. Episode three explores how mob-affiliated figures, such as Louis “Butchie” Peraino, parlayed the money they made from producing porno flicks into purchasing and distributing legitimate films (in his case, titles such as Andy Warhol’s Frankenstein, Enter the Dragon, Dark Star and The Texas Chainsaw Massacre), thus creating an early model for independent film-making that we’d see take off in the 90s.Alongside pornography, the other big revenue stream for Hollywood mobsters was cocaine, which became the drug de rigueur of the town’s elite. Robert Evans and his fall from grace become the focus for much of this episode, particularly his involvement in the disastrous production of the 1984 historical crime drama The Cotton Club. Reuniting with Godfather director Francis Ford Coppola in the hopes of recreating that film’s success, Evans made a desperate decision to secure funding by partnering with two members of Florida’s cocaine cartel. The subsequent falling-out between the pair resulted in a highly publicized murder trial that would destroy what was left of Evans’s reputation (at least until his unlikely third-act reinvention 20 years later).View image in fullscreenRobert Evans in 1974.Photograph: Jeff Robbins/APThese stories are just a sampling of those covered in Hollywood Crime Story, which, by its directors’ own admission, barely scratches the surface. Inspired during the development of respective docuseries about Marylin Monroe and Elvis Presley’s connections to the mob, Patterson found that “Once you start diving into it, another story pops up, and another story pops up, and another story pops up. The hardest part was deciding what to include in the three episodes.”To that end, Patterson is greatly helped by the expert team he assembled behind and in front of the camera, a mix of mob historians, such as senior director of education at Las Vegas’s Mob Museum Claire White and author Gus Russo, and film experts like Jonathan Kuntz and Christina Newland. The documentary succeeds not only as a breezy, but expertly researched look behind the Hollywood curtain, but also as a critical examination of the mob genre itself, its evolution from the silent era to the final decade of the 20th century. Patterson explains his decision to end in 1990 by asking, “Has there been a truly great gangster movie since Goodfellas? They either tend to look to the past or they’re on TV.”Regardless of one’s opinion on post-2000 mob cinema, Patterson notes that “Organized crime in Hollywood ranges today from Ukrainian mobsters taking over streaming services to African gangs running piracy, etc, etc. We don’t live in the world of concentrated power in either a physical or psycho-geographic Hollywood any more.”However diffuse organized crime’s impact is on the industry in today’s digital age, you can bet the relationship remains a symbiotic one, with movies influencing how gangsters think and act, and vice versa, ad infinitum.Hollywood Crime Story: The Mob Takes Over the Movies airs on Sundance Now and is available on AMC+This article was amended on 14 August 2026. It was originally stated that Lana Turner was married to Johnny Stompanato, but they only dated.Explore more on these topicsDocumentaryFactual TVTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Real Kyle McCarren review – musical eulogy to lost bandmate strikes a chord | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Andy Roninson’s tribute to a friend who died aged 21 combines original rock, soul and folk songs in a considered exploration of grief
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Andy Roninson’s tribute to a friend who died aged 21 combines original rock, soul and folk songs in a considered exploration of grief
Content: Singing seance … Andy Roninson and Sean McVerry in The Real Kyle McCarren.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/the GuardianView image in fullscreenSinging seance … Andy Roninson and Sean McVerry in The Real Kyle McCarren.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/the GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewThe Real Kyle McCarren review – musical eulogy to lost bandmate strikes a chordPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghAndy Roninson’s tribute to a friend who died aged 21 combines original rock, soul and folk songs in a considered exploration of griefChris WiegandFri 14 Aug 2026 06.18 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 06.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThey say don’t speak ill of the dead – how about singing instead? Based on real events, this new US musical is designed as a loving but warts-and-all eulogy. His friend and bandmate Kyle, who died out of the blue at the age of 21, was a rock for him, says creatorAndy Roninson. “But in a Sisyphus way.”Roninson narrates and plays the keys in a concert-style show that mostly unfolds in the days just after the death. It’s that strange period where a private sense of loss collides with congregation and you see the deceased through the eyes of mutual acquaintances, which can be jarring. This is exactly Andy’s experience as he’s outraged to find another so-called “best friend” Liam (Vincent Jamal Hooper) delivering a speech at the memorial, while tiptoeing around Kyle’s formidable mother (Jaygee Macapugay) and encountering Kyle’s ex (Sarah Coffey). Each of them has a solo tribute, covering a pleasing variety of rock, soul and folk (Coffey’s plaintive ballad stands out).Sean McVerry, who wrote the music and lyrics with book-writer Roninson, is ever-present as Kyle himself, frequently ribbing Andy.View image in fullscreenCongregation … Vincent Jamal Hooper, Jaygee Macapugay and Sarah Coffey in The Real Kyle McCarren.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/the GuardianThis is an earnest, assured and polished production, co-directed by Lonny Price and Matt Cowart, with some well-crafted songs. Roninson is aJonathan Larson Grantrecipient and his musical – set in “upstate wherever in the year 2000-who-cares” sometimes shares the off-kilter neuroses and wit ofthe Rent creator. Songs are presented in original ways, from Liam’s eulogy to Kyle and Andy jamming together as teens to one of his recordings being recreated between the cast when a CD starts skipping.You and Me (and Whoever Comes Next) review – theatre crafted with love and careRead moreThe challenge is to make us feel Kyle’s loss while telling (never really showing) his story in retrospect and to round out his character largely through others’ reminiscences. Despite the talent on stage, and some acute insights into the grieving process (especially how you lose a part of yourself when a friend dies), Kyle remained elusive for me. Perhaps that’s because the focus is not on any key incident of his life but on sketches of its aftermath. We’re told he could be an asshole but there’s little nitty-gritty, conflicted emotion or overarching plot to go with that. If the show broke out of its concert format, and perhaps added some fuller flashbacks, the songs would still soar and the real Kyle McCarren might properly emerge.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026TheatreMusicalsEdinburgh festivalDeath and dyingFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Joseph Morpurgo: Highlander 70 review – a dork’s last day at school is one to remember | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: This one-man comic play, told at breakneck speed and featuring West Side Story-like dance-numbers, is highly entertaining
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: This one-man comic play, told at breakneck speed and featuring West Side Story-like dance-numbers, is highly entertaining
Content: Ladling on the poignancy … Joseph MorpurgoView image in fullscreenLadling on the poignancy … Joseph MorpurgoEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewJoseph Morpurgo: Highlander 70 review – a dork’s last day at school is one to rememberPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghThis one-man comic play, told at breakneck speed and featuring West Side Story-like dance-numbers, is highly entertainingBrian LoganFri 14 Aug 2026 04.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s as ifJoseph Morpurgohad never been away. The Londoner made a splash on the fringe a decade ago with severalhigh-concept comedy shows, of which thrift-shop source material and multimedia presentation were standout features. After a nine-year absence, the same is true of Highlander 70, a one-man comic play built exclusively around an American high-school yearbook salvaged from half a century ago. Drawing on that book’s text and (mainly) innocent black-and-white photographs of wholesome teens, Morpurgo cobbles together a breakneck tale of dorky David Moon’s last day of school. He must navigate assembly, the big game, graduation – and then he’s free. “What could possibly go wrong?”View image in fullscreenInnocent photographs of wholesome teens … Joseph Morpurgo: Highlander 70In Morpurgo’s telling, plenty, as our juvenile hero (face painted grey, the better to resemble his monochrome original) embarks on a quest to recover his missing diary, which contains mortifying evidence of a crush on schoolmate Beth. Standing in his way, the school’s martinet principal, its bully Roscoe Peltz and his crew of unconvincing tough guys, and a dance-hall full of dangerously intoxicated adolescents.Moon/Morpurgo navigates all this with frenetic energy on stage and on an upstage screen, where images from the yearbook (with DIY animation and voiceovers attached) accompany or undercut the narrative to droll effect.The overarching joke here is the daftness of the project, the thought of Morpurgo poring over this random artefact from the past, looking for each tiny incongruity (a curious facial expression in the background; an odd diagram on the blackboard) around which a gag might be built, or a story told. The tale that emerges (squeaky-clean David learns to live a little) is simple but stirring, and Morpurgo ladles on poignancy at the end with an imagined “where are they now?” sequence. There are lulls – including an audience participation sequence I’m not sure justifies itself – but far more highs, such as the West Side Story-alike teenage bully dance number.For the most part, Highlander 70 keeps you highly entertained as Morpurgo sets every US high-school cliche spinning off in unlikely directions, distilling amid the nonsense both teen spirit and the bittersweet ineffability of the photographed past.AtPleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalFestivalsComedy (Culture)Comedy (Stage)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Nicole Kidman opens up about divorce from Keith Urban – and ‘throwing my career away’ for Tom Cruise | Nicole Kidman | The Guardian
description: Actor, 59, reflects on high-profile marriages in Vogue interview, saying she felt ‘deeply vulnerable’ after split from Urban
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: Actor, 59, reflects on high-profile marriages in Vogue interview, saying she felt ‘deeply vulnerable’ after split from Urban
Content: Nicole Kidman said of her life: ‘You make all these plans and you have all these ideas of what it’s all going to be like and then it’s… not.’Photograph: Marechal Aurore/Abaca/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenNicole Kidman said of her life: ‘You make all these plans and you have all these ideas of what it’s all going to be like and then it’s… not.’Photograph: Marechal Aurore/Abaca/ShutterstockNicole KidmanNicole Kidman opens up about divorce from Keith Urban – and ‘throwing my career away’ for Tom CruiseActor, 59, reflects on high-profile marriages in Vogue interview, saying she felt ‘deeply vulnerable’ after split from UrbanSian CainFri 14 Aug 2026 00.32 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 12.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNicole Kidman has opened up about her divorce from Keith Urban and reflected on her marriage to Tom Cruise, saying she was warned being his wife would overshadow her career.Ina new interview with Vogue, the 59-year-old actor spoke about going through two divorces under intense media scrutiny: with Cruise, who she married in 1990 and divorced in 2001, and musician Urban, who she married in 2006.Kidman filed for divorce from Urban in September 2025citing marital difficulties and irreconcilable differences, with the separation finalised out of court by January.‘We laced Nicole into her corset and her rib broke again’: Moulin Rouge at 25 – an oral history by cast and crewRead moreKidman said her second divorce had been a difficult period in her life, adding: “But at the same time I’m like, ‘OK, I didn’t expect this. I had a different view of what my life was going to be, but this is what it is now.’ You make all these plans and you have all these ideas of what it’s all going to be like and then it’s … not. You have to adjust. You adapt. The future, it’s completely unknown to me right now.”Asked if it had also been a “scary” time, Kidman said: “There was a point where I was very fearful and deeply vulnerable, which is exposing. And then at the same time [I’m] going: ‘Well, I can either really not confront it and just curl up, or I can just go forward with an enormous amount of hope.’”Asked if her split from Cruise had been “useful” for weathering the scrutiny around her second divorce, Kidman said: “It’s all new. Every time!”View image in fullscreenTom Cruise and Nicole Kidman at the premiere of his film Jerry Maguire in Rome, 1997.Photograph: Maurizio Brambatti/PAOf her marriage to Cruise, who she married when she was 23 and he was 28, she said, “Suddenly I was 22, 23 years old and I had this huge movie star husband. But it just seemed completely natural. We just fell madly in love and it was that simple. I remember people saying to me, ‘OK, well this is really going to affect your career’. I’m like, ‘I don’t care. I’m in love. I want to be married.’“And then I was his wife and they were like, ‘See, we told you.’ I’m like, ‘So what? I wasn’t meant to marry the man I love? Of course I’ll throw my career away. I don’t care.’”In the Vogue interview, Kidman also revealed she sometimes goes dancing in disguise, saying: “I’ll put on glasses. Sometimes I’ll wear a wig to hide, a little dark wig, and then I can just dance. As long as I’m surrounded by people – like, I take people with me – then I’m fine. I need it.”Explore more on these topicsNicole KidmanTom CruisenewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Lydia West’s offbeat college campus murder mystery  | Television | The Guardian
description: She stars as a grungy student in Australian dramedy He Had It Coming. Plus: Frank Skinner’s very funny standup special. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: She stars as a grungy student in Australian dramedy He Had It Coming. Plus: Frank Skinner’s very funny standup special. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Wrong place, wrong time … Lydia West (left) and Natasha Liu Bordizzo in He Had It Coming.Photograph: Lisa Tomasetti/BBC/2025 Jungle Entertainment Pty Ltd, Stan Entertainment Pty Ltd, Screen AustraliaView image in fullscreenWrong place, wrong time … Lydia West (left) and Natasha Liu Bordizzo in He Had It Coming.Photograph: Lisa Tomasetti/BBC/2025 Jungle Entertainment Pty Ltd, Stan Entertainment Pty Ltd, Screen AustraliaTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Lydia West’s offbeat college campus murder mysteryShe stars as a grungy student in Australian dramedy He Had It Coming. Plus: Frank Skinner’s very funny standup special. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Jack Seale,Phil Harrison,Priya ElanandSimon WardellFri 14 Aug 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHe Had It Coming11.15pm, BBC ThreeLydia West stars in this offbeat Australian comedy-drama about a murder on a university campus. It follows a grungy feminist art student, Elise (West), and her unlikely new influencer mate, Barbara (Natasha Liu Bordizzo), who get drunk and deface a statue – only to wake up and find that the institution’s star athlete was killed in the same spot overnight. Can they cover their tracks?Hollie RichardsonBeethoven’s Seventh at the Proms7pm, BBC FourThe Los Angeles Philharmonic returns to theProms, conducted by surprise World Cup final half-time show participant Gustavo Dudamel. It’s an evening of vibrant rhythm and vital energy, as Beethoven’s ecstatic Seventh Symphony is paired with Mexican composer Gabriela Ortiz’s Revolución diamantina.Jack SealeBergerac9pm, BBC TwoThis reboot emphasises the darker aspects of detective Jim Bergerac’s character. As the endgame approaches, Bergerac seems to have the measure of Pippa Haywood’s Margaret. But there’s a danger that his emotional investment in catching Cate’s killer might blow him off course.Phil HarrisonFrank Skinner: 30 Years of Dirt9pm, Sky OneA welcome return to the warm bosom of the standup special for the one-time national treasure. Skinner riffs on pensioner-age concerns, including the appearance of his long-term partner (“She doesn’t even have laughter lines!”), Harold Shipman and landlines.Priya ElanGrimsburg10pm, Sky OneView image in fullscreenA homage to American teen fiction … Grimsburg.Photograph: Fox/2025 by Fox Media Inc.More adult animated fun from hapless detective Marvin Flute (voiced by Jon Hamm) whose titular town has become ever more comically crime-ridden. This time, a homage to a particular genre of American teen fiction as Flute visits a summer camp where a slasher is leaving a trail of bloody destruction.PHAnn Droid10.40pm, BBC OneRobots go camping – what could possibly go wrong? Diane Morgan’s comedy drama about a widow and her carer robot just gets funnier and more poignant as Sue (Sue Johnston) and Linda (Morgan) stay at a campsite. But as the series heads to its end, so too does the question of Linda’s future.HRFilm choiceHamnet (Chloé Zhao, 2025), 8.10am, 8pm, Sky Cinema PremiereView image in fullscreenMarried to the Bard … Jessie Buckley as Agnes in Hamnet.Photograph: Agata Grzybowska/Focus FeaturesFrom a Roman muscle man in Gladiator II to William Shakespeare, Paul Mescal has certainly been showing his range of late. But in Chloé Zhao’s version of Maggie O’Farrell’s superb novel, he has to play second fiddle toJessie Buckley. It’s her Oscar-winning turn as Agnes – the Bard’s unsung wife – that gives the drama its gut-wrenching power. Agnes is the heart to Will’s brain, more attuned to the mysteries of the natural world, and aware that his genius will take him away from her. But their differing reactions to a family tragedy push them further apart … Hamnet is a difficult book to adapt, its potency coming from its unarticulated emotions, but Zhao has pulled it off brilliantly.Simon WardellOn Falling (Laura Carreira, 2024), 11.05pm, BBC TwoPortuguese immigrant Aurora (Joana Santos) works as a “picker” in an Amazon-style warehouse in Scotland. It’s a monotonous but time-sensitive job that has reduced her to a zombie-like state; she’s too tired and poor to enjoy her free time and struggles to connect with her mostly foreign colleagues and flatmates. And when her phone needs a costly repair, that’s all it takes to tip her over the edge. Laura Carreira’s debut feature is heart-breaking social realism with a Ken Loach feel, but where he rails at capitalism’s evils, Carreira sees bureaucratic indifference.SWLive sportChampionshipfootball: Wolves v Blackburn, 7.15pm, Sky Sports Main Event.The opening match of the season at Molineux.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightHamnetPaul MescalChloé ZhaoJessie BuckleyFrank SkinnerPromsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best recent crime and thrillers – review roundup | Books | The Guardian
description: The Amateur by Chris Bohjalian; Claws Out! by Bella Mackie; Plant Lady by Minyoung Kang; Children of Wolves by Lawrence Osborne; Mad Mabel by Sally Hepworth
Author: Laura Wilson
Headline: The Amateur by Chris Bohjalian; Claws Out! by Bella Mackie; Plant Lady by Minyoung Kang; Children of Wolves by Lawrence Osborne; Mad Mabel by Sally Hepworth
Content: Incisive social satire … Bella Mackie.Photograph: Kate Peters/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIncisive social satire … Bella Mackie.Photograph: Kate Peters/The GuardianCrime and thrillers roundupBooksReviewThe best recent crime and thrillers – review roundupThe Amateur by Chris Bohjalian; Claws Out! by Bella Mackie; Plant Lady by Minyoung Kang;Children of Wolves by Lawrence Osborne; Mad Mabel by Sally HepworthLaura WilsonFri 14 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 08.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenThe Amateurby Chris Bohjalian (Hutchinson Heinemann, £18.99)American bestseller Bohjalian deserves to be far better known in the UK, although, as the first line of his 26th novel points out, “It is neither virtue nor might that rules the world; it’s luck”. Mira Winston’s luck began early, as she was born into a rich family, clever enough to secure a place at Yale, and a talented enough golfer to consider turning pro, but things change dramatically in 1978 when, at the age of 18, a ball she hits on a driving range smashes the temporal bone of a young caddy, killing him almost instantly. The freak accident turns out to be rather more complicated than first thought, not least because it becomes karmically conflated, in Mira’s mind, with her relationship with a married man twice her age. Told as a memoir, with Mira looking back on the derailment of her life and chronicling society’s changing perceptions of agency and privilege, this literary thriller is a masterfully executed ace.View image in fullscreenClaws Out!by Bella Mackie (Borough, £20)Mackie’s third novel centres on Diana, a manipulative grifter whose previous three husbands have died, apparently of natural causes. She’s in the process of getting her feet under the fourth mark’s prosperous Hampstead table when she encounters opposition. David Farrand’s “entitled but otherwise entirely average” daughter Catriona isn’t going to give up her father or her inheritance without a fight, and when she starts investigating Diana’s past, she discovers that her former stepchildren are convinced of foul play. Meanwhile, Diana’s own son, a feckless charmer, is also hoping to benefit from his mother’s matrimonial plans. Some readers may find the arch authorial tone grating, and the sharp-eyed will spot at least one major plot development before it occurs, but the incisive social satire, vinegary humour and expert pacing will keep you laughing as you turn the pages.Plant Ladyby Minyoung Kang, translated by Shanna Tan (Doubleday, £14.99)In a fictional Korean city, green-fingered trauma survivor Yoohee realises her dream of opening a plant shop. Although she remains courteous and self-effacing, her long-held conviction that humans, like plants, repay attention and tenderness, has worn thin, and when an errant boyfriend fails to improve, she repurposes him as fertiliser. She begins offering her overwhelmingly female customer base an additional service, ridding them of abusive men, but a young detective notices that the shop is the only common point of reference in a string of otherwise unconnected disappearances, and a game of cat and mouse ensues. This “weird girl” tale of female revenge is politely told, the mechanics of dismemberment happening off the page, and although the villains tend towards the cartoonish, the atmosphere is such that one can almost inhale the damp, scented air of our heroine’s lush botanical haven as she calmly puts the world to rights.View image in fullscreenChildren of Wolvesby Lawrence Osborne (Chatto & Windus, £18.99)Osborne’s books often feature morally ambiguous expats in exotic locations; here it’s American investigator Tyler Sedgewick, in Turkey to track down Chana Knight at the behest of her father. Posing as a writer, Tyler worms his way into the young woman’s friendship group; Chana, Adam, Diana and Marco are the delinquent, sensation-seeking offspring of wealthy parents, who first met at a California reform school for rich kids, and became self-styled radicals. Now, they have walked out of their respective lives with the intention of atoning for their privileged existences through a “meaningfully violent act” against “a prominent American target”. Tyler, who has become dangerously drawn to Chana, does not realise the extent to which he is being used, and soon attracts the attention of the Turkish intelligence agency. There are echoes of both Graham Greene and Patricia Highsmith here, but Osborne’s sense of place and ability create an undercurrent of menace all his own.View image in fullscreenMad Mabelby Sally Hepworth (Macmillan, £16.99)The titular character of Australian Hepworth’s latest is a stroppy, sarcastic 81-year-old, living under a pseudonym in a quiet Melbourne suburb. More than 60 years earlier, Mabel Waller became the youngest person in Australian history to be convicted of murder. Now she keeps herself to herself, but Persephone, the lonely young daughter of a neighbour, is determined to be friends, and slowly Mabel, whose own desolate childhood with her wealthy but uninterested parents is gradually revealed in flashbacks, begins to thaw. But someone has discovered her past and is sending anonymous letters, and when the elderly man next door dies unexpectedly, she becomes the prime suspect. Although crime fiction aficionados may figure out at least one plot twist early on, Mabel’s cantankerous facade, behind which the fuzzy outlines of loss, trauma and misunderstanding gradually sharpen into focus, and the growing warmth of the intergenerational friendship, make this a genuinely moving and surprisingly funny read.Explore more on these topicsBooksCrime and thrillers roundupFictionThrillersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Rebecca Perry: ‘Lorca hit me like a bolt of lightning’ | Culture | The Guardian
description: The poet and novelist on the power of fairytales, being inspired by Frank O’Hara and the joys of Doris Lessing
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The poet and novelist on the power of fairytales, being inspired by Frank O’Hara and the joys of Doris Lessing
Content: ‘Percival Everett made me feel I might be able to write a novel’ … Rebecca Perry.Photograph: Ross JonesView image in fullscreen‘Percival Everett made me feel I might be able to write a novel’ … Rebecca Perry.Photograph: Ross JonesThe books of my lifeCultureRebecca Perry: ‘Lorca hit me like a bolt of lightning’The poet and novelist on the power of fairytales, being inspired by Frank O’Hara and the joys of Doris LessingRebecca PerryFri 14 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 05.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMy earliest reading memoryReading On the Ning Nang Nong by Spike Milligan, aged five or so, sitting on the floor of the bedroom I shared with my brother – who, in my memory, was sitting on the carpet next to me.My favourite book growing upI had a collection of fairytales in a big yellow hardback, which I was totally entranced by from around the age of seven to 10. I’ll never forget the feeling of despair on turning the page and discovering that the Little Mermaid had become foam on the surface of the water; it was a very early lesson in the helplessness of the reader in the face of a story’s destiny. In particular, though, I loved a Scottish fairytale called The Black Bull of Norroway, which I think, in many ways, has been under the surface of everything I’ve ever written.The book that changed me as a teenagerCollected Plays by Federico García Lorca, which I studied for GCSE drama and led me to seek out his poetry. It would be impossible for me to think about my adolescent relationship to reading, and my relationship as an adult to language, without Lorca. I remember these lines from City That Does Not Sleep hitting me like a bolt of lightning: “… and the man who rushes out with his / spirit broken will meet on the street corner / the unbelievable alligator quiet beneath / the tender protest of the stars”.The writer who changed my mindFrank O’Hara, which I know is one of the most predictable answers a poet can give, but for good reason. All of the poetry I’d studied up to the point of discovering him felt deeply serious, almost something not to be touched. Then you read O’Hara and it’s like: OK, life!The book that made me want to be a writerI really don’t think this is something that happened to me. I have just written for as long as I can remember and, at a certain point as an adult, I realised that normal living people can write books if they want to, if they’re lucky, and that maybe I would like to try to do that. To answer a slightly different question,Percival Everett’s astonishing The Treeswas the book that made me feel I might be able to write a novel.The book I rereadAnne Carson’s Glass and God, in particular The Glass Essay. It’s basically perfect – my go-to text for resetting my brain and being reminded, within the space of a page, about the capacities of writing.The book I could never read againJK Rowling’s Harry Potter series was a huge part of my childhood, but it’s art that’s firmly not to be separated from artist, in this case.The book I discovered later in lifeI don’t think I read Doris Lessing’s The Golden Notebook until I was in my 30s – but really, any time is the perfect time to discover this novel.The book I am currently readingA proof of Compensation by Augustine Cerf, which so far is brilliant, and My Garden (Book) by Jamaica Kincaid, which I often pick up and read a page or two of between other things. I’m also rereading Doom Painting by AK Blakemore, out in September. It’s a phenomenal achievement – I don’t know how she did it.My comfort readThe poetry collection Adam by Gboyega Odubanjo, who died in 2023. I keep this book on the shelf directly above my desk and when the loss of him feels particularly impossible, I take it down, read a poem and remember he’s there on the page.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMay We Feed the King by Rebecca Perry is published by Granta. It won the 2026 Waterstones debut fiction prize and islonglisted for the Booker prize. To support the Guardian order your copy atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsCultureThe books of my lifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Kristen Schaal: The Legend of Crystal Shell review – flighty Conchords comic is still kooking on gas | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: As a half-horse half-woman who dreams of being a unicorn and performing Swan Lake, Schaal sheds little light but has plenty of sparkle
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: As a half-horse half-woman who dreams of being a unicorn and performing Swan Lake, Schaal sheds little light but has plenty of sparkle
Content: Wilfully dotty … Kristen Schaal in The Legend of Crystal Shell at Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenWilfully dotty … Kristen Schaal in The Legend of Crystal Shell at Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewKristen Schaal: The Legend of Crystal Shell review – flighty Conchords comic is still kooking on gasPleasance Courtyard, EdinburghAs a half-horse half-woman who dreams of being a unicorn and performing Swan Lake, Schaal sheds little light but has plenty of sparkleBrian LoganFri 14 Aug 2026 11.54 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 11.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor a happy handful of years in the noughties, around the time she made her TV name onFlight of the Conchords’ sitcom, Kristen Schaal was a fringe fixture, award-nominated in 2008 for her two-hander with Kurt Braunohler,Double Down Hearts. Ifthose showsfound Schaal kooking on gas, about as wilfully dotty and insubstantial as you’d ever wish comedy to be, the intervening two decades seem to have changed her not a jot.The Legend of Crystal Shell, her two-hander with John Roberts, casts the comic actor as a half-woman, half-horse, overcoming a lifetime of shame to deliver a performance of Tchaikovsky’s Swan Lake for tonight’s audience. It plays as if written by a primary schoolchild high on pick’n’mix, and is endearing and nonplussing in equal measure.It begins with Schaal confined to a cardboard refrigerator-cum-horsebox, shyly announcing herself to the crowd. She emerges, to recount her origin story, as the progeny of her mum’s unlikely tryst with a stallion called Shimmer. We meet her friend Arnold the (suspiciously dormant) mouse. She reads non sequitur poems and tries to catch fairies in a net.View image in fullscreenHorsing about … Kristen Schaal and John Roberts.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianA flightier confection it would be hard to imagine, and my patience was fraying with it until – at the blast of a trumpet – Crystal’s long-lost dad makes an appearance. That multiplies the cast, at least, if not the significance, as this wannabe unicorn starts singing about the malfunctioning healing powers of his “teeny tiny horn”.So what does all this horsing about amount to? They’re both compelling performers: Schaal the otherworldly womanchild, Roberts her Fonz-alike father. There’s something almost audacious in the randomness of the play’s narrative development, as if they’d set themselves the challenge of accepting every first idea, however arbitrarily it advances the plot. There are hints too, if tenuous, that Crystal’s late blooming may be a metaphor for the menopause. If so, it sheds little light, but plenty of sparkle, as Schaal’s alter ego grows her own twinkling uni-horn and puts a life of meekness behind her. There’s nothing meek about Schaal’s comedy, whose take-it-as-you-find-it idiosyncracy is easy to admire and, usually, to indulge.At Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh until 16 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Kristen SchaalComedy (Stage)Edinburgh festivalTheatreComedy (Culture)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Murakami saw his book come alive!’: the Japanese company bringing the author’s science fiction masterpiece to the stage | Theatre | The Guardian
description: A play based on the writer’s dreamlike novel Hard-Boiled Wonderland and the End of the World is touring the world, riding a wave of interest in Japanese culture. Its creators talk about how they adapted the famously cryptic tale
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A play based on the writer’s dreamlike novel Hard-Boiled Wonderland and the End of the World is touring the world, riding a wave of interest in Japanese culture. Its creators talk about how they adapted the famously cryptic tale
Content: Skull set … Narushi Ikeda in End of the World and Hard-Boiled WonderlandPhotograph: Takahiro WatanabeView image in fullscreenSkull set … Narushi Ikeda in End of the World and Hard-Boiled WonderlandPhotograph: Takahiro WatanabeTheatre‘Murakami saw his book come alive!’: the Japanese company bringing the author’s science fiction masterpiece to the stageA play based on the writer’s dreamlike novel Hard-Boiled Wonderland and the End of the World is touring the world, riding a wave of interest in Japanese culture. Its creators talk about how they adapted the famously cryptic taleMarigold WarnerFri 14 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTatsuya Fujiwara is no stranger to London’s Barbican theatre. It was here nearly 30 years ago that one of Japan’s biggest film stars, now 44, made his stage debut. He was just 15, plucked out of an audition of more than 5,000 hopeful youngsters by the revered theatre director Yukio Ninagawa for his play Shintoku-Maru. It kickstarted Fujiwara’s career, and three years later he landed a role in the cult dystopianfilm Battle Royale, going on to star in hit TV dramas and blockbuster films, all the while continuing to perform in Ninagawa’s acclaimed productions.Now, Fujiwara returns to where it all began, to perform in a stage adaptation of Haruki Murakami’s science fiction novel Hard-Boiled Wonderland and the End of the World. The story alternates between two seemingly unrelated narratives: a cyberpunk thriller set in Tokyo, and a surreal fantasy that unfolds within a mysterious walled town. Directed by the French choreographer Philippe Decouflé, the play premiered in Tokyo in January, toured Japan until March, then Singapore in April. After the Barbican run this autumn, the tour will wrap up in Paris.“When performing in Japan, you become accustomed to your own audience,” says Fujiwara. “You develop a feel for what reaches them and how they receive you. The moment you cross a border, that certainty disappears.”View image in fullscreenFlowered up … Tatsuya Fujiwara and Miu Tomita in End of the World and Hard-Boiled Wonderland.Photograph: Takahiro WatanabeWe meet in April, backstage at the Esplanade theatre in Singapore just a few hours before the production’s first performance to an English-speaking audience. (The play is performed in Japanese, with English surtitles.) The response was rapturous, the audience more animated than with any performance during the Japan run, according to the director and cast. The Singapore house laughed freely, while in Japan the comic moments did not land with such warmth.Whether that’s due to cultural differences in self-expression or humour is up for debate, but backstage during intermission the cast are giddy. “It definitely gives us confidence for London,” says the director.This play arrives at a time when Japanese culture is experiencing a global boom, particularly in London. The last five years alone have seen a cluster of UK exhibitions about Japan. The British Museum has curated shows on manga, Hokusai and the samurai; the V&A did the history of kimonos; Oxford’s Ashmolean explored art and photography from Tokyo; and Somerset House celebrated 50 years of Hello Kitty. However, productions that have broken through to a mainstream audience overseas have largely been based on anime and manga. This summer saw a musical adaptation of Death Note at the Barbican, as well as Pretty Guardian Sailor Moon at the West End’s Here at Outernet and Koko in Camden Town, and Spirited Away, which enjoyed a six-month run at the London Coliseum in 2024.double quotation markToday, there is a curiosity about Japanese storytelling and aesthetics. Audiences approach our work with more familiarity“The barriers are considerably lower,” says Miyako Kanamori, senior executive and veteran producer at HoriPro. As one of Japan’s largest entertainment companies, HoriPro has been exporting Japanese theatre to the UK for many decades. “Thirty years ago, when we first brought [Yukio] Ninagawa’s productions to Britain, that cultural landscape simply did not exist. Today, there is a far broader curiosity about Japanese storytelling and aesthetics, and I feel audiences approach our work with a greater sense of familiarity.” Perhaps now is the time for homegrown theatre to shine. Plus, as a global bestseller, Murakami’s name carries instant esteem and recognition.However, the world of Murakami does not naturally lend itself to the stage. His novels can be cryptic and allegorical, making them hard to adapt for its native audience, let alone an international one.Hard-Boiled Wonderland and the End of the Worldspans 400 pages and features curious creatures such as unicorns and the “Murks”, monsters that lurk in the sewers. Fujiwara plays Watashi, the protagonist ofthe cyberpunk narrative the Hard-Boiled Wonderland,a human data processor known as a “Calcutec” who is essentially a cyborg. He encrypts data using a technique known as “shuffling”, described as a supernatural kind of mind alteration. His routine job slowly reveals a darker conspiracy buried deep within his own consciousness.View image in fullscreenPage turners … Tatsuya Fujiwara and Misato Morita in End of the World and Hard-Boiled Wonderland.Photograph: Takahiro WatanabeThe parallel narrative is even more peculiar. End of the World unravels within a mythical walled town. Upon entering, the second protagonist, Boku – played on alternating nights by Kiita Komagine and Ryunosuke Shimamura –is stripped of his shadow and all his memories, and tasked with reading dreams from the skulls of dead unicorns. The two plots eventually converge, and while they are both totally removed from the reality we know, the stories are strangely relatable.Murakami wrote the novel more than 40 years ago, but in an age of AI and algorithmic control, his questions about what remains when memory and selfhood are stripped are more pertinent now than ever.“At first I thought it was impossible to do anything with [the material],” says Decouflé, who is best known for directing music videos for New Order and Fine Young Cannibals, as well as France’s 1992 Winter Olympics opening ceremony. “I’m not Japanese, so I can never fully grasp what lies beneath the text, but then I thought: ‘They’ve asked me to do it, so I’m going to do it my way, with my dreams, my ideas, my vision.’”For the production company, bringing in a European director with a background in movement was a deliberate decision. Having worked on several adaptations of Murakami’s novels – Ninagawa’s Kafka on the Shore in 2015 and Simon McBurney’s The Wind-Up Bird Chronicle in 2023 – producer Kanamori learned that expressing the spiritual and psychological dimensions of the author’s world through dialogue alone was “profoundly difficult”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShe came to realise that “music and physical expression might offer a more truthful theatrical language for his work”, particularly for a play that was intended to be performed to a non-Japanese-speaking audience. Working closely with Japanese scriptwriter Ako Takahashi to decode the text, Decouflé has made a highly visual adaptation. He casts ballerinas as unicorns, dressing them in golden leotards and pointe shoes with stilted forelimbs. Street dancers armoured in urchin-like spikes writhe and scuttle through the sewers, while Tokyo-based dancer Rikubouz moves in long, liquid phrases to connect the two worlds between scenes.Murakami came to rehearsals himself. “He was always very contained, very still,” says Decouflé. “And then suddenly he saw the stage. He saw it alive. And I could see that he was happy – happy that I had given life to his dreams, to his book.” After the premiere, the author made a short speech. “He said something like: ‘I wrote this novel 40 years ago, and I had forgotten everything. Tonight, you all reminded me of what I created.’”View image in fullscreenShuffle vision … Tatsuya Fujiwara in End of the World and Hard-Boiled WonderlandPhotograph: Takahiro WatanabeDecouflé had made two productions in Japan before – once 30 years ago, another 15 years ago – and has observed the rise of Japanese dance in that time. “Thirty years ago, we could not find dancers of the quality we needed. Even 15 years ago it was so-so. And now Japan has some extraordinary dancers.” He was also impressed by the professionalism of the performers. “I never heard anyone complain,” he says. “I gave them hard work, I really pushed them. And at the end, they were overjoyed. It was a great luxury to work that way.”Cultural exchange has always been a crucial part of Japan’s story and how its art travels. Back in the Edo period, artisans commonly used discarded Ukiyo-e prints to package ceramics. These were later discovered by the impressionists, inspiring the Japonisme movement and artists such as Monet, Van Gogh and Klimt. The dialogue that followed, between eastern aesthetics and western modernism, moulded the development of modern art on both sides.Perhaps something of that pattern persists here. The play’s star hopes international interest in Japanese theatre will also ignite a new energy back home. “It would be amazing if theatre in Japan could one day command the kind of broad cultural engagement it has in the UK, where it’s truly part of public life,” says Fujiwara, who knows better than most what it takes to carry culture across borders. At the Barbican in 2015, performing Ninagawa’s Hamlet on Shakespeare’s home turf, the pressure was paralysing.“It’s a bit like a British company staging kabuki in Japan,” he says. “But this time it’s different because it’s Murakami. There’s more room to breathe, and more hope that we can offer something that reaches people broadly.”End of the World and Hard-Boiled Wonderlandis at Barbican theatre, London, 8 to 11 October.Explore more on these topicsTheatreDanceScience fiction booksJapanfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Dear Michelle Kwan review – fire and ice in a whirlwind figure-skating comedy | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Four skaters enter into feral competition in this darkly funny yet flimsily plotted play about female teenhood
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Four skaters enter into feral competition in this darkly funny yet flimsily plotted play about female teenhood
Content: You root for each of them … Dear Michelle KwanPhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenYou root for each of them … Dear Michelle KwanPhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewDear Michelle Kwan review – fire and ice in a whirlwind figure-skating comedytheSpace Triplex, EdinburghFour skaters enter into feral competition in this darkly funny yet flimsily plotted play about female teenhoodArifa AkbarFri 14 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 04.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe title refers to thefigure-skating legendand Olympian who, in the noughties, captivated the US with her performances on ice, winning a total of five world championships. Here, the four teen skaters trying to make it big worship her, quite literally, invoking her for strength on and off the ice.It is a great central idea with moments of frozen action as each girl sends a wish, a fear or prayer up to a godlike, absent Kwan in their most anxious or exhilarated moments. Christie Spessard’s play has verve, capturing the extremes of adolescent life and competitive sport. Energetically directed by Ryan Pangracs, it is full of humour with some zingers and movement that contains a true sense of gliding.There is Dahlia (Isabella Fay), who is desperately trying to please her mother through her skating, and the ambitious Marnina (played by Spessard), whose sister has died, and who is striving to have her own solo moment in the annual show for which they are training. Courtney (Skyler Sajewski) and Iris (Hannah Breshears) make up the group but are a little less coloured in.There are some echoes ofI, Tonyain the feral competition between the girls. Their bullying, emotional manipulative and physically abusive trainer, Eve (Jasmyn Donya Molaei), brings black humour. “You can handle a little pain,” she tells them, and considers them to be her daughters, but this element could benefit from developing spikier and more serious undercurrents.Spin Cycle review – romcom hits full speed as couple air their dirty laundryRead moreSo could the relationships between the characters; there is a hint of same-sex longing for two of them alongside Marnina’s grief and Dahlia’s family traumas. But you don’t quite get to know them enough, and the interesting issues they raise around teenhood remain buried beneath humour and camaraderie.The plot is flimsy too. The girls are training for an annual holiday show and get snowed in by a blizzard. This opens up the ground for conflict or bonding between them, and there is some of this, but it feels too slight: not quite emotional or dramatic enough.Thankfully there is so much energy and charisma in the performances that it becomes sheer good fun to watch. The characters are endearing too: they perform their numbers at the end and you find yourself rooting for each of them. A play brimming with potential brilliance.AttheSpace Triplex, Edinburgh, until 29 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalFestivalsComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Add to playlist: the heartbreak post-mortems of Cape Town’s Rowlene and the week’s best new tracks | Music | The Guardian
description: The South African singer has been a memorable guest artist, but the unhurried, emotional tracks on new album Some Strings Attached show she’s ready for the spotlight
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: The South African singer has been a memorable guest artist, but the unhurried, emotional tracks on new album Some Strings Attached show she’s ready for the spotlight
Content: An R&B balladeer at heart … RowleneView image in fullscreenAn R&B balladeer at heart … RowleneAdd to playlistMusicAdd to playlist: the heartbreak post-mortems of Cape Town’s Rowlene and the week’s best new tracksThe South African singer has been a memorable guest artist, but the unhurried, emotional tracks on new album Some Strings Attached show she’s ready for the spotlightMary Chiney andLaura SnapesFri 14 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 08.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFromCape Town, South AfricaRecommended if you likeSummer Walker, SZA, ShekhinahUp nextSome Strings Attached out nowRowlene Bosman learned to sing in a Cape Town school choir, and the discipline never left her: she is a precision vocalist in a scene that rewards volume. Most South Africans first heard her in 2018, delivering the hook onNasty C’s SMA– she was the first signing to his Tall Racks label – and the featured artist circuit kept her busy for years. But while South African pop stampeded towards amapiano, Rowlene held her ground as a balladeer, writing slow, confessional R&B in which heartbreak is examined instead of danced away. Her 2020 debut album 11:11, a set of aching, close-quarters soul songs, brought a South African music award nomination for best pop album, and three of her originals –Cupid,Stayand the Nasty C collaborationI Need You– landed on the soundtrack of Netflix’s SA teen crime drama Blood & Water, carrying her voice far beyond home.Hurts 2b Reminded, from her new albumSome Strings Attached, is the best argument yet for that patience. Over spare, unhurried production with a faint Afropop pulse ticking underneath, she sings about the ambush of memory: the places and small details that resurrect someone you thought you had let go. The twist is who she is mourning: not the dead, nor an ex, but friends who are alive and well yet simply elsewhere, people whose lives moved on without her. Losing them, she has said, was the price of finding herself. After 10 years of stealing the show from other artists, she sounds ready to headline her own.Mary ChineyThis week’s best new tracksView image in fullscreenHayley Williams.Photograph: Zachary GrayPower Snatch – Born DeadParamore’sHayley Williamscontinues her fruitful artistic evolution with her new band’s surprise second EP. Balancing murky alt-rock grandeur and serpentine intimacy, this highlight winds its vines around you. [Stream atBandcamp]Heavensouls – Dawn of the CityChidi Obialo, 20, has already released an album of the year in Westside Trapped. Now comes a 10-minute odyssey evoking a malfunctioning Dance Dance Revolution machine, dreamy chiptune and frenetically lapping IDM. [Stream atBandcamp]Sophia Stel – Now I’ve Got a Lot You KnowThe breakout Vancouver star’s latest song threatens to spill from robot ballad to confetti-canon rager, although the EDM risers that peak two minutes in bring surprising clarity and warmth to her devotional.Axel Boman and Superpitcher – True CrimeNew Boman is always cause for celebration, not least when it’s seven delicious minutes of ribboning, swirling synth trills undercut by a beat as fine and spangly as tinsel fronds.King Gizzard& the Lizard Wizard – Kill for the Steel“We don’t wish death upon you,” a alien voice incants reassuringly on the latest from Gizz’s Cyberdog techno turn; instead, their apparent wish is a state of dripping, warehouse-induced transcendence. [Stream onBandcamp]Shabazz Palaces – Ahh World (I Won the Alpha Bet)Ishmael Butler delivers life lessons – never gossip, hit fastballs, take risks – on a shadowy, bassy track so cool and imperious you could imagine it emanating from an ancient court.Garefowl – Buthaigir/PuffinFrom the Scottish archipelago of St Kilda come this avian-inspired group, whose new album for AD93 contemplates the island’s birds. The lead single is a gorgeous, violin-led lament.Laura SnapesSubscribe to the Guardian’s rolling Add to Playlist selections on Spotify – or transfer it toApple,Tidalor other servicesThis article was amended on 14 August 2026. Ishmael Butler’s son does not appear on the new Shabazz Palaces song as previously stated.Explore more on these topicsMusicAdd to playlistSouth AfricaPop and rockR&BfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Open Mike Eagle and Kenny Segal: Doomed! review – caustic, crushing breakup album flirts with catharsis | Music | The Guardian
description: The rapper-producer duo muster a breakup record with glistening beats and lovelorn lyrics that mull over grievances without resolve
Author: Will Pritchard
Headline: The rapper-producer duo muster a breakup record with glistening beats and lovelorn lyrics that mull over grievances without resolve
Content: True stories told loosely … Kenny Segal, left, and Open Mike Eagle.View image in fullscreenTrue stories told loosely … Kenny Segal, left, and Open Mike Eagle.MusicReviewOpen Mike Eagle and Kenny Segal: Doomed! review – caustic, crushing breakup album flirts with catharsis(Backwoodz)The rapper-producer duo muster a breakup record with glistening beats and lovelorn lyrics that mull over grievances without resolveWill PritchardFri 14 Aug 2026 03.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTough as they may be, breakups make for good material. Doomed! is Open Mike Eagle’s entry into that wide canon – sitting alongside Tyler, the Creator’s Igor and Ye’s 808s & Heartbreak in the alt-rap subcategory – and finds the LA-via-Chicago rapper every bit as wide-eyed, caustic and, at-times, crushing as those who’ve Kübler-Rossed their way out of a relationship before him. Out of lemons, lemonade, and all that.View image in fullscreenOpen Mike Eagle and Kenny Segal: Doomed!In fact, without the disintegration of his five-year relationship, he and Kenny Segal – the feted Low End Theory-reared producer who helms the entire project – might have been resigned to merely cropping up as occasional features on each other’s records forever. The breakup gave sessions a focal point, and half a decade’s grievances to mull. Or, as Eagle puts it languidly over lounge glockenspiel on Streets of Rage: Public Arguments Edition: “These is true stories told loosely.”Emotions run high, and stretch scenarios to absurd shapes: the tragicomic image of failing to scribe initials into wet concrete, or the relationship’s “Covid growth spurt”. It’s the sound of Open Mike Eagle replaying every row and coming up with the ideal comeback just a few months too late. It’s also funny, if excruciatingly so: “I’d rather tongue kiss a bug zapper,” he offers on Don’t Go Look. Segal’s beats keep things interesting – a glistening cascade of keys on She Swear I’m Colorblind, the slow-motion corrode of Watching a Movie Called Freedom by Myself – but Eagle’s verses, still raw, never quite touch catharsis.Explore more on these topicsMusicRapreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Henry Threadgill, Vijay Iyer, Dafnis Prieto: Fifteen review – Pulitzer winner stirs gorgeous improv patterns | Music | The Guardian
description: By turns gleeful, sensitive, urgent and ruminative, this is a brilliant set that plays to the trio’s formidable strengths
Author: John Fordham
Headline: By turns gleeful, sensitive, urgent and ruminative, this is a brilliant set that plays to the trio’s formidable strengths
Content: Brilliant … (from left) Dafnis Prieto, Henry Threadgill and Vijay Iyer.Photograph: Michael WilsonView image in fullscreenBrilliant … (from left) Dafnis Prieto, Henry Threadgill and Vijay Iyer.Photograph: Michael WilsonJazz album of the monthMusicReviewHenry Threadgill, Vijay Iyer, Dafnis Prieto: Fifteen review – Pulitzer winner stirs gorgeous improv patterns(Nonesuch)By turns gleeful, sensitive, urgent and ruminative, this is a brilliant set that plays to the trio’s formidable strengthsJohn FordhamFri 14 Aug 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThough the century-old Pulitzer prize – launched as a celebration of the craft and social necessity of good news reportage – was eventually expanded to include fiction and music by 1943, the US-born art of jazz has only been represented by Ornette Coleman and Wynton Marsalis in their lifetimes, Duke Ellington, John Coltrane and Thelonious Monk posthumously – and most recentlyHenry Threadgill, for his four-part suiteIn for a Penny, In for a Pound, in 2016.View image in fullscreenHenry Threadgill, Vijay Iyer, Dafnis Prieto: FifteenPublisher Joseph Pulitzer once declared his dreams for his readership were “to arrest their attention, enlist their sympathy … stimulate their imagination, convince their reason, and awaken their conscience”. Contemporary-classical composer and flautist Threadgill has been doing all that with his music,his personal story, his internationalism and his charisma since the 1960s. Now 82, he releases Fifteen, joining him in a brilliant trio featuring pianist/composer Vijay Iyer and creative Cuban percussionist Dafnis Prieto.The album title references the number of years since this collective originally convened on a fundraiser for New York’sJazzgallery. It’s simpler and more explicitly improv-oriented than Threadgill’s Pulitzer winner, the instrumentally diverse, polyphonically dizzying In for a Penny: all three members here are simultaneously composers and free-improvisers who cherish the communality of recurring patterns in ways some free-jazz players avoid.Trio Piece is begun by Prieto and Iyer in staccato interval-hops and asymmetrical snare-drum snaps before Threadgill’s skimming flute lines glide in. Last Night is an urgently pressing piano groove powered by Iyer against Prieto’s supple, sensuous drum sounds, while Threadgill’s own Where Coconuts Fall is a rumination for piano, frothing cymbals and imploring alto-sax long tones. Prieto’s closing On the Way is a coquettish Latin frolic, edited by the stately Threadgill to clipped sonic punctuation marks, but gleefully stormed all over by Prieto and Iyer. Hearteningly delightful contemporary music-making.Also out this monthBassist/composerLinda May Han Ohalso celebrated the arts of the jazz trio onStrange Heavenslast year, but the Malaysia-born bassist/composer gets even more closely conversational onBeneath Lifted Skies (Biophilia)in a duo partnership with Chilean saxophone starMelissa Aldanathat will entrance jazz traditionalists and newcomers alike. A hurtling interchange on the Charlie Parker classic Anthology, lyrically haunting wanderings on Wayne Shorter’s Dance Cadaverous and Oh’s beautiful solo reflections on Billie Holiday’s God Bless the Child are among 15 exquisite vignettes, likely destined for the end-of-year faves lists. Three-volume set The Riverside Years 1959-1962 (Acrobat) captures the effortless lyrical fluency of short-lived guitar geniusWes Montgomeryin some of his hottest company, including saxist Johnny Griffin and Miles Davis pianist Wynton Kelly between those years. And innovative UK-based guitarist/composerNicolas Meierdraws on the work of Argentine composer Astor Piazzolla, flamenco and new configurations of his jazz, Turkish and Middle Eastern roots onElysian Drift (MGP).Explore more on these topicsMusicJazz album of the monthJazzreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Hillborg: Lost Landscapes album review – sonic imagination and luminous colours | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Unconventional instrumentation adds to the filmic feeling of these three works by the Swedish composer, played on this recording by a powerhouse orchestra on top form
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: Unconventional instrumentation adds to the filmic feeling of these three works by the Swedish composer, played on this recording by a powerhouse orchestra on top form
Content: Stylistically eclectic: composer Anders HillborgPhotograph: https://www.hillborg.com/View image in fullscreenStylistically eclectic: composer Anders HillborgPhotograph: https://www.hillborg.com/Classical musicReviewHillborg: Lost Landscapes album review – sonic imagination and luminous coloursGothenburg Symphony Orchestra/Kuusisto/Lubman/Falk Winland(Alpha)Unconventional instrumentation adds to the filmic feeling of these three works by the Swedish composer, played on this recording by a powerhouse orchestra on top formClive PagetFri 14 Aug 2026 06.06 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 06.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnders Hillborg’s stylistically eclectic work resists easy categorisation as these three rewarding works, performed by the Gothenburg Symphony Orchestra, demonstrate. Lost Landscapes opens with signatureglissandi, features a filmic, jazz-inflected chase and ends in an orchestral death spiral. Pekka Kuusisto draws out its luminous colours and richly clustered harmonies.View image in fullscreenAnders Hillborg: Lost Landscapes.Photograph: Alpha ClassicsThe Strand Settings, a four-movement song cycle to texts by Canadian poet Mark Strand, was composed at the behest of Renée Fleming. Nature, the elements and a certain forlorn eroticism infuse poetry that Hillborg responds to with tonal and dynamic restraint. Gently pulsing strings with piquant woodwind and brass build atmospheric soundscapes over which Swedish soprano Ida Falk Winland spins haunting vocal lines in impeccable English.Finally, Sound Atlas, stylishly conducted by Brad Lubman, showcases Hillborg’s sonic imagination and affection for unusual instruments. Here it’s theverrophone, invented by German musician Sascha Reckert, where the rims of glass tubes are rubbed with wet fingers, similar to playing wine glasses. The orchestra is often instructed to play slightly sharp or flat, their microtonal clashes lending the work a spectral quality. A pair of gleaming slow movements pitch into the glittering Vaporised Toy Pianos followed by the roiling Vortex before concluding with Hymn, a noble finale in the manner of Sibelius.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com.
