title: ‘It’s one huge adventure playground’: readers’ best summer trips in the lakes and mountains of Europe | Europe holidays | The Guardian
description: From the Alpine meadows of Bavaria to a pristine lake in Italy and the pilgrim routes of the Pyrenees, here are some of your favourite discoveries.
Author: Guardian readers
Headline: From the Alpine meadows of Bavaria to a pristine lake in Italy and the pilgrim routes of the Pyrenees, here are some of your favourite discoveries.
Content: Haldensee is in western Austria, a couple of hours’ drive from Munich.Photograph: Westend61/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHaldensee is in western Austria, a couple of hours’ drive from Munich.Photograph: Westend61/Getty ImagesReaders' travel tipsEurope holidays‘It’s one huge adventure playground’: readers’ best summer trips in the lakes and mountains of EuropeFrom the Alpine meadows of Bavaria to a pristine lake in Italy and the pilgrim routes of the Pyrenees, here are some of your favourite discoveries.Tell us about alesser known European island– the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucherGuardian readersFri 14 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 10.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLate summer hiking in the Austrian AlpsHaldensee is a clear, sparkling cold lake located at the bottom of the Tannheimer Tal valley in the Austrian Alps (about 90 miles south-west of Munich). We visited last year, just when summer was on its way out, and it was too cold to skinny-dip in the lake (unless you were very brave). Nonetheless, if you’re a hiker, a ski lift takes you up into the Allgäu Alps where you can walk through dense forest toBad Kissinger Hütteserving refreshingapfelschorle, warming soups and seasonal bakes to refuel for the journey downhill. When going down, we were accompanied by tinkling cattle, ambling along the mountain-side springs, which made the experience so much more memorable.KovidaMountain tracks of Lake Garda, ItalyView image in fullscreenMountain bikers on the Strada del Ponale at Lake Garda.Photograph: Image Professionals /AlamyNorthern Lake Garda, where the mountains tower above the lake, is one huge adventure playground: walking, cycling, climbing, boat trips and all manner of watersports on the lake. There are castles, waterfalls and valley cycle trails. The oldPonalemountain road might be the pick for cycling (best on ebike) and walking. It winds through tunnels and clings to the rock with spectacular views over the lake. AtPonale Altoenjoy a hearty pasta dish washed down with a local beer or wine, before returning downhill all the way.Dave ThomasProfileReaders' tips: send a tip for a chance to win a £200 voucher for a Coolstays breakShowGuardian Travel readers' tipsEvery week we ask our readers for recommendations from their travels. A selection of tips will be featured online and may appear in print. To enter the latest competition visit thereaders' tips homepage-Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Swiss bliss near Mont BlancView image in fullscreenThere are loads of great walking choices from La Fouly just to the east of the Mont Blanc massif.Photograph: DanielSkip the crowds of Chamonix and spend a week atLa Fouly, in south-west Switzerland. Some walking routes are busy (it is a hub for the famous Tour du Mont Blanc walk) but there are plenty of walks to choose from, many of which are not on the main trail. Walk to theLacs de Fenêtre, where you can hear the gurgling burps of rock ptarmigans at first light, and the shrieks of marmots as you descend back down into the valley. We camped by cool, fast-flowing rivers atCamping des Glaciersin La Fouly.DanielMeadows and cowbells in SloveniaView image in fullscreenThe Logar valley in Slovenia.Photograph: Aliaksandr Mazurkevich/AlamyThe loudest sound in Slovenia’sLogar Valleyis usually a cowbell. A narrow road runs through flower-filled meadows to the foot of the Kamnik-Savinja Alps, but it’s best explored on foot or by bike, stopping at the little farms that sell homemade cheese and apple juice. Follow the easy trail to the 90-metreRinka waterfall, then linger over lunch at one of the mountain inns to enjoy the view. I stayed overnight in a family-run guesthouse, and by early evening the day visitors had gone, leaving the valley almost silent except for swallows and grazing cattle.Susanna CDragonflies and lilies on Italy’s secret lakeView image in fullscreenLago di Monate is north-west of Milan.Photograph: Panther Media Global/AlamyThe spring-fed Lago di Monate, between the much larger lakes of Maggiore and di Varese, has possibly the freshest swimming water in Italy, chiefly because of its longstanding ban on motorboats. You can hire paddleboards to cross the calm surface to vast lily beds, blooming in summer and alive with dragonflies. The grassy beach with sunbeds and umbrellas atIl Coppaleis very reasonable with evening meal (fresh fish, naturally) on their terrace at about €25 with a view over the lake to the Alps.Tim LeadbetterAlpine ambience in BavariaView image in fullscreenLödensee in Upper Bavaria.Photograph: Image Professionals /AlamyLooking for a reasonable budget autumnal trip, a search on the usual sites led us to Bavaria, and the outdoorsy town of Ruhpolding. Alpine atmosphere was immediately delivered, with a charming unpretentious ambience. There is a really impressive waterpark and cool blue lakes, such as Lödensee and Weitsee. Hikes through classical Alpine scenery took us to analm,a mountain refuge in high meadows where local milk and beer was served with platters of meat and cheese. A little further away the huge Chiemsee gave us a day at the beach. A stop in Munich on the way back allowed us to visit the excellent BMW museum, part of which is free.Brian LowryCycling the foothills of the French PyreneesView image in fullscreenThe town of Foix in the foothills of the Pyrenees.Photograph: Fred P/AlamyCycling theVelosudthis summer was the perfect trip to the mountains without having to cycle up or down them. We spent two weeks leisurely following the signposted route in the foothills of the Pyrenees, often alongside rivers, with mountain views every day. It’s all either traffic-free or on very quiet roads, and passes by spa towns such as Salies-du-Salat, the beautiful Foix and Mirepoix, and lovely, low-key but well equipped campsites (always with swimming pool, aperitif and morning croissants).RowanA cross-border trek on the Camino FrancésView image in fullscreenA pilgrims’ shrine on the Way of St James near Roncesvalles.Photograph: J Meyers Foreman/AlamyI’ve walked close to 2,000km of the Camino de Santiago, traversing Spain from the Pyrenees to the Galician coast and following the crashing waves of the Atlantic Portuguese coast in northern Portugal. One of the most stunning stretches of the Camino Francés (part of the Camino de Santiago) takes you from the French Pyrenean town of St-Jean-Pied-de-Port to the Spanish village of Roncesvalles. It’s a very tough climb, but it’s well worth the effort. In the early morning mist, as you approach the border with Spain, the panoramic views from above the cloud line will take your breath away. A truly spectacular experience.Stephen TaylorTuscany’s wild sideView image in fullscreenThe Alpi Apuane are in the far north of Tuscany,  inland from La Spezia, Liguria.Photograph: AlamyIt’s amazing that the Alpi Apuane are not better known. This raw, jagged cluster of marble peaks forms a dramatic backdrop to the bucket-and-spade beaches of northern Tuscany. These mountains are laced with challenging trails, including the multi-dayVia Vandelli, linking Modena to the coast. The valleys shelter quiet, refreshing streams and half-forgotten villages. Above the treeline, the hiker is rewarded with expansive views of the mountains, the sea, and the surreal marble quarries hewn from the mountainsides. This is the wild side of Tuscany.RobertWinning tip: The Vosges mountains by trainView image in fullscreenThe Vosges’ Wormsa valley, just west of Colmar, is brilliant walking country.Photograph: Juergen Feuerer/AlamyThe Vosges mountains in eastern France are made up of forest-covered rounded peaks calledballons, and are accessible by train. The line between Colmar and Metzeral provides easy access into the Wormsa valley, where forest paths climb past streams to the peaceful Lac du Fischboedle, surrounded by trees. From there you can climb the third highest mountain in the Vosges, Hohneck (1,363 metres), for sweeping views towards the Alps. The food in the region is delicious, especially tarte flambée (flammekueche), a traditional thin flatbread topped with creme fraiche, onions and bacon.HannahView image in fullscreenExplore more on these topicsEurope holidaysReaders' travel tipsWalking holidaysAlps holidaysSwimming holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cocktail of the week: Whiteley’s at Six Senses’ strawberry & basil margarita – recipe | Cocktails | The Guardian
description: A vibrant and playful twist on the classic cocktail, with a bright, citrus kick and a subtle herbal note
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A vibrant and playful twist on the classic cocktail, with a bright, citrus kick and a subtle herbal note
Content: Whiteley’s strawberry and basil margarita.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.View image in fullscreenWhiteley’s strawberry and basil margarita.Photograph: Rob Lawson/The Guardian. Drink styling: Seb Davis.The good mixerCocktailsCocktail of the week: Whiteley’s at Six Senses’ strawberry & basil margarita – recipeA vibrant and playful twist on the classic cocktail, with a bright, citrus kick and a subtle herbal noteAdrian Gonzalez ParrondoFri 14 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFresh, vibrant and full of summer character, this is a playful twist on the classic. It’s juicy and refreshing, with a bright, citrus kick and a subtle, herbal note that keeps things light and balanced. It also works very well with non-alcoholic tequila. If you like, double the syrup quantities, because it’s delicious drizzled over pancakes or diluted with sparkling water for a refreshing, summery drink.Strawberry and basil margaritaServes1For the strawberry syrup (for 6 serves)75g fresh strawberries, hulled and chopped75ml agave syrupFor the drink50ml tequila– just use your favourite (we useThe Lost Explorer Tequila Blanco)Juice of1lime25mlstrawberry syrup(see above and method)2 basil leavesFirst, make the syrup. Put the chopped strawberries and agave in a blender and blitz smooth. Fine strain into a clean jar, then seal and store in the fridge, where it’ll keep for about a fortnight.To build the drink, put everything in a shaker filled with ice, add a basil leaf, seal and shake hard. Strain into a rocks glass filled with fresh ice, garnish with the second basil leaf and serve.Adrian Gonzalez Parrondo, director of bars,Six Senses, London W2Explore more on these topicsCocktailsThe good mixerSpiritsFoodSummer food and drinkFruitHerbs and spicesMexican food and drinkrecipesShareReuse this content

title: Helen Goh’s recipe for frozen Eton mess with plum, coconut and raspberry | Dessert | The Guardian
description: The classic British dessert, but with a frozen twist, captures all of the charm of the original with a welcome chill for summer
Author: Helen Goh
Headline: The classic British dessert, but with a frozen twist, captures all of the charm of the original with a welcome chill for summer
Content: Helen Goh’s frozen Eton mess with plum, coconut and raspberry.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Prop styling: Lucy Turnbull. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.View image in fullscreenHelen Goh’s frozen Eton mess with plum, coconut and raspberry.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The Guardian. Food styling: Katie Smith. Food styling assistant: Phoebe Altman.The sweet spotDessertHelen Goh’s recipe for frozen Eton mess with plum, coconut and raspberryThe classic British dessert, but with a frozen twist, captures all of the charm of the original with a welcome chill for summerHelen GohFri 14 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIlove the glorious unruliness of Eton mess, all billowy cream, crushed meringue and tumbling fruit. This frozen version captures all of that charm but in a sliceable, make-ahead dessert that’s perfect for August entertaining. The fruit can even be cooked a day in advance, leaving little more to do than whip everything together before freezing. Thanks to the condensed milk, the cream freezes surprisingly softly, while the meringue keeps its gentle chew and the toasted coconut adds a welcome crunch and nuttiness. Late summer plums bring a lovely tartness that balances the sweetness beautifully, though apricots, peaches and nectarines would also work well.Frozen Eton mess with plum, coconut and raspberryWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep10 minCook40 minFreeze8 hr+Serves8For the fruit400g red plums(about 5 medium fruit), stoned and quartered40g caster sugar2 tsp lemon juice1 pinch fine sea salt120g raspberries, plus a few extra to decorateFor the ice-cream150g coconut condensed milk, or regular condensed milk250ml double cream1 tsp vanilla extract½ tsp fine sea salt120g shop-bought meringues, roughly broken50g toasted coconut chips, plus 15g extra to decorateStart by cooking the fruit, as it needs to cool completely before being folded into the ice-cream. Put the plums, sugar, lemon juice and salt in a medium pan on a medium heat. Cover partially with a lid and leave to cook gently for about 10 minutes, until the plums soften and collapse. Add the raspberries, stir gently for about a minute, just until they begin to soften, then take off the heat.Strain the fruit through a fine-mesh sieve set over a bowl, reserving both the fruit and its juices separately. Return the juices to the pan and simmer on a medium-high heat for three to five minutes, until reduced to a lightly syrupy consistency. Pour into a small jug and leave both the syrup and the fruit to cool completely.Line a 20cm x 10cm loaf tin with baking paper, leaving plenty of overhang on all sides. Put the condensed milk, cream, vanilla and salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment. Whisk on medium-high until the mixture holds firm peaks. Fold in the broken meringues and toasted coconut chips, until evenly incorporated, then add the cooled fruit. Fold gently a few times, just so the fruit remains in generous ripples, rather than becoming fully incorporated.Spoon the mix into the lined tin and smooth out the surface with a spatula. Tap the tin firmly on a work surface a few times to knock out any air pockets, then fold the paper overhang over the top and freeze overnight, or for at least eight hours.To serve, briefly wrap the outside of the tin with a hot, damp tea towel, then use the paper overhang to lift the ice-cream on to a platter. Spoon over the reserved fruit syrup, scatter with the extra toasted coconut and decorate with a few extra raspberries.
